profileDesc.creation:
Initially created: 2025-12-06T12:10:47.398+09:00 by chris Translate the following text from Classical Chinese into English.
Requirements: 1. The text contains page numbers in square brackets, such as [01], [02], etc. - These must be passed through unchanged. - Each page number must appear in exactly the same position in the translation as in the source. - The number of page markers in the output must match the input exactly.
2. Personal names, place names, titles, and other proper nouns should be rendered in Hànyǔ Pīnyīn with tone marks.
3. Do NOT transcribe the full Classical Chinese text into Pinyin.
4. Do NOT include explanatory notes, annotations, or commentary — output only the English translation.
5. The target language is English.
Input text:

p.seg: Sīmǎ Guāng
compiled by imperial command.
Later
The Zhū clan was originally from Dàngshān.
Dàngshān,
during the Warring States period, belonged to Liáng territory.
Tàizǔ started his enterprise as Military Governor of Xuānwǔ;
the Xuānwǔ Army was based in Biànzhōu,
ancient Dàliáng.
Gradually growing stronger and more prosperous,
he was promoted to Prince of Liáng,
and his state was accordingly named Liáng.
The *Zīzhì Tōngjiàn* had already recorded the Xiāo Liáng dynasty before this period,
hence this is referred to as Hòuliáng (Later Liáng).
Tàizǔ Shénwǔ Yuánshèng Xiàohuángdì (The August Emperor, Martial, Sagely, Filial)
His surname was Zhū,
his given name Wēn.
He was from Wǔgōu Lǐ, Dàngshān, Sòngzhōu.
He deserted Huáng Cháo and submitted to Táng,
and was granted the name Quánzhōng.
Upon ascending the throne,
he changed his name to Huǎng.
Kāipíng First Year
(*Dīngmǎo*, 907 CE)
He ascended the throne in the fourth month of this year,
and the era name was changed.
1 Spring,
first month,
on the *xīnsì* day,
the Prince of Liáng rested his troops at Bèizhōu.
Returning from Cāngzhōu,
he rested his troops in Bèizhōu,
also because of the provisions from Wèibó.
2 Yáng Wò, Military Governor of Huáinán, concurrently Grand Mentor and Supreme Commander of the Expeditions of All Routes East, Prince of Hóngnóng Commandery, having seized Jiāngxī,
meaning he had also annexed Zhōng Kuāngshí's territory.
The matter is seen in the previous volume, Tiānyòu 3rd year.
said to Zhōu Yǐn, the Judicial Commissioner:
"You sold out another's state;
how can you face me again!"
And so he killed him.
This was because Yǐn had said that Wò was incapable of shouldering the responsibility,
and intended to submit his state to Liú Wēi.
The matter is seen in the previous volume, Tiānyòu 2nd year.
*fù*,
read as *fú yòu fān*.
Having expelled Wáng Màozhāng,
and then killed Zhōu Yǐn,
it was natural that others would feel insecure.
Lǚ Shīzhōu, Commander of the Hēiyúndū, and Qí Zhāng, Vice Commander, led troops to garrison Shànggāo.
Shànggāo is within the bounds of Gāo'ān County, Hóngzhōu.
During the Sòng dynasty, Shànggāo County was established,
subordinate to Jūnzhōu,
95 *lǐ* southwest of the prefecture.
Sòng Bái said: Shànggāo County was originally the upper town of Gāo'ān County,
because its terrain was high,
it was called Shànggāo.
During the Shēngyuán reign of Southern Táng, Shànggāo Post Station was established,
and in the Bǎodà 10th year, it was promoted to a county.
Having repeatedly achieved merits,
Wò became wary of him.
Shīzhōu, afraid, discussed with Qí Zhāng, saying:
"Lord Mǎ is generous and tolerant,
referring to Mǎ Yīn.
Would it be acceptable?"
Zhāng said:
"You must plan this matter yourself;
my tongue may be cut out,
but I dare not reveal it!"
Shīzhōu then fled to Húnán,
and Zhāng allowed his family to escape.
Lù Zhèn's *Jiǔ Guó Zhì* says: Lǚ Shīzhōu's father, Kē, served Yáng Xíngmì with bravery,
accumulating merits,
and was appointed Commander of the Hēiyúndū.
When Kē died,
Shīzhōu succeeded him,
and said to himself,
"A general's family for three generations cannot preserve wealth and status,"
and often indulged in drinking cups;
when drunk, he would surely rise and dance,
or beat time and sing wildly,
then weep with emotion.
Xíngmì heard of this and suspected him,
and secretly sent men to scout his movements.
Shīzhōu felt insecure,
and so conspired with Qí Zhāng and fled to Húnán.
According to this, he was suspected by Wò,
not Xíngmì.
*nú*,
pronounced *nú*,
meaning children.
He was from Yángzhōu.
Wò was in mourning,
he was in mourning for his father Xíngmì.
He made music,
a sentence break.
One candle cost tens of thousands of *qián*.
Sometimes he would ride out alone,
his followers scrambling along the road,
not knowing where he was going.
Zhāng Hào and Xú Wēn, the commanders of the Left and Right Guards, tearfully remonstrated.
The Shu commentary says: *yá* refers to
a flag,
those who held the *yá* were named after it.
They were divided into left and right contingents,
hence called Left and Right Guards.
I believe the *yá* troops guarded the prefectural *yá*.
"If you think I am untalented,
why don't you kill me and do it yourself!"
The two men were afraid.
Wò selected strong warriors,
calling them
"East Courtyard Cavalry,"
and widely appointed his confidants as generals and officials;
those appointed, relying on their power, became arrogant and tyrannical,
disregarding veteran officials.
Hào and Wēn secretly plotted rebellion.
During the time of Wò's father, Xíngmì,
there were several thousand imperial guards encamped within the *yáchéng*.
The Shu commentary says: In ancient times, when an army marched, there was a *yá*,
where the revered person was located.
Later generations then called the place they governed *yá*,
calling it *yáchéng*,
which is the same as *yáchéng*.
Since that area was used as an archery ground,
Hào and Wēn were consequently fearless.
The historian says Yáng Wò removed his own claws and teeth.
When Wò was stationed in Xuānzhōu,
In Tiānyòu 1st year,
Yáng Wò was stationed in Xuānzhōu;
in the 2nd year, he was summoned to succeed.
And when he succeeded to the throne,
he was summoned back to Guǎnglíng.
Hào and Wēn sent three generals to follow Qín Péi to attack Jiāngxī;
taking advantage of their garrisoning Hóngzhōu,
they falsely accused them of plotting rebellion,
and ordered a separate general, Chén Yòu, to go and execute them.
The historian says Zhāng Hào and Xú Wēn again clipped Wò's claws and teeth.
On the sixth day, he arrived in Hóngzhōu,
and in plain clothes, carrying a short weapon, went straight into Qín Péi's tent.
Péi was greatly alarmed.
Yòu informed him of the reason,
informed him of the reason why he entered directly.
Yòu enumerated the crimes of Sī Qíng and others,
arrested and beheaded them.
When Wò heard that the three generals were dead,
he became even more wary of Hào and Wēn,
and wanted to execute them.
On the *bǐngxū* day,
Wò attended to affairs in the morning.
Hào and Wēn led two hundred *yá* soldiers,
with bared blades, directly into the courtyard.
Wò said:
"Do you truly intend to kill me?"
They replied:
"We dare not;
we only wish to execute those around Your Highness who are disrupting government!"
They then enumerated the crimes of more than ten of Wò's confidants,
dragged them down,
and killed them with iron clubs.
This was called
"armed remonstrance."
The *Zuǒ Zhuàn* says: Yù Quán strongly remonstrated with the Marquis of Chǔ,
who did not heed him;
he confronted him with weapons,
and the Marquis, afraid, complied,
then Yù Quán himself cut off his own feet.
Zhāng Hào and Xú Wēn justified their actions as armed remonstrance,
but they were criminals like Yù Quán.
Hào and Wēn gradually executed them according to law;
thereupon, all military and political power returned to the two men,
and Wò could not control it.
This set the stage for Hào and Wēn to assassinate Wò.
3 Initially,
King Liáng, seeing that all the prefectures north of the Yellow River had submitted,
with only Yōu and Cāng yet to be conquered,
therefore launched a large expedition against them,
intending to solidify the loyalty of the other prefectures.
Soon after, Lùzhōu rebelled internally,
and the King burned his camps and returned.
The details are in the previous volume, Tiānyòu 3rd year.
"Returned" (還),
read as "cóng xuān fān" (從宣翻),
also as the character itself.
Fearing that this might cause disloyalty both domestically and abroad,
he wished to swiftly accept the abdication to stabilize the situation.
On the *dīnghài* day,
the King stayed in a residence in Wèi,
suffering from an illness,
and lay in his mansion.
Luó Shàowēi, fearing the King might attack him,
entered to see the King and said:
"Currently, those who raise armies and trouble Your Majesty
all do so under the pretext of supporting the Táng dynasty.
It would be better for Your Majesty to quickly eliminate Táng to cut off their hopes."
Although the King did not explicitly agree, he was grateful for the suggestion,
and so he quickly returned.
On the *rényín* day,
he arrived at Dàliáng.
On the *jiǎchén* day,
Táng Zhāoxuān Dì sent the Imperial Censor-in-Chief Xuē Yíjǔ to Dàliáng to comfort the King.
Yíjǔ requested an audience with the rites of a subject.
The King invited him to ascend the steps.
Yíjǔ said:
"Your Highness's merits and virtues reside among the people;
the three spirits have changed their choice.
The 'three spirits'
refer to the spirits of Heaven, Earth, and Man.
This means that the hearts of Heaven, Earth, and Man have all abandoned the Táng dynasty,
and have chosen and appointed a new ruler.
How dare this subject defy this!"
Thereupon, he bowed and performed the dance facing north in the courtyard.
The King turned his body to avoid it.
Yíjǔ returned
and reported to the Emperor, saying:
"The Grand Marshal has the intention of accepting the abdication!"
The Emperor then issued an edict.
"Emperor" (帝)
refers to Táng Zhāoxuān Dì.
"Grand Marshal" (元帥)
refers to King Liáng.
He also sent the Chancellor with a letter to persuade the King;
the King declined.
4 The Hédōng army was still stationed at Chángzǐ,
intending to spy on Zézhōu.
The *Jiǔyù Zhì* states: Chángzǐ
is 140 *lǐ* southwest of Zézhōu.
In the first year of Tàipíng Xīngguó of Emperor Tàizōng of Sòng, Báoyì Jūn was changed to Báopíng Jūn,
to avoid the former name of the imperial residence.
This is recorded by the historiographers to avoid the taboo name of the imperial temple.
However, observing that Kāng Huáizhēn was ordered to dispatch troops from Jīngzhào and Tónghuá to garrison Jìnzhōu,
it is likely that two prefectural armies were dispatched from Fūzhōu eastward to garrison Jìnzhōu.
For if Huáizhēn were to dispatch Jīngzhào and Tónghuá troops from Xíngzhōu,
the distance would be great and difficult to traverse.
Xíngzhōu is near Lùzhōu,
and it should also be prepared for the Hédōng army's arrival,
so there is no reason to make Huáizhēn leave Xíngzhōu and garrison Jìnzhōu.
I presume
"Báopíng"
should also be written as
"Bǎodà."
According to Ōuyáng Xiū's *History*, in Huáiyīng's biography, it is also written as
"Báoyì,"
probably because the Báoyì Jiedushi was only abolished after the victory at Měiyuán.
Zhū Quánzhōng was eager to usurp Táng,
and had no time to raise an army to attack Lùzhōu,
merely making his own preparations.
Therefore, Lùzhōu was able to strengthen its defenses even further.
5 In the second month,
Táng ministers jointly submitted a memorial requesting Emperor Zhāoxuān to abdicate.
On the *rénzǐ* day,
an edict ordered the Chancellor to lead the hundred officials to the Grand Marshal's Residence to urge him to ascend the throne.
King Liáng had established the Grand Marshal's Residence in Dàliáng.
"Xiàng shuài" (相帥)
is read as "lǜ" (率).
Thereupon, court officials, regional governors, and even those from Húnán and Língnán, successively submitted memorials urging him to ascend the throne.
6 In the third month,
on the *guǐwèi* day,
the King appointed Lǐ Sī'ān, the Prefect of Bózhōu, as the Northern Route Army Commander,
leading troops to attack Yōuzhōu.
This was to attack Liú Rén'gōng.
7 On the *gēngyín* day,
Emperor Zhāoxuān of Táng issued an edict sending Xuē Yíjǔ again to Dàliáng to convey the intention of abdication.
He also ordered Sū Xún, Minister of Rites, to carry the memorials of the hundred officials to Dàliáng.
8 Qián Liú, King of Wú and Jiedushi of Zhènhǎi and Zhèndōng, sent his sons Chuánliáo and Chuán'guàn to suppress Lú Jí in Wēnzhōu.
9 On the *jiǎchén* day,
Emperor Zhāoxuān of Táng issued an imperial decree abdicating the throne to Liáng.
The *Kǎoyì* states: The *Shílù*, Xuē Jūzhèng's *Wǔdài Shǐ*, and *Táng Yúlù* all say it was in the fourth month,
that the Táng Emperor issued an imperial decree to the Chancellor Zhāng Wénwèi and others to prepare the imperial carriage to welcome the Liáng court,
but without a specific day.
The *Wǔdài Tōnglù* says it was the *dīngwèi* day of the fourth month.
The *dīngwèi* day
is the first day of the fourth month.
The *Jiù Táng Shū* says it was the *jiǎchén* day of the third month.
The *jiǎchén* day
is the twenty-seventh day of the third month.
The *Táng Nián Bǔlù* states: On the *jiǎzǐ* day, the twenty-seventh day of the third month, this imperial decree was issued,
and on the *wùchén* day of the fourth month, Zhū Quánzhōng ascended the throne.
This is even more erroneous.
According to this year, the first day of the third month was *wùyín*,
and the first day of the fourth month was *dīngwèi*.
We now follow the *Jiù Táng Shū*.
Sū Xún, Minister of Rites, was his deputy.
The envoy for the abdication ceremony
presented the abdication scroll and seals,
escorted by the imperial guards and the grand ceremonial procession.
Táng possessed eight imperial seals of transmission.
Empress Wǔ hated the character *xǐ* (璽, seal),
and changed it to *bǎo* (寶, treasure),
so the eight seals for the transmission of the mandate were all re-engraved with the character *bǎo*.
Xuē Yíjǔ, Imperial Censor-in-Chief, was appointed the Envoy for Escorting the Golden Seals.
The *Táng Liùdiǎn* states: The Son of Heaven's eight seals,
made of jade,
are sealed with clay.
The seals of the Empress and Crown Prince are called *bǎo* (treasures),
and are made of gold.
He led the hundred officials with the imperial carriage to Dàliáng.
The *Táng Liùdiǎn* states: The grand imperial carriage system comprised five carriages,
all with accompanying carriages;

there were also the south-pointing chariot, odometer chariot, white egret chariot, phoenix banner chariot, evil-repelling chariot, leather canopy chariot, plough-root chariot, sedan chair, four-direction viewing chariot, sheep chariot, yellow axe chariot, and leopard tail chariot,
with twelve attendant carriages.
For the standard imperial carriage system, five accompanying carriages were reduced,
along with the white egret, evil-repelling, sedan, and four-direction viewing chariots,
and one-quarter of the attendant carriages.
"Shuài" (帥)
is read as "lǜ" (率).
Yáng Shè's son, Níngshì, an official of the Imperial Archives,
In the third year of Zhēngguān,
the Imperial Archives were established within the Department of the Palace Secretariat,
with other officials concurrently holding positions,
or talented individuals of lower rank also referred to as "Archivists" (zhígǎn),
with the Chancellor overseeing the compilation.
After the Tiānbǎo era,
other officials concurrently holding historical positions were called "Compilers of the Imperial Archives" (shǐguǎn xiūzhuàn),
and those newly entering were called "Archivists" (zhígǎn).
In the first year of Yuánhé,
Chancellor Péi Jì proposed that
those holding historical positions who had ascended to court were "Compilers,"
with higher-ranking officials overseeing the archives,
and those not yet ascended to court were "Archivists."
said: "My lord is the Chancellor of Táng,
and the state has come to this;
this cannot be said to be without fault.
Moreover, to personally hand over the Son of Heaven's imperial seals and ribbons to another,
although it may preserve wealth and honor,
what about a thousand years from now!
Why not refuse it!"
Shè was greatly alarmed and said:
"You will destroy my clan!"
His expression was disturbed for several days because of this.
Cè
was from Dūnhuáng.
Guāngfēng
was the son of Yǐn.
Zhào Yǐn is mentioned in volume 252, Yīzōng's Xiántōng 13th year.
10 Liú Rén'gōng, Jiedushi of Lúlóng,
was arrogant, extravagant, greedy, and tyrannical.
He constantly worried that the city of Yōuzhōu was not secure,
and built a mansion on Mount Dà'ān.
The *Xuē Shǐ* states: To the west of Yōuzhōu is a famous mountain called Mount Dà'ān.
"This mountain is steep and isolated on all four sides;
a small force can control a large one here."
Its buildings were grand and magnificent,
comparable to those of an emperor.
He selected beautiful women to fill it.
He refined elixirs with alchemists,
seeking immortality.
He collected all the money within his territory
and buried it on the mountaintop;
he ordered the common people to use purple clay to make money.
He also prohibited tea merchants from Jiāngnán from entering his territory,
and personally collected mountain herbs and trees to make tea,
which he then sold.
Rén Gōng had a beloved concubine, Lady Luó.
His son, Shǒu Guāng, had an affair with her.
Rén Gōng flogged Shǒu Guāng with a staff and banished him,
no longer counting him as a son.
He was not ranked among his other sons.
Wherever they passed, they burned and plundered everything.
Summer,
fourth month,
on the Jǐyǒu day,
they reached directly beneath the walls of Yōuzhōu city.
Rén Gōng was still at Dà'ān Shān,
the city had no defenses,
and was almost indefensible.
Shǒu Guāng led his troops in from outside,
ascended the walls to resist the attack;
and also led troops out to fight Sī'ān,
whereupon Sī'ān was defeated and retreated.
Shǒu Guāng then proclaimed himself Jiédùshǐ,
and ordered his generals, Lǐ Xiǎoxǐ and Yuán Xíngqīn, to lead troops to attack Dà'ān Shān.
Rén Gōng dispatched troops to resist the attack,
but was defeated by Xiǎoxǐ.
Rén Gōng was captured and brought back,
and imprisoned in a separate room.
Rén Gōng's generals, aides, and personal attendants,
all those whom Shǒu Guāng had always disliked, were killed.
Wáng Sītóng, Commander-in-Chief of Yínhúpiào, led 3,000 of his troops.
Lǐ Chéngyuē, Inspector of the Eight Armies of Shānhòu, led 2,000 of his troops.
Lúlóng considered the four prefectures of Guī, Tán, Xīn, and Wǔ as Shānhòu.
They fled to Lǐ Kèyòng.
Not long after,
they also fled to Hédōng.
The Hédōng Jiédùshǐ, Jìn Wáng Kèyòng, appointed Chéngyuē as Commander of Kuāngbà,
and Sītóng as Commander of Fēiténg.
Sītóng's mother
was the daughter of Rén Gōng.
Kuāngbà and Fēiténg
were both names of military units established by Jìn Wáng.
11 The Liáng
King first held court at Jīnxiáng Diàn.
Wáng Pǔ's *Wǔdài Huìyào* states: "When Liáng received the abdication and established its capital at Dàliáng,
the main hall was renamed Chóngyuán Diàn,
the East Hall was renamed Xuándé Diàn,
the Inner Hall was renamed Jīnxiáng Diàn,
Wànsuì Táng was renamed Wànsuì Diàn,
and the gates followed the names of the halls.
Xuē Shǐ says: Liáng proclaimed itself to rule by the virtue of Metal,
and moreover, Fújiàn presented parrots,
and various prefectures successively presented white crows, white rabbits, and white lotus with joined stalks.
This was considered an auspicious sign corresponding to the Metal element's destiny.
Therefore, the hall was named Jīnxiáng."
These were the officials that Liáng itself established.
He referred to himself as "guǎrén."
On the Xīnhài day,
an order was issued that all memorials, petitions, registers, and records should omit the Táng era names,
and only state the month and day.
On the Bǐngchén day,
Zhāng Wénwèi and others arrived at Dàliáng.
12 Lú Jí heard that Qián Chuánliáo and others were approaching,
and led his navy to resist them at Qīng'ào.
Qīng'ào is in the sea northeast of Wēnzhōu,
commonly known as Qīng'ào Mén.
By advancing boats through Qīng'ào Mén, one enters Wēnzhōu;
beyond it is the open ocean.
Ào,
pronounced 'wū dào fān' (fanqie).
A bay or inlet in the sea is called 'ào'.
"All of Jí's elite troops are here;
we cannot fight them."
So, they abandoned their boats at Āngù,
and took a shortcut to attack Wēnzhōu.
Āngù
was Zhāng'ān during the Hòuhàn.
Jiàn,
pronounced 'gǔ xiàn fān' (fanqie).
On the Wùwǔ day,
Wēnzhōu fell,
and Jí was captured and beheaded.
In the second year of Tiānyòu (905),
Lú Jí had taken Wēnzhōu;
by this time, he was defeated and perished.
(The King) ordered Chuánliáo and others to move their troops to attack Lú Yuē at Chǔzhōu.
13 On the Rénxū day,
the Liáng Wáng changed his name to Huàng.
The King's elder brother, Quányù, hearing that the King was about to ascend the imperial throne,
said to the King:
"Zhū Sān,
can you truly become the Son of Heaven?!"
On the Jiǎzǐ day,
Zhāng Wénwèi and Yáng Shè rode in chariots from Shàngyuán Yì, escorting the imperial edicts and seals.
Various departments each prepared ceremonial guards and imperial equipage to lead the way,
and all the officials followed behind.
These were the officials of Táng.
Cóng,
pronounced 'cái yòng fān' (fanqie).
The King wore the imperial robe and crown,
and immediately ascended the imperial throne.
Zhāng Wénwèi and Sū Xún presented the imperial edict, ascended the hall, and read it aloud.
Yáng Shè, Zhāng Cè, Xuē Yíjǔ, and Zhào Guāngféng, in succession, presented the imperial seal, ascended the hall,
and after reading it,
(The character) 'yǐ'
means 'bì' (finished).
led all the officials in dancing and offering congratulations.
The Emperor then feasted with Wénwèi and others at Xuándé Diàn.
The Emperor raised his wine and said:
"I have not governed for long,
this is all due to the efforts of you gentlemen in recommending and supporting me."
Wénwèi and others were ashamed and fearful,
prostrating themselves and unable to respond.
Only Sū Xún, Xuē Yíjǔ, and Zhāng Yī, the Minister of Punishments,
lavishly praised the Emperor's merits and virtues, claiming they were in accordance with Heaven and people's will.
The Emperor again played *bo* and drank with his imperial relatives by blood and marriage in the palace.
Zōng
refers to relatives with the same surname;
qī
refers to relatives with different surnames.
Fù,
pronounced 'fú yòu fān' (fanqie).
Zhū Quányù suddenly threw the dice, scattering them in the basin.
Bào Hóng's *Bójīng* says: "The *Chǔcí* mentions *kūnbì* and elephant chess, both being types of liùbó."
Kūnbì
are jade chopsticks,
each player throws six chopsticks,
and moves six pieces,
hence it is called liùbó.
Twelve pieces are used,
six white pieces,
six black pieces.
The thrown heads are called *qióng*.
The *qióng* have five colors.
Those carved with one stroke are called *sài*.
Those carved with two strokes are called *bái*.
Those carved with three strokes are called *hēi*.
Those not carved,
among the five *sài*,
are called 'five *sài*'.
According to Ōu Shǐ,
what is called 'throwing *qióng*' here
is actually dice.
Bèng,
pronounced 'běi mèng fān' (fanqie).
The *Kǎoyì* says: Wáng Rényù's *Yùtáng Xiánhuà* says:
"The dice were tossed several times.
Guǎng Wáng Quányù suddenly stopped and did not throw them,
but looked at Liáng Zǔ and said,
again calling out 'Zhū Sān',
Liáng Zǔ's expression changed.
Guǎng Wáng said: 'You love these many high offices you hold,
but will your family be safe in the long run?'
Thereupon, (the Emperor) became furious,
threw the gaming pieces down the steps,
struck the basin and shattered it,
and glared angrily and muttered,
which did not cease for several days."
Now we follow Wáng Yǔchēng's *Wǔdài Shǐ Quēwén*.
"Zhū Sān,
you were originally a commoner from Dàngshān.
You followed Huáng Cháo as a bandit.
The Son of Heaven appointed you as Jiédùshǐ of the Four Circuits.
Liáng Wáng first governed the Four Circuits;
see scroll 262, the first year of Tiānfù under Táng Zhāozōng.
How could you, in a single day, destroy the Táng house's three-hundred-year-old altars of soil and grain?
Táng received the abdication in the first year of Wǔdé (618),
in the year of Zhuóyōng Shètígé.
The throne was abdicated to Liáng
in the year of Qiángyǔ Dān'è (907).
It enjoyed the country for 290 years.
Your family is bound to be exterminated.
What's the point of gambling!"
The Emperor was displeased and stopped.
On the *yǐchǒu* day,
an order was issued to the relevant officials to report to Heaven, Earth, the imperial ancestral temple (Zōngmiào), and the altars of land and grain (Shèjì).
On the *dīngmǎo* day,
envoys were dispatched to issue proclamations to the prefectures and garrisons.
All stated that the abdication was received from Táng.
On the *wùchén* day
a great amnesty was granted.

The *Kǎoyì* (Critical Analysis) states: The *Liáng Shílù* (Veritable Records of Liáng), *Biān Yílù* (Compilations of Leftover Records), *Xuē Shǐ* (History by Xuē), and *Táng Yúlù* (Remaining Records of Táng) all do not mention a great amnesty;
this account follows Ouyáng Shǐ.
The reign era was changed to Kāipíng.
Táng Zhāoxuān Dì was enfeoffed as Jìyīn Wáng,
Jìyīn Prefecture of Cáozhōu.
*Jì*,
pronounced like *zǐlǐ*.
All Táng central and local former officials' ranks and titles remained as before.
Biànzhōu was made Kāifēng Fǔ,
and designated Dōngdū;
the former Dōngdū was made Xīdū;
the former Xījīng was abolished,
and Jīngzhào Fǔ was made Dà'ān Fǔ,
with Yòuguó Jūn established at Dà'ān Fǔ.
Táng designated Cháng'ān as Xījīng,
and Luòyáng as Dōngjīng.
Now Liáng's capital is Dàliáng,
which is east of Luòyáng,
so Luòyáng was designated Xīdū,
Dàliáng was Dōngdū,
and Cháng'ān was Dà'ān Fǔ.
In *Tōngjiàn*, volume 264, the fourth month of Tiānyòu first year of Táng Zhāozōng,
it is already recorded,
"Wèibó was renamed Tiānxíong Jūn,"
which likely also came from Zhū Quánzhōng's intention.
This is a re-occurrence,
but it is unknown in which year the army's name was changed.
*Gēng*,
pronounced like *gōnghéng*.
Hedged it with thorns,
using a phrase from the *Zuǒ Zhuàn*.
*Jiàn*,
pronounced like *zàidiān*,
means "to enclose."
14 On the *xīnwèi* day,
Mǎ Yīn, Jìedùshǐ of Wǔ'ān, was made Chǔ Wáng.
Mǎ Yīn bypassed the rank of Jùn Wáng,
and was directly enfeoffed as a king,
a special favor at the beginning of the reign.
15 Jìng Xiáng, *Zhǎng Shūjì* of Xuānwǔ and Tàifǔ Qīng, was appointed *Zhī Chóngzhèng Yuàn Shì*.
The Liáng Chóngzhèng Yuàn performed the duties of the Táng Shūmì Yuàn;
later, the Shūmì Yuàn was abolished and its functions absorbed into the Chóngzhèng Yuàn.
He participated in discussions and presented proposals,
received imperial edicts within the palace,
and proclaimed them to the prime ministers for implementation.
If prime ministers had any requests to present when not in audience, or needed to make further requests after receiving an edict,
they would record the details and submit them via the Chóngzhèng Yuàn,
and upon receiving the imperial decree, it would be proclaimed back to the prime ministers.
Xiáng was a profound
and resourceful person;
he served in the secretariat for over thirty years.
During the Guāngqǐ era of Xīzōng,
Jìng Xiáng joined the Biàn secretariat.
By this time, it was twenty years,
so the history mistakenly wrote
"thirty"
for
"twenty."
The emperor entrusted everything to him.
Xiáng devoted himself assiduously to his duties,
working day and night without sleep.
He himself said that he only found rest on horseback.
The emperor was violent and difficult to approach,
and no one could fathom him,
but Xiáng alone understood his intentions.
If there was something objectionable,
Xiáng never spoke out directly,
but merely subtly indicated his doubts;
the emperor would then grasp the point
and often change his plans accordingly.
During the transition of imperial power,
Xiáng's strategies were instrumental.
16 Imperial great-great-grandfathers and great-great-grandmothers, and those since, were all posthumously honored as emperors and empresses.
*Wǔdài Huìyào* states: Liáng took Shùnchén Zhū Hǔ as its progenitor,
and forty-two generations later, to Àn,
who was posthumously honored as Sùzǔ Xuānyuán Huángdì,
and Lady Fàn was posthumously honored as Xuānxī Huánghòu;
Àn's son Màolín was posthumously honored as Jìngzǔ Guāngxiàn Huángdì,
and Lady Yáng was posthumously honored as Xiào Huánghòu;
Màolín's son Xìn was posthumously honored as Xiànzǔ Zhāowǔ Huángdì,
and Lady Liú was posthumously honored as Zhāoyì Huánghòu.
Xìn's son was Chéng.
His birth mother, Lady Wáng, was posthumously honored as Wénhuì Huánghòu.
17 Initially,
when the emperor was Jìedùshǐ of the Four Garrisons,
all records of storehouses were managed by the Jiànchāng Yuàn;
at this time,
his adopted son Yǒu Wén, *Jìedù Fùshǐ* of Xuānwǔ, was made Kāifēng Yǐn and *Pàn Yuàn Shì*,
in charge of all national finances and grain.
Yǒu Wén was originally the son of the Kāng family.
18 On the *yǐhài* day,
an edict was issued to strip Lǐ Kèyòng of his official titles and ranks.
Lǐ Kèyòng claimed Táng official titles
and used Táng's reign era name.
How could Liáng strip him of them?
The history merely records Liáng's initial policies.
Regarding "Tiānyòu,"
Xīchuān used
the "Tiānfù"
reign era name;
in Tiānfù fourth year,
the Liáng Wáng abducted Táng Zhāozōng and moved him to Luò,
changing the reign era to Tiānyòu.
Hédōng and Xīchuān considered that the one who abducted the Son of Heaven and moved the capital was Liáng,
and that Tiānyòu was not a Táng era name
and should not be used.
So they used Tiānfù fifth year.
In this year, Liáng destroyed Táng,
Hédōng used Tiānyòu fourth year,
and Xīchuān still used Tiānfù.
They acknowledged vassalage and offered tribute.
The Shǔ Wáng and Hóngnóng Wáng issued a joint declaration to all circuits,
Yáng Wò of Huáinán was enfeoffed as Hóngnóng Wáng.
But none responded.
The Shǔ Wáng then deliberated claiming emperorship,
issuing an edict to officials and common people under his rule;
he also sent a letter to the Jìn Wáng, saying:
"Let us each become emperor of a region,
and after Zhū Wēn is pacified,
we shall seek a Táng imperial clansman to establish him,
and then return to our vassal states."
The Jìn Wáng replied, refusing,
saying:
"I swear that in this life I dare not lose my integrity."
The history states that although Lǐ Kèyòng was of barbarian descent, he remained a Táng subject his entire life,
which was also due to his loyal and pure nature.
At the end of Táng, when eunuchs were executed,
the imperial edict reached Hédōng,
and the Jìn Wáng hid the supervising eunuch Zhāng Chéngyè at Húlǜ Sì,
executing a condemned criminal instead to comply with the edict.
See volume 264, Táng Zhāozōng Tiānfù third year.
Húlǜ Sì
was probably established by the Húlǜ clan during their prosperity, when Gāo Qí established its hegemonic residence in Jìnyáng.
He was reinstated as supervising eunuch,
and treated with greater generosity;
Chéngyè also exerted himself fully for him.
Qí Wáng governed his army with great leniency,
treating his officers and soldiers simply.
When someone reported that his general Fú Zhāo was in rebellion,
Qí Wáng went directly to Fú Zhāo's house,
dismissed all his attendants,
slept soundly for a night, and then returned;
because of this, everyone was pleased and submitted;
however, his military governance lacked discipline.
When he heard that Táng had fallen,
due to his weak army and limited territory,
he dared not claim emperorship,
but merely opened a Qí Wáng Fǔ,
appointed numerous officials,
named his residence a palace,
and his wife was called empress.
Lǐ Màozhēn made himself Qí Wáng,
and his wife was called empress;
his wife's status surpassed that of her husband.
These military strongmen,
taking advantage of the times to usurp titles,
privately adopted names to designate themselves—
how can one discuss proper etiquette with them!
Their whips, fans, and commands often imitated those of an emperor.
"Whip" refers to the
鸣鞭 (*míngbiān*, cracking whip);
"fan" refers to the
雉尾扇 (*zhìwěishàn*, pheasant-tail fan).
According to Táng regulations: when the Son of Heaven held court,
as he emerged from the inner palace, whips were cracked to give warning;
after exiting the western side door, a fan was requested.
When the fan closed,
the Son of Heaven ascended the throne;
when the fan opened,
all officials finished their audience.
Luó Yǐn, *Jìedù Pànguān* of Zhènhǎi, urged Wú Wáng Qián Liú to raise an army to attack Liáng,
saying:
"Even if there is no success,
you can still retreat and hold Hángzhōu and Yuèzhōu,
and declare yourself Eastern Emperor;
why should you cross your arms and serve the bandit,
bringing eternal shame?!"
Qián Liú initially thought that Yǐn had been ill-treated by Táng,
and must bear resentment.
But upon hearing his words,
though he could not adopt his advice,
he respected him greatly.
19 In the fifth month,
on the *dīngchǒu* day (the first day of the month),
Xuē Yí Jǔ, *Yùshǐ Dàfū*, was appointed *Zhōngshū Shìláng* and *Tóng Píngzhāng Shì*.
20 Wáng Róng, Zhào Wáng and *Jìedùshǐ* of Wǔshùn, was promoted to *Shǒu Tàishī*;
Luó Shàowēi, Yè Wáng and *Jìedùshǐ* of Tiānxíong, was promoted to *Shǒu Tàifù*;
and Wáng Chǔzhí, *Jìedùshǐ* of Yìwǔ, concurrently held the title of *Shìzhōng*.
21 Qìdān sent its minister Páohú Mèilǎo to establish friendly relations,
the Emperor sent Tàifǔ Shàoqīng Gāo Qí to reciprocate.
Initially,
the Qìdān had eight tribes.
Ōuyáng Xiū said: The chieftain of the Qìdān was called Dàhè Shì,
later divided into eight tribes: one was the Dànlìjiē Bù,
two was the Yǐshìhuó Bù,
three was the Shíhuó Bù,
four was the Nàwěi Bù,
five was the Pínmò Bù,
six was the Nèihuìjī Bù,
seven was the Jíjiě Bù,
and eight was the Xīwà Bù.
The leader of a tribe was called Dàrén.
Lù Zhèn's Jiǔguó Zhì says: The Qìdān
are descended from the ancient Xiōngnú.
They have long resided in the midst of the Liáozé,
on the south bank of the Huángshuǐ,
1,100 *lǐ* south of Yúguān,
and Yúguān is 700 *lǐ* south of Yōuzhōu.
The Kǎoyì says: Sū Féngjí's Hàn Gāozǔ Shílù says:
"The Qìdān originally had the surname Dàhè Shì,
later divided into eight clans: one was Lìjiē Dǐ,
two was Yǐshīhuó Dǐ,
three was Shíhuó Dǐ,
four was Nàwěi Dǐ,
five was Pínmò Dǐ,
six was Nèihuìjī Dǐ,
seven was Jíjiě Dǐ,
and eight was Xīwà Dǐ.
They governed forty-one counties,
each with a magistrate.
The leaders of the eight clans
were all called Dàrén,
and styled Cìshǐ.
They often nominated one person to be king,
establishing banners and drums to honor him.
Every three years,
they would rank their names to rotate the position."
The Zhuāngzōng Lièzhuàn says:
"In the late Xiántōng era,
their king was named Xí'ěr.
His territory gradually expanded,
and he repeatedly came to pay tribute.
During the Guāngqǐ era,
their king was named Qīndé.
Taking advantage of the many troubles in the Central Plains
and the unpreparedness of the northern border,
he gradually encroached upon the various tribes.
The Dádá, Xī, Shìwéi and their like
were all driven to servitude."
The Hàn Gāozǔ Shílù and Táng Yúlù both say:
"Around the Xī and Zhāo eras,
their king, Yēlǜ Ābǎojī, relied on his strength and courage.
He resisted the other tribes and refused to rotate,
styling himself Tiānhuáng Wáng.
Later, the various tribes invited him
and requested to use the old system.
Ābǎojī had no choice but to
transfer the banners and drums,
and said: 'I have been a leader for nine years,
and the number of Hàn people I have acquired is quite large.
I wish to use the ancient Hàn city to lead my own tribe,
command the Hàn people to defend it,
and establish myself as a separate tribe.'
The various tribes assented.
Soon, he devised a strategy to annex the other tribes again,
presumptuously claiming the title of Emperor,
and his territory grew daily.
During the Dàshùn era,
Wǔhuáng of the Later Táng sent envoys to form an alliance with him,
holding a grand meeting at the eastern city of Yúnzhōu.
He invited him into his tent,
and they pledged brotherhood."
The Zhuāngzōng Lièzhuàn also says:
"When Qīndé's rule declined,
Ābǎojī's clan flourished,
and he proclaimed himself King.
In the second year of Tiānyòu,
he greatly plundered our Yúnzhōng.
Tàizǔ sent envoys to form an alliance,
and subsequently met with him in person at the eastern city of Yúnzhōu.
He invited him into his tent,
and they pledged brotherhood,
saying: 'The Táng dynasty has been usurped by rebellious officials.
I will launch a major campaign this winter.
My brother should assist me with 20,000 elite cavalry
to jointly recover Biàn and Luò.'
Ābǎojī agreed.
After Ābǎojī returned,
Qīndé transferred the affairs of the state to him."
Jiǎ Wěi's Bèishǐ says:
"Wǔhuáng met Ābǎojī at the old city of Yúnzhōu,
and they formed a bond of brotherhood.
At that time, their troops were arrayed five *lǐ* apart.
Messengers rode back and forth with cups on horseback,
performing the rituals of exchange.
Ābǎojī was pleased and
said to Wǔhuáng: 'Among our barbarian chieftains,
the old custom is to retire after three years.
If I see you someday in the future,
will we still treat each other with courtesy?'
Wǔhuáng said: 'I received the court's decree to garrison Tàiyuán,
and there is also a system of transfer.
However, as long as one does not abdicate, it is fine.
Why worry about retirement!'
From this, Ābǎojī followed his teaching
and refused to be replaced by the other tribes."
Zhào Zhìzhōng's Lǔtíng Zájì says:
"Tàizǔ's taboo name was Yì,
his barbarian name was Ābǎojǐn,
and another taboo name was Wòlǐ.
Tàizǔ was intelligent from birth.
The leaders of the eight tribes loved his heroism and courage,
so they removed their former leader, Āniǎn Shì, and returned to their own tribe,
establishing Tàizǔ as king."
It also says:
"Whenever a king was established,
the chieftains of all the tribes would gather for a meeting.
One who possessed virtue, conduct, and accomplishments would be chosen.
If no disasters occurred,
and livestock flourished,
and the people lived in peace,
then the king would not be replaced;
if not,
the chieftains would convene the tribes and select another person as king;
thus, the king, by barbarian law,
would willingly step down,
and not be harmed by the multitude."
It also says:
"There were Hán Zhīgǔ, Hán Yǐng, Kāng Méi, Wáng Zòushì, and Wáng Yù,
all Chinese,
who together urged Tàizǔ not to abdicate."
The Xīn Tángshū records many different names for the eight Qìdān tribes compared to the Hàn Gāozǔ Shílù,
probably because the eras were distant
and the barbarian language was not constant,
but in reality, they were the same.
Ābǎojī said,
"I have been a leader for nine years,"
which means he had already long resisted abdication in his state,
not due to Wǔhuáng's teaching.
We now follow the Hàn Gāozǔ Shílù.
Furthermore, the Táng Yúlù previously states,
"During the Qiánníng era,
Liú Rén'gōng garrisoned Yōuzhōu.
Ābǎojī invaded,
and Rén'gōng captured his wife's elder brother, Shùlǜ Ābō.
From then on, for over ten years, he could not cross the frontier,"
but later it says,
"during the Dàshùn era, he met Wǔhuáng in Yúnzhōng."
However, Dàshùn was before Qiánníng.
Rén'gōng only became the Jìedù of Yōuzhōu in the second year of Qiánníng;
he was not in the Dàshùn era.
Also, Wǔhuáng said:
"The Táng dynasty has been usurped by rebellious officials.
I will launch a major campaign this winter."
This was not an event during the Dàshùn era.
The Táng Yúlù is mistaken.
The Biān Yílù also states:
"In the fifth month of the second year of Kāipíng,
Qìdān King Ābǎojī and former King Qīndé offered tribute."
This means that at that time, the seven tribes still existed.
They agreed among themselves
to nominate one person as king,
establish banners and drums to command the various tribes,
and every three years, they would take turns replacing each other.
In the late Xiántōng era,
a man named Xí'ěr became king,
and his territory began to expand.
Afterwards, Qīndé became king,
taking advantage of the many troubles in the Central Plains,
and frequently raided the border.
When Ābǎojī became king,
he was particularly heroic and courageous.
The Five Clans of Xī
The Five Clans of Xī are:
one, the Āhuì Bù;
two, the Chǔhé Bù;
three, the Àoshī Bù;
four, the Dùjī Bù;
five, the Yuánsìzhé Bù.
Each had a Rǔhézhǔ as its chieftain.
Ōuyáng Xiū said: The Xī resided in Yīnliángchuān at the end of the Táng dynasty,
west of Yíngfǔ,
and northwest of Yōuzhōu,
both several hundred *lǐ* away.
They were divided into five tribes: one was the Āhuì Bù,
two was the Yòumǐ Bù,
three was the Yuèzhì Bù,
four was the Nùjiē Bù,
and five was the Hēiqì Zhībù.
Later, they migrated several hundred *lǐ* northeast of Yōuzhōu.
Sòng Bái said: The Xī resided in Yīnliángchuān,
500 *lǐ* east of Yíngfǔ,
and 900 *lǐ* southwest of Yōuzhōu.
To the southeast, they bordered the sea,
across 3,000 *lǐ* of mountains and rivers.
Later, they migrated to Pípáchuān.
The Shìwéi originally had over twenty tribes,
and seven clans among them were close to the Qìdān.
Ābǎojī's surname was Yēlǜ Shì.
Ōu Shǐ Sìyífùlù says: Ābǎojī used the name of the place of his dwelling, Héngzhàng, as his surname,
said Shìlǐ.
Shìlǐ,
the translator called him Xiélǜ.
He refused to be replaced.
After a long time,
Ābǎojī returned from attacking the Huángtóu Shìwéi,
and the Qībù ambushed him at the border,
demanding what was agreed upon.
It was the agreement for a replacement every three years.
He handed over the banner and drum,
and also said:
“I have been king for nine years,
and I have acquired many Hàn people.
I request to lead my clans
to reside in Gǔhànchéng,
to guard it with the Hàn people,
and to form a separate tribe.”
The Qībù assented.
Hànchéng
was the former Huáyán county of the Hòuwèi.
The Hànbù records:
Huáyán county belonged to Yúyáng Jùn.
Emperor Míng of the Hòuhàn changed its name to Yántián.
The Shuǐjīngzhù states: The Dàyúhé flows southeast from the south of Mìyúnchéng,
passing south of Huáyán county, formerly of Ānzhōu, Yúyáng Jùn of the Hòuwèi.
Huáyán
was commonly called Húyánchéng,
two hundred lǐ northwest of Yùyízhèn.
Ōuyáng Xiū said: Hànchéng is on the Luánhé southeast of Tànshān.
Sòng Bái said: The Qìdān reside in the middle of Liáozé,
on the south bank of the Huángshuǐ.
Liáozé is one thousand one hundred thirty lǐ from Yúguān,
and Yúguān is one hundred seventy-four lǐ from Yōuzhōu.
Its land borders the sea to the southeast,
the Liáohé to the east,
encloses Lěngxíng to the west,
and borders Sōngxíng Shān to the north.
It spans three thousand lǐ east to west,
the land has many pines and willows,
and the marshes have many cattails and reeds.
Ābǎojī resided in Hànchéng,
five hundred fifty lǐ northwest of Tánzhōu.
North of the city is Lóngmén Shān,
north of the mountain is Tànshān,
and west of Tànshān is the contiguous border between the Qìdān and Shìwéi.
This land is the upper source of the Luánhé,
and to its west are the benefits of salt lakes,
which is the Hòuwèi’s Huáyán county.
There are benefits from salt ponds.
After this, Ābǎojī gradually used his army to attack and annihilate the Qībù,
and re-united them into one state.
He then invaded the Shìwéi and Nǚzhēn to the north.
The Nǚzhēn
are descendants of the Sùshèn clan,
and the Hēishuǐ Mòhé are from their land.
Those who entered Liáodōng and were registered were called Shú Nǚzhēn,
those living wild outside the border were called Shēng Nǚzhēn,
and those in the furthest reaches were called Huángtóu Nǚzhēn.
He attacked the Xī,
annihilated them,
then re-established a Xī king and had the Qìdān supervise their army.
All the various tribes in the northeast feared and submitted to him.
That year,
Ābǎojī led a force of three hundred thousand to raid Yúnzhōu.
King Jìn allied with him,
met him at Dōngchéng,
pledged brotherhood,
invited him into his tent,
drank freely,
shook hands in utmost joy,
and agreed to jointly attack Liáng this winter.
Kǎoyì said: Táng Tàizǔ Jìniánlù records:
“Tàizǔ, seeing Ābǎojī’s clan party gradually strengthening,
summoned him.
In the fifth month of Tiānyòu 2 (905 CE),
Ābǎojī led his thirty thousand tribesmen to the east city of Yúnzhōu,
discussed matters in the tent,
shook hands joyfully,
pledged brotherhood,
and left after ten days.
He left his son Gǔdōushèlì and leader Jǔbǐngméi as hostages,
agreeing to launch a major campaign across the river in early winter to restore the rightful rule,
but it was stopped when Emperor Zhāozōng encountered robbers.”
Ōuyáng Shǐ said:
“As the Liáng were about to usurp the Táng,
King Jìn Lǐ Kèyòng sent envoys to the Qìdān.
Ābǎojī, with an army of three hundred thousand, met Kèyòng at the east city of Yúnzhōu,
shook hands and pledged brotherhood,
and set a date to jointly raise an army to attack Liáng.”
Upon examination, the Yúnzhōu meeting,
in Zhuāngzōng Lièzhuàn and Xuēshǐ, is placed in Tiānyòu 4 (907 CE),
but Jìniánlù alone places it in Tiānyòu 2 (905 CE);
it also says
“agreed to jointly recover Biàn and Luò this winter,
but it was stopped when Emperor Zhāozōng encountered robbers.”
If this were the case, it should have been before Emperor Zhāozōng’s death in Tiānyòu 1 (904 CE),
not in Tiānyòu 2.
Moreover, if Emperor Zhāozōng encountered robbers, it would have been even more appropriate to raise an army to suppress them,
so why was it stopped?
According to Wǔhuáng,
“The Táng court was usurped by treacherous officials,”
this is a statement from the fourth year;
that winter Wǔhuáng fell ill,
which is probably why the army was not dispatched.
We follow this now.
“As he is coming,
he can be captured,”
the King said:
“To break faith with barbarians when the enemy is not yet vanquished is the way to self-destruction.”
Ābǎojī stayed for ten days and then left.
King Jìn presented him with tens of thousands of gold and silk.
Ābǎojī left three thousand horses
and tens of thousands of various animals in return.
Ābǎojī returned and broke the alliance,
instead attaching himself to the Liáng,
which caused King Jìn to resent him.
The Tōngjiàn, in the Tángjì, writes
“Lǐ Kèyòng,”
showing the distinction between ruler and subject;
in the Liángjì, it writes
“King Jìn,”

The cases of Wú and Shǔ follow the same principle.
On the day of Jǐmǎo,
Zhāng Quányì, the Henán Yǐn and concurrent Jiéduéshǐ of Héyáng, was made King Wèi;
Qián Liú, the Jiéduéshǐ of Zhènhǎi and Zhèndōng and King Wú, was made King Wúyuè;
Liú Yǐn, the Jiéduéshǐ of Qīnghǎi, and Wáng Shěnzhī, the Jiédué of Wēiwǔ, were promoted to concurrent Shìzhōng.
After

“shǐ”.
From the time Emperor Wǔ of Sòng, a descendant of Péngchéng, rose in Jiāngnán,
many later considered the Liú of Péngchéng to be a distinguished clan.
Liú Yǐn was enfeoffed as King Dàpéng,
the intention was probably derived from this.
On the day of Guǐwèi,
Gāo Jìchāng, acting administrator of Jīngnán Liúhòu, was made Jiéduéshǐ.
Jīngnán formerly governed eight prefectures:
Jīng, Guī, Xiá, Kuí, Zhōng, Wàn, Lǐ, Lǎng,
a total of eight prefectures.
Rebellions followed one after another,
and all the prefectures were occupied by neighboring circuits,
leaving only Jiānglíng.
When Jìchāng took office,
the cities and towns were ruined,
and the population was depleted.
Jìchāng settled the scattered populace,
and the people all returned to their livelihoods.
On the day of Yǐyǒu,
he established his elder brother Quányù as King Guǎng,
his son Yǒuwén as King Bó,
Yǒuguī as King Yǐng,
Yǒuzhāng as King Fú,
Yǒuzhēn as King Jūn,
Yǒuyōng as King Hè,
and Yǒuhuī as King Jiàn.
Yǒuwén, as an adopted son, was placed above the other sons.
Yǒuguī’s regicide
sowed the seeds of disaster here.
On the day of Xīnmǎo,
the old residence in Dōngdū was converted into Jiànchānggōng,
and the Administrator of the Jiànchāngyuàn was renamed Jiànchānggōngshǐ.
Xuēshǐ said: Initially,
when the Emperor was founding his enterprise,
because the records of the four garrisons’ troops, horses, and storages were numerous and complex,
he established the Jiànchāngyuàn to manage them.
At this time, it was changed to a palace,
probably to emphasize its importance.
Sòng Bái said: In this year, the Zhōngshūménxià proposed changing the Administrator of the Jiànchāngyuàn to Jiànchānggōngshǐ,
and further requested that the old mansion in the capital be made Jiànchānggōng.
On the day of Rénchén,
Kāng Huáizhēn, the Jiéduéshǐ of Bǎopíng, was ordered to lead an army of eighty thousand to join the Wèibó army in attacking Lùzhōu.
They attacked the Jìn general Lǐ Sìzhāo.
On the day of Jiǎwǔ,
an imperial edict abolished the Shūmìyuàn,
and all its duties were transferred to the Chóngzhèngyuàn,
with Jìng Xiáng, who was in charge of the Yuàn affairs, appointed as Yuànshǐ.
Kǎoyì said: The Shílù records:
“On the Xīnwèi day of the fourth month,
Xiáng was appointed Administrator of Chóngzhèngyuàn affairs.
On the Jiǎwǔ day of the fifth month,
an imperial edict announced that the Shūmìyuàn should be renamed Chóngzhèngyuàn,
and Xiáng was first appointed Yuànshǐ.”
It seems that the name Chóngzhèngyuàn already existed,
and at this point, the duties of the Shūmìyuàn were simply merged entirely into the Chóngzhèngyuàn.
Sū Xún (蘇循), Minister of Rites, and his son, 起居郎 Kǎi (楷), considered themselves to have rendered meritorious service to Liáng (梁).
In the second year of Tiānyòu (天祐) of Emperor Zhāoxuān (昭宣) of Táng (唐), Sū Xún (蘇循) had vigorously promoted the transfer of the throne.
Hence, he considered himself to have rendered meritorious service.
Xún (循) hoped day and night to become a chancellor.
The emperor disdained his character.
According to the Imperial Annals of the Old Book of Táng (舊唐書帝紀): In the second year of Tiānyòu (天祐) of Emperor Zhāoxuān (昭宣),
Sū Kǎi (蘇楷) submitted a memorial refuting the posthumous title of Zhāozōng (昭宗).
Quánzhōng (全忠) was suspicious and discerning.
After Kǎi (楷) refuted the posthumous title, Quánzhōng (全忠) deeply despised him.
After the succession had been accomplished,
both father and son were expelled,
and not allowed to remain at court.
Xiáng (翔) said to the emperor,
"Sū Xún (蘇循)
is an owl and a vulture of Táng (唐),
who sells out his country for personal gain.
He should not be allowed to stand in a revitalized court."
On the day Wùxū (戊戌),
an edict ordered Xún (循) and Zhāng Yī (張禕), Minister of Punishments, along with fifteen other people, to retire from office.
Kǎi (楷) was dismissed and sent back to his hometown.
Xún (循) and his son then went to Hézhōng (河中) to seek refuge with Zhū Yǒuqīan (朱友謙).
This was the basis for Sū Xún's (蘇循) flattery of Táng Zhuāngzōng (唐莊宗) in the early days of Tóngguāng (同光).
Lú Yuē (盧約) surrendered Chǔzhōu (處州) to Wúyuè (吳越).
In the first year of Zhōnghé (中和) of Emperor Xīzōng (僖宗),
Lú Yuē (盧約) occupied Chǔzhōu (處州),
and it fell at this time.
The surrender
caused the population to fluctuate.
The King of Hóngnóng (弘農王) appointed Liú Cún (劉存), Inspector of Èyuè (鄂岳), as Commander of All Forces for the Southwest Front;
Chén Zhīxīn (陳知新), Prefect of Yuèzhōu (岳州), as Commander of the Yuèzhōu (岳州) Militia;
Liú Wēi (劉威), Inspector of Lúzhōu (廬州), as Aid-and-Reinforcement Envoy;
and the separate general Xǔ Xuányīng (許玄應) as Supervisor of the Army.
They led a naval force of thirty thousand to attack Chǔ (楚).
Mǎ Yīn (馬殷), the King of Chǔ (楚), was greatly alarmed.
Yáng Dìngzhēn (楊定真), Commander of Jìngjiāng (靜江) Army, congratulated him, saying,
"Our army will win!"
Yīn (殷) asked why.
Dìngzhēn (定真) said,
"Indeed, fear in battle leads to victory,
while arrogance leads to defeat.
Now the Huáinán (淮南) troops are heading straight for our city,
which shows their arrogance and contempt for the enemy;
but the King shows signs of fear,
which is why I know we will surely win."
Yīn (殷) ordered Qín Yànhuī (秦彥暉), the City Commander,
The City Commander
commanded all the troops stationed in Tánzhōu (潭州).
Huáng Fán (黃璠), Deputy Commander of the Naval Forces, led three hundred warships to garrison at Liúyángkǒu (瀏陽口).
Wú (吳) established Liúyáng (瀏陽) County in Chángshā (長沙),
which Suí (隋) abolished;
in the second year of Jǐnglóng (景龍), it was re-established at the old site,
belonging to Tánzhōu (潭州).
According to the Jiǔyù Zhì (九域志): The county is one hundred sixty *lǐ* northeast of the prefecture.
According to the Shuǐjīng Zhù (水經註): The Xiāng (湘) River flows north past the west of Hàn Línxiāng (漢臨湘) County,
and the Liú (瀏) River flows from the northwest of the county into it,
where there was a Liúkǒu (瀏口) garrison.
Fán (璠),
pronounced *fú yuán fán*.
Liú (瀏),
pronounced *lì zhōu fán*.
Cún (存) and others encountered heavy rain and
led their troops back to the north of Yuèdī (越堤).
Yànhuī (彥暉) pursued them.
Cún (存) fought several battles without success,
so he sent a letter to Yīn (殷) feigning surrender.
Yànhuī (彥暉) sent a message to Yīn (殷), saying,
"This must be a trick;
do not accept!"
Cún (存) and Yànhuī (彥暉) arranged their forces across the water.
Cún (存) called out from afar,
"It is inauspicious to kill those who surrender. Do you not consider your descendants, my lord?"
Yànhuī (彥暉) said,
"If the enemy enters our territory and we do not attack, why bother about descendants!"
He advanced with drums and shouts.
Cún (存) and others fled.
Huáng Fán (黃璠) crossed the river from Liúyáng (瀏陽)
and joined Yànhuī (彥暉) in a combined attack,
thoroughly defeating them.
They captured Cún (存) and Zhīxīn (知新).
The Kǎoyì (考異) says: The Biānyílù (編遺錄) states:
"In the fourth month of the fourth year of Tiānyòu (天祐),
the Húnán (湖南) army, led by Chén Shào (陳卲), reported victory.
The Huáinán (淮南) and Lángzhōu (朗州) forces, combining by land and water, rushed into their territory.
Mǎ Yīn (馬殷) launched his fleet at Liúyáng Jiāngkǒu (瀏陽江口) and utterly defeated the rebel party,
capturing the self-proclaimed Jiédùshǐ (節度使) of Èzhōu (鄂州), Liú Cún (劉存)."
According to Xuē Shǐ (薛史), Liáng Jì (梁紀),
Mǎ Yīn (馬殷) reported defeating the Huái (淮) invaders in the sixth month;
according to the Wú Shǐ (吳史) of the Shíguó Jìnián (十國紀年),

Tens of thousands of soldiers died,

Wēi (威) escaped with the remaining forces,

For Chén Zhīxīn (陳知新) taking Yuèzhōu (岳州), see the previous volume, previous year.
Jiàn (艦),

Sōu (艘),

He comforted and exhorted them.
Both men cursed, saying,

So they were executed.
The history praises Liú Cún (劉存) and Chén Zhīxīn (陳知新) as loyal and courageous.
They were the confidants of the King of Hóngnóng (弘農王)
and often participated in government affairs.
Zhāng Hào (張顥) and Xú Wēn (徐溫), taking advantage of their defeat,
arrested and executed them.
King Yīn (殷) of Chǔ (楚) sent troops to join Péng Gān (彭玕), Prefect of Jízhōu (吉州), in attacking Hóngzhōu (洪州),
but they failed.
For Péng Gān (彭玕) joining Chǔ (楚), see the previous volume, third year of Tiānyòu (天祐) of Emperor Zhāoxuān (昭宣) of Táng (唐).
Kāng Huáizhēn (康懷貞) arrived at Lùzhōu (潞州).
Lǐ Sìzhāo (李嗣昭), Jiédùshǐ (節度使) of Zhāoyì (昭義) of Jìn (晉), and Lǐ Sìbì (李嗣弼), Deputy Envoy, closed the city gates and held firm.
Huáizhēn (懷貞) attacked day and night,
but after half a month, failed to take it.
He then built fortifications and dug centipede trenches to besiege it,
cutting off communication both inside and out.
The King of Jìn (晉) appointed Zhōu Déwēi (周德威), Commander of all Fān (蕃) and Hàn (漢) troops, as Commander of the Mobile Army.
Zhōu Déwēi (周德威) commanded all the Fān (蕃) and Hàn (漢) troops and
was a great general of Hédōng (河東).
In the Five Dynasties period,
each frontier command had its own Commander,
but the duties of the appointed officials sometimes differed.
For example, Zhōu Déwēi (周德ēi) was Commander of Fān (蕃) and Hàn (漢) troops,
meaning all Fān (蕃) and Hàn (漢) troops were under his command;
a Commander of the Mobile Army meant all troops in the mobile camp were under his command;
Ān Yuánxìn (安元信), Commander of the Tiělín (鐵林) Corps,
was merely the commander of a single corps of the Tiělín (鐵林) Army.
Historians should seek the meaning according to their categories.
The history states that Jìn (晉) deployed its entire nation to save Lùzhōu (潞州).
Shuài (帥),
read as *lǜ*.
Kèxiū (克脩) was the son;
Kèxiū (克脩) was the younger brother of the King of Jìn (晉),

Jìn (晉) forces attacked Zézhōu (澤州),
attacking Zézhōu (澤州) to counter Kāng Huáizhēn (康懷貞)'s rear.
On the day Jiǎyín (甲寅),
Hán Jiàn (韓建), Jiédùshǐ (節度使) of Pínglú (平盧), was appointed Sītú (司徒) and Tóng Píngzhāngshì (同平章事).
Léi Yàngōng (雷彥恭), Jiédùshǐ (節度使) of Wǔzhēn (武貞), joined Chǔ (楚) forces to attack Jiānglíng (江陵).
Gāo Jìchāng (高季昌), Jiédùshǐ (節度使) of Jīngnán (荊南), led his troops to garrison at Gōng'ān (公安).
Gōng'ān (公安) was Hàn Chánlíng (漢孱陵) County.
In the late Hàn (漢) period,
Liú Bèi (劉備) garrisoned here
and renamed it Gōng'ān (公安).
During Táng (唐), it belonged to Jiānglíng (江陵) Prefecture.
According to the Jiǔyù Zhì (九域志): It is ninety *lǐ* south of the prefecture.
Yàngōng (彥恭) was defeated,
and the Chǔ (楚) forces also fled.
After Liú Shǒuguāng (劉守光) imprisoned his father,
see the event in the fourth month above.
He sent an envoy to request an appointment.
In autumn,
the seventh month,
on the day Jiǎwǔ (甲午),
Shǒuguāng (守光) was appointed Jiédùshǐ (節度使) of Lúlóng (盧龍) and Tóng Píngzhāngshì (同平章事).
Qǔ Yù (曲裕), Jiédùshǐ (節度使) of Jìnghǎi (靜海), died.
Qǔ Yù (曲裕) is Qǔ Chéngyù (曲承裕).
On the day Bǐngshēn (丙申),
his son, Háò (顥), who was provisionally managing the succession, was appointed Jiédùshǐ (節度使).
The Kǎoyì (考異) states: No other book specifies Háò's (顥) relation to Yù (裕).
According to Xuē Shǐ (薛史):
"In the sixth month,
on the day Bǐngchén (丙辰),
Yù (裕) died.
In the seventh month,
on the day Bǐngshēn (丙申),
Qǔ Hàò (曲顥), Sīmǎ (司馬) of Jìnghǎi (靜海) Mobile Command, who was provisionally managing the succession, was reinstated as Ānnán Dūhù (安南都護)
and concurrently Jiédùshǐ (節度使)."
Since it says
"reinstated,"
it is known that he was his son.
"Hángyíng" (行營)
should be
"Hángjūn" (行軍).
Léi Yàngōng (雷彥恭) attacked Yuèzhōu (岳州),
but failed.
After Léi Yàngōng (雷彥恭) attacked Jīngnán (荊南) with Chǔ (楚),
he then attacked Chǔ's (楚) Yuèzhōu (岳州),
which shows his duplicity.
On the day Bǐngwǔ (丙午),
Zhāng Quányì (張全義), Yin of Hénán (河南), was granted the name Zōngshì (宗奭).
The Emperor's former name was Quánzhōng (全忠),
hence Quányì's (全義) name was changed to Zōngshì (宗奭).
On the xīn-hài day,
Wúyuè Wáng Qián Liú was appointed concurrently as the Jiédu Shǐ of Huáinán,
and Chǔ Wáng Mǎ Yīn concurrently as the Jiédu Shǐ of Wǔchāng,
each serving as the Zhāotǎo Zhìzhì Shǐ of their respective circuits.
The intention was to have Liǎngzhè and Húnán attack Hóngnóng Wáng Yáng Wò,
by first granting them the two prefectures under the Yáng family's control.
40 Jìn’s Zhōu Déwēi established a camp at Gāohé.
Gāohé is southeast of Túnliú County, Lùzhōu.
Wǔ was defeated.
Qīn Qí,
the imperial guards of Liáng,
were cavalry.
On the dīng-sì day,
the Emperor appointed Lǐ Sī’ān, the Cìshǐ of Bózhōu, to replace Huái Zhēn as the Xíngyíng Dūtǒng of Lùzhōu,
and demoted Huái Zhēn to Xíngyíng Dōuyúhòu.
Sī’ān led Héběi troops westward.
Shàngdǎng is high ground,
west of the Héběi prefectures,
hence "westward."
The character shàng
is pronounced shí zhǎng.
He then built a double wall,
to defend against internal assaults
and to repel external relief forces,
which was called a jiāzhài (flanking stockade).
He mobilized the people of Shāndōng to transport military provisions.
Déwēi's light cavalry raided them daily.
Sī’ān then built a covered passageway from the southeast mountain pass,
connecting it to the jiāzhài.
Déwēi and his generals repeatedly attacked it,
demolishing walls and filling trenches,
dozens of times within a day and a night.
The Liáng troops were exhausted from their constant efforts.
Whenever those from the jiāzhài came out to forage,
Déwēi would always raid them.
Consequently, the Liáng troops remained behind their walls and did not venture out.

Léi Yàngōng attacked Cényáng and Gōng’ān.
The Jiǔyù Zhì states: Gōng’ān County in Jiānglíng Fǔ has Cényáng Town.
Cén
is pronounced chú zhēn.
Yàngōng was as greedy and cruel as his father.
Léi Yàngōng was the son of Mǎn.
The area between Jīng and Hú often suffered from his depredations;
moreover, he was allied with Huáinán.
On the bǐng-shēn day,
an imperial edict stripped Yàngōng of his official titles and ranks,

42 The Shǔ Wáng convened his generals and aides to discuss proclaiming himself emperor.
They all said:
"Although Your Highness is loyal to Táng,
Táng has already perished.
This is what is meant by 'Heaven grants, but one does not take it'! "
Fēng Juān alone submitted a proposal requesting that the Shǔ Wáng merely declare himself regent,
saying:
"While the court thrives, it is not improper to serve as a minister;
while the rebels exist, it is not right to join them in evil."
The King did not follow this advice,
and Juān secluded himself at home.
Fēng Juān, the grandson of Fēng Sù,
after the fall of the Táng dynasty,
upheld his loyalty to the former sovereign,
showing a marked difference from people like Wéi Zhuāng and Zhāng Gé.
He led his officials and people in weeping for three days;
on the jǐ-hài day,
he ascended the imperial throne.
Wáng Jiàn's courtesy name was Guāngtú,
and he was from Wǔyáng, Xǔzhōu.
The Kǎoyì states: Zhuāngzōng Lièzhuàn:
"After Tàizǔ's demise,
Jiàn proclaimed himself emperor in Chéngdū,
with the era name Wǔchéng."
Xuē Shǐ and Táng Yú Lù:
"In the ninth month of Tiānyòu fifth year,
Jiàn proclaimed himself emperor in Chéngdū,
with the era name Wǔchéng."
Jiǔguó Zhì:
"In the seventh month of this year, he ascended the imperial throne,
and the following year changed the era name."
Sòng Xiáng Jìnián Tōngpǔ:
"In the autumn of Tiānyòu fourth year, he proclaimed himself emperor,
and the next year changed the era name."
Ōuyáng Shǐ and Shíguó Jìnián:
"In the ninth month of Tiānfù seventh year, he ascended the throne,
and the following year changed the era name."
We follow this last account.
On the xīn-chǒu day,
the former Dōngchuān Jiédu Shǐ and concurrently Shìzhōng Wáng Zōngjí was appointed Zhōngshū Lìng,
Wéi Zhuāng was appointed Zuǒ Sànqí Chángshì and Pàn Zhōngshū Ménxià Shì,
and Lángzhōu Fángyù Shǐ Táng Dàoxí was appointed Nèi Shūmì Shǐ.
Zhuāng was
the grandson of Jiàn Sù.
Wéi Jiàn Sù was a chancellor at the end of Tiānbǎo.
Although the Shǔ Lord was illiterate,
he enjoyed discussing with scholars,
and had a rough understanding of their principles.
At that time, many Táng noble families had fled to Shǔ to escape chaos.
The Shǔ Lord treated them with respect and employed them,
having them restore former institutions.
Thus, his institutions and culture retained the legacy of Táng.
Historians say that the Shǔ Lord rose from the ranks of soldiers but was able to personally employ Confucian scholars.
The Shǔ Lord's eldest son, Jiàoshūláng Zōngrén, was disabled by illness when young.
His second son, Mìshū Shàojiān Zōngyì, was made Suì Wáng.
43 In winter,
in the tenth month,
Gāo Jìchāng dispatched his general Ní Kěfú to join Chǔ general Qín Yànhuī in attacking Lángzhōu.
Léi Yàngōng sent an envoy to request surrender to Huáinán,
and also sent an urgent appeal for help.
Hóngnóng Wáng sent general Líng Yè with a naval force to encamp at Píngjiāng,
and Lǐ Ráo with infantry and cavalry to encamp at Liúyáng to rescue him.
Chǔ Wáng Yīn sent Yuèzhōu Cìshǐ Xǔ Déxūn with troops to resist them.
Líng Yè advanced and encamped at Lángkǒu.
The Lángshǔi flows southwest from Chén and Jǐn Prefectures into Lángzhōu territory,
passes through the prefectural city and enters the Dàjiāng,
which is called Lángkǒu.
(Déxūn's men) covered their heads with branches and leaves,
carried long sabers, and floated down the river.
They attacked the camp at night,
and also set fires,
causing panic among Yè's troops.
Déxūn advanced with his main army and attacked them,
completely routing them.
He pursued them to Lùjiǎ Zhèn,
captured Yè;
he also broke through the Liúyáng stockade,
captured Lǐ Ráo;
and returned after plundering Shànggāo and Tángnián.
In Tiānbǎo second year of Táng, a mountain cave was opened,
and Tángnián County was established,
subordinate to Èzhōu.
44 In the eleventh month,
on the jiǎ-shēn day,
Jiāmǎ Zhǐhuīshǐ Yǐn Hào attacked and captured the Jiāngzhě Lǐng stockade in Jìnjiāng.
Liáng's Xīdū had a Jiāmǎ camp.
Jiāngzhě Lǐng is west of Chángzǐ County, Lùzhōu,
and leads to Diāokē Lǐng via the northern route.
45 Yìchāng Jiédu Shǐ Liú Shǒuwén heard that his younger brother Shǒuguāng had imprisoned their father,
gathered his generals and officials, and wept loudly, saying:
"I never imagined our family would produce such an evil creature!
It is better for me to die than to live. I swear to you gentlemen that I will subjugate him!"
He then raised troops to attack Shǒuguāng,
with alternating victories and defeats.

The Emperor then ordered all soldiers to tattoo their faces to mark their military unit.

Guān refers to a strategic pass that must be traversed;

15 After Wáng Zōngjí [王宗jí], Grand Preceptor of Shǔ [蜀], was dismissed from his post as chancellor,

He submitted a memorial, stating:
“Your servant holds the rank of a great minister,

In matters of the state,
our joys and sorrows are shared.
Now, the heir apparent is not yet established,

If Your Majesty deems Zōngyì [宗懿] capable of succession,
an early ceremony of investiture should be held,
and your servant appointed as Grand Marshal,
to command all six armies.
However, if the times are difficult,

Your servant requests to establish a Grand Marshal's office,
cast seals for the six armies,
and personally oversee all levies and deployments for expeditions.
Your servant will carry out all these matters independently.

The Shǔ [蜀] ruler was enraged,
