and Zhāng Cè [張策], Hànlín Xuéshì Chéngzhǐ [翰林學士承旨], was appointed Xíngbù Shìláng [刑部侍郎],
both as Tóng Píngzhāngshì [同平章事].
Yú Jīng [兢] was the elder brother's son of
Yú Cóng [于琮].
Yú Cóng [于琮] is mentioned in the annals of Táng Xuān Jì [唐宣紀] and Xī Jì [僖紀].
18 Jiázhài [夾寨] reported that the Jìn [晉] troops in Yúwú [余吾] had withdrawn.
The emperor believed that since reinforcements could not come again,
Lùzhōu [潞州] was certainly conquerable.
On the day of Bǐngwǔ [丙午],
he returned south from Zézhōu [澤州].
On the day of Rénzǐ [壬子],
he arrived at Dàliáng [大梁].
The Liáng [梁] troops in Jiázhài [夾寨] also no longer maintained their defenses.
Troops must not be without preparations.
With preparations, there is no disaster.
Now, with the Liáng [梁] army,
the ruler is arrogant above,
and the generals are lazy below.
Their defeat is thus deserved.
“Shàngdǎng [上黨] is the barrier of Hédōng [河東].
Without Shàngdǎng [上黨],
there is no Hédōng [河東].
Lùzhōu [潞州]
is Shàngdǎng [上黨] Commandery.
When they heard I was newly enthroned,
they thought a young boy was not skilled in military affairs.
Xián [閑] means 'skilled.'
If we select elite troops and rush there at double speed,
taking them by surprise,
we will surely defeat them.
To assert prestige and establish hegemony,
as stated by Jìn Xiānzhěn [晉先軫] in the Zuǒzhuàn [左傳],
this opportunity must not be missed!”
Zhāng Chéngyè [張承業] also advised him to proceed.
Then he sent Zhāng Chéngyè [承業] and the judicial official Wáng Jiān [王緘] to request troops from Fèngxiáng [鳳翔].
Qí Wáng Lǐ Màozhēn [岐王李茂貞] was based in Fèngxiáng [鳳翔].
Qí Wáng [岐王] was old and infirm,
his army weak and treasury exhausted,
so he could not respond.
Jìn Wáng [晉王] held a grand review of his soldiers,
and appointed Dīng Huì [丁會], former Military Governor of Zhāoyì [昭義], as Commander-in-Chief.
Dīng Huì [丁會] surrendered Lùzhōu [潞州] to Jìn [晉],
as seen in volume 264, Tiānyòu [天祐] 3rd year of Táng Zhāoxuān Dì [唐昭宣帝].
On the day of Jiǎzǐ [甲子],
he led Zhōu Déwēi [周德威] and others to depart from Jìnyáng [晉陽].
19 Huáinán [淮南] sent troops to raid Shíshǒu [石首].
In the fourth year of Wǔdé [武德] of Táng [唐], Shíshǒu [石首] County was established by dividing Huáróng [華容] County,
named after Shíshǒu [石首] Mountain north of the county,
and belonged to Jiānglíng [江陵] Prefecture.
The Jiǔyù Zhì [九域志] places it two hundred *lǐ* southeast of the prefecture.
Sūn Jiàn [孫鑑] said: “From Ānlù [安陸] to Jìnglíng [竟陵],
both post stations are on flat ground.
To the south, reaching the Great River,
there are no hills or obstacles.
Crossing the river to Shíshǒu [石首],
shallow hills first appear.
It is called Jìnglíng [竟陵] because the hills end here.
It is called Shíshǒu [石首] because the rocks begin here.”
They also sent their general Lǐ Hòu [李厚] with fifteen thousand marines to advance towards Jīngnán [荊南].
Gāo Jìchāng [高季昌] met them in battle
and defeated them at Mǎtóu [馬頭].
Jīngnán [荊南] was administered from Jiānglíng [江陵],
on the north bank of the river.
The south bank was called Mǎtóu’àn [馬頭岸],
directly opposite Shāshì [沙市].
20 On the day of Jǐsì [己巳],
the Jìn Wáng’s [晉王] army encamped at Huángniǎn [黃碾],
forty-five *lǐ* from Shàngdǎng [上黨].
Huángniǎn [黃碾] Village is in Lùchéng [潞城] County of Lùzhōu [潞州].
Niǎn [碾] is pronounced Niǔ Shàn fān [紐善翻].
On the first day, Xīnwèi [辛未],
the Jìn Wáng [晉王] ambushed his troops below Sānchuígāng [三垂岡].
Sānchuígāng [三垂岡] is southeast of Túnliú [屯留] County.
He advanced directly to Jiázhài [夾寨].
The Liáng [梁] army had no scouts,
and did not expect the arrival of the Jìn [晉] troops.
The generals and soldiers had not yet risen,
and the camp was thrown into chaos.
Jìn Wáng [晉王] ordered Zhōu Déwēi [周德威] and Lǐ Sìyuán [李嗣源] to divide their forces into two routes.
Zhōu Déwēi [德威] attacked the northwest corner,
and Lǐ Sìyuán [嗣源] attacked the northeast corner,
filling the moats, burning the camps,
and charging in with drums and shouts.
The Liáng [梁] army was utterly routed,
fleeing south.
Fú Dàozhāo [符道昭], the Commander-in-Chief, fell from his horse
and was killed by the Jìn [晉] soldiers.
Their losses of generals, officers, and soldiers numbered in the tens of thousands,
and abandoned provisions, supplies, and weapons piled up like mountains.
Zhōu Déwēi and others arrived below the city walls
and called out to Lǐ Sìzhāo, saying:
"The late king has passed away.
The current king has come in person
and broken the enemy's flanking encampments.
The enemy has already left.
You can open the gates!"
Sìzhāo did not believe them
and said:
"This must be a trick by the enemy,
sent to deceive me."
He intended to shoot them.
His attendants stopped him.
Sìzhāo said:
"If the king has indeed come,
can I see him?"
The king himself went forward and called out to him.
Sìzhāo saw the king in white mourning clothes
and wept so bitterly that he nearly fainted,
his breath almost failing him.
幾 (jǐ)
is pronounced "jū yī."
Thereupon, he opened the gates.
Initially,
Déwēi and Sìzhāo had a feud.
Jìn Wáng Kèyòng, on his deathbed, said to Jìn Wáng Cúnyù:
"Jìntōng is loyal and filial;
I love him deeply.
If he doesn't emerge from the heavy siege now,
could it be that Déwēi has not forgotten their old grievances?
You must convey this intention of mine to him.
If the Lùzhōu siege is not lifted,
I will not rest in peace even in death."
Jìntōng
was Sìzhāo's nickname.
Jìn Wáng Cúnyù told this to Déwēi,
who was moved to tears.
From then on, he fought with great vigor at the flanking encampments.
Once he met Sìzhāo,
they became as close as before.
Kāng Huáizhēn fled back from Tiānjǐng Guān with over a hundred cavalrymen.
The Emperor heard that the flanking encampments could not be held
and was greatly alarmed.
After a while, he sighed, saying:
"If one is to have a son, he should be like Lǐ Yàzǐ!
Kèyòng will not perish!
As for my sons,
they are merely pigs and dogs!"
An imperial edict ordered all localities to rally and settle the scattered soldiers.
Zhōu Déwēi and Lǐ Cúnzhāng, capitalizing on their victory, pressed on to Zézhōu.
The Prefect Wáng Bān had long lost popular support,
and the populace would not serve him.
Lónghǔ Tǒngjūn Niú Cúnjié led troops from Xīdū to reinforce the routed soldiers of the flanking encampments.
The Lónghǔ Jūn was the same as the Táng Lóngwǔ Jūn.
When Liáng received the abdication from Táng,
they changed
"wǔ"
to
"hǔ."
Wáng Pǔ's Wǔdài Huìyào says: In the first year of Kāipíng,
in the fourth month,
the Left and Right Zhǎngzhí were changed to the Left and Right Lónghǔ Jūn.
Also, Liáng designated Luòyáng as Xīdū.
Cúnjié said to his troops:
"Zézhōu is a strategic location
and must not be lost.
Even without an imperial edict,
we must rescue it."
The troops were all unwilling,
saying:
"The Jìn forces' morale is sharp,
and we are outnumbered."
Cúnjié said:
"To see danger and not rescue is not righteous.
To fear a strong enemy and avoid them is not courageous."
Thereupon, he took up his riding whip and led his troops forward.
策 (cè)
refers to a horsewhip.
The people inside the city had already set fires and were making a clamor,
intending to respond to Jìn Wáng.
Bān closed the inner city and defended himself.
When Cúnjié arrived,
order was restored.
The Kǎoyì says: Ōuyáng Shǐ states:
"Cúnjié followed Kāng Huáiqīng in attacking Lùzhōu and served as the commander of the field formations.
The Jìn troops had already broken the flanking city.
Cúnjié returned with his remaining troops.
When he reached Tiānjǐng Guān,
he heard that the Jìn troops were attacking Zézhōu and went to rescue it."
The Liáng Lièzhuàn says:
"When Zézhōu was on the verge of falling,
Hé'nán Yǐn Zhāng Zōngshì summoned Lónghǔ Tǒngjūn Niú Cúnjié to discuss.
Cúnjié led his own army, as well as the Right Shénwǔ and Yǔlín armies, to reinforce the returning army from Shàngdǎng.
When he reached Tiānjǐng Guān,
he immediately led his troops forward to rescue Zézhōu."
Xuē Shǐ also agrees.
We note that if Cúnjié had fled from the flanking city,
he would have passed Zézhōu first,
and then reached Tiānjǐng Guān.
How could he have already passed it and then returned to rescue it?
Therefore, we follow the Liáng Lièzhuàn and Xuē Shǐ.
The enemy dug tunnels around the city walls to attack it.
Cúnjié resisted day and night,
for a total of thirteen days.
Liú Zhījùn led troops from Jìnzhōu to rescue it.
Previously, Liú Zhījùn had been ordered to rest his troops in Jìnzhōu.
The Jiǔyù Zhì says: Jìnzhōu is 310 lǐ southeast of Zézhōu.
They retreated to secure Gāopíng.
Gāopíng
was the territory of Xiǎnshì County during the Hàn dynasty.
Later, the Northern Wèi established Gāopíng County.
During the Táng dynasty, it belonged to Zézhōu.
The Jiǔyù Zhì says: It is 83 lǐ northeast of the prefecture.
The Kǎoyì says: Zhuāngzōng Lièzhuàn and Zhū Wēn Zhuàn state:
"Lǐ Cúnzhāng attacked Zézhōu,
and Prefect Wáng Bān abandoned the city and left.
Zé and Lù were both pacified."
We do not adopt this account.
Jìn Wáng returned to Jìnyáng,
rested his troops, and distributed rewards.
He appointed Zhōu Déwēi as Zhènwǔ Jiédùshǐ and Tóng Píngzhāngshì.
He ordered the prefectures and counties to recommend talented individuals,
dismiss corrupt and cruel officials,
lighten taxes and levies,
care for orphans and the poor,
redress grievances and abuses,
and prohibit treachery and theft.
The region was greatly reformed.
Because Hédōng was geographically small and had few soldiers,
he trained his soldiers and prohibited cavalry from mounting their horses unless they saw the enemy.
Once formations were set,
no one was allowed to overstep their boundaries,
or to leave a gap to avoid danger.
They were to advance by separate routes simultaneously,
and their meeting times were not allowed to deviate by a single moment.
Those who were late were to be beheaded;
this was military law.
晷 (guǐ)
is pronounced "jū wěi" and refers to a sundial.
If the appointed time was noon,
and the sundial indicated past noon without arrival, that constituted a deviation.
Others can be inferred similarly.
Day and night were divided into one hundred *kè*.
Therefore, he was able to conquer Shāndōng
and take Hénán,
due to the精整 (jīngzhěng) discipline of his soldiers.
Initially,
when Jìn Wáng Kèyòng pacified Wáng Xíngyú (see Volume 260, Táng Zhāozōng Qiánníng, second year),
regional governors often issued their own decrees.
The King was ashamed to be like them,
and always reported to the court when appointing officials.
By this time,
Jìn Wáng Cúnyù began to appoint officials on his own authority.
Jìn Wáng esteemed Zhāng Chéngyè,
valuing his role in resolving the crisis involving Lǐ Kèníng.
Whenever he visited Zhāng Chéngyè's residence,
he would ascend the hall and bow to his mother,
bestowing very generous gifts.
The siege of Lùzhōu had lasted for years,
and more than half of the soldiers and common people had died from freezing and starvation,
leaving the markets and streets desolate.
Lǐ Sìzhāo encouraged farming and sericulture,
lightened taxes, and relaxed punishments.
Within a few years,
the military city was fully restored.
Shǐ Jiù speaks of Lǐ Sìzhāo's achievements in governing Lùzhōu.
The Jìngjiāng Jiédùshǐ and Tóng Píngzhāngshì Lǐ Qióng died.
Lǐ Qióng captured Jìngjiāng (see Volume 262, Táng Zhāozōng Guānghuà, third year).
On the day Rénshēn,
Xǔzhōu Zhōngwǔ Jūn was renamed Kuāngguó Jūn;
Tóngzhōu Kuāngguó Jūn was renamed Zhōngwǔ Jūn;
and Shǎnzhōu Bǎoyì Jūn was renamed Zhènguó Jūn.
On the day Yǐhài,
the Chǔ army raided Èzhōu.
Qín Péi, the prefect appointed by Huáinán,
attacked and defeated them.
In 24, Zhāng Hào (張顥), the commander of the Left Fang Guard of Huáinán (淮南), and Xú Wēn (徐溫), the commander of the Right Fang Guard, monopolized military and political power.
The heart of the King of Hóngnóng (弘農), Wēi (威), was not at peace.
Yáng Wò (楊渥) was posthumously named King Wēi.
The two felt uneasy,
and together conspired to assassinate the King,
dividing his territory to submit to Liáng (梁).
On the day of Wùyín (戊寅),
Hào sent his associates Jǐ Xiáng (紀祥) and others to assassinate the King in his bedchamber.
Kǎoyì (考異) states: Wúlù (吳錄):
"Hào sent Jǐ Xiáng, Chén Huī (陳暉), Lí Fán (黎璠), Sūn Yīn (孫殷), and others to seize Wò in his bedchamber,
and assassinated him."
It does not mention Xú Wēn,
probably because Xú Xuàn (徐鉉) concealed it for Wēn.
Xuē Shǐ (薛史) followed this, but Jiāngnán Biélù (江南別錄) mentions using only the Left Fang Guard's troops.
Ōuyáng Shǐ (歐陽史) says:
"Wēn and Hào together sent assassins to kill Wò,
agreeing to divide his territory to submit to Liáng."
According to this, Wēn and Hào jointly commanded the Fang Guards,
if Wēn was not involved in the conspiracy,
Hào would certainly not dare to assassinate Wò alone.
We now follow Jiāngnán Biélù.
Shíguó Jìnián (十國紀年) states:
"Zhāng Hào wished to declare himself acting Military Governor (liúhòu, 留後) of Huáinán,
and sent his submission to Liáng,
exchanging Huáinán for control of Càizhōu (蔡州)."
Xú Wēn said: "Yángzhōu (揚州) to Biànzhōu (汴州) is only three thousand lǐ (里) round trip.
The military government will surely fall into chaos if it is without a master for more than a month.
It is better to establish someone,
and then make plans."
According to this, if Hào declared himself acting Military Governor,
there would already be a master.
We do not adopt this.
He was twenty-three years old.
On the day of Jǐmǎo (己卯),
Hào gathered the generals and officials in the government courtyard.
Along the paths, in the courtyard, and in the main hall, white blades were arrayed,
ordering all generals to dismiss their retinues before entering.
Qù (去), pronounced Qiāng Lǚ Fān (羌呂翻).
(Phonetic gloss for 去).
Cóng (從), pronounced Cái Yòng Fān (才用翻).
(Phonetic gloss for 從).
"The heir apparent has passed away,
who should be the master of the military government?"
He asked three times, but no one responded, and Hào's expression grew increasingly angry.
The staff officer Yán Kěqiú (嚴可求) stepped forward and secretly advised:
"The military government is vast,
and its four borders are fraught with danger.
It is impossible for it not to have a master;
however, today it may be too hasty."
Hào said:
"What do you mean by 'hasty'?"
Kěqiú said:
"Liú Wēi (劉威), Táo Yǎ (陶雅), Lǐ Yù (李遇), Lǐ Jiǎn (李簡)—
Liú Wēi is in Lúzhōu (廬州),
Táo Yǎ is in Shèzhōu (歙州),
Lǐ Yù is in Xuānzhōu (宣州),
Lǐ Jiǎn is in Chángzhōu (常州).
If you establish yourself now,
will these people be willing to submit to you?
It would be better to establish a young master and assist him.
Which of the generals would dare not to follow!"
Hào was silent for a long time.
Kěqiú then dismissed his attendants,
quickly wrote a letter and put it in his sleeve,
then waved to his colleagues to go to the commissioner's residence (shǐzhái, 使宅) to offer congratulations.
The residence of the Military Governor (jiédùshǐ, 節度使) is called the commissioner's residence.
The congratulators wished to congratulate the new ruler.
Shǐ (使), pronounced Shū Lì Fān (疏吏翻).
(Phonetic gloss for 使).
Upon arrival,
Kěqiú knelt and read it.
It was the instruction of the Grand Madam Shǐ (史).
According to Lù Zhèn's (路振) Jiǔguó Zhì (九國志),
Wò's mother, Lady Shǐ, was enfeoffed as Wǔchāng Jùnjūn (武昌郡君).
She was probably honored as Grand Madam after Wò succeeded to the throne.
"The former King's (xiānwáng, 先王) undertaking was difficult.
This section,
whenever it mentions 'former King,' refers to Yáng Xíngmì (楊行密).
Lóngyǎn (隆演) should succeed to the throne next.
The generals should not fail the Yáng (楊) clan,
and should guide him well."
The wording was clear and firm.
Hào's expression showed dejection.
Because of its righteous message,
he dared not oppose it.

So, he enthroned Wēi Wang's younger brother, Lóngyǎn, proclaiming him acting Military Governor of Huáinán and Supreme Commander of all armies on the Eastern Front (Dōngmiàn Zhū Dào Xíngyíng Dūtǒng, 東面諸道行營都統).
Yáng Lóngyǎn, courtesy name Hóngyuán (鴻源), was Yáng Xíngmì's second son.
Xuē Shǐ and Lù Zhèn's Jiǔguó Zhì both render
"Lóngyǎn"
as
"Wèi" (渭).
The Deputy Supreme Commander (fù dūtǒng, 副都統), Zhū Jǐn (朱瑾), went to Kěqiú's residence
and said:
"I, Jǐn, at sixteen or seventeen, was already wielding a spear and leaping on a horse,
charging formidable enemies,
never intimidated.
Today, facing Hào, I involuntarily sweated.
You rebuked him to his face as if no one else was present;
I now realize my courage is but that of a common man,
far inferior to yours."
He then treated him as an elder brother.
Hào appointed Xú Wēn as the Surveillance Commissioner of Zhèxī (浙西),
garrisoned at Rùnzhōu (潤州).
Yán Kěqiú persuaded Wēn, saying:
"If you abandon the Fang Guards and go to an outer command,
Hào will surely lay the blame for the regicide on you."
Wēn was startled and said:
"If so, what should I do?"
Kěqiú said:
"Hào is stubborn and ignorant in affairs.
If you can listen to me,
I will plan for you."
At that time, the Deputy Envoy (fùshǐ, 副使) Lǐ Chéngsì (李承嗣)—
Lǐ Chéngsì was then the Deputy Envoy of the Huáinán Expeditionary Army.
Kěqiú also persuaded Chéngsì, saying:
"Hào's fierce power is such,
now sending Xú outside cannot be without reason,
and I fear it is not to your advantage either."
Chéngsì deeply agreed.
Kěqiú went to see Hào and said:
"When you send General Xú (Xú Gōng, 徐公) outside,
everyone says you want to seize his military power and kill him.
Such widespread talk is also to be feared."
Hào said:
"The Right Fang Guard wanted it"—
"The Right Fang Guard" refers to Xú Wēn by his official title.
"It has already been carried out."
"It has become a deed."
Kěqiú said:
"Stopping it is easy."
The next day,
Kěqiú invited Hào and Chéngsì to visit Wēn together.
Kěqiú glared at Wēn and reprimanded him, saying:
"The ancients did not forget the kindness of a single meal,
let alone you, an old general of the Yáng clan!
Now that the young heir is newly enthroned,
at a time of many affairs,
can you seek personal safety outside?
Is that acceptable?"
Wēn apologized, saying:
"If you gentlemen tolerate me,
how dare I act on my own initiative!"
Thus, he did not depart.
Hào knew that Kěqiú secretly sided with Wēn.
That night,
he sent assassins to stab him.
Kěqiú knew he could not escape,
and asked to write a farewell letter to the Prefect (fǔzhǔ, 府主).
Fǔzhǔ refers to Lóngyǎn.
Kěqiú took up his brush without fear.
The assassins, who could recognize characters,
saw that his words were loyal and resolute,
and said:
"You are a virtuous man,
we cannot bear to kill you."
They plundered his property to report back,
saying:
"We pursued him but did not catch him."
Hào angrily said:
"I wanted Kěqiú's head,
what use is property!"
Xú Wēn and Yán Kěqiú plotted to execute Zhāng Hào.
Yán Kěqiú said:
“It cannot be done without Zhōng Tàizhāng.”
As for Zhōng Tàizhāng,
he was a native of Héféi,
and at that time held the title of General of the Left Gate Guard.
A critical comparison notes: The Wú Jì records it as
“Zhōng Zhāng.”
The Shí Guó Jìnián records it as
“Zhōng Tàizhāng,”
and we follow this version.
Zhái Qián informed him.
When Zhōng Tàizhāng heard this, he was pleased,
and secretly gathered thirty strong men.
At night,
they pricked their blood and drank it as an oath.
On the morning of Dīnghài,
they went straight in and decapitated Zhāng Hào in the Yátáng.
The Yátáng
was the place where the Left and Right Yá Commanders managed affairs.
Xú Wēn then publicly denounced Zhāng Hào's crime of regicide,
and had Jǐ Xiáng and others dismembered in the marketplace.
He went to the Western Palace to inform the Grand Lady.
The Western Palace in Guǎnglíng
was where Yáng Xíngmì's Shǐ Fūrén resided.
She wept bitterly and said:
“My son is young and immature,
and such misfortune has befallen us.
I wish to protect my entire family and return to Lúzhōu.
That would be your kindness, Sire!”
Xú Wēn said:
“Zhāng Hào committed regicide and rebellion;
he could not but be executed.
Madam, you should make yourself comfortable!”
Earlier,
when Xú Wēn and Zhāng Hào plotted to assassinate King Wēi,
Xú Wēn said:
“If we involve both the Left and Right Yá soldiers,
their hearts will certainly not be united.
It would be better to use only our own soldiers.”
Zhāng Hào disagreed,
so Xú Wēn said:
“Then let's use only your soldiers.”
Zhāng Hào followed this.
At this point,
when the rebellious faction was thoroughly investigated,
they were all Left Yá soldiers.
Because of this, people believed that Xú Wēn genuinely had no knowledge of the plot.
Considering the circumstances and assigning guilt,
Xú Wēn should have been in the same category as Zhāng Hào;
yet Xú Wēn was spared the charge of regicide,
and subsequently monopolized the government of the State of Wú.
Perhaps Heaven blessed him.
治 (zhì),
pronounced 'zhí'.
All matters of the military government were decided by him.
He appointed Yán Kěqiú as the Sīmǎ of Yángzhōu.
Xú Wēn was resolute and decisive by nature.
He lived a simple and frugal life.
Although he was illiterate,
he had others read judicial and litigation documents to him and made his decisions,
all of which were reasonable and appropriate.
Before this,
when Zhāng Hào was in power,
punishments were cruel and excessive,
and he allowed his personal guards to plunder the markets and towns.
Xú Wēn said to Yán Kěqiú:
“The great matter has been settled.
We, along with gentlemen like yourself, should strive to implement good governance,
so that people can sleep peacefully with their clothes off.”
He then established laws and regulations,
prohibited violence and oppression,
and upheld the major principles.
The military and common people found peace in this.
An ancient person once said:
“Even a thief has his principles.”
However, one who steals goods is a petty thief,
while one who steals a state is a great thief.
Observing Xú Wēn's theft of the state,
how could this saying deceive me!
He entrusted financial matters to the Zhījìguān, Luò Zhīxiáng.
The Zhījìguān
was similar to the Dùzhīláng of Tiāntái.

The barbarians observed the national situation before deciding to come and go.

環 (huán),
pronounced 'huàn'.

Léi Yànhuī beat drums, shouted, broke through the gate, and entered.

occupied Lǎngzhōu in the first year of Zhōnghé of Emperor Xīzōng of Táng,

A critical comparison notes: The Liáng Tàizǔ Shílù states:

a victory was reported from the Lǎngzhōu front.
Yàngōng drowned in the river.”
We now follow the Annal.
He was sent to Dàliáng.

Before this,
Xiàng Huái, Cìshǐ of Lǐzhōu, was in league with Yàngōng.

雍 (yōng),
pronounced 'yōng'.
In the sixth month,
on Rènyín,
Liú Zhījùn was appointed Xīlù Xíngyíng Dūzhāotǎoshǐ to resist them.
29Wáng Shīfàn, the Jīnwú Shàngjiāngjūn, resided in Luòyáng.
Zhū Yǒuníng's wife tearfully complained to the Emperor, saying:
“Your Majesty has transformed your family into the state,
and all your clan members have received honor and favor.
My husband alone was unfortunate;
because of Wáng Shīfàn's rebellion,
he died on the battlefield.
(Zhū Yǒuníng's death is mentioned in Volume 264, Tiānfù 3rd year of Táng Zhāozōng.)
I truly grieve for him!”
The Emperor said:
“I almost forgot about this traitor!”
On Jǐyǒu,
he sent an envoy to Luòyáng to exterminate his clan.
The envoy first dug a pit beside the residence,

Wáng Shīfàn grandly arranged a banquet,
and sat in a row with his clan members.
He said to the envoy:
“Death is something no one can escape,
let alone those who are guilty!
I do not wish for the piled bodies to be out of order by age.”
After the wine was served,
he ordered them, from youngest to oldest,
to be led into the pit and executed.
A total of two hundred people died.

33Gāo Yù, the Pànguān of Húnán, requested permission for the people to collect tea themselves and sell it to northern merchants,

In autumn,
in the seventh month,
Mǎ Yīn memorialized to establish Huítóuwù in Biàn, Jīng, Xiāng, Táng, Yǐng, and Fù prefectures.

were similar to today's trading markets.)
They would sell tea to trade for silk floss and warhorses, and then return.

The edict granted permission.
Húnán thus became prosperous and abundant.

the generals and officials of Huáinán requested Lǐ Yǎn,
to (acting on imperial authority) confer on Yáng Lóngyǎn the titles of Huáinán Jiédùshǐ, Dōngmiàn Zhūdào Xíngyíng Dūttǒng, Tóng Píngzhāngshì, and Prince of Hóngnóng.
(Lǐ Yǎn's acting on imperial authority began in Volume 263, Tiānfù 2nd year of Táng Zhāozōng.)
Zhōng Tàizhāng's reward was meager.
(This was the reward for killing Zhāng Hào.)
More than a year later,
he, while drunk, argued with other generals and brought this up.
Someone informed Xú Wēn,
stating that Zhōng Tàizhāng harbored resentment,
and requested his execution.
Xú Wēn said:
“This is my fault.”
He promoted him to Cìshǐ of Chúzhōu.

Jǐngrén is Màozhāng;

what power do monks have!"
The history says that Zhài Zàiyòng was good at nurturing soldiers and was not misled by heterodox doctrines.

The empress

Map of Jīn people's territory: Xīzhōu Shílóu County has Shàngpíng Pass.

is the mouth of the Hàn River entering the Jiāng,

Shātóu is now Shātóu Market, south of Jiānglíng city.

was originally Suíhuà County, Shǐ'ān Commandery during the Suí.

Gōngzhōu
was originally the territory of Měnglíng County during the Hàn.

In the fifth year of Xīníng, Méngzhōu was abolished,

Then, nurturing soldiers and resting the people,

Tāo took them all,

Only Qiánlíng

Yōng,

Yīzhèng,

1 In spring,

the fourth month,

13 The Huáinán army besieged Sūzhōu,

Sūn Yǎn of Línhǎi, a general of Wúyuè, placed wheels on the ends of poles,
and let down ropes with pointed tools to dismantle them (the siege engines).
The attackers were fully exposed.
When trebuchets arrived, nets were deployed to repel them,
and the Huáinán people could not capture the city.
Wúyuè Wáng Qián Liú sent his staff commander Qián Biāo,
and Xíngjūn Fùshǐ Dù Jiànhuī and others to lead troops to relieve it.
Sūzhōu had a waterway connecting to the city.
The Huáinán forces set up nets with bells suspended in the water,
knowing if fish or turtles passed by.
Sīmǎ Fú, Yóuyì Dūyúhòu of Wúyuè, wanted to secretly enter the city,
so he used a pole to touch the net.
The enemy heard the bells and raised the net,
allowing Fú to pass through.
He stayed in the water for three days
before he was able to enter the city.
Because of this, the city's commands corresponded with those of the relief army,
and the enemy considered it divine.
Wúyuè Wáng Qián Liú once visited his governmental garden
and observed a gardener, Lù Rénzhāng, who was skillful in horticulture, and took note of him.
"Zhì" (志) means
to remember in one's heart.
"Bèi" (被)
is pronounced as "pí yì".
He (Sīmǎ Fú) indeed delivered the message and returned.
Qián Liú treated him (Lù Rénzhāng) like his own grandson,
and he was successively promoted to Lǐangfǔ Jūliáng Dūjiāshǐ.
"Lǐangfǔ" (兩府) refers to the two *jiédù* administrations of Zhènhǎi and Zhèndōng.
Rénzhāng
was a native of Mùzhōu.
On a Xīnhài day,
the Wúyuè forces attacked the Huáinán forces from both inside and outside,

capturing their general Hé Lǎng and over thirty others,

Zhōu Běn fled by night,
and was again pursued and defeated at Huángtiāndàng.
This Huángtiāndàng is not the Huángtiāndàng in the Great River of Zhēnjzhōu.
According to the memorial of Jiá Dǎn, a native of Kūnshān County, Píngjiāng Prefecture, in the third year of Xīníng of the Sòng dynasty, concerning water conservancy,
there are Chángdàng and Huángtiāndàng in the area of Chángzhōu County;
this is that one.
The character "bài" (敗)
is pronounced as "bǔ mài".
Many banners were planted among the wild rice and water caltrops.
"Gū" (菰)
is the same as "jiǎng" (蔣).
"Zhì" (幟)
is pronounced as "chāng zhì".
14 Lǐ Yànbó, Bǎodà Jiédùshǐ appointed by the King of Qí,
(Kǎoyì states: The Yílù and Wǔdàishǐ record
"Yànróng".
We now follow Liú Shù's Guǎngběn.)
and Yán Hóngyǐ, Dūjiāng of Fūzhōu, surrendered with their city.
On a Jǐwèi day,
Gāo Wànxīng was made Bǎosài Jiédùshǐ,

Liáng thus took the two garrisons of Fūfāng and Dānyán.
15 Huáinán first established official examinations,
with Luò Zhīxiáng in charge of them.
Since the period of chaos,
the system of official examinations had been abandoned,
so Yáng Shì's ability to re-establish it is recorded.
16 In the fifth month,
on the dìngmǎo day,
the Emperor ordered Liú Zhījùn (劉知俊) to take Bīnzhōu (邠州) while riding on his victory;
Zhījùn (知俊) found it difficult.
Lǐ Jìhuī (李繼徽) occupied Bīnzhōu (邠州),
and had support from Fèngxiáng (鳳翔).
Therefore, Liú Zhījùn (劉知俊) considered it difficult to take.
So, he was recalled.
17 Wáng Chóngshī (王重師), Jìnguó (佑國) Jìedùshǐ, had garrisoned Cháng'ān (長安) for several years.
When the Emperor was in Hézhōng (河中),
he was angered that Chóngshī's (重師) tributes were not timely.
On the jǐsì day,
Chóngshī (重師) was summoned to court.
Liú Hàn (劉捍), Zuǒ Lónghǔ Tǒngjūn, was made Jìnguó Liúhòu.
18 On the guǐyǒu day,
the Emperor departed Hézhōng (河中);
on the jǐmǎo day,
he arrived at Luòyáng (洛陽).
When Liú Hàn (劉捍) arrived in Cháng'ān (長安),
Wáng Chóngshī (王重師) showed him no courtesy.
Hàn (捍) slandered him to the Emperor,
saying that Chóngshī (重師) was secretly communicating with Bīn (邠) and Qí (岐).
On the jiǎshēn day,
Chóngshī (重師) was demoted to Xīzhōu (溪州) Cìshǐ.
Soon after, he was granted death by suicide,
and his clan was exterminated.
This laid the groundwork for Liú Zhījùn (劉知俊) to kill Liú Hàn (劉捍) and rebel.
19 Liú Shǒuwén (劉守文) attacked Liú Shǒuguāng (劉守光) repeatedly for years without success.
Liú Shǒuwén (劉守文) had been attacking Shǒuguāng (守光) since the first year;
this matter was first mentioned in the previous volume.
He used heavy bribes to attract the multitudes of the Qìdān (契丹) and Tǔyùhún (吐谷渾),
gathering forty thousand to garrison Jìzhōu (薊州).
Shǒuguāng (守光) met them in battle at Jīsū (雞蘇).
According to Xuē Shǐliáng Jì,
in this year Liú Shǒuguāng (劉守光) reported
that he battled his brother Shǒuwén (守文) west of Jìzhōu (薊州),
and captured Shǒuwén (守文) alive.
This is probably Jīsū (雞蘇).
Shǒuwén (守文), on a single horse, stood before the battle formation,
and tearfully said to his troops:
"Do not kill my brother!"
Yuán Xíngqīn (元行欽), a general of Shǒuguāng (守光), recognized him,
went straight forward and captured him.
Liú Shǒuguāng (劉守光) imprisoning his father's son is
a villain of the world.
Liú Shǒuwén (劉守文) had publicly announced his crimes and set out to punish him,
meaning execution without pardon.
A small lack of patience ruined a great matter;
becoming a captive
was his own doing.
Shǒuguāng (守光) imprisoned him in a separate room,
fenced with thorny bushes,
and rode his victory to advance and attack Cāngzhōu (滄州).
Lǚ Yǎn (呂兗) and Sūn Hè (孫鶴), Jìedù Pànguān of Cāngzhōu (滄州), nominated Shǒuwén's (守文) son Yánzuò (延祚) as commander,
and defended the city.
Yǎn (兗)
was from Āncì (安次).
Āncì (安次)
was a Hàn (漢) county,
belonging to Yōuzhōu (幽州) in the Táng (唐) dynasty,
located one hundred thirty lǐ southeast of the prefecture.
Shuài (帥)
is pronounced like suǒ lèi.
20 Liú Zhījùn (劉知俊), Zhōngwǔ Jìedùshǐ and concurrently Shìzhōng,
last year changed Tóngzhōu Kuāngguó Jūn to Zhōngwǔ Jūn;
this matter is mentioned in the previous volume.
Seeing the Emperor's suspicion and cruelty grow daily,
he felt uneasy internally.
And when Wáng Chóngshī (王重師) was executed,
Zhījùn (知俊) became even more afraid.
The Emperor was about to campaign against Hédōng (河東);
Hédōng (河東)
refers to Jìn (晉).
He wanted to make Zhījùn (知俊) the Western Route Xíngyíng Dōutǒng;
and because Zhījùn (知俊) had achievements at Dān (丹) and Yán (延),
he heavily rewarded him.
Zhījùn's (知俊) younger brother, Zhīhuàn (知浣), Right Bǎoshèng Zhǐhuīshǐ, was with the Emperor in Luòyáng (洛陽).
He secretly sent someone to tell Zhījùn (知俊):
"If you enter, you will surely die."
He also told the Emperor
that he wished to lead his brothers and nephews to welcome Zhījùn (知俊).
The Emperor permitted it.
In the sixth month,
on the yìwèi (乙未) new moon,
Zhījùn (知俊) reported,
"I have been detained by the military and civilians,"
and then surrendered Tóngzhōu (同州) to Qí (岐).
The Kǎoyì says: The Shílù states:
"In the sixth month, on the gēngxū day,
Zhījùn (知俊) rebelled in his own prefecture.
His official titles and ranks were stripped, and an army was dispatched to suppress him."
The Biānyílù states:
"In the sixth month,
on the yìwèi day,
it was first reported that the local military and civilians detained him,
and soon it was heard that the envoys were captured and would be sent to Fèngxiáng (鳳翔)."
The Biānyílù is based on the day the report arrived,
and the Shílù is based on the day of the stripping of titles.
All were shackled and sent to Qí (岐).
He sent troops to attack Huàzhōu (華州),
driving out Cìshǐ Cài Jìngsī (蔡敬思).
The Jiǔyù Zhì states: Tóngzhōu (同州) is seventy lǐ south of Huàzhōu (華州).
Huà (華)
is pronounced like hù huà.
He secretly sent people with heavy bribes to entice the generals in Cháng'ān (長安),

send him to Qí (岐),

Zhījùn (知俊) sent an envoy to request troops from Qí (岐),

He wrote a letter to the King of Jìn (晉) saying:

21 On the dīngwèi day,
Hán Xùn (韓遜), Shuòfāng Jìedùshǐ, reported the capture of Yánzhōu (鹽州),

In the late Táng (唐),
Yánzhōu (鹽州) directly reported matters to the imperial court,
and was not subordinate to Língxià (靈夏).
By this time, Líng (靈) and Yán (鹽) were reunited into one commandery.
22 The Emperor sent a close official to convey to Liú Zhījùn (劉知俊):
"I have treated you very generously,
why do you suddenly betray me?"
Zhījùn (知俊) replied:
"I do not betray kindness,
but merely fear the extermination of my clan like Wáng Chóngshī (王重師)."
The Emperor again sent someone to tell him:
"Liú Hàn (劉捍) said Chóngshī (重師) secretly allied with Bīn (邠) and Qí (岐).
I now regret it without being able to undo it;
Hàn's (捍) death is not enough to atone for the mistake."
Zhījùn (知俊) did not reply.
On the gēngxū day,
an imperial edict stripped Zhījùn (知俊) of his official titles and ranks.
Yáng Shīhòu (楊師厚), Shānnán Dōngdào Jìedùshǐ, was made Xīlù Xíngyíng Zhāotǎoshǐ,

On the xīnhài day,
the Emperor departed Luòyáng (洛陽).
When Liú Xún (劉鄩) arrived east of Tóngguān (潼關),
he captured thirty men including Lìn Rúhǎi (藺如海), who were Liú Zhījùn's (劉知俊) ambush soldiers on the road.
He released them and made them guides.
Liú Zhījùn (劉知俊) had already taken Tóngguān (潼關),
and had ambushed troops along the road outside the pass to watch.
Liú Xún (劉鄩) instead captured and used them as local guides.
Shǐ Zhào says: Lìn (藺)
is a surname.
Their ancestor, Hàn Xiànzǐ's great-great-grandson, was named Kāng (康),
who received an allotment of land at Lìn (藺),
and thus adopted the surname.
After lingering for several days,
he arrived below the pass.
The pass official admitted him.
Rúhǎi (如海) and others arrived afterward.
The pass official, unaware that they had been captured,
also admitted them.
Xún's (鄩) troops, taking advantage of the open gate, advanced directly,
and thus captured Tóngguān (潼關).
They pursued and caught Zhīhuàn (知浣),
capturing him.
On the guǐchǒu day,
the Emperor arrived at Shǎn (陝).
23 Wáng Xíngsī (王行思) and others, Dānzhōu Mǎjūn Dōutóu, revolted.
Cìshǐ Sòng Zhīhuì (宋知誨) fled back.

Zhījùn (知俊) wanted to ride lightly to the traveling court to apologize,

Yáng Shīhòu (楊師厚) and others arrived at Huàzhōu (華州).
Niè Shǎng (聶賞), Zhījùn's (知俊) general, opened the gate and surrendered.
Zhījùn (知俊) heard that Tóngguān (潼關) had not been held,

In a panic and at a loss,
on the yǐmǎo day,
he fled with his whole family to Qí (岐).
Yáng Shīhòu (楊師hòu) arrived at Cháng'ān (長安).
Qí (岐) troops had already occupied the city.
Shīhòu (師厚), with a surprise force, rapidly advanced along the Nánshān (南山),

On the gēngshēn day,
Liú Xún (劉鄩) was appointed acting Jìnguó Liúhòu.
The King of Qí (岐) treated Liú Zhījùn (劉知俊) with great courtesy,
making him Zhōngshū Lìng.
The territory was narrow,
with no frontier commandery to place him in,

A hoofprint cannot hold a foot-long carp.
This laid the groundwork for Liú Zhījùn (劉知俊) to flee to Shǔ (蜀).
25 Liú Shǒuguāng (劉守光) sent an envoy to submit a memorial reporting his victory,

He also sent a letter to the King of Jìn (晉),

Liú Shǒuguāng (劉守光) repeatedly vacillated between Liáng (梁) and Jìn (晉),
believing he had a clever plan,

26 Wēi Quánfěng (危全諷), the Cìshǐ (刺史) of Fǔzhōu (撫州), proclaimed himself the Jìedùshǐ (節度使) of Zhènnán (鎮南),

The Táng (唐) dynasty had established the Zhènnán (鎮南) army in Hóngzhōu (洪州),
and Fǔ (撫), Xìn (信), Yuán (袁), and Jí (吉) were all within its jurisdiction.
Wēi Quánfěng (危全諷) proclaimed himself Jìedù (節度),
raised an army to attack Hóngzhōu (洪州),
wanting to annex and possess it.
The Jiǔyù Zhì (九域志) states: Fǔzhōu (撫州) is two hundred and nine lǐ (里) northwest of Hóngzhōu (洪州).
Shuài (帥),

The generals and officials were all fearful.
Jìedùshǐ (節度使) Liú Wēi (劉威) secretly sent an envoy to Gǔanglíng (廣陵) for urgent help,
and daily summoned his aides for banquets.
Quánfěng (全諷) heard of this,
and encamped at Xiàngyátán (象牙潭),

Xiàngyátán (象牙潭) is northeast of Jīnxī Xiàn (金溪縣) in Fǔzhōu (撫州).
Chǔ Wáng (楚王) Yīn (殷) sent the Zhǐhuīshǐ (指揮使) Yuàn Méi (苑玫).
Yuàn (苑),
is a surname.

Qí (齊) had a Dàfū (大夫) Yuàn Héjì (苑何忌).
Méi (玫),
is pronounced Mò-bēi.
Méi (玫),
was from Cáizhōu (蔡州);
Yànzhāng (彥章),
was Gān (玕)'s elder brother.
Péng Gān (彭玕) is mentioned in volume two hundred sixty-five, Tiānyòu (天祐) third year of Táng Zhāoxuān Dì (唐昭宣帝).
Xú Wēn (徐溫) asked Yán Kěqiú (嚴可求) about generals.
Kěqiú (可求) recommended Zhōu Běn (周本).
So Běn (本) was made Xīnán Miàn Xíngyíng Zhāotǎo Yìngyuán Shǐ (西南面行營招討應援使),

Běn (本) had previously failed in attacking Sūzhōu (蘇州),

Kěqiú (可求) forcibly roused him from his bedchamber.
Běn (本) said:
"In the Sūzhōu (蘇州) campaign,
the enemy could not defeat me,
but the authority of the main general was too light.
Now I must be put in charge,

Kěqiú (可求) agreed to this.
Běn (本) said:
"The Chǔ (楚) people are merely supporting Quánfěng (全諷),
they do not wish to take Gāo'ān (高安).
If I defeat Quánfěng (全諷),
the reinforcing army will surely return."
Yuánbīng (援兵),
refers to the troops besieging Gāo'ān (高安).
Huán (還),
is pronounced cóng-xuān.
Passing through Hóngzhōu (洪州).
Liú Wēi (劉威) wanted to reward the army,
but Běn (本) refused to stay.
Someone said:
"Quánfěng (全諷)'s army is strong,
you should observe the situation before advancing."
Běn (本) said:
"The bandits are ten times our number.
If our army hears this, they will surely be afraid.
It is better to strike while our morale is high."
27 Autumn,
seventh month,
Jiǎzǐ (甲子),
Liú Shǒuguāng (劉守光) was made Yān Wáng (燕王).
28 The Liáng (梁) army captured Dānzhōu (丹州),

29 Lǐ Chóu (李稠), the Cìshǐ (刺史) of Shāngzhōu (商州), drove the soldiers and people westward,
intending to flee to Shǔ (蜀).
Kǎoyì (考異) says: Xuē Shǐ (薛史) says:

Bǐngyín (丙寅),

"The Shāngzhōu (商州) generals and officials, seeing Chóu (稠) driving the common people to flee west,

They temporarily ordered Dōuyáyá (都押牙) Lǐ Mín (李玟) to manage the prefectural affairs."
We follow this now.
30 Gēngwǔ (庚午),
Yòuguó Jūn (佑國軍) was renamed Yǒngpíng (永平).
In Kāipíng (開平) first year, Yòuguó Jūn (佑國軍) was moved to Cháng'ān (長安),
now renamed Yǒngpíng (永平).
31 The Hédōng (河東) army raided Jìnzhōu (晉州),
plundering as far as Yáocí (堯祠) before leaving.
Yáo (堯)'s capital was Píngyáng (平陽),
where there was a shrine ten lǐ (里) east of Fénchéng (汾城) on the eastern plain.
Píngyáng (平陽) was Línfén Xiàn (臨汾縣) during the Táng (唐) dynasty,

32 Guǐyǒu (癸酉),
the Emperor departed Shǎnzhōu (陝州);
Yǐhài (乙亥),
arrived at Luòyáng (洛陽),

33 Initially,
the Emperor summoned Yáng Shīhòu (楊師厚), the Jìedùshǐ (節度使) of Shānnán Dōngdào (山南東道),
wanting him to supervise the generals in attacking Lùzhōu (潞州).
He appointed Wáng Bān (王班), formerly Liúhòu (留後) of Yǎnhǎi (兗海), as Liúhòu (留後)
to garrison Xiāngzhōu (襄州).
Kǎoyì (考異) says: Xuē Shǐ (薛史) writes "
Wáng Bān (王班)",
we now follow Shílù (實錄).
It should be noted that Bān (班) relied on the brave men around him,
and did not take them seriously,
often humiliating them in public.
Wùyín (戊寅),
they were banished to guard the western border.
That night,
they rebelled,
killed Bān (班),
and acclaimed Dōuzhǐhuīshǐ (都指揮使) Liú Bǐ (劉邠) of Yǒngqiū (雍丘) as Liúhòu (留後);
Bǐ (邠) feigned compliance,
and the next day,
fled with Zhǐhuīshǐ (指揮使) Wáng Yánshùn (王延順) to the Emperor's residence.
Kǎoyì (考異) says: Yáo Yǐ (姚顗)'s Míngzōng Shílù (明宗實錄) and Xuē Shǐ (薛史)'s Bǐ (邠) biography both state:
"The next day, he received congratulations,
and entertained the soldiers in the courtyard.
He had armed men hidden under a canopy,
and in the middle of the banquet, he executed all the rebel generals and reported it.
For his merit, he was made Fùzhōu Cìshǐ (復州刺史)."
However, the Liáng Zǔ Shílù (梁祖實錄) says:
"In the eighth month, Dīngyǒu (丁酉), gifts were bestowed upon Bǐ (邠) and Wáng Yánshùn (王延順),
for their return from the rebellion of opposing generals."
The edict for executing Lǐ Hóng (李洪) and others in the Biānyílù (編遺錄) says:
"He first supported Liú Bǐ (劉邠),
then fled and returned to loyalty."
If Bǐ (邠) had executed the rebel generals the next day,
how could Xiāngzhōu (襄州) only be recovered in the ninth month!
Probably Bǐ (邠) escaped and returned to court,
and when Liáng (梁) fell and he entered Táng (唐),
he falsely claimed to have executed the rebel generals to boast,
and the historians, unable to verify,
simply wrote it down.
It was annexed to Shǔ (蜀).
Soon after,
Yáng Qián (楊虔), the Cìshǐ (刺史) of Fángzhōu (房州), also rebelled and defected to Shǔ (蜀).
34 Wēi Quánfěng (危全諷) was at Xiàngyátán (象牙潭),
with camps and stockades along the creek,
extending for dozens of lǐ (里).
Gēngchén (庚辰),
Zhōu Běn (周本) arrayed his troops across the creek,
first sending weak soldiers to test the enemy;
Quánfěng (全諷)'s soldiers crossed the creek to pursue them.
Běn (本) attacked them when they were halfway across,
unleashing his troops.
Quánfěng (全諷)'s army was routed,
trampling each other,
and many drowned.
Běn (本) divided his troops to cut off their retreat,
capturing Quánfěng (全諷) and five thousand officers and soldiers.
Taking advantage of the victory, he captured Yuánzhōu (袁州),
seized Cìshǐ (刺史) Péng Yànzhāng (彭彥章),
and advanced to attack Jízhōu (吉州).
The Jiǔyù Zhì (九域志) says: Yuánzhōu (袁州) is three hundred and fifteen lǐ (里) south of Jízhōu (吉州).
Wēi Zǐchàng (危仔倡), the Cìshǐ (刺史) of Xìnzhōu (信州), requested to surrender.
In the second year of Táng Xīzōng (唐僖宗)'s Zhōnghé (中和) era,
Wēi Quánfěng (危全諷) occupied Fǔzhōu (撫州),
and Zǐchàng (仔倡) occupied Xìnzhōu (信州).
By this time, both had fallen.
Xíngyíng Dōuzhǐhuīshǐ (行營都指揮使) Mǐ Zhìchéng (米志誠), Dōuwèi (都尉) Lǚ Shīzào (呂師造), and others defeated Yuàn Mín (苑玟) at Shànggāo (上高).
Péng Gān (彭玕), the Cìshǐ (刺史) of Jízhōu (吉州), led several thousand people to flee to Chǔ (楚).
In the third year of Táng Zhāozōng (唐昭宗)'s Tiānyòu (天祐) era, Péng Gān (彭玕) defected to Chǔ (楚).
He married his daughter to his son Xīfàn (希範).
Huáinán (淮南) appointed Zhāng Jǐngsī (張景思), the Zuǒ Xiānfēng Zhǐhuīshǐ (左先鋒指揮使), to govern Xìnzhōu (信州),
and sent Xíngyíng Dōuyúhòu (行營都虞候) Gǔ Yán (骨言) with five thousand soldiers to escort him.
Gǔ (骨),
is a surname.
In the early Táng (唐) dynasty, there was Gǔ Yí (骨儀).
He fled to Wúyuè (吳越).
Wúyuè Wáng (吳越王) Qián Liú (錢鏐) appointed Zǐchàng (仔倡) as Huáinán Jìedù Fùshǐ (淮南節度副使),
and changed his surname to Yuán (元).
Ōushǐ Shíguó Shìjiā (歐史十國世家) says: Qián Liú (錢鏐) disliked the surname Wēi (危),
and changed it to Yuán (元).
Gēng (更),
is pronounced gōng-héng.
Hóngnóng Wáng (弘農王), because he had once been benevolent to Wǔzhōng Wáng (武忠王),
released him and provided him with generous provisions.
Yáng Xíngmì (楊行密) was posthumously named Wǔzhōng (武忠).
At that time, the Huáinán (淮南) generals debated, saying:
"Formerly, when the late king attacked Zhào Huáng (趙鍠),
Quánfěng (全諷) repeatedly supplied our army."
So they released him.
Lú Guāngchóu (盧光稠), the Cìshǐ (刺史) of Qiánzhōu (虔州), surrendered his prefecture to Huáinán (淮南).
Thus, all the territory in Jiāngxī (江西) fell into the hands of the Yáng (楊) family.
Guāngchóu (光稠) also sent an envoy to defect to Liáng (梁).
35 On the *jiǎyín* day,
the Emperor's illness slightly improved,
and he began to hold court again.
From the *yǐhài* day of the seventh month, when he fell ill,
it had been forty days in total until this time.
朝 (*cháo*):
pronounced *zhí yáo fān* (variant pronunciation for *cháo*);
same below.
36 Kāng Huáizhēn, Military Governor of Zhènguó, was appointed Deputy Commander of the Western Route Expeditionary Army.
37 The Lord of Shǔ ordered Crown Prince Zōngyì to oversee the six armies,
opened the Yǒnghé Mansion,
and carefully selected court officials as his staff.
38 On the *xīnyǒu* day,
Zhāng Jìngfāng, Prefect of Jūnzhōu, reported the capture of Fángzhōu.
Yáng Qián presented Fángzhōu, which had been attached to Shǔ, to the Emperor.
According to the *Jiǔyù Zhì*: Jūnzhōu is two hundred and fifteen *lǐ* south of Fángzhōu.
39 The King of Qí wanted to send Liú Zhījùn to lead troops to attack Líng and Xià,
and also agreed with the King of Jìn to attack Jìn and Jiàng.
The King of Jìn led his troops south,
first sending Zhōu Déwēi and others to lead troops out of Yīndì Pass to attack Jìnzhōu.
The Prefect Biān Jìwēi defended it with all his might.
The Jìn troops dug tunnels,
collapsing more than twenty *bù* of the city wall.
The city's defenders fought desperately to repel them,
and the wall was rebuilt overnight.
An imperial edict ordered Yáng Shīhòu to lead troops to relieve Jìnzhōu.
Zhōu Déwēi used cavalry to control the strategic passes of Méngkēng.
Méngkēng is east of the Fénshǔi,
extending over three hundred *lǐ* east to west,
with impassable trails.
Upon reaching Jìnzhōu,
the Jìn troops lifted the siege and fled.
The *Kǎoyì* says: The *Shílù* states:
"They killed and captured rebel generals such as Xiāo Wàntōng,
and the rebels consequently abandoned their camp and fled."
The *Zhuāngzōng Shílù* states:
"When the Biàn army reached Méngkēng,
Zhōu Déwēi engaged them in battle,
defeating them,
beheading two hundred.
Shīhòu retreated to Jiàngzhōu.
In this engagement,
the junior general Xiāo Wàntōng died in battle.
Shīhòu advanced his camp to Píngyáng,
and Déwēi withdrew his troops."
Both armies claimed victory,
but if Xiāo Wàntōng had been killed,
how could Shīhòu have retreated to Jiàngzhōu?
If he was defeated and retreated,
how could he then advance his camp to Píngyáng?
If Déwēi had won the battle,
why would he have withdrawn his troops immediately?
It is likely that the Jìn army was actually defeated and fled,
and the *Zhuāngzōng Shílù* falsely claimed victory.
40 Lǐ Hóng raided Jīngnán.
Gāo Jìchāng sent his general Ní Kěfú to defeat him.
An imperial edict ordered Chén Huī, Commander of Infantry and Cavalry, to lead troops to join the Jīngnán army to suppress Hóng.
41 The Lord of Shǔ appointed Wáng Kǎi, Imperial Censor-in-Chief, as Minister of the Central Secretariat and Grand Chancellor.
42 Chén Huī's army arrived at Xiāngzhōu.
Lǐ Hóng engaged them in battle,
suffering a great defeat,
and Wáng Qiú died.
In the ninth month,
on the *dīngyǒu* day,
they captured its city,
beheaded a thousand rebel soldiers,
and captured Lǐ Hóng and Yáng Qián, sending them to Luòyáng
where they were executed.
43 On the *dīngwèi* day,
Wáng Tán, Military Governor of Bǎoyì, was appointed Commander of the East Route Expeditionary Army for Lùzhōu.
44 Liú Shǒuguāng reported sending his son Jìwēi, Commander of the Central Army, to appease the officials and people of Cāngzhōu;
on the *wùshēn* day,
Jìwēi was appointed Acting Military Governor of Yìchāng.
45 On the *xīnhài* day,
Hán Jiàn, Grand Preceptor, was dismissed from his post of Grand Tutor;
Yáng Shè, Left Grandee Secretary and Grand Chancellor, was dismissed from his original post.
Zhào Guāngféng, Grand Master of Sacrifices, was appointed Minister of the Central Secretariat;
Dù Xiǎo, Gentleman of the Palace and Minister of Works, was appointed Minister of Revenue,
both serving as Grand Chancellors.
The Liáng changed the title Hàlín Chéngzhǐ to Hàlín Fèngzhǐ
due to the imperial taboo on the character chéng
(the given name of the temple ancestor), to avoid using the taboo character.
However,
the character 誠 (*chéng*)
and
the character 承 (*chéng*)
have different pronunciations (different *fǎnqiè*).
He was the son of Ràng Néng.
Dù Ràngnéng died in national calamity, as seen in volume 259, second year of Jǐngfú, Tang Zhāozōng.
46 Huáinán sent an envoy, Zhāng Zhīyuǎn, to establish friendly relations with Fújiàn;
Zhīyuǎn was arrogant and rude,
so Mǐn Wáng Shěnzhī executed him
and submitted his memorial to the Emperor.
上 (*shàng*):
pronounced *shí zhǎng fān* (variant pronunciation for *shàng*).
Shěnzhī was frugal and simple by nature,
often wearing hemp sandals.
His official residence was humble and dilapidated,
never having been repaired.
He leniently applied laws and lightly taxed,
making both public and private coffers rich and the territory peaceful.
Every year, tribute was sent by sea to Dēng and Lái,
but four or five out of ten ships were lost at sea.
Sending tribute from Fújiàn to Dàliáng
by land would require passing through Qú and Xìn, then crossing the river in the territory of Ráo and Chí,
then crossing the Huái in Shū, Lú, and Shòu,
before entering Liáng territory.
However, from Xìn and Ráo to Lú and Shòu, all belonged to the Yáng clan,
and the Zhū and Yáng were hereditary enemies,
so passage could not be granted.
Therefore, tribute was sent by sea.
Now, from Fúzhōu-yáng, passing Wēnzhōu-yáng,
taking Tái Zhōu-yáng, passing Tiānménshān, entering Míngzhōu Xiàngshān-yáng,
passing Cénjiāng,
skirting Lièjiǎng,
heading directly northeast across the great ocean to the shores of Dēng and Lái.
The winds and waves were extremely perilous,
hence many were drowned.
47 In winter,
the tenth month,
on the *jiǎzǐ* day,
Hú Xiùlín, Director of the Astronomical Bureau of Shǔ, presented the Yǒngchāng Calendar,
which was put into use.
Ōuyáng Xiū said: The Yǒngchāng Calendar was only used in their state;
it is now lost
and no longer seen.
48 Gāo Lǐ, Prefect of Húzhōu, was fierce and cruel by nature.
He once summoned the prefectural officials and discussed, saying:
"I want to kill all the common people,
is that acceptable?"
An official replied:
"If so,
from where would the taxes come?
You should select those who deserve to be killed and kill them."
At that time, Lǐ conscripted civilians into soldiers.
When there were rumors of discontent,
Lǐ gathered all the civilian soldiers at Kāiyuán Temple.
Kāiyuán Temples exist in various prefectures today,
having been established during the Kāiyuán era of the Tang dynasty.
Those who entered were killed;
more than half died.
Those outside realized what was happening and set fire, creating chaos.
Lǐ closed the city gates and conducted a massive search,
killing three thousand people in total.
Wúyuè Wáng Liú wanted to execute him.
On the *wùchén* day,
Lǐ rebelled with the prefecture and defected to Huáinán.
Gāo Lǐ and his son, with a single prefecture,
had long lived between Qián and Yáng,
constantly shifting allegiance to survive.
Now, exclusively defecting to Huáinán,
Qián's army will arrive.
The *Jiǔyù Zhì* says: Rénfú County in Hángzhōu has the town of Língpíng.
Note that Rénfú County was originally Qiántáng County.
In the early Tàipíng Xīngguó era of the Sòng dynasty, Qiántáng County was renamed Rénfú.
This was likely because there was already a place named Yìhé,
and also to avoid the old name of Tàizōng's princely residence,
so it was changed to Rénfú.
49 In the eleventh month,
on the *jiǎwǔ* day,
the Emperor offered a thanksgiving sacrifice at the Round Mound (Yuánqiū);
"offering thanksgiving" means
thanking Heaven for having obtained the realm.
According to Ōu Shǐ (Ōuyáng Xiū's history),
on this day,
the sun reached its southernmost point (winter solstice).
Xú Wúdǎng's commentary says: It doesn't say "performed rites at the southern suburban altar"
because the ceremony was somewhat simpler than the southern suburban altar rites.
On the *wùxū* day,
a general amnesty was declared.
Yèwáng Luó Shàowēi (羅紹wēi) contracted a form of palsy.
He submitted a memorial stating:
"The former great garrisons of Wèibó (魏博)
often had outside armies.
I wish to have a meritorious and prominent minister garrison it.
Your servant requests to retire and return to his residence."
When the Emperor heard this,
he pounded the table and his expression changed.
Pounding the table and his expression changing
was not out of pity for Luó Shàowēi's (羅紹wēi) illness.
Wèibó (魏博) was a great garrison
that had been hereditary for 150 years.
To suddenly resign the garrison and request a replacement
was beyond expectation.
Joy overflowed within him,
so much so that he was unaware of his hand pounding and his expression changing.
On the day *jǐhài* (己亥),
his son Luó Zhōuhàn (羅周翰) was made Deputy Military Governor of Tiānxíong (天雄),
administering the prefecture.
He said to the envoy:
"Return quickly and tell your lord:
Eat more for my sake!
If something untoward were to happen
(meaning death),
now that Zhōuhàn (周翰) leads the military administration,
I still hope you will recover."
The *Kǎoyì* (考異) states: In the *Liáng Gōngchén Lièzhuàn* (梁功臣列傳):
"Since the founding of the imperial court,
whenever there were major affairs, envoys were sent down to consult.
Shàowēi (紹wēi) had foresight and strategized,
also sending letters to offer advice.
If they met halfway,
their intentions would align five or six times out of ten.
Tàizǔ (太祖) sighed, saying: 'He is the only one who exhausts his loyalty and effort.'"
It also says:
"He had three sons: the eldest was Luó Tíngguī (羅廷規),
Sīnóng Qīng (司農卿),
who married Princess Ānyáng (安陽),
and later Princess Jīnhuá (金華),
but died young.
The second was Luó Zhōuhàn (羅周翰),
who was reinstated as Yúnhuī Jiāngjūn (雲麾將軍),
appointed acting Military Governor of Tiānxíong (天雄),
soon after made acting Sītú (司徒),
and then officially appointed Military Governor of Wèibó (魏博),
but also died young.
The third was Luó Zhōujìng (羅周敬)."
Xuē Shǐ (薛史) also agrees.
The *Shílù* (實錄) states:
"On the day *jǐhài* (己亥),
Sīmén Lángzhōng (司門郎中) Luó Tíngguī (羅廷規) was made Deputy Military Governor of Wèibó (魏博),
administering the prefecture,
and his name was changed to Zhōuhàn (周翰).
At that time, Yèwáng Shàowēi (鄴王紹wēi) was gravely ill,
worried about future matters,
and therefore submitted the request."
The *Zhuāngzōng Lièzhuàn* (莊宗列傳) states:
"After Shàowēi (紹wēi) died,
Wēn (溫) appointed his son Zhōuhàn (周翰) to succeed him in governance."
The *Zhuāngzōng Shílù* (莊宗實錄) states:
"Shàowēi (紹wēi) levied heavy taxes and collected much,
emptying his treasury to serve Wēn (溫).
If there was a slight transgression,
Wēn (溫) would immediately send someone to insult him.
Shàowēi (紹wēi) felt ashamed and regretful of his strategy to weaken himself,
so he secretly recruited soldiers and bought horses,
secretly planning to overthrow Wēn (溫),
and bribed Wēn (溫) even more heavily.
Wēn (溫) found his subservience strange,
feared he was harboring wicked schemes but couldn't detect them.
So he bestowed several concubines upon Shàowēi (紹wēi),
all of whom were favored.
Less than half a year later,
Wēn (溫) recalled them,
and through this, obtained knowledge of his secret affairs."
There is an internal contradiction.
Xuē Shǐ (薛史) also states:
"In the summer of the 4th year of Kāipíng (開平),
an edict was issued for Princess Jīnhuá (金華) to become a nun,
residing in Xuánjìng Sì (玄靜寺) in Sòngzhōu (宋州).
This was Tàizǔ (太祖) extending his grace to the Luó (羅) family,
allowing her to complete her wifely virtue."
The *Táng Yúlù* (唐餘錄) and Ōuyáng Shǐ (歐陽史) both agree;
only the *Táng Zhuāngzōng Shílù* (唐莊宗實錄) differs.
Upon examination, during Jūndì's (均帝) time, Zhào Yán (趙巖) and others said
"Luó Shàowēi (羅紹wēi) was respectful at first but arrogant later;
Tàizǔ (太祖) often harbored deep anger,"
which seems to align with this statement.
However, if Liáng Zǔ (梁祖) had heard of Shàowēi's (紹wēi) secret plot,
he would certainly not have allowed Zhōuhàn (周翰) to remain in Wèi (魏).
It is suspected that the Later Táng (後唐) historians,
because Shàowēi (紹wēi) was very close to Liáng (梁),
disliked him,
and thus included this rumored account.
We now follow the majority of texts.
The change of Tíngguī's (廷規) name to Zhōuhàn (周翰)
is also perhaps an error in the *Shílù* (實錄).
Qíwáng (岐王) wished to capture Língzhōu (靈州) to settle Liú Zhījùn (劉知俊),
and also to use it as a grazing land for horses. He sent Zhījùn (知俊) to lead troops to attack it himself.
Shuòfāng Jiédùshǐ (朔方節度使) Hán Xùn (韓遜) reported the emergency.
An edict ordered Zhènguó Jiédùshǐ (鎮國節度使) Kāng Huáizhēn (康懷貞) and Gǎnhuà Jiédùshǐ (感化節度使) Kòu Yànqīng (寇彥卿) to lead troops to attack Bīnnìng (邠寧) to relieve it.
Huáizhēn (懷貞) and the others were victorious wherever they went,
capturing Níngzhōu (寧州) and Yǎnzhōu (衍州),
and taking the southern city of Qìngzhōu (慶州).
The Prefect Lǐ Yànguǎng (李彥廣) surrendered.
Níngzhōu (寧州), Qìngzhōu (慶州), and Yǎnzhōu (衍州) were all under the jurisdiction of the Jìngnàn (靜難) army,
belonging to the territory of Qí (岐).
In the 5th year of Zhōuxíandé (周顯德), Yǎnzhōu (衍州) was abolished and became Dìngpíng Zhèn (定平鎮),
subordinate to Fénzhōu (汾州).
The *Jiǔyù Zhì* (九域志) states: In the 5th year of Xīníng (熙寧), Dìngpíng Xiàn (定平縣) of Fénzhōu (汾州) was made subordinate to Jīngzhōu (涇州),
60 *lǐ* (里) south of the prefecture.
When Liú Zhījùn (劉知俊) heard of this,
in the 12th month,
on the day *jǐchǒu* (己丑),
he lifted the siege of Língzhōu (靈州)
and led his troops back.
The Emperor urgently recalled Huáizhēn (懷貞) and the others,
sending troops to meet and reinforce them at Sānyuán Qīnggǔ (三原青谷).
Huáizhēn (懷貞) and the others returned,
reaching Sānshuǐ (三水).
Sānshuǐ (三水) was an ancient county in the Hàn (漢) dynasty,
and belonged to Bīnnán (邠南) in the Táng (唐) dynasty.
The *Jiǔyù Zhì* (九域志) states: It is 60 *lǐ* (里) northeast of the prefecture.
Xuē Shǐ (薛史) says: Zhījùn (知俊) ambushed and attacked Huáizhēn (懷貞) and the others at Chángchéng Lǐng (長城嶺) in Bīnnán (邠南).
The *Wǔdài Huìyào* (五代會要) states: In the 1st year of Kāipíng (開平), the Left and Right Qīnsuí Jūn (親隨軍) cavalry were reorganized into the Left and Right Lóngxiáng Jūn (龍驤軍).
Huáizhēn (懷貞), along with his subordinate generals Lǐ Déyù (李德遇), Xǔ Cóngshí (許從實), and Wáng Shěnquán (王審權),
marched separately,
and none met with the reinforcing troops.
Upon reaching Shēngpíng (昇平),
Shēngpíng Xiàn (昇平縣) was established by dividing Yíjūn (宜君) in the 12th year of Tiānbǎo (天寶) of the Táng (唐) dynasty,
belonging to Fángzhōu (坊州).
Huáizhēn (懷貞) suffered a great defeat,
barely escaping with his life.
The armies of Déyù (德遇) and the others were all lost.
Qíwáng (岐王) appointed Zhījùn (知俊) as Zhāngyì Jiédùshǐ (彰義節度使),
garrisoning Jīngzhōu (涇州).
Wáng Yànzhāng (王彥章) was exceptionally brave and fierce.
In every battle, he used two iron spears,
each weighing a hundred *jīn* (斤).
One was placed in the saddle,
and one in his hand.
He was unstoppable wherever he went,
and people at the time called him Wáng Tiěqiāng (王鐵槍) (Iron Spear Wang).
Shǔzhōu (蜀州) Prefect Wáng Zōngbiàn (王宗弁) claimed illness,
retired to Chéngdū (成都),
and secluded himself at home.
Wáng Zōngbiàn (王宗弁) was originally Lù Biàn (鹿弁).
The ruler of Shǔ (蜀) adopted him as a son,
and bestowed his surname and given name.
He was promoted to acting Tàibǎo (太保),
but he firmly declined,
telling people:
"The incorruptible are content and without worry,
while the greedy worry and are never satisfied.
I am a humble person; to have reached this position is enough.
How can I endlessly seek advancement!"
The ruler of Shǔ (蜀) admired his resolve and granted his wish,
showering him with additional gifts.
Zōngbiàn's (宗弁) request for retirement
was due to the Shǔ (蜀) ruler's suspicion and jealousy.
Liú Shǒuguāng (劉守光) had besieged Cāngzhōu (滄州) for a long time but could not take it.
Liú Shǒuguāng (劉守光) had attacked Cāngzhōu (滄州) since the fifth month.
It was still firmly defended.
Food in the city was exhausted.
The common people ate mud from *jǐn* (菫) plants,
the soldiers ate human flesh,
and donkeys and horses ate each other's manes and tails.
Lǚ Yǎn (呂兗) selected weak men and women,
fed them *qúmài biàn* (麴丏) (fermented grains) and cooked them,
to provide food for the army.
This was called the 'Slaughtering Office' (Zǎishā Wù, 宰殺務).
1st month,
on the day *yǐwèi* (乙未),
Liú Yánzuò (劉延祚), at the end of his strength, surrendered.
At that time, Liú Jìwēi (劉繼威) was still young.
Liú Jìwēi (劉繼威) was Shǒuguāng's (守光) son.
This sets the stage for Zhāng Wànjìn (張萬進) to kill Liú Jìwēi (劉繼威).
Lǚ Yǎn (呂兗)'s clan was exterminated, but Sūn Hè (孫鶴) was spared.
Yǎn Zǐqí,
at fifteen years old,
his retainer Zhào Yù deceived the executioner, saying:
"This is my younger brother;
do not kill him indiscriminately."
The executioner believed him,
and thus carried him away to escape.
Qí's feet hurt and he could not walk,
so Yù carried him on his back,
changed their names,
and begged for food on the road,
barely managing to escape.
Qí felt the destruction of his family keenly,
and studied diligently to establish himself.
Jìn Wáng heard of his reputation,
and appointed him as the Judgement Officer of Dàizhōu.
Sūn Hè ultimately could not escape execution,
yet Lǚ Qí was able to establish himself.
Is it heaven's will?
Or human effort!
2. On the Xīnchǒu day,
Lú Guāngchóu was appointed as the Acting Military Governor of Zhènnán.
Lú Guāngchóu surrendered Qiánzhōu to Liáng.
The Zhènnán Army was stationed in Hóngzhōu,
which by this time was already under the control of Huáinán.
3. Liú Shǒuguāng requested that his father, Rén Gōng, be allowed to retire.
On the Bǐngwǔ day,
Rén Gōng was appointed Grand Tutor
and retired.
Shǒuguāng soon sent men to secretly assassinate his elder brother Shǒuwén,
then blamed the killers and executed them.
4. In the second month,
Wàn Quán'gǎn returned from Qí to Guǎnglín.
The previous year, Huáinán had sent Wàn Quán'gǎn as an envoy to Jìn and Qí.
The heir to Wú Wáng,
Táng Zhāozōng had enfeoffed Yáng Xíngmì as Wú Wáng in Tiānfù 2nd year.
Now Qí Wáng, by his authority, elevated Lóngyǎn to heir.
5. Gāo Lǐ sought help from Wú.
The Wú Prefect of Chángzhōu, Lǐ Jiǎn and others, led troops to respond to him.
The Huzhou generals Shèng Shīyǒu and Shěn Xíngsī closed the city gates and did not let them in;
Lǐ then led his five thousand subordinates and fled to Wú.
According to records, in Tiānfù 4th year of Táng Zhāozōng, Lǐ Yànhuī fled to Huáinán,
and Qián Liú took Húzhōu.
In Tiānfù 2nd year, Xú Xǔ caused unrest in Hángzhōu.
The Prefect of Húzhōu, Gāo Yàn, sent his son Wèi to assist.
In Tiānyòu 3rd year of Táng Zhāoxuān Dì, Yàn died,
and his son Lǐ took his place,
until he was defeated now.
The character "帥" (shuài)
is pronounced as "率" (shuài).

The Emperor ordered Yāyá (押衙) Dài Hànchāo (戴漢超) to carry an imperial decree and letters from the Six Zhèn (鎮) to Yōuzhōu (幽州),
which read: 'On the 27th day of the third month of Tiānyòu (天祐) 8th year,

Sòng Yáo (宋瑤), Jìedùshǐ (節度使) of Tiāndé Jūn (天德軍), Zhōu Déwēi (周德威), Jìedùshǐ (節度使) of Zhènwǔ (振武), Lǐ Sìzhāo (李嗣昭), Jìedùshǐ (節度使) of Zhāo Yì (昭義), Wáng Chǔzhí (王處直), Jìedùshǐ (節度使) of Yì Dìng (易定), Wáng Róng (王鎔), Jìedùshǐ (節度使) of Zhènzhōu (鎮州), and Jìn Wáng (晉王), Jìedùshǐ (節度使) of Hé Dōng (河東) and Shàngshū Lìng (尚書令), respectfully present this imperial patent to confer upon Yān Wáng (燕王), Jìedùshǐ (節度使) of Lúlóng (盧龍) and Hénghǎi (橫海) armies, Jiǎnjiào Tàishī (檢校太師) and concurrently Zhōngshū Lìng (中書令), the titles of Shàngshū Lìng (尚書令) and Shàngfù (尚父).'
In the fifth month,
envoys from the Six Zhèn (鎮) arrived,
and the Biàn (汴) envoys also gathered.
In the sixth month,
Shǒuguāng (守guāng) ordered the relevant departments to finalize the ceremonies for Shàngfù (尚父) and Cǎifǎngshǐ (採訪使)."
Liáng Tàizǔ Shílù (梁太祖實錄) makes no mention of Shǒuguāng's (守guāng) affairs,
only Biān Yílù (編遺錄) states:
"On the Rénchén (壬辰) day of the third month,
Géménshǐ (閤門使) Wáng Tóng (王瞳) and Shòu Zhǐ (受旨) Shǐ Yànhuán (史彥㣥) were dispatched to carry imperial gifts to Liú Shǒuguāng (劉守光) in Yōuzhōu (幽州).
On the Jiǎwǔ (甲午) day,
Shǒuguāng (守guāng) repeatedly submitted memorials,
generally stating that since Zhèn (鎮) and Dìng (定) had made peace with Hé Dōng (河東),
and concurrently dispatched envoys, he requested that the Tiānyòu (天祐) era name be used in his territory.
Shǒuguāng (守guāng) soon seized Wáng Tóng (王瞳), Shǐ Yànhuán (史彥㣥), and their entire entourage and imprisoned them.
They were released several days later."
According to Zhuāngzōng Shílù (莊宗實錄) and Nántáng Lièzǔ Shílù (南唐烈祖實錄), both state
"On the Xīnhài (辛亥) day of the third month, Jìn Wáng (晉王) sent Dài Hànchāo (戴漢āo) to propose Shǒuguāng (守guāng) as Shàngfù (尚父)."
Xīnhài (辛亥) is the 27th day of the third month.
Rénchén (壬辰) is the 8th day of the third month,
how could Wáng Tóng (王瞳) and others already be in Yōuzhōu (幽州)!
Jiǎwǔ (甲午) is the 10th day of the third month,
how could Shǒuguāng (守guāng) submit a memorial saying
"the Six Zhèn (鎮) propose your servant as Shàngfù (尚父)"!
The dates in Biān Yílù (編遺錄) are often incorrect,
so it is not adopted here.
10 The Emperor ordered Yáng Shīhòu (楊師厚) to lead thirty thousand troops to garrison Xíngzhōu (邢州).
This was to attack Zhào (趙).
11 The Shǔ (蜀) generals attacked the Qí (岐) troops,
defeating them repeatedly.
In autumn,
in the seventh month,
the Shǔ (蜀) ruler returned west,
leaving yùyíngshǐ (御營使) Chāng Wáng Zōnghuì (昌王宗鐬) to garrison Lìzhōu (利州).
12 On the Xīnchǒu (辛丑) day,
the Emperor escaped the summer heat at Zhāng Zōngshì's (張宗奭) residence.
Zhāng Quányì (張全義) was granted the name Zōngshì (宗奭) in Kāipíng (開平) first year, as seen in the previous volume.
According to Xuē Shǐ (薛史),
Zhāng Zōngshì's (張宗奭) private residence was in the Huìjié Fāng (會節坊) of Luòyáng (洛陽).
Zōngshì's (宗奭) son, Jìzuò (繼祚), overcome with indignation and shame,
wanted to assassinate him.
Zōngshì (宗奭) stopped him, saying:
"Our family was once in Héyáng (河陽),
besieged by Lǐ Hǎnzī (李罕之),
as seen in Volume 257, Táng Xīzōng Wéndé (唐僖宗文德) first year.
Thanks to his rescue,
we are able to have what we have today;
this kindness must not be forgotten."
So he stopped.
On the Jiǎchén (甲辰) day,
he returned to the palace.
13 Zhào Wáng Róng (趙王鎔), seeing Yáng Shīhòu (楊師厚) in Xíngzhōu (邢州),
was greatly frightened.
Jiǔyù Zhì (九域志) states: Xíngzhōu (邢州) is only 144 *lǐ* north of Zhàozhōu (趙州).
The army was at his border,
hence he was greatly frightened.
Jìn Wáng (晉王) considered Róng (鎔) an old friend of his father,
and treated him with great respect.
Róng (鎔) had previously been an equal of Jìn Wáng Kèyòng (晉王克用) in serving Táng (唐),
and they also had good relations.
Jìn Wáng (晉王) said:
"Zhū Wēn's (朱溫) evil is extreme;
Heaven will punish him.
Even people like Shīhòu (師厚) cannot save him.
Should there be any invasion,
I will personally lead my troops to confront them.
Uncle, do not worry about it."
Róng (鎔) raised a goblet to offer a toast,
calling Jìn Wáng (晉王) "Fourtysixth Maternal Uncle".
Jìn Wáng (晉王) was the forty-sixth.
Jìn Wáng (晉王) cut a piece of his collar as an oath,
promising to marry his daughter to him.
From then on, the alliance between Jìn (晉) and Zhào (趙) was solidified.
14 In the eighth month,
on the Gēngshēn (庚申) day,
the Shǔ (蜀) ruler arrived in Chéngdū (成都).
He returned from Lìzhōu (利州).
Yān Wáng Shǒuguāng was about to declare himself emperor.
Many of his generals and aides secretly discussed that it was inappropriate.
Shǒuguāng then set up an axe and a chopping block in the courtyard.
Zhì [chopping block],
is a wooden block for beheading.
"Any who dare to remonstrate shall be executed!"
Sūn Hè said,
"When Cāngzhōu was defeated,
I should have died,
but the King spared my life.
This event is mentioned in the previous volume, Kaīpíng Four.
Fēn,
pronounced fúwèn.
Liú Shǒuguāng imprisoned his father and killed his brother.
It would be righteous for the people of Yōu and Cāng not to share the same sky with him.
Sūn Hè received the trust of Liú Shǒuwén,
but was unable to die for him.
Instead, he carried the grace of Shǒuguāng's saving his life,
and remonstrated faithfully unto death.
This is to be able to die but not to die,
and to be able to live without dying.
Today,
how can I cherish my life and forget such grace!
I secretly believe that becoming emperor today is not advisable."
Shǒuguāng was enraged,
made him lie on the chopping block,
and ordered his soldiers to [AS-FE47] and eat him.
Hè cried out,
"Within a hundred days,
a great army will arrive!"
Shǒuguāng ordered his mouth to be stopped with earth,
and had him chopped into small pieces.
On the day of Jiǎzǐ,
Shǒuguāng ascended the imperial throne,
proclaiming his dynasty Great Yān,
and changing the reign title to Yìngtiān.
He appointed Liáng envoy Wáng Tóng as Left Chancellor,
Lúlóng Judge Qí Shè as Right Chancellor,
and Shǐ Yàn'ěng as Censor-in-Chief.
The Kǎoyì states: The compiled Yílù says Vice Censor-in-Chief.
Now following the Zhuāngzōng Shílù.
The Qìdān captured Píngzhōu,
causing alarm and disturbance among the Yān people.
Sòng Bái said: Píngzhōu,
in the time of Shùn, was within the territory of Yíngzhōu, one of the twelve provinces.
In the Zhōuguān Zhífāng, it was in the land of Yōuzhōu,
in the Spring and Autumn period, it was the land of the Shānrong Gūzhú and Báidí Féizǐ states,
and in the Hàn dynasty, it was the land of Féirú and Shíchéng.
In the early Wǔdé period of the Táng dynasty, Píngzhōu was established in Lúlóng.
On the day of Yǐhài,
Wáng Zōngkǎn, Wáng Zōnghè, Táng Dàoxí, and Wáng Zōngshào fought them at Qīngní Lǐng.
Qīngní Lǐng is fifty lǐ northwest of Chángjǔ Xiàn in Xīngzhōu.
It has ten thousand-ren cliffs,
and is often covered in clouds and rain,
so travelers often encounter muddy bogs.
The Cavalry and Infantry Commander Wáng Zōnghào fled to Xīngzhōu,
and drowned in the river.
This river
is the Jiālíng Jiāng.
Previously,
the Infantry Commander-in-Chief Wáng Zōngwǎn had built a city west of the county,
named Ānyuǎn Jūn.
The Jiǔyù Zhì states: Xī Xiàn is one hundred lǐ west of Xīngyuán Fǔ.
Zhījùn and Jìchóng pursued and besieged it.
The common opinion was to abandon Xīngyuán,
but Dàoxí said,
"Without Xīngyuán, there is no Ānyuǎn,
and Lìzhōu will then become enemy territory."
The Jiǔyù Zhì states: Xīngyuán is one hundred lǐ west to Xī Xiàn,
Xī Xiàn is forty-five lǐ to the border of Lìzhōu,
and from the border to Lìzhōu is two hundred and sixty-four lǐ.
The Shǔ ruler appointed Chāngwáng Zōnghuì as the Aīnyuán Zhāotǎo Shǐ (Supporting and Suppressing Envoy),
and Dìngróng Tuánliàn Shǐ Wáng Zōngbō as the Sì Zhāotǎo Mǎbù Dūzhīhuīshǐ (Fourth Suppressing Envoy and Commander-in-Chief of Cavalry and Infantry).
The Shǔ ruler had previously dispatched three suppressing envoys to attack Qí,
and now again appointed Wáng Zōnghuì as the Aīnyuán Zhāotǎo Shǐ,
making him the fourth suppressing envoy.
They fortified between the Lián and Ràng rivers.
The Lián river flows out from the northern valley of Dàbā Shān.
The Ràng river,
its source is in the Lián river,
after irrigating the fields, it flows southeast to the side of the ancient Liánshuǐ City.
The two rivers are southeast of Nánzhèng Xiàn.
Dù Yòu said: Mǐnzhōu Chāngmíng Xiàn has Liánshuǐ and Ràngshuǐ.
Sòng Bái's Xù Tōngdiǎn: The county has Qīnglián Xiāng and Ràngshuǐ Xiāng.
They greatly defeated them at Míngzhū Qǔ.
The next day, they fought again at Fúkǒu,
beheading Lǐ Yànchēn, the Governor of Chéngzhōu.
In the ninth month,
the Emperor's illness slightly improved.
Hearing that Jìn and Zhào planned to invade,
he personally led troops to resist them.
On the day of Wùxū,
Zhāng Zōngshì was appointed Protector of the Western Capital.
On the day of Gēngzǐ,
the Emperor departed Luòyáng.
On the day of Jiǎchén,
he arrived at Wèizhōu.
While he was eating,
a report from the front arrived that the Jìn army had already exited Jǐngxíng.
The Emperor hastily ordered his carriage northward towards Xíngmíng,
traveling day and night at double speed.
On the day of Bǐngwǔ,
he arrived at Xiāngzhōu.
The Jiǔyù Zhì states: Wèizhōu is one hundred and twenty-five lǐ north to Xiāngzhōu,
and from Xiāngzhōu further north one heads towards Xíngmíng.
Qù,
pronounced qīyù.
Then he stopped.
Lǐ Sī'ān, the Governor of Xiāngzhōu, did not expect the Emperor's sudden arrival,
and was completely unprepared,
for which he was stripped of his official rank and titles.
Qián Biāo, the Governor of Húzhōu, was a drunkard and murderer.
Fearing that Wúyuè Wáng Liú would punish him,
in winter,
tenth month,
on the first day of Xīnhài,
he killed the Supervising Commissioner Pān Cháng and the Investigating Official Zhōng Āndé,
and fled to Wú.
The Jìn King heard that Yān Lord Shǒuguāng had proclaimed himself emperor,
and laughed heartily, saying,
"When he seeks a longevity prophecy for his reign,
I shall inquire about his tripods."
He used the stories of King Chéng of Zhōu seeking a longevity prophecy and the Chu princes inquiring about the tripods to ridicule Shǒuguāng.
The Jìn King sent the Deputy Prefect of Tàiyuán, Lǐ Chéngxūn.
Chéngxūn arrived at Yōuzhōu,
using the etiquette for envoys from neighboring states.
The Yān official for diplomatic reception said,
"Our King is now Emperor,
so you should declare yourself a subject when you have an audience."
Chéngxūn replied,
"I received my appointment from the Táng court as Deputy Prefect of Tàiyuán.
The King of Yān may make his own subjects within his territory,
but how can he make an envoy from another state his subject!"
Shǒuguāng was angry,
and imprisoned him for several days.
He then brought him out and asked,
"Will you be my subject?"
Chéngxūn said,
"If the King of Yān can make my King his subject,
then I request to be his subject;
otherwise,
there is only death!"
Shǒuguāng ultimately could not make him yield.
The Shǔ ruler went to Lìzhōu.
Hearing that Wáng Zōngkǎn had been defeated by Qí,
he therefore returned to Lìzhōu to provide support.
Wáng Cóng, the Usher of the Juéyún Army, defeated the Qí army,
captured their general Lǐ Yàntài,
and captured or beheaded three thousand five hundred heads.
On the day of Yǐmǎo,
the Live Capture General Péng Jūnjí broke two Qí strongholds,
capturing or beheading three thousand heads.
Wáng Zōngkǎn sent his subordinate general Lín Sī'è to travel through the heart of Bā to Níxī.
Bāzhōu is in the middle of the Three Bā,
hence called Zhōngbā.
South of Xīngyuán there is a great road,
passing through Gūyún Liǎngjiǎo,
and crossing Mǐcāng Shān leads to Bāzhōu.
According to the account of the Later Táng's campaign against Shǔ and their return,
Wèiwáng Jìjí and Lǐ Shàochēn's army passed by Shěníxī,
which should be north of Jiànzhōu in the Lìzhōu area.
The Shǔ ruler ordered Wáng Zōngbì, the Commander-in-Chief for Road Opening, to lead troops to relieve Ānyuǎn,
and fought Liú Zhījùn at Xiégǔ,
On the 21st *jiǎyín* night,
Dì Fā (帝發) departed from Xiāngzhōu (相州).
On *yǐmǎo* (乙卯),
he arrived at Huánshuǐ (洹水).
That night,
a border official reported that the Jìn (晉) and Zhào (趙) armies were advancing south.
The Emperor immediately moved his troops.
On *bǐngchén* (丙辰),
he reached Wèixiàn (魏縣).
Huánshuǐ (洹水) is in the western part of Wèizhōu (魏州), within Chéng'ān Xiàn (成安縣).
The *Jiǔyù Zhì* (九域志) states: Chéng'ān Xiàn (成安縣) in Wèizhōu (魏州) has Huánshuǐ Zhèn (洹水鎮).
Chéng'ān Xiàn (成安縣) is thirty-five *lǐ* (里) west of the prefecture.
Wèixiàn (魏縣) is thirty-five *lǐ* (里) west of Wèizhōu (魏州).
"The Shātuó (沙陀) have arrived!"
The officers and soldiers were terrified,
many deserted,
and severe punishments could not stop them.
Soon after, another report came that there were no bandits,
and only then did order return among all ranks.
The morale of a defeated army,
once lost, never recovers;
this is what is meant.
*Fù* (復)
is pronounced *fú yòu fān* (扶又翻).
On *wùwǔ* (戊午),
Bèizhōu (貝州) reported that the Jìn (晉) army had attacked Dōngwǔ (東武),
but soon withdrew.
The Emperor, having repeatedly suffered setbacks at Jiāzhài (夾寨) and Bǎixiāng (柏鄉) –
the defeat at Jiāzhài (夾寨) is recorded in volume 266, during Kāipíng (開平) 2nd year;
the defeat at Bǎixiāng (柏鄉) is recorded in the previous volume for this year –
desired to avenge his disgrace.
His spirits were low,
and he was often agitated and angry.
Meritorious officials and veteran generals were often executed for minor offenses,
increasing the fear in people's hearts.
The *Xuē Shǐ Běnjì* (薛史本紀) states: When the Emperor arrived at Xiāngzhōu (相州),
Dèng Jìyún (鄧季筠), Left Lóngxiáng (龍驤) Metropolitan Drill Instructor, Hé Língchóu (何令稠), Wèibó (魏博) Cavalry Metropolitan Commander, and Chén Língxūn (陳令勳), Right Flank Cavalry Metropolitan Commander,
were all腰斩 (yāozhǎn) at the army gate
because their horses were thin;
next, at Wèixiàn (魏縣),
Huáng Wénjìng (黃文靖), Vanguard Commander, was executed.
The Emperor, in his fury, acted rashly
to avenge the disgrace of two defeats.
Had he indeed encountered the Jìn (晉) and Zhào (趙) forces,
he would surely have been defeated again.
On *rénwǔ* (壬午),
the Emperor returned south.
On the 22nd, Yān (燕) Lord Shǒuguāng (守光) gathered his generals and officials to plan an attack on Yìdìng (易定).
Féng Dào (馮道) of Jǐngchéng (景城), a staff officer in Yōuzhōu (幽州), thought it was not yet feasible;
Jǐngchéng Xiàn (景城縣) belonged to Yíngzhōu (瀛州) in the Hàn (漢) dynasty and was an old county name.
He was imprisoned,
but someone rescued him,
and he was spared.
Dào (道) fled to Jìn (晉).
Zhāng Chéngyè (張承業) recommended him to the Jìn (晉) King,
who appointed him as his chief secretary.
From then on, Féng Dào (馮道) served the Táng (唐), Jìn (晉), Hàn (漢), and Zhōu (周) dynasties,
reaching the highest positions among officials.
Yet, no remonstrances or arguments are heard from him.
Perhaps he learned a lesson from the misfortune of remonstrating with Shǒuguāng (守光).
On *dīnghài* (丁亥),
Wáng Chǔzhí (王處直) appealed to Jìn (晉) for help.
On the 23rd, Dùan Míngyuǎn (段明遠), Prefect of Huáizhōu (懷州), had a sister who was a beauty.
On *wùzǐ* (戊子),
the Emperor arrived at Huòjiā (獲嘉).
The *Jiǔyù Zhì* (九域志) states: Huòjiā Xiàn (獲嘉縣) is one hundred and fifty *lǐ* (里) northeast of Huáizhōu (懷州).
The Emperor was pleased.
Dùan Míngyuǎn (段明遠) later changed his name to Níng (凝).
He gained favor and trust through this,
and rose to the position of a great general,
which ultimately led to the downfall of Liáng (梁).
On the 24th *gēngyín* (庚寅),
Gāo Wànxīng (高萬興), Jìedùshǐ (節度使) of Bǎosài (保塞), reported that he had dispatched Metropolitan Commander Gāo Wànjīn (高萬金) with troops to attack Yánzhōu (鹽州),
and its Prefect Gāo Xíngcún (高行存) surrendered.
The *Kǎoyì* (考異) states: The *Shílù* (實錄) says:
"On *dīngwèi* (丁未) in the 6th month of Kāipíng (開平) 3rd year,
Hán Xùn (韓遜) of Língwǔ (靈武) reported the recapture of Yánzhōu (鹽州)
and the capture of the pseudo-Prefect Lǐ Jìzhí (李繼直) and sixty-two others.
" Regarding the surrender of Gāo Xíngcún (高行存) in this year,
it says: "Yánzhōu (鹽州) is interlaced with Túbō (吐蕃) and Dǎngxiàng (党項) territories,
serving as a vital pass between the two regions.
Moreover, the benefits of the salt marshes at Wūchí (烏池)
constantly attracted the barbarians and Qiāng (羌) tribes.
In the early Jiànzhōng (建中) era of Táng (唐), it was captured by Túbō (吐蕃)
who razed its walls before leaving.
As a result, Yín (銀), Xià (夏), Níng (寧), Yán (延) up to Língwǔ (靈武)
were guarded annually by no fewer than forty thousand soldiers from Hénán (河南), Shāndōng (山東), Huáinán (淮南), Qīng (青), Xú (徐), Jiāng (江), Zhè (浙) and other circuits,
known as the Autumn Defense.
In Zhēnyuán (貞元) 9th year,
when court affairs were somewhat settled,
Marshal Hún Jiān (渾瑊) was ordered to lead thirty thousand troops to retake the area
and build a hundred-yard wall there.
From then on, barbarian incursions ceased,
and border troubles ended.
During the Táng (唐) revolution,
it was lost again.
Now, with merely a partial force,
this vital stronghold has been quickly recovered.
The right arm of the nation,
may its affliction now cease!"
Many of Lǐ Màozhēn's (李茂貞) adopted sons have the character
"Jì" (繼)
in their names.
The recovery in Kāipíng (開平) 3rd year
seems to belong to Fèngxiáng (鳳翔).
Now it is recovered again,
and it says
"the Táng (唐) revolution lost it."
There must be a mistake in one of the accounts,
or perhaps it was gained in Kāipíng (開平) and then lost again.
On the 25th *rénchén* (壬辰),
the Emperor arrived at Luòyáng (洛陽),
and his illness recurred.
