On the 26th, Shǔ (蜀) King Zōngbì (宗弼) defeated the Qí (岐) army at Jīnniú (金牛),
capturing sixteen stockades,
taking over six thousand captives and decapitated heads,
and capturing their general Guō Cún (郭存) and others.
On *bǐngshēn* (丙申),
Wáng Zōnghuì (王宗鐬) and Wáng Zōngbò (王宗播) defeated the Qí (岐) army at Huángniúchuān (黃牛川),
capturing their general Sū Hòu (蘇厚) and others.
On *dīngyǒu* (丁酉),
the Shǔ (蜀) Lord traveled from Lìzhōu (利州) to Xìngyuán (興元).
Once the relief forces had gathered,
the Ānyuǎn (安遠) army sighted their banners –
the banners here refer to those of the Shǔ (蜀) Lord –
and,
together with the relief forces,
attacked the Qí (岐) army from both sides,
greatly defeating them.
They captured twenty-one stockades
and decapitated their general Lǐ Tíngzhì (李廷志) and others.
On *jǐhài* (己亥),
the Qí (岐) army lifted the siege and fled.
They lifted the siege of Ānyuǎn (安遠) and fled.
And were defeated again.
On *gēngzǐ* (庚子),
the Shǔ (蜀) Lord returned west.
After the Qí (岐) army was defeated and fled,
he returned.
Shí Jiǎnyǒng (石簡顒), a trusted aide of the Qí (岐) King, slandered Líu Zhījùn (劉知俊) to the Qí (岐) King,
who then took away his troops.
Lǐ Jìchóng (李繼崇) spoke to the King, saying:
"Zhījùn (知俊) is a brave man;
he came to us when he was in dire straits.
It is inappropriate to dismiss him due to slander."
The King then executed Jiǎnyǒng (簡顒) to appease him.
Jìchóng (繼崇) invited Zhījùn (知俊) and his entire clan to reside in Qínzhōu (秦州).
Lǐ Jìchóng (李繼崇) was garrisoned in Qínzhōu (秦州) at the time.
Jìchóng (繼崇) soon proved unable to hold Qínzhōu (秦州),
and Líu Zhījùn (劉知俊) consequently also surrendered to Shǔ (蜀).
On the 27th *wùshēn* (戊申),
Yān (燕) Lord Shǒuguāng (守光) led twenty thousand troops to attack Yìdìng (易定)
and besieged Róngchéng (容城).
Róngchéng (容城) was a Hàn (漢) county name,
belonging to Yìzhōu (易州) in the Táng (唐) dynasty,
and Xióngzhōu (雄州) in the Sòng (宋) dynasty.
In the 28th, 12th month,
on *yǐmǎo* (乙卯),
Mǎ Cóng (馬賨), Acting Commissioner of Lángzhōu (朗州), was made Jìedùshǐ (節度使) of Yǒngshùn (永順) and *Tóng Píngzhāngshì* (同平章事).
On the 29th, Lú Yánchāng (盧延昌), Acting Commissioner of Zhènnán (鎮南), indulged in excessive hunting,
so Lí Qiú (黎球), Commander of Bǎishèng (百勝) Army, killed him
and established himself.
He planned to kill Tán Quánbō (譚全播),
but Quánbō (全播) feigned illness and requested retirement,
thus being spared.
On *bǐngchén* (丙辰),
Qiú (球) was made Fángyùshǐ (防禦使) of Qiánzhōu (虔州).
Not long after,
Qiú (球) died,
and Yájìang (牙將) Lǐ Yàntú (李彥圖) temporarily managed the prefectural affairs.
Quánbō (全播) increasingly claimed to be gravely ill.
Líu Yán (劉巖), hearing of Quánbō's (全播) illness,
dispatched troops to attack Sháozhōu (韶州),
and captured it.
Prefect Líao Shuǎng (廖爽) fled to Chǔ (楚).
Chǔ (楚) King Yīn (殷) memorialized for him to be made Prefect of Yǒngzhōu (永州).
On the 30th *dīngsì* (丁巳),
the Shǔ (蜀) Lord arrived at Chéngdū (成都).
He returned to Chéngdū (成都) from Xìngyuán (興元).
On the 31st *wùwǔ* (戊午),
Qǔ Měi (曲美), Acting Commissioner of Jìnghǎi (靜海), was made Jìedùshǐ (節度使).
On the 32nd *guǐhài* (癸亥),
Yáo Yànzhāng (姚彥章), Xíngjūn Sīmǎ (行軍司馬) of Jìngjiāng (靜江), was made Níngyuǎn (寧遠) Jìedù Fùshǐ (節度副使)
and provisionally governed Róngzhōu (容州),
at the request of Chǔ (楚) King Yīn (殷).
Líu Yán (劉巖) sent troops to attack Róngzhōu (容州).
Yīn (殷) dispatched Metropolitan Commander Xǔ Déxūn (許德勳) with Guìzhōu (桂州) troops to relieve it.
Yànzhāng (彥章) was unable to defend,
so he relocated the people of Róngzhōu (容州) and its official treasury to Chángshā (長沙).
Yán (巖) then took control of Róngguǎn (容管) and Gāozhōu (高州).
On the 33rd *jiǎzǐ* (甲子),
the Jìn (晉) King dispatched Zhōu Déwēi (周德威), General Commander of Fān (蕃) and Hàn (漢) cavalry and infantry,
with thirty thousand troops to attack Yān (燕),
to relieve Yìdìng (易定).
In this 34th year,
the Shǔ (蜀) Lord made Pān Kàng (潘炕), Internal Privy Council Commissioner, Jìedùshǐ (節度使) of Wǔtài (武泰).
The Táng (唐) dynasty established the Wǔtài (武泰) Army in Qiánzhōu (黔州).
1 In spring,
in the first month,
Zhōu Déwēi marched eastward from Fēihú,
setting out from Dàizhōu via Fēihú.
Sòng Bái said: Fēihú County
was territory of Dài Commandery in the Hàn dynasty.
Cáo Wèi enfeoffed Yuè Jìn as Marquis of Guǎngchāng State.
During the Later Zhōu, Guǎngchāng County was established in Wǔlóngchéng;
in the Suí dynasty, it was renamed Fēihú County,
named after Fēihúkǒu to the north of the county.
King of Zhào
was Wáng Róng.
Yìwǔ
was Wáng Chùzhí.
On the day Bǐngxū,
the armies of the three garrisons advanced to attack Qígōuguān in Yān,
and captured it;
the three garrisons were
Bìng, Zhèn, and Dìng.
Qígōuguān was south of Zhuōzhōu
and north of the Jùmǎhé River in Yìzhōu.
From the pass westward to Yìzhōu was sixty *lǐ*.
From the Jùmǎhé River eastward to Xīnchéng County was forty *lǐ*.
On the day Wùzǐ,
Zhuōzhōu was besieged.
Sòng Bái said: Zhuōzhōu
was the ancient land of Zhuōlù.
Emperor Gāo of Hàn established Zhuō Commandery;
Wèi renamed it Fányáng Commandery,
taking its name from Hàn Zhuō County being north of the Fàn River.
In Dàlì 4 of the Táng dynasty, Zhuōzhōu was established.
South to Mòzhōu was one hundred sixty *lǐ*;
northeast to Yōuzhōu was one hundred twenty *lǐ*.
Liú Qùfēi, a retainer of Liú Shǒuqí, shouted loudly below the city walls,
saying to Zhī Wēn:
“Little Master Liú from Hédōng has come to avenge his father;
how does this concern you that you hold out so firmly?”
Shǒuqí removed his helmet and encouraged him.
Liú Shǒuqí defected to Jìn;
see volume 266, Kāipíng 1.
Láo,
pronounced *lìdào fān*.
So he surrendered.
Zhōu Déwēi was jealous of Shǒuqí's achievements
and slandered him to the King of Jìn;
this was Zhōu Déwēi's narrow-mindedness.
Jiàng,
pronounced *hùjiāng fān*.
Shǒuqí feared being punished,
and fled with Qùfēi and the *jìnshì* Zhào Fèng.
The Emperor appointed Shǒuqí as the Administrator of Bózhōu.
Qùfēi and Fèng
were both from Yōuzhōu.
Previously,
Yān ruler Shǒuguāng had registered all able-bodied men in his territory,
tattooing their faces to turn them into soldiers;
even scholars were not exempt.
Fèng feigned being a monk and fled to Jìn,
and Shǒuqí took him as a retainer.
On the day Dīngyǒu,
Déwēi arrived below the city walls of Yōuzhōu,
and Shǒuguāng came to ask for help.
In the second month,
the Emperor's illness slightly improved.
He debated personally leading an attack on Zhèn and Dìng to rescue him.
2 The Emperor heard that Qí and Shǔ were attacking each other.
On the day Xīnyǒu,
he sent Grand Master of Luxuries Lú Pín and others as envoys to Shǔ,
sending a letter to the Shǔ ruler,
addressing him as elder brother.
The Emperor and the Shǔ ruler had both risen from humble beginnings.
Shǔ had strong armies and treacherous terrain,
and the Emperor judged that his own strength could not subdue it,
so he used the courtesies of an allied state
and addressed him as elder brother.
3 On the day Jiǎzǐ,
the Emperor departed from Luòyáng.
Many accompanying officials, fearing the Emperor's unpredictable executions,
were reluctant to travel.
The Emperor heard of this
and grew even angrier.
That day,
he arrived at Báimǎdùn.
He granted food to his accompanying officials,
many of whom had not yet arrived,
so he sent cavalry to urge them on the road.
Left Sanqí Chángshì Sūn Zhì, Right Jiànyì Dàfū Zhāng Yǎn, and Bīngbù Lángzhōng Zhāng Jùn arrived last.
The Emperor ordered them beaten to death.
Yǎn
was Zōngshì's nephew.
On the day Bǐngyín,
the Emperor arrived at Wǔzhì.
The *Jiǔyù Zhì* states: Wǔzhì County is eighty *lǐ* east of Huáizhōu.
On the day Dīngmǎo,
he arrived at Huòjiā.
The Emperor recalled Lǐ Sī'ān's shortcomings in providing supplies last year,
demoted him to Sīhù of Liǔzhōu,
and when announcing his dismissal, praised Míngyuǎn's ability, saying:
“Observing Míngyuǎn's loyalty and diligence,
how does Sī'ān's rebellion and arrogance compare!”
Soon after, Sī'ān was exiled to Yázhōu
and then granted death.
At that time, those exiled to distant places were all granted death.
Liǔzhōu was far beyond the mountain ranges,
and Yázhōu required crossing whale-infested waters again;
how could Sī'ān possibly have reached it!
On the day Yǐhài,
the Emperor arrived at Wèizhōu.
He ordered the Grand Commander of the Expedition and Xuānyì Military Governor Yáng Shīhòu, and his deputy, former Héyáng Military Governor Lǐ Zhōuyí, to besiege Zǎoqiáng.
He ordered the Commander of Recruitment and Reception and Pínglú Military Governor Hè Délún, and his deputy, Tiānpíng Acting Military Governor Yuán Xiàngxiān, to besiege Tiáoxiàn.
The *Jiǔyù Zhì* states: Zǎoqiáng County is fifty-five *lǐ* southeast of Zhènzhōu.
Tiáoxiàn is one hundred fifty *lǐ* northeast of Jìzhōu.
Sòng Bái said: Tiáoxiàn was the Hàn Marquisate of Tiáo;
in Kāihuáng 5 of the Suí dynasty, Tiáo County was renamed Tiáoxiàn.
Tiáo
is pronounced *tiáo*.
Héxī Hú people;
Xiàngxiān
was from Xiàyì.
On the day Wùyín,
the Emperor arrived at Bèizhōu.
4 The tribal chiefs Sòng Yè and Chāng Shīyì of Chénzhōu led their followers to surrender to Chǔ.
King Yīn of Chǔ appointed Yè as Administrator of Chénzhōu,
and Shīyì as Administrator of Xùzhōu.
5 The Emperor traveled day and night.
In the third month,
on the day Xīnsì,
he arrived south of Xiàbó
and ascended Guān Jīn's tomb.
Southeast of the ancient city of Hàn Guānjīn County was a green hill,
which was the tomb of Dòu Hòu's father, Shàoxiāo, from Emperor Wén of Hàn's time.
Xiāo was a local,
who, during the chaos of Qín,
hid himself by fishing and died by falling into an abyss.
When Emperor Jǐng ascended,
the Empress sent envoys to fill the abyss and bury her father,
raising a large tomb southeast of Guānjīn city.
The county residents called it Dòu's Green Hill.
Not knowing it was the Emperor,
they rushed forward to press him.
Someone reported:
“The Jìn army has arrived in great numbers!”
The Emperor abandoned his traveling tent
and quickly led his troops to Zǎoqiáng,
joining with Yáng Shīhòu's army.
Xí
was from Zhàozhōu.
Zǎoqiáng was small but strongly fortified.
The Zhào people gathered several thousand elite soldiers to defend it.
Shīhòu attacked it fiercely,
but after several days it did not fall.
The walls were damaged and repaired repeatedly,
and the dead and wounded numbered in the tens of thousands.
This refers to the dead and wounded among the attacking soldiers.
They considered surrendering.
One soldier indignantly said:
“Ever since the defeat at Báixiāng,
the bandits have glared at us Zhèn people with fierce anger.
To surrender to them now
is like throwing oneself into the jaws of tigers and wolves.
In such desperate straits,
what use is my life!
I ask to go alone and test them.”
At night,
he was lowered from the city wall
and went to the Liáng army, feigning surrender.
Lǐ Zhōuyí summoned him and asked about the city's defenses.
He replied:
“It will not be easy to take in less than half a month.”
Then he plotted, saying:
“Móu”
should be written
“Qǐng”.
“Since I have pledged my allegiance,
I wish to obtain a sword
and, risking my life, be the first to ascend
and take the head of the defending general.”
Zhōuyí did not permit it,
and made him carry a burden and follow the army.
The soldier found an opportunity and used the burden to strike Zhōuyí's head,
knocking him to the ground.
His attendants arrived to help,
and he was saved.
The Emperor heard of this
and grew even angrier.
He ordered Shīhòu to attack day and night.
On the day Bǐngxū,
he captured it,
killing everyone regardless of age,
filling the city with blood.
Initially,
Dì led his troops across the river,
claiming 500,000 men.
Jìn Xīnzhōu Cìshǐ Lǐ Cúnshěn was stationed at Zhàozhōu,
and, concerned about the small number of his troops,
his Bìjiàng Zhào Xíngshí requested to enter Tǔmén to avoid them.
Cúnshěn refused.
"Entering Tǔmén means retreating to Jìnyáng!"
Cúnshěn said to Shǐ Jiàntáng and Lǐ Sìgōng:
"Our King is currently occupied with affairs in Yōují,
with no troops coming here.
The matters in the south are entrusted to a few of us.
Now, Xiànyàn is in urgent peril;
how can we just sit and watch!
If the bandits capture Xiànyàn,
they will surely invade Shēn and Jì to the west,
and our troubles will deepen.
We must use an ingenious strategy with you gentlemen to defeat them."
Cúnshěn then led his troops to hold Xiàbóqiáo.
The Zhāngshuǐ river flows past Xiàbóxiàn;
it was a bridge spanning the Zhāngshuǐ.
Jiàntáng divided his subordinates into five detachments,
each with one hundred men.
One went to Héngshuǐ,
one to Nángōng,
one to Xìndū.
Xìndū,
an ancient county of Hàn,
was under Jìzhōu in Táng times.
Although its administrative seat was within the city walls,
the territory it governed encompassed the near suburbs of Jìzhōu.
He personally led one detachment deep into the territory,
and he and Sìgōng captured all the woodcutters and fodder gatherers of the Liáng army they encountered,
seizing several hundred people.
The next day, they met at Xiàbóqiáo,
killed them all,
and left a few, severing their arms and letting them go,
saying:
"Go tell Zhū Gōng for us: 'The Jìn King's grand army has arrived!'"
At that time, Xiànyàn had not yet fallen.
Dì led Yáng Shīhòu's 50,000 troops
to join Hè Délún in attacking it.
On the day Dīnghài,
they first arrived west of the county.
Before they could set up camp,
Jiàntáng and Sìgōng, each leading three hundred cavalry,
displaying the flags, banners, and uniforms of the Liáng army,
mingled with the woodcutters and fodder gatherers.
As evening approached,
they reached Délún's camp gate,
killed the guards,
set fires, shouted loudly,
shot arrows wildly,
and galloped about.
When night fell,
they each took severed heads and captives and departed.
There was great confusion in the camp,
and they did not know what to do.
The armless men returned again, saying:
"The Jìn army has arrived in great force!"
Dì was greatly alarmed,
burned his camp, and fled in the night.
With Zhū Wēn's cunning
and Yáng Shīhòu's support,
if they had met another enemy,
they might still have maintained order amidst the chaos.
Now, Shǐ Jiàntáng and others, with their surprise troops, disrupted them,
leading them to fall into disarray,
to the point of scattering and being unable to recover.
This was because the commanders, high and low, already harbored a fear of Jìn.
They took a winding route for one hundred and fifty *lǐ*,
arriving at Jìzhōu on the morning of Wùzǐ.
The farmers of Xiànyàn all carried hoes and brandished clubs to pursue them,
abandoning countless military supplies and equipment.
Afterwards, cavalry were again sent to scout,
and they reported:
"The Jìn army has truly not arrived;
these were merely Vanguard Shǐ's skirmishers."
The Jìn King had appointed Shǐ Jiàntáng as Commander of the Vanguard,
hence the稱.
He personally commanded the six armies,
yet fled at the sight of the enemy's skirmishers,
hence his shame;
his army had sallied out repeatedly and been defeated repeatedly,
hence his fury.
He could not control himself,
indicating the extremity of his state.
He could not ride in a shoulder palanquin.
He stayed in Bèizhōu for more than ten days,
before his various armies finally reassembled.
Such was the extent of their dispersion that it took a long time for them to regroup.
6 Yìchāng Jiédùshǐ Liú Jìwēi was young,
and his debauchery and cruelty resembled his father.
Liú Jìwēi's father was Shǒuguāng.
Wàn Jìn was enraged
and killed him.
The next morning,
he summoned the grand general Zhōu Zhīyù
and informed him of the situation.
Wàn Jìn proclaimed himself Liúhòu
and appointed Zhīyù as Zuǒ Dū Yāyá.
On the day Gēngzǐ,
he sent an envoy to present a memorial requesting surrender,
and also sent an envoy to surrender to Jìn.
The Jìn King ordered Zhōu Déwēi to pacify him.
Zhīyù felt uneasy
and thus fled to Dì.
Dì established the Guīhuàjūn for him,
appointed Zhīyù as its Commandery Commander,
and all soldiers who came from Héshuò
were attached to it.
On the day Xīnchǒu,
Wàn Jìn was appointed Yìchāng Liúhòu.
On the day Jiǎchén,
Yìchāng was renamed Shùnhuàjūn,
and Wàn Jìn was appointed Jiédùshǐ.
This sets the stage for Yáng Shīhòu to abduct and relocate Zhāng Wànjìn.
7 On the day Yǐsì,
Dì departed Bèizhōu;
on the day Dīngwèi,
he arrived at Wèizhōu.
Bèizhōu is two hundred and ten *lǐ* south of Wèizhōu.
8 On the day Wùshēn,
Zhōu Déwēi sent Bìjiàng Lǐ Cúnhuī and others to attack Wǎqiáo Guān.
The Jiǔyùzhì states: Wǎqiáo Guān is one hundred and twenty *lǐ* south of Zhuōzhōu.
Yán,
a native of Yōuzhōu,
had a superficial knowledge of books and historical records.
The Jìn King wanted him to tutor his son Jìjí,
but Yán firmly declined.
The Jìn King was angry
and was about to execute him.
The Jiàoliànshǐ Mèng Zhīxiáng, barefoot, entered to remonstrate, saying:
"While powerful enemies remain,
how can Your Highness, in a fit of anger, slay a righteous man who has embraced us?"
This meant it was not the way to attract and win over the people of Yān.
Zhīxiáng,
son of Qiān.
Mèng Qiān surrendered Xíngzhōu to Jìn,
then betrayed Jìn and surrendered Xíngzhōu to Liáng.
Mèng Zhīxiáng begins here.
Lǐ Kèrang,
brother of Jìn King Kèyòng.
9 Wú Zhènnán Jiédùshǐ Liú Wēi,
Shèzhōu Guānchásǐ Táo Yǎ,
Xuānzhōu Guānchásǐ Lǐ Yù,
Chángzhōu Cìshǐ Lǐ Jiǎn,
were all former generals of Wǔzhōng Wáng,
and had rendered great service.
Yáng Xíngmì was posthumously honored as Wǔzhōng Wáng.
Xú Wēn, from the position of Yòuyá Zhǐhuīshǐ, wielded political power.
See volume 266, Kāipíng first year.
Lǐ Yù was especially vehement,
often saying:
"Who is Xú Wēn?
I have never met him,
yet he suddenly governs the state!"
The Guǎnyìshǐ Xú Jiè was sent as an envoy to Wúyuè.
On his way, he passed through Xuānzhōu.
Wēn sent Jiè to persuade Yù to come and see the new King.
Yù initially agreed.
Jiè said:
"If you do not,
if you do not..."
This means 'if you do not do as I say'.
Yù angrily said:
"You say I am rebelling,
but isn't killing the Shìzhōng not rebellion?"
Shìzhōng
refers to Wēiwáng.
Yáng Wò was posthumously honored as Wēiwáng.
Lǐ Yù openly accused Xú Wēn of killing him.
Wáng Tán, Deputy Commissioner of Huáinán Commandery, was appointed Xuānzhōu Zhìzhìshǐ.
"Wáng Tán"
should perhaps be
"Wáng Tán" with a different character.
The Dū Zhǐhuīshǐ Chái Zàiyòng was sent to lead troops from Shēng, Rùn, Chí, and Shè to install Tán in Xuānzhōu.
Shēngzhōu Deputy Commissioner Xú Zhīgào served as his deputy.
Yù refused to be replaced.
Zàiyòng attacked Xuānzhōu,
but after more than a month, could not conquer it.
10Summer,
fourth month,
on the day Guǐchǒu,
Chǔ Wáng Yīn was appointed Jiédùshǐ of Wǔ'ān, Wǔchāng, Jìngjiāng, and Níngyuǎn,
and Dūtǒng of the mobile armies on all four fronts of Hóng and È.
This was intended to make him attack Yáng's Hóng and È.
On the 11th day, *yǐmǎo*,
Bó Wáng Yǒuwén came to court,
coming to court at Wèizhōu Traveling Palace.
On the day *dīngsì*,
the Emperor departed from Wèizhōu;
on the day *jǐwèi*,
he arrived at Líyáng,
where he was delayed by illness;
on the day *yǐchǒu*,
he arrived at Huázhōu.
From Líyáng to Huázhōu
is merely across the Great River.
The old city of Huázhōu is now submerged in the river.
On the 12th day, the Qiānghú chieftain Dǒng Zhuó of Wéizhōu rebelled,
and the Lord of Shǔ dispatched Zhào Chuò, the Commander of the Imperial Guard, to suppress him.
On the 13th day, *jǐsì*,
the Emperor arrived at Dàliáng.
The Emperor heard that Lǐngnán and Chǔ were at war with each other.
On the day *jiǎxū*,
he appointed Wéi Jiǎn, the Right Sanjì Chángshì, and others as peace envoys to Tán and Guǎng,
to resolve the conflict.
On the 15th day, *wùyín*,
the Emperor departed from Dàliáng.
Zhōu Déwēi reported to Jìn Wáng
that with too few troops it would be insufficient to attack the city,
stating that Yōuzhōu was large and fortified,
and could not be attacked with a small force.
Lǐ Sìyuán attacked Yíngzhōu,
and its Prefect Zhào Jìng surrendered.
In the fifth month,
on the day *jiǎshēn*,
the Emperor arrived at Luòyáng,
his illness having greatly worsened.
Sīkōng, Ménxià Shìláng, and Tóng Píngzhāngshì Xuē Yíyǔ passed away.
The Lord of Yān, Shǒu Guāng, dispatched his general Shàn Tíngguī with ten thousand elite troops to sally forth and engage in battle.
They met Zhōu Déwēi at Lóngtóu Gāng.
Lóngtóu Gāng is located southeast of Yōuzhōu city.
The *Kǎoyì* says: The *Zhuāngzōng Shílù* records it as
“Yángtóu Gāng,”
but we now follow the *Zhuāngzōng Lièzhuàn*.
The *Zhuāngzōng Shílù*:
“On the first day of the fourth month, *jǐmǎo*,
Zhōu Déwēi captured Shàn Tíngguī,
and advanced his army to Dàchéng Zhuāng.”
Xuē Shǐ and the biography of Zhōu Déwēi in the *Zhuāngzōng Lièzhuàn* state,
“Tíngguī was captured on the seventh day of the fifth month,
and on the twelfth day, they reached Dàchéng Zhuāng.”
We now follow this account.
[Tíngguī said,] “Today I shall surely capture Zhōu Yángwǔ and present him.”
Yángwǔ
was Déwēi’s nickname.
During the battle,
seeing Déwēi in the formation,
he seized his spear and pursued him alone on horseback.
The spear reached Déwēi’s back,
but Déwēi turned his body to dodge it,
then wielded his club to counter-attack and knock Tíngguī off his horse.
Shàn Tíngguī’s horse was galloping at full speed,
and he could not stop its momentum.
Zhōu Déwēi turned his body to avoid its thrust,
and as the horse passed slightly forward,
Déwēi was already within spear range.
He wielded his club and struck Tíngguī.
Where could Tíngguī dodge?
This is why he fell from his horse.
In hand-to-hand combat,
a saber is not as good as a club;
this is what is meant.
He was placed at the camp gate.
The Yān army retreated and fled.
Déwēi led his cavalry to pursue them,
and the Yān army suffered a great defeat,
with three thousand heads taken.
Tíngguī was
a valiant Yān general.
The Yān people lost him,
and their morale was crushed.
On the day *jǐchǒu*,
Shǔ granted a general amnesty.
Lǐ Yù’s youngest son was a *yájiàng* in Huáinán,
and Yù loved him dearly.
Xú Wēn captured him
and displayed him beneath the walls of Xuānzhōu city.
His son wept and cried for his life,
and Yù, because of this, could not bear to fight.
Those who undertake great deeds should not care for their families.
Since Lǐ Yù was an enemy of Xú Wēn,
how could he care for just one son?
[Xú Wēn] used the order of Wú Wáng to persuade him,
saying:
“If you are truly determined to rebel,
I ask that you be executed to make an example;
otherwise,
follow me and surrender.”
Yù then opened the gates and surrendered.
Wēn ordered Chái Zàiyòng to execute him
and exterminate his clan.
Thereupon, the generals began to fear Wēn,
and none dared to disobey his commands.
“Generals”
refers to people like Liú Wēi and Táo Yǎ.
Xú Zhīgào was promoted to Prefect of Shēngzhōu for his merits.
Zhīgào served Wēn very diligently,
enduring hardship and humiliation,
sometimes not untying his belt all night.
Because of this, Wēn especially loved him,
and often said to his sons:
“Can you serve me as well as Zhīgào?”
Xú Wēn, by serving Yáng Xíngmì well, usurped the power of Wú;
Xú Zhīgào, by serving Xú Wēn well, usurped the power of the Xú clan.
Was it Heaven,
or man?
[Wēn] focused solely on military affairs,
not caring about the welfare of the people;
Zhīgào, in Shēngzhōu,
uniquely selected honest officials,
reformed and clarified governance and education,
and attracted scholars and officials from all directions,
spending his family wealth without reservation.
Sòng Qíqiū, a *jìnshì* from Hóngzhōu,
was skilled in the art of vertical and horizontal alliances.
He sought an audience with Zhīgào,
who was impressed by him,
and appointed him as a *tuīguān*.
He, along with the *pànguān* Wáng Lìngmóu and *cānjūn* Wáng Hóng, were solely responsible for strategy and deliberation,
with the *yálì* Mǎ Rényù, Zhōu Zōng, and Cáo Cóng as his confidants.
Rényù was
from Péngchéng;
Zōng
was from Liánshuǐ.
This laid the groundwork for Zhīgào’s usurpation of the Yáng clan.
In the intercalary month,
on the day *rénxū*,
the Emperor’s illness worsened significantly.
He said to his close ministers:
“I have managed the empire for thirty years.
The Emperor began his enterprise when he garrisoned Xuānwǔ in the third year of Zhōnghé under Emperor Xīzōng of Táng;
this was the beginning of his enterprise.
By this year, it had been thirty-one years.
He referred to Jìn.
*Niè*,
read *yú liè* (*yùliè*) [tone: *niè*, meaning 'illegitimate offspring'].
Heaven has robbed me of years.
When I die,
my sons will not be their match,
and I will have no burial ground!”
He then choked up and sobbed,
fainting and then reviving.
To gasp and then resume breathing is to revive.
Gāo Jìchāng secretly harbored the ambition to seize Jīngnán.
He therefore memorialized to build an outer city wall for Jiānglíng,
expanding it.
On the 24th day, *bǐngyín*,
Shǔ Ménxià Shìláng and Tóng Píngzhāngshì Wáng Kǎi was dismissed and made Bīngbù Shàngshū.
The Emperor’s eldest son, Chén Wáng Yǒuyù, had died early.
The second son, adopted son Bó Wáng Yǒuwén,
Yǒuwén’s original surname was Kāng,
and his given name was Qín.
He was often left to guard Dōngdū,
and concurrently served as the commissioner of Jiànchāng Gōng.
The Emperor had converted his old residence in Dàliáng into Jiànchāng Gōng.
His mother was a camp courtesan from Bózhōu,
and he served as the Commander-in-Chief of the Left and Right Kònghè divisions.
The third son, Jūn Wáng Yǒuzhēn,
served as the Commander-in-Chief of the infantry and cavalry in Dōngdū.
Initially,
Yuánzhēn Empress Zhāng was stern, orderly, and highly intelligent,
and the Emperor respected and feared her.
After the Empress died,
Empress Zhāng died in the first year of Tiānyòu of Táng Zhāozōng.
Although his sons were in other places,
the Emperor often summoned their wives to attend him,
and he frequently had illicit relations with them.
Yǒuwén’s wife, Lady Wáng, was beautiful,
and the Emperor especially favored her.
Although he had not yet made Yǒuwén the Crown Prince,
the Emperor’s intention was always inclined towards him.
Yǒuguī’s heart was not at peace.
Yǒuguī once committed an offense,
and the Emperor flogged him,
making Yǒuguī even more uneasy.
The Emperor became very ill,
and ordered Lady Wáng to summon Yǒuwén to Dōngdū,
wishing to bid him farewell
and entrust him with the affairs of the future.
Yǒuguī’s wife, Lady Zhāng, also attended the Emperor morning and evening,
and knowing this,
secretly told Yǒuguī, saying:
"Dàjiā has given the imperial seal to Lady Wáng, who is taking it to Dōngdū;
we are surely doomed to die soon."
The couple wept together.
Some attendants then advised them, saying:
"In urgent situations, stratagems arise;
why not make other plans?
The opportunity must not be missed!"
An ancient said:
"When one is lewd and not a father,
there will surely be disaster from one's sons."
How true this is!
Shuō,
is pronounced "shì ruì" (式芮).
In the sixth month,
on the Dīngchǒu day,
the Emperor ordered Jìng Xiáng to send Yǒuguī out as the Prefect of Láizhōu,
and immediately ordered him to proceed to his post.
The imperial decree had already been announced,
but the official edict had not yet been issued.
Jìng Xiáng was then Xuānzhèngshǐ,
so he was made to issue the edict.
Xiáng had assisted the Emperor for many years;
there was no major military or state plan in which he did not participate.
He reconciled matters as they arose,
diverting the Emperor's violent temper to achieve success,
and his achievements were not small.
While critically ill, the Emperor ordered Yǒuguī to go away.
If Xiáng had been able to devise a plan for this,
then there would surely have been a way to deal with Yǒuguī,
and the Emperor would have avoided the disaster of being stabbed.
When one falls and is not helped,
what use is that minister!
Yǒuguī became even more afraid.
On the Wùyín day,
Yǒuguī changed his clothes and secretly entered the Zuǒ Lónghǔ Army,
met with the Commander Hán Qíng,
and told him the situation.
Qíng also saw that many meritorious officials and veteran generals were executed for minor offenses,
feared for his own safety,
and so they conspired together.
When both officials and sons are rebellious,
it is also because of those above them who cause it.
Bèi,
is pronounced "pí yì" (皮義).
They lay in ambush inside the palace.
The Liáng used the imperial guards as the Kònghè Army.
When they reached the sleeping chamber,
all those attending the Emperor scattered and fled.
The Emperor rose in shock,
and asked:
"Who are the rebels?"
Yǒuguī said:
"It is no one else."
The Emperor said:
"I always suspected this villain;
I regret not killing him earlier.
How can Heaven and Earth tolerate such rebellion from you!"
Yǒuguī said:
"Old villain, may you be torn into ten thousand pieces!"
Yǒuguī’s servant Fény Tíng’è stabbed the Emperor in the abdomen,
the blade exiting through his back.
Yǒuguī himself wrapped the body in a tattered felt blanket
and buried it in the sleeping chamber;
he was sixty-one years old.
Yì,
is pronounced "yú jì" (於計).
He sent the court attendant Dīng Zhāopǔ to ride quickly to Dōngdū,
ordering Prince Jūn, Yǒuzhēn, to kill Yǒuwén.
On the Jǐmǎo day,
a fabricated edict declared:
"Prince Bó, Yǒuwén, plotted rebellion,
and sent troops to storm into the palace.
Thanks to the loyalty and filial piety of Prince Yǐng, Yǒuguī,
who led troops to execute him,
Our person was preserved.
However, due to the shock, Our illness
has become even more critical.
It is fitting that Yǒuguī provisionally manage the affairs of the military and the state."
Hán Qíng, advising Yǒuguī,
extensively distributed gold and silk from the imperial treasury
to the various armies and officials to win their favor.
On the Xīnsì day,
Dīng Zhāopú returned
and heard that Yǒuwén was already dead.
Then the mourning was announced,
the imperial will was proclaimed,
and Yǒuguī ascended the throne as Emperor.
At this time, with recent internal turmoil in the court,
people inside and outside were agitated.
The soldiers in Xǔzhōu spread news of change among themselves,
but the Kuāngguó Jiedushi, Hán Jiàn, paid no attention
and made no preparations.
On the Bǐngshēn day,
the Mǎbù Dūzhīhuīshǐ, Zhāng Hòu, rebelled,
killing Jiàn.
The Kǎoyì states: The Zhuāngzōng Shílù records
that Jiàn was killed in the ninth month.
We now follow Xuē Shǐ.
On the Jiǎchén day,
Hòu was made Prefect of Chénzhōu.
26 In autumn,
in the seventh month,
on the Dīngwèi day,
a general amnesty was declared.
27 The Tiānxíong Jiédùshǐ, Luó Zhōuhàn, was young and weak,
and all military and governmental affairs were decided by the Yánèi Dūzhīhuīshǐ, Pān Yàn.
The Běimiàn Dū Zhāotǎoshǐ and Xuānyì Jiédùshǐ, Yáng Shīhòu, was garrisoned in Wèizhōu,
and had long intended to seize control,
but feared the majesty and strictness of Tàizǔ,
and dared not act.
At this point,
Shīhòu stayed at the Tóngtái驛,
which was named after the Tóngquè Terrace.
However, the Tóngquè Terrace was in Yè,
not in Wèizhōu.
He seized and killed him,
led his troops into the Yáchéng,
and assumed his position to handle affairs.
On the Rénzǐ day,
an edict made Shīhòu the Tiānxíong Jiédùshǐ.
The Kǎoyì states: The Liáng Gōngchén Lièzhuàn, Yáng Shīhòu Zhuàn says:
"When Tàizǔ first abandoned the realm,
many prefectures and administrations took advantage of the situation to rebel.
The Wèi Yánèi Dūzhīhuīshǐ, Pān Yàn, and generals Zāng Yánfàn and Zhào Xùn plotted rebellion;
there was a secret informant,
and Shīhòu deployed troops to capture and
execute them.
In the seventh month, he was appointed Wèibó Jiédùshǐ."
Xuē Shǐ’s Shīhòu Zhuàn is largely similar.
We now follow Zhuāngzōng Lièzhuàn, Zhū Yǒuguī Zhuàn, and Zhuāngzōng Shílù.
In the first year of Wéndé of Táng Xīzōng,
Luó Hóngxìn obtained Wèibó,
and it was passed down from son to grandson before it was lost.
28 Hán Qíng, the Shìwèi Zhūjūnshǐ, was appointed Kuāngguó Jiédùshǐ.
Hán Qíng received the jiedushi title as a fellow conspirator.
29 On the Jiǎyín day,
Wúyuè Wáng, Liú, was additionally granted the title Shàngfù.
30 On the Jiǎzǐ day,
Prince Jūn, Yǒuzhēn, was appointed Kāifēng Yǐn and Dōngdū Liúshǒu.
31 Shǔ Crown Prince Yuántǎn changed his name to Yuányīng.
Zōngyì changed his name to Yuántǎn,
as seen in the previous volume, Kāipíng fourth year.
According to Ōu Shǐ,
Shǔ Lord Jiàn once obtained a bronze tablet in Shífǎng County
with over twenty characters.
Jiàn took it as an auspicious omen,
and then used it to name his sons;
hence, he again changed his name to Yuányīng.
Gēng,
is pronounced "gōng héng" (工衡).
32 On the Bǐngyín day,
the Jiànchānggōng Shǐ was abolished,
and Hénán Yǐn, Zhāng Zōngshì, was appointed Guójìshǐ,
who took charge of all the gold and grain throughout the realm that previously belonged to the Jiànchānggōng.
When Liángzǔ accepted the abdication,
he appointed Prince Bó, Yǒuwén, as Jiànchānggōng Shǐ,
exclusively in charge of gold and grain.
Since Yǒuguī had killed Yǒuwén,
he therefore abolished this position and established the Guójìshǐ.
33 In the eighth month,
three thousand soldiers of the Lóngxiáng Army garrisoned in Huáizhōu,
(garrisoned in Huáizhōu to guard against the Jìn people descending from Shàngdǎng via Tàiháng to spy on Luòyáng),
plundered wherever they went.
On the Wùzǐ day,
Hóng Yànwēi, the Dōngjīng Mǎbùjūn Dūzhīhuīshǐ, and Dù Yànqiú, the Zuǒ Yàowǔ Zhīhuīshǐ, were sent to suppress them.
On the Gēngyín day,
the rebellious troops were defeated,
and their commander Liú Chóngyù was captured at Yānlíng.
On the Jiǎwǔ day,
he was executed.
This laid the groundwork for Yǒuzhēn to raise an army of righteousness to execute Yǒuguī.
34 After Yǐng Wáng Zhū Yǒuguī 友珪 usurped the throne,
many veteran generals were enraged.
Although he showered them with favors and courtesy,
they remained displeased.
When the envoy bearing news of mourning arrived in Héchōng 河中,
Hùguó Jiédùshǐ 護國節度使 Jì Wáng Zhū Yǒuqīan 友謙 wept and said,
"The late emperor spent several decades establishing his dynastic foundation.
The recent upheaval in the palace
is truly scandalous.
As a regional governor,
I am secretly ashamed of it."
Zhū Yǒuqīan 友謙 was originally Zhū Jiǎn 朱簡, a yájiāng 牙將 from Shǎnzhōu 陝州.
In the late Táng 唐, he attached himself to Zhū Wēn 朱溫,
who bestowed upon him the name Yǒuqīan 友謙
and ranked him among his sons.
Therefore, he took this opportunity to denounce Zhū Yǒuguī's 友珪 patricidal act.
According to ancient law,
a minister who murders his sovereign,
or a son who murders his father,
is to be executed without pardon if he holds office.
Thus, for Zhū Yǒuguī's 友珪 crime,
all subjects and sons of the Liáng 梁 dynasty were permitted to execute him.
He justified himself with an imperial edict
and also summoned Yǒuqīan 友謙.
Yǒuqīan 友謙 said to the envoy,
"Who is the one who has been enthroned?
The late emperor did not pass away naturally.
I shall go to Luòyáng 洛陽 to punish the culprit.
Why would I be summoned!"
On the day Wùxū 戊戌,
Hán Qíng 韓勍, the Shìwèi Zhūjūnshǐ 侍衞諸軍使, was appointed Xīmiàn Xíngyíng Zhāotǎoshǐ 西面行營招討使
to command the armies to attack him.
Zhū Yǒuqīan 友謙 allied Héchōng 河中 with Jìn 晉 to seek aid.
In the ninth month,
on the day Dīngwèi 丁未,
Kāng Huáizhēn 康懷貞, the Gǎnhuà Jiédùshǐ 感化節度使, was appointed Héchōng Dū Zhāotǎoshǐ 河中都招討使,
with Hán Qíng 韓勍 as his deputy.
35 Zhū Yǒuguī 友珪 considered Jìng Xiáng 敬翔, Bīngbù Shàngshū 兵部尚書 and Zhī Chóngzhèngyuànshì 知崇政院事, to be Tàizǔ's 太祖 confidant.
Fearing that Jìng Xiáng 敬翔 would be disloyal to him,
he wanted to relieve him of his inner post.
"Inner post"
refers to Zhī Chóngzhèngyuànshì 知崇政院事.
On the day Gēngwǔ 庚午,
Jìng Xiáng 敬翔 was appointed Zhōngshū Shìláng 中書侍郎 and Tóng Píngzhāngshì 同平章事.
On the day Rénshēn 壬申,
Lǐ Zhèn 李振, the Hùbù Shàngshū 戶部尚書, was made Chóngzhèngyuànshǐ 崇政院使.
Jìng Xiáng 敬翔 often claimed illness and did not participate in affairs.
Jìng Xiáng 敬翔 and Lǐ Zhèn 李振 were both meritorious officials who helped found the previous dynasty at this time.
Lǐ Zhèn 李振 replacing Jìng Xiáng 敬翔 as Chóngzhèngyuànshǐ 崇政院使 meant that Lǐ Zhèn 李振 was complicit with Zhū Yǒuguī 友珪.
Although Jìng Xiáng 敬翔 claimed illness and did not participate,
if judged by the ancient law that a minister lives and dies with his lord,
he would also not escape death.
36 Kāng Huáizhēn 康懷貞 and others, along with Niú Cúnjié 牛存節, the Zhōngwǔ Jiédùshǐ 忠武節度使, amassed an army of fifty thousand and encamped west of Héchōngchéng 河中城,
attacking it with great urgency.
The Jìn Wáng 晉王 dispatched his generals Lǐ Cúnshěn 李存審, Lǐ Sìgōng 李嗣肱, and Lǐ Sì'ēn 李嗣恩 with troops to relieve it,
defeating the Liáng 梁 army at Húbì 胡壁.
Lǐ Sì'ēn 李嗣恩
was originally a man of the Luò 駱 clan.
The "Yì'ér Zhuàn" 義兒傳 in Ouyáng Xiū's 歐陽修 history states
that Lǐ Sì'ēn's 李嗣恩 original surname was Luò 駱,
and he was a man of the Tǔyùhún 吐谷渾 tribe.
37 When Wú Wǔzhōng Wáng 吳武忠王 was ill,
Zhōu Yǐn 周隱 requested to summon Líu Wēi 劉威,
a matter mentioned in volume 265 under the second year of Tiānyòu 天祐 of Táng 唐.
This was resented by the Shuàifǔ 帥府.
"Shuàifǔ 帥府"
refers to Guǎnglíng Shuàifǔ 廣陵帥府.
The character "shuài 帥"
is pronounced as suǒ lèi.
Xú Wēn 徐溫 was about to attack him.
Wēi's 威 retainer Huáng Nà 黃訥 advised Wēi 威, saying,
"Although you have been deeply slandered,
you have done nothing to warrant rebellion.
If you travel in a light boat to pay respects to the court,
then all suspicion will vanish."
Wēi 威 followed his advice.
Táo Yǎ 陶雅, hearing of Lǐ Yù's 李遇 defeat,
also grew fearful.
He went with Wēi 威 to Guǎnglíng 廣陵,
where Xú Wēn 徐溫 treated them with great respect,
observing the same etiquette as when serving Wǔzhōng Wáng 武忠王.
He generously bestowed upon them official titles and ranks,
which pleased Yǎ 雅 and others, winning their allegiance.
From then on, everyone respected Xú Wēn 徐溫.
Huáng Nà 黃訥
was from Sūzhōu 蘇州.
Xú Wēn 徐溫, along with Wēi 威 and Yǎ 雅, leading generals and officials, requested Lǐ Yǎn 李儼,
who by imperial authority added the titles of Tàishī 太師 and Wú Wáng 吳王 to the heir to the Wú 吳 King, Lóngyǎn 隆演.
The conferment of the title "Heir to the Wú King, Lóngyǎn 隆演,"
was by Lǐ Màozhēn's 李茂貞 imperial authority.
Yáng Xíngmì 楊行密 had respected Lǐ Yǎn 李儼's imperial authority through his envoy.
Xú Wēn 徐溫 and others, based on this precedent, made their request to Lǐ Yǎn 李儼.
The character "shuài 帥"
is read as "shuài 率".
Lóngyǎn 隆演 remained Huáinán Xíngjūn Sīmǎ 淮南行軍司馬.
Xú Wēn 徐溫 sent Wēi 威 and Yǎ 雅 back to their garrisons.
Líu Wēi 劉威 was garrisoned at Hóngzhōu 洪州,
and Táo Yǎ 陶雅 at Shèzhōu 歙州.
Xú Wēn 徐溫 treated Wēi 威 and Yǎ 雅 as he would Yáng Xíngmì 楊行密.
To be noble and yet not forget old ties,
one must be capable of feigning emotion;
as for sending Wēi 威 and Yǎ 雅 back to their garrisons,
not only did people of the time admire him,
but Wēi 威 and Yǎ 雅 were also truly won over.
From ancient times,
the dispositions of heroes have always differed,
but their ability to manage affairs of the time according to their disposition is consistent.
Those who are good at studying history should not overlook this!
38 On the day Xīnsì 辛巳,
Shǔ 蜀 changed Jiànnán Dōngchuān 劍南東川 to Wǔdéjūn 武德軍.
39 Zhū Yǒuqīan 友謙 again sent an urgent appeal to Jìn 晉.
In winter,
the tenth month,
the Jìn Wáng 晉王 personally led his army westward from Zélù 澤潞,
instead of marching south from Tàiyuán 太原 through Fén 汾 and Jìn 晉.
The character "jiāng 將"
is pronounced as jìliàng.
Sòng Bái 宋白 said: Xièxiàn 解縣 was an old Hàn 漢 county,
which the Later Wèi 後魏 renamed Běixièxiàn 北解縣.
According to previous records, Xièxiàn 解縣 was within Línjìnxiàn 臨晉縣 territory.
In the sixteenth year of Kāihuáng 開皇 of the Suí 隋, Xièxiàn 解縣 was established here.
It was abolished in the second year of Dàyè 大業.
In the ninth year, Yúxiāngxiàn 虞鄉縣 was moved from Suíhuà gùchéng 綏化故城 to the former county seat.
In the first year of Wǔdé 武德 of Táng 唐, Yúxiāngxiàn 虞鄉縣 was renamed Xièxiàn 解縣,
and another Yúxiāngxiàn 虞鄉縣 was established in the Púzhōu 蒲州 area.
The Jiǔyù Zhì 九域志 states: Xiè 解 is ninety-five lǐ 里 east of Púzhōu 蒲州,
and Yúxiāng 虞鄉 is sixty lǐ 里 east of Púzhōu 蒲州.
The character "xiè 解"
is pronounced as hù mǎi.
The Kǎoyì 考異 states: The "Zhuāngzōng Tóngguāng Sìnián Shílù" 莊宗同光四年實錄, "Zhuāngzōng Lièzhuàn" 莊宗列傳, Xuē Shǐ 薛史, and "Táng Yú Lù Zhū Yǒuqīan Zhuàn" 唐餘錄朱友謙傳 all state
that he "met the Biàn 汴 army at Píngyáng 平陽
and thoroughly defeated them."
This account follows the "Zhuāngzōng Tiānyòu Jiǔnián Shílù" 莊宗天祐九年實錄.
A thousand heads were cut off,
and the pursuit continued to Báijìnglǐng 白徑嶺 before returning.
Báijìnglǐng 白徑嶺 is east of Ānyìxiàn 安邑縣 in Héchōng 河中.
They retreated to Shǎnzhōu 陝州.
The Jiǔyù Zhì 九域志 states: Héchōng 河中 is two hundred thirty-eight lǐ 里 south of Shǎnzhōu 陝州.
The character "shǎn 陝"
is pronounced as shī rǎn.
The Jiǔyù Zhì 九域志 states: Yīshìxiàn 猗氏縣 is ninety-five lǐ 里 northeast of Héchōngfǔ 河中府.
Zhū Yǒuqīan 友謙 dismantled his military defenses
and went to the Jìn Wáng's 晉王 tent,
bowing to him as his maternal uncle.
The Jìn Wáng 晉王 arranged a feast with music that night,
and Yǒuqīan 友謙 became greatly intoxicated.
The Jìn Wáng 晉王 had him stay overnight in the tent,
and Yǒuqīan 友謙 slept soundly,
snoring freely.
Zhū Yǒuqīan 友謙 used this to show his complete trust in the Jìn Wáng 晉王,
with no suspicion or estrangement.
The character "hān 鼾"
is pronounced as xià dàn.
40 After Yáng Shīhòu 楊師厚 gained control of the troops of Wèibó 魏博,
and also held the position of Dū Zhāotǎoshǐ 都招討使,
many elite guards were under his command,
and he could deploy troops from all garrisons.
His power and influence were immense.
He held Yǐng Wáng Zhū Yǒuguī 友珪 in contempt
and often acted independently without consulting him.
Zhū Yǒuguī 友珪 worried about this.
He issued an edict summoning him,
stating,
"There are military matters concerning the northern border
that I wish to discuss with you in person."
As Yáng Shīhòu 楊師厚 was about to depart,
his close confidants all advised him, saying,
"Going will surely lead to unforeseen dangers."
Yáng Shīhòu 楊師厚 said,
"I know his character.
Even if I go,
what can he do to me!"
Thereupon, he led over ten thousand elite soldiers,
crossed the river, and headed for Luòyáng 洛陽.
Zhū Yǒuguī 友珪 was greatly alarmed.
On the day Dīnghài 丁亥,
he arrived at the Dūmén 都門.
The outer city gate is called Dūmén 都門.
He entered with over ten people to see the king.
Zhū Yǒuguī 友珪 was pleased.
He used sweet words and humble expressions to appease him
and bestowed upon him vast riches.
On the day Guǐsì 癸巳,
Yáng Shīhòu 楊師厚 was sent back.
41 In the eleventh month,
Zhào 趙 general Wáng Démíng 王德明 led thirty thousand troops to plunder Wǔchéng 武城.
Wǔchéng 武城 was the Hàn 漢 county of Dōngwǔchéngxiàn 東武城縣,
and belonged to Bèizhōu 貝州 in Táng 唐.
The Jiǔyù Zhì 九域志 states: it is fifty lǐ 里 east of the prefecture.
They attacked Zōngchéng 宗城
and took it.
On the day Guǐchǒu 癸丑,
Yáng Shīhòu 楊師厚 laid an ambush at Tángdiàn 唐店,
ambushing and
thoroughly defeating them,
beheading over five thousand.
On the *jiǎyín* day of the 42nd year,
Shénwǔ Yuánshèng Xiàohuángdì was buried at Xuānlíng.
Xuānlíng is located in Yīquè County, Hénán.
In the 43rd year, Chén Zhāng and others, vice-envoy of the Huáinán Military Commissioner of Wú, led a naval force to raid Chu's Yuèzhōu.
They captured its Prefect, Yuàn Méi.
In the first year of Kāipíng,
Chu had taken Yuèzhōu.
In the third year,
Yuàn Méi surrendered to Chu,
and now he was captured by Huáinán.
Méi had surrendered to Chu from Jiāngxī,
and Chu had ordered him to guard Yuèzhōu.
Zhāng and others advanced to attack Jīngnán.
Gāo Jìchāng dispatched his general Ní Kěfú to resist them.
Wú, fearing that Chu forces would rescue Jīngnán,
sent Liú Xìn, the Prefect of Fúzhōu, to lead troops from the five prefectures of Jiāng, Fú, Yuán, Jí, and Xìn, and station them in Jízhōu,
to reinforce Zhāng.
Stationing troops in Jízhōu was to project power,
as if they were preparing to advance and attack Tán and Héng,
to tie up Chu's forces.
In the 44th year, in the twelfth month,
on the *wùyín* day,
Wáng Zōngfén, the commander of the marching army of Shǔ, attacked Qí's Wénzhōu.
He captured it,
and its defending general Lǐ Jìkuí fled.
Wénzhōu
was the land of ancient Yīnpíng.
*Jiàng*,
pronounced *liàng*;
the same below.
In the 45th year,
Liú Xùn, the commander of Xízhōu, killed the Prefect
and surrendered the prefecture to Jìn.
The King of Jìn appointed him as the Prefect of Yíngzhōu.
Xùn
was a native of Yǒnghé.
Yǒnghé County belonged to Xízhōu,
the land of Hàn's Húdiàn County.
During the Suí, it became Yǒnghé County.
The *Jiǔyù Zhì* says: It is 100 *lǐ* west of the prefecture.
In the 46th year, Lǐ Yàntú, the Defense Commissioner of Qiánzhōu, died.
The people of the prefecture supported Tán Quánbō to manage the affairs of the prefecture,
and sent envoys to pledge allegiance.
An imperial edict appointed Quánbō as the Defense Commissioner of Bǎishèng and the Military and Trade Commissioner of Qián and Sháozhōu.
Qiánzhōu previously had a Bǎishèng Command,
which now became the name of the military prefecture.
The “Kāitōngshǐ” [Military and Trade Commissioner]
meant to open up roads
to the south, reaching Jiāo and Guǎng.
In the 47th year, Gāo Jìchāng sent out troops,
claiming to assist Liáng in attacking Jìn.
He advanced to attack Xiāngzhōu.
Kǒng Qíng, the Military Commissioner of Shānnán Dōngdào, defeated him.
From then on, the tribute route was cut off.
Since Gāo Jìchāng had fallen out with Kǒng Qíng,
the route to Liáng was cut off,
and he no longer paid tribute.
*Bài*,
pronounced *bò*.
He was from Yǎnzhōu.
Jūnwáng, supreme,
personal name Yǒuzhēn,
the third son of Tàizǔ.
Wáng Pǔ's *Huìyào* says: The fourth son of Tàizǔ,
whose mother was Empress Yuánzhēn, née Zhāng.
Upon enthronement,
he changed his name to Tián,
and later again changed it to Huáng.
I, the annotator, believe that Wáng Pǔ's statement of "fourth son"
includes the adopted son, Bówáng Yǒuwén, in the count.
The 3rd year of Qiánhuà
(*guǐyǒu*, 913 CE)
1 In spring,
in the first month,
on the *dīngsì* day,
Zhōu Déwēi of Jìn captured Yān's Shùnzhōu.
In the 4th year of Zhēngguān of Táng, after pacifying the Tujue,
their tribes were organized into the four prefectures of Shùn, Yòu, Huà, and Cháng.
In the 6th year, Shùnzhōu was provisionally established in Wǔliǔshù, south of Yíngzhōu.
Shěn Kuò said: Thirty *lǐ* northeast of Yōuzhōu is Wàngjīngguǎn.
Traveling a little north of east for over ten *lǐ*, one reaches the ancient Great Wall.
Another twenty *lǐ* brings one to Zhōngdùn.
Then, crossing Sūnhóuhé and traveling twenty *lǐ*, one reaches Shùnzhōu,
whose northern plain is flat
and fertile for cultivation.
Another seventy *lǐ* to the northeast leads to Tánzhōu.
The Jīn People's Frontier Map says: Shùnzhōu is 115 *lǐ* from Yānjīng.
The *Xiōngnú Xūzhī* says: Shùnzhōu is ninety *lǐ* south of Yānjīng.
The distances recorded vary,
so they are all preserved here.
Sòng Bái said: Yōuzhōu is eighty *lǐ* northeast of Shùnzhōu.
During the Great Yuán, Shùnzhōu administered Huáiróu and Mìyún counties,
belonging to Dàtóng
[Dū].
2 On the *guǐhài* day,
Yǐngwáng Yǒuguī offered sacrifices at the Tàimiào.
On the *jiǎzǐ* day,
he sacrificed at the Huánqiū,
granted a general amnesty,
and changed the era name to Fènglì.
The *Kǎoyì* says: The biography of Zhuāngzōng states
"on the seventh day,"
while the *Shílù* states
"on the *gēngxū* day,
Yǒuguī sacrificed at the Huánqiū
and changed the era name."
We follow Xuē Shǐ here.
3 Chén Zhāng of Wú attacked Jīngnán,
but was unsuccessful and returned.
Jīngnán forces and Chu forces met at Jiāngkǒu to intercept him.
Jiāngkǒu
is Jīngjiāngkǒu.
*Huán*,
pronounced *xuán*,
also as written.
Two hundred boats were arranged in a single line,
passing through in the night.
The troops of the two garrisons suddenly came out to pursue them,
but could not catch up.
4 Zhōu Déwēi of Jìn captured Yān's Ānyuǎnjūn.
Chéng Xíngyán and other generals of Jìzhōu surrendered to Jìn.
5 In the second month,
on the *rénwǔ* day,
Shǔ granted a general amnesty.
6 After Yǐngwáng Yǒuguī had achieved his ambition,
he quickly became extravagant and dissolute.
Both inside and outside the court, there was widespread indignation.
Although Yǒuguī enticed them with gold and silk,
none ultimately sided with him.
The imperial son-in-law, Duwei Zhào Yán,
was the son of Zhāo Chōu.
Zhāo Chōu had guarded Chénzhōu
and rendered meritorious service by resisting Huáng Cháo,
as seen in the annals of Táng Xīzōng.
Yán was married to Tàizǔ's daughter, Princess Chánglè.
He was Tàizǔ's nephew.
Yuán Xiàngxiān's father, Jìngchū,
was married to Tàizǔ's younger sister, Grand Princess Wàn'ān.
Jūnwáng Yǒuzhēn secretly plotted with them to execute Yǒuguī.
Yán said:
"The success or failure of this matter
rests with Commander Yáng Lìnggōng.
Yáng Shīhòu held the office of Zhōngshūlìng [Chancellor]
and was the Northern Front Grand Commander,
hence the title.
Our plan can be immediately carried out."
At that time, the heavy troops of Liáng were all in Yáng Shīhòu's hands,
and his reputation and achievements were admired by all.
Therefore, they wanted him to convey the message to the imperial guards.
"Yǐngwáng usurped the throne and murdered the sovereign.
The hopes of the people rest with Dàliáng.
If you, Sir, seize this opportunity to bring it to fruition,
this will be an unparalleled achievement."
They also promised to reward him with 500,000 *mín* of military funds on the day of success.
Shīhòu discussed it with his subordinate generals and advisors,
saying:
"When Yǐngwáng committed regicide,
I could not immediately punish him.
Now that the relationship between sovereign and subject is established,
is it permissible to change plans without reason?"
Someone said:
"Yǐngwáng personally murdered his sovereign and father;
he is a rebel.
Jūnwáng raises an army to avenge;
this is righteousness.
To uphold righteousness and punish the rebel,
what 'sovereign and subject' is there!
If he, one morning, defeats the rebel,
how will you position yourself, Sir?"
Shīhòu said:
"I almost made a wrong calculation."
Thereupon, he sent his general Wáng Shùnxián to Luòyáng
to secretly plot with Yuán Xiàngxiān,
and dispatched Zhū Hànbīn, a native of Qiáo, the Commander of Foot and Horse Troops of the Commander's Office, to lead troops and station them in Huázhōu as an external response.
Qiáo
was a Hàn county,
and during Táng, it belonged to Bózhōu.
He also secretly finalized the plan with Xiàngxiān.
Yǒu-Guī was punishing the mutineers of the Lóngxiāng Army.
Last year, the Lóngxiāng Army in Huáizhōu mutinied.
治 (zhì),
pronounced zhí zhī fān.
Those captured were executed with their families,
and it had not ceased for a year.
At that time, some Lóngxiāng Army soldiers were garrisoned in Dàliáng.
Yǒu-Guī summoned them.
Jūn-Wáng thereupon had someone incite their troops, saying:
"The Emperor considers the troops stationed in Huáizhōu to be rebels,
and intends to summon you all to bury you alive."
Kǎoyì says: The biographies of Zhuāngzōng and Zhū Yǒu-Zhēn, and Xuē Shǐ and Ōuyáng Shǐ's record of the last emperor state:
"The Left and Right Lóngxiāng Divisions were garrisoned in Biàn,
and Yǒu-Zhēn falsely issued Yǒu-Guī's edict
to recall them to Luòxià."
Zhuāngzōng Shílù states:
"Yǒu-Guī suspected them and summoned them."
According to Liáng Tàizǔ Shílù, it says:
"On bǐng xū,
Dōngjīng reported that the Lóngxiāng Army, having received an edict to return to Xījīng,
was unwilling to set off."
It was in fact Yǒu-Guī who summoned them,
not Yǒu-Zhēn who forged the edict,
but merely incited them by saying they would be buried alive.
No one knew what to do.
On bǐng xū,
Jūn-Wáng reported that the Lóngxiāng Army was apprehensive
and unwilling to advance.
On wù zǐ,
the Lóngxiāng officers saw Jūn-Wáng
and tearfully pleaded for a path to life.
The King said:
"The Late Emperor fought alongside you for over thirty years,
establishing the imperial enterprise.
Now the Late Emperor has been assassinated,
where can you escape death?"
He then took out a portrait of Tàizǔ and showed it to them, weeping, saying:
"If you can go to Luòyáng yourselves and avenge this humiliation,
then calamity will turn into fortune."
All the troops leaped up, shouting "Long live!",
and requested weapons.
The King supplied them.
At dawn on gēng yín,
Yuán Xiàngxiān and others led several thousand imperial guards and stormed into the palace.
Yǒu-Guī, hearing of the change,
fled with his wife Zhāng Shì and Fèng Tíng-È to beneath the north wall tower.
As he was about to scale the wall,
he realized he could not escape.
He ordered Tíng-È to kill his wife first,
and then kill himself.
Tíng-È also committed suicide by slitting his own throat.
The more than one hundred thousand troops plundered the city,
and before the Biàn troops even reached Luòyáng,
the imperial guards had already killed Yǒu-Guī.
Dù Xiǎo, Middle Secretariat Attendant and Grand Councilor, and Lǐ Tǐng, Academician-in-waiting, were both killed by the mutinous soldiers.
Yú Jīng, Palace Secretariat Attendant and Grand Councilor, and Lǐ Zhèn, Commissioner of the Department of State Affairs, were wounded.
The situation was stabilized by dusk.
Xiàngxiān and Yán Jì carried the imperial seal to Dàliáng to welcome Jūn-Wáng.
The King said:
"Dàliáng is where the state was founded;
Liáng Zǔ, starting as Military Commissioner of Xuānwǔ, consolidated various circuits."
He then ascended the imperial throne in Dàliáng,
re-proclaimed the year as Qiānhuà 3rd year,
posthumously demoted Yǒu-Guī to a commoner,
and restored Bó-Wáng Yǒu-Wén's official titles.
7 On bǐng shēn,
Jìn's Lǐ Cún-Huī attacked Yān's Tánzhōu,
and the prefect Chén Què surrendered the city.
It should be known: Tánzhōu is 160 lǐ south of Yānjīng,
and 190 lǐ southeast of Jìzhōu.
Sòng Bái says: Tánzhōu
is the ancient land of Báitán.
8 Shǔ's Táng Dào-Xí returned from Xīngyuán
and was reinstated as Commissioner of Military Affairs.
Crown Prince Yuán-Yīng publicly enumerated Dào-Xí's faults.
疏 (shū)
means to list.
To list his faults one by one in the imperial court during an assembly,
hence "tíng shū."
The Shǔ ruler was displeased.
On gēng zǐ,
Dào-Xí was appointed Grand Tutor to the Crown Prince.
9 In the third month,
on jiǎ chén shuò,
Jìn's Zhōu Dé-Wēi captured Yān's Lú
[lú]
10On dīng wèi,
the Emperor changed his name to Huáng;
after some time,
he was again named Zhèn.
11On gēng xū,
Yáng Shī-Hòu was additionally appointed Middle Secretariat Administrator,
granted the title of Yè-Wáng,
and was not addressed by his personal name in edicts.
All matters, big or small, were decided only after consulting him.
12The Emperor sent an envoy to recruit Zhū Yǒu-Qiān;
Yǒu-Qiān again declared himself a vassal,
adopting the Liáng reign title.
Last year, Zhū Yǒu-Qiān submitted to Jìn;
though he now again declared himself a vassal,
he was secretly allied with Jìn.
13On bǐng chén,
the Emperor's younger brother Yǒu-Jìng was enfeoffed as Kāng-Wáng.
14On yǐ chǒu,
Jìn general Liú Guāng-Jùn captured Gǔběikǒu.
To the east of Yānlè County in Tánzhōu, there are two garrisons, Dōngjūn and Běikǒu.
Běikǒu
is a pass in the Great Wall.
Shěn Kuò says: Fifty lǐ northeast of Tánzhōu is Jīngōuguǎn.
From the inn, travel slightly northeast,
alternating between plains and wetlands,
for over thirty lǐ to Zhōngdùn.
After the dùn,
turn and head north through a gorge,
cross the Luán Shuǐ,
continue for over thirty lǐ,
then turn sharply into a mountain crevice to cross;
this is what is called Gǔběikǒu.
It should be known: Hǔběikǒu is 300 lǐ south of Yānjīng.
Fifteen lǐ north of Chāngpíng County in Yōuzhōu is Jūndū Xíng,
and thirty-five lǐ northwest is Nàkuǎn Guān,
which is the old Jūyōng Pass.
15On wù chén,
Dài Sī-Yuǎn, acting military commissioner of Bǎoyì, was appointed Military Commissioner
and garrisoned Xíngzhōu.
The Táng Zhāoyì Army governed the five prefectures of Lù, Zé, Xíng, Míng, and Cí.
During the late Táng wars,
Jìn gained Lùzhōu,
and still considered it the Zhāoyì Army.
From Mèng Fāng-Lì to Liáng,
Xíng, Míng, and Cí prefectures were made the Zhāoyì Army,
thus resulting in two Zhāoyì Armies.
Now Liáng renamed Xíng, Míng, and Cí as the Bǎoyì Army,
and the Bǎoyì Army of Shǎnzhōu as the Zhènguó Army.
Kǎoyì says: Xuē Shǐ's biography of Sī-Yuǎn states:
"During the Zhēnmíng era,
he was acting military commissioner of Xíngzhōu.
When Zhāng Wàn-Jìn killed Liú Jì-Wēi,
Sī-Yuǎn was ordered to garrison it."
However, Wàn-Jìn's killing of Jì-Wēi happened earlier.
Here, we follow the basic annals.
16 Yān zhǔ Liú Shǒuguāng (燕主守光) ordered General Yuán Xíngqīn (元行欽) to lead seven thousand cavalry
to graze horses north of the mountains,
and recruit soldiers from north of the mountains to respond to the Qìdān (契丹).
Liú Shǒuguāng (劉守光) sought aid from the Qìdān (契丹),
hence he sent Yuán Xíngqīn (元行欽) to recruit soldiers north of the mountains to respond to them,
serving as an external reinforcement.
Jìn (晉) Lí Sìyuán (李嗣源) divided his troops to take the eight garrisons beyond the mountains,
all of which were captured.
The Jìn Wáng (晉王) appointed his younger brother, Cúnjǔ (存矩), as the Cìshǐ (刺史) of Xīnzhōu (新州) to oversee them.
This laid the groundwork for Cúnjǔ’s (存矩) downfall due to arrogance and laziness.
Lí Sìyuán (李嗣源) advanced to attack Wǔzhōu (武州),
and Gāo Xíngguī (高行珪) surrendered the city.
Yuán Xíngqīn (元行欽) heard of this,
and led his troops to attack Xíngguī (行珪).
Xíngguī (行珪) sent his younger brother, Xíngzhōu (行周), as a hostage to the Jìn (晉) army to request aid.
Lí Sìyuán (李嗣源) led his troops to rescue him.
Xíngqīn (行欽) lifted the siege and departed.
Sìyuán (嗣源) and Xíngzhōu (行周) pursued him to Guǎngbiānjūn (廣邊軍).
Guǎngbiānjūn (廣邊軍) was located north of Huáiróng Xiàn (懷戎縣), Guīzhōu (媯州),
which was the old Báiyúnchéng (白雲城).
Sòng Bái (宋白) said: Guǎngbiānjūn (廣邊軍) is one hundred thirty *lǐ* (里) north of Guīzhōu (媯州).
The Gāo (高) brothers Xíngzhōu (行周) originally hailed from Diāokē Cūn (鵰窠村) in Guǎngbiānjūn (廣邊軍).
Xíngqīn (行欽), exhausted, surrendered.
Sìyuán (嗣源), admiring his bravery and prowess,
adopted him as a son.
Kǎoyì (考異) states: The *Zhuāngzōng Shílù* (莊宗實錄)
has “Xíngzhōu (行周)”
written as
“Xíngwēn (行溫)”.
Zhāng Zhāozhōu Tàizǔ Shílù (張昭周太祖實錄) records:
“Yānchéng (燕城) was in dire straits,
its armored soldiers dispersed.
Liú Shǒuguāng (劉守光) summoned Yuán Xíngqīn (元行欽).
Xíngqīn’s (行欽) subordinate generals, believing Shǒuguāng (守光) was doomed to fail,
and that answering the summons would be futile,
requested Xíngqīn (行欽) to become the Yān (燕) commander,
styling himself Liúhòu (留後).
Xíngqīn (行欽) had no alternative
and said to his generals: ‘If I am to be commander,
I must also return to Yōuzhōu (幽州).’
The multitude agreed.
Xíngqīn (行欽), seeing Xíngguī (行珪) in Wǔzhōu (武州),
feared him as a future threat.
He then sent men to Huáiróng (懷戎) to capture Xíngguī’s (行珪) son,
and bound him to follow him.
Upon reaching Wǔzhōu (武州),
Xíngqīn (行欽) said to Xíngguī (行珪): ‘The officers and soldiers have made me Liúhòu (留後).
Let us, father and son, go together,
first secure the military headquarters,
and then surrender to Tàiyuán (太原).
If you do not comply,
I will certainly kill your son.’
Xíngguī (行珪) said: ‘The Great King entrusted you with his personal troops,
and you immediately plotted rebellion.
I would rather die than follow you.’
His son wept and pleaded with Xíngguī (行珪).
Xíngguī (行珪) said: ‘Grand Lord Yuán (元公) is plotting rebellion,
how can one obediently follow?
I bid you farewell.’
Xíngguī (行珪) held the city for over a month.
Food in the city was exhausted,
and the soldiers showed signs of hunger.
Xíngguī (行珪) then gathered the residents and said to them: ‘It is not that I do not pity your families, elders,
but unfortunately, the soldiers lack food.
You may cut off my head and surrender,
and you will immediately see peace.’
Xíngguī (行珪) had governed with kindness,
and the crowd wept, saying: ‘We are willing to offer our private provisions to aid the army,
and defend to the death together.’
That night, he lowered his brother Xíngzhōu (行周) by rope to the Jìn (晉) army as a hostage,
begging for military rescue.
Zhōu Déwēi (周德威) ordered Lí Sìběn (李嗣本), Lí Sìyuán (李嗣源), and Ān Jīnquán (安金全) to rescue Wǔzhōu (武州).
By the time they arrived,
Xíngqīn (行欽) had already lifted the siege.
Sìyuán (嗣源) and Xíngguī (行珪) pursued him to Guǎngbiānjūn (廣邊軍).
Xíngqīn (行欽) led his cavalry to resist.
Xíngguī (行珪) called out to Xíngqīn (行欽), saying: ‘We both served the Liú (劉) family.
I defended the city for the Liú (劉) family,
while you usurped the title of Liúhòu (留後).
Whose fault is this?
In today’s matter,
why trouble the troops?
Let us contend against each other to decide the outcome.’
Xíngqīn (行欽) was fierce and brave,
exceptional in horsemanship and archery.
He replied, ‘Agreed!’
Xíngzhōu’s (行周) horse stumbled slightly,
about to fall.
Sìyuán (嗣源) leaped onto his horse to save him,
striking Xíngqīn (行欽), nearly making him fall.
Xíngqīn (行欽) straightened himself, drew his bow, and shot Sìyuán (嗣源),
hitting his thigh and piercing through the saddle.
Sìyuán (嗣源) pulled out the arrow.
In eight battles,
he drew his bow seven times,
striking Xíngqīn (行欽) with arrows.
Yet Xíngqīn (行欽), foaming blood, fought fiercely and did not give up.
That night,
Xíngqīn (行欽) was in dire straits,
firmly holding Guǎngbiānjūn (廣邊軍).
The Jìn (晉) army surrounded him.
Sìyuán (嗣源) sent a person to tell him: ‘
We are both generals,
there is no need for verbal persuasion.
The situation can be assessed;
come quickly to meet me, and I will certainly protect your reputation and career.’
The next day,
Xíngqīn (行欽) came out, with hands bound, and surrendered.
Sìyuán (嗣源) poured wine for him,
patted his back, and said: ‘My son, you are a brave man.’
He adopted him as a foster son.
Capturing living enemies on the battlefield
always yielded gains,
and his name became well-known in the army.”
The *Zhuāngzōng Shílù* (莊宗實錄), *Xuē Shǐ Jì* (薛史紀), *Yuán Xíngqīn Zhuàn* (元行欽傳), and *Míngzōng Shílù* (明宗實錄) all state
that “Xíngqīn (行欽), hearing that Xíngguī (行珪) had surrendered to Jìn (晉),
led his troops to attack him.”
Only the *Zhōu Tàizǔ Shílù Gāo Xíngzhōu Zhuàn* (周太祖實錄高行周傳) states
that “Xíngqīn (行欽) styled himself Liúhòu (留後),
and Xíngguī (行珪) defended the city,
refusing to comply.”
However, it is feared that at the time of Xíngzhōu’s (行周) death,
it had been a long time since the fall of Yān (燕),
and Xíngzhōu’s (行周) position and prestige were eminent.
His disciples and former officials exaggerated the virtues of him and his brother,
hence this account differs significantly from other versions.
We now follow the majority of texts.
After pulling it out,
in the late Táng (唐), Rúzhōu (儒州) was established east of Guīzhōu (媯州),
administering Jìnshān (晉山) County.
Xíngzhōu (行周) remained to serve Sìyuán (嗣源),
often sharing command of the Yábīng (牙兵) with Sìyuán’s (嗣源) foster son Cóngkē (從珂) to accompany him.
Cóngkē’s (從珂) mother, Madame Wèi (魏氏),
was from Zhènzhōu (鎮州).
She was first married to a man surnamed Wáng (王),
and gave birth to Cóngkē (從珂).
Sìyuán (嗣源), while fighting in Hébĕi (河北) with Jìn Wáng Kèyòng (晉王克用),
acquired Madame Wèi (魏氏),
making her his concubine.
Hence Cóngkē (從珂) became Sìyuán’s (嗣源) son.
When he grew up,
he was known for his courage and strength,
and became famous.
Sìyuán (嗣源) loved him.
This is the beginning of Lǐ Cóngkē (李從珂).
Kǎoyì (考異) states: Zhāng Zhāo (張昭), when compiling the *Táng Fèidì Shílù* (唐廢帝實錄) at the beginning of the dynasty, recorded:
“The deposed emperor’s personal name was Cóngkē (從珂),
the eldest son of Emperor Míngzōng (明宗皇帝).
His mother was Empress Xuānxuàn Wèi (宣憲皇后魏氏),
from Píngshān (平山), Zhènzhōu (鎮州).
In the late Zhōnghé (中和) era,
Emperor Míngzōng (明宗) campaigned in Shāndōng (山東),
garrisoning Píngshān (平山), and acquired Empress Wèi (魏后).
The Emperor was born in the outer dwelling on the twenty-third day of the first month of Guāngqǐ (光啟) first year.
As the Zhào (趙) people broke their alliance
and warfare did not cease,
communication was cut off.
When the Emperor was just ten years old,
he was able to return to his family.
At that time, Emperor Míngzōng (明宗) was a裨將 (píjiàng) [minor general],
broad-minded and unable to manage household affairs.
Empress Cáo (曹后) was also neglectful in planning.
The sole reliance for their livelihood
was Empress Xuānxuàn (宣憲).
Empress Cáo (曹后) had not yet conceived,
but was diligent in managing the household.
The Emperor, with his subordinates Wáng Jiànlì (王建立) and Huángfǔ Lì (皇甫立),
traveled back and forth from Dàiběi (代北) to provide supplies.
Empress Cáo (曹后) pitied him
and treated him no differently from her own son.”
*Xuē Shǐ* (薛史) states:
“The last Emperor’s personal name was Cóngkē (從珂),
originally surnamed Wáng (王),
from Zhènzhōu (鎮州).
His mother was Empress Xuānxuàn Wèi (宣憲皇后魏氏),
who gave birth to the Emperor in Píngshān (平山) in the first year of Guāngqǐ (光啟).
During the Jǐngfú (景福) era,
Emperor Míngzōng (明宗), as a cavalry general under Emperor Wǔ (武皇),
campaigned in Píngshān (平山),
encountered Madame Wèi (魏氏),
and captured her.
The Emperor was then over ten years old.
Emperor Míngzōng (明宗) adopted him as his son.”
Liú Shù (劉恕) used the *Fèidì Lù* (廢帝錄)
and believed that after Emperor Míngzōng (明宗) ascended the throne, he did not establish Cóngkē (從珂) but wished to establish Cóngróng (從榮).
After Cóngróng (從榮) died,
the succession was passed to Cónghòu (從厚),
hence everyone called Cóngkē (從珂) an adopted son.
However, Zhāng Zhāo (張昭) served Emperor Míngzōng (明宗) as a historian,
and compiled the *Fèidì Lù* (廢帝錄) in a later dynasty,
without anything to conceal,
and did not mention adopted son.
The matter thus seems credible.
Yet Lǐ Kèyòng (李克用) had never campaigned in Shāndōng (山東) before the first year of Guāngqǐ (光啟).
Moreover, if Cóngkē (從珂) were indeed Emperor Míngzōng’s (明宗) son,
Emperor Míngzōng (明宗) would surely not have abandoned him to establish Cóngróng (從榮).
Cóngkē (從珂) also would not have submitted.
We now follow *Xuē Shǐ* (薛史).
17. Lǐ Tāo (李濤), Grand Commissioner for Pacification of the Wú (吳) Traveling Secretariat, led a force of twenty thousand out of Qiānqiū-lǐng (千秋嶺),
attacking Wúyuè’s (吳越) Yīyǐn-jūn (衣錦軍).
From the southeast of Hángzhōu (杭州), crossing Qiānqiū-lǐng, one reaches Hángzhōu’s Lín’ān-xiàn (臨安縣).
Xuē Shǐ (薛史) says,
in the second year of Kāipíng (開平) of Liáng (梁), Lín’ān-xiàn’s Guǎngyì-xiāng (廣義鄉) was renamed Yīyǐn-xiāng (衣錦鄉).
Shuài (帥)
is pronounced luǜ (率).
Yī (衣)
is pronounced like yù jǐ (於既).
Chuán Liáo (傳璙), Administrator of Mùzhōu (睦州), was made Commander-in-Chief for Recruitment and Recovery,
leading a naval force to attack Wú’s Dōngzhōu (東洲) to divide their military strength.
Dōngzhōu (東洲)
is Chángzhōu (常州) Dōngzhōu.
Liáo (璙)
is pronounced like lì diào (力弔),
and also like lì xiǎo (力小).
18. In summer,
in the fourth month,
on the guǐwèi (癸未) day,
Yuán Xiàngxiān (袁象先) was appointed Military Governor of Zhènnán (鎮南) and
Commander of the Zhènnán Army.
Hóngzhōu (洪州)
then belonged to Wú.
This refers to a nominal military governorship,
which existed in both the Five Dynasties and Ten Kingdoms.
19. Jìn’s (晉) Zhōu Déwēi (周德威) advanced his army, pressing on the southern gate of Yōuzhōu (幽州).
On the rénchén (壬辰) day,
Yān’s (燕) lord Shǒuguāng (守光) sent an envoy to present a letter to Déwēi to request peace,
the words being extremely humble and sorrowful.
Déwēi said:
"The Great Yān (燕) Emperor has not yet performed the suburban sacrifice to Heaven;
why is he so submissive?
Hàn’s (漢) Zhào Wēn (趙溫) said: A true man should soar like an eagle;
how can he cower like a hen?
To form an alliance and continue good relations
is not something I have heard of."
He did not reply to the letter.
Shǒuguāng (守光) was afraid,
and again sent someone to plead for mercy.
Déwēi then reported this to the King of Jìn (晉).
20. The path through Qiānqiū-lǐng (千秋嶺) was perilous and narrow.
Qián Chuán’guàn (錢傳瓘) sent men to fell trees to cut off the rear of the Wú (吳) army and attack them.
The Wú army suffered a great defeat,
capturing Lǐ Tāo (李濤) and over three thousand soldiers and returning.
21. On the jǐhài (己亥) day,
Jìn’s (晉) Liú Guāngjùn (劉光濬) captured Yān’s (燕) Píngzhōu (平州),
seizing Administrator Zhāng Zàijí (張在吉).
In the fifth month,
Guāngjùn (光濬) attacked Yíngzhōu (營州),
and Administrator Yáng Jìng (楊靖) surrendered.
Sòng Bái (宋白) said: From Píngzhōu (平州) northeast to Yíngzhōu (營州) is six hundred and ninety lǐ.
22. On the yǐsì (乙巳) day,
the Shǔ (蜀) lord appointed Wáng Kǎi (王鍇), Minister of War, as Vice Director of the Central Secretariat and Grand Chancellor.

23. Yáng Shīhòu (楊師厚) and Liú Shǒuqí (劉守奇), leading ten thousand troops from Biàn (汴), Huá (滑), Xú (徐), Yǎn (兗), Wèi (魏), Bó (博), Xíng (邢), and Míng (洺), extensively plundered the territory of Zhào (趙).
Yáng Shīhòu (楊師厚), seeing Yān (燕) and Jìn (晉) engaged in war,
took advantage of the void to plunder Zhào (趙).
He hastened to Zhàozhōu (趙州).
Shǒuqí (守奇) entered from Bèizhōu (貝州) and hastened to Jìzhōu (冀州).
The Jiǔyù-zhì (九域志) states: From Bǎixiāng (柏鄉) north to Zhàozhōu (趙州) is over seventy lǐ;
From Bèizhōu (貝州) north to Jìzhōu (冀州) is over one hundred and twenty lǐ.
Qù (趣)
is pronounced like qī yù (七喻).
On the gēngxū (庚戌) day,
Shīhòu (師厚) arrived at Zhènzhōu (鎮州).
The Jiǔyù-zhì (九域志) states: From Zhàozhōu (趙州) north to Zhènzhōu (鎮州) is ninety-five lǐ.
They burned its pass city.
On the rénzǐ (壬子) day,
Shīhòu (師hòu) withdrew his troops from Jiǔmén (九門) to Xiàbó (下博).
Shǒuqí (守奇) led his troops to join Shīhòu (師hòu) in attacking Xiàbó (下博),
and captured it.
Jìn (晉) generals Lǐ Cúnshěn (李存審) and Shǐ Jiàntáng (史建瑭) garrisoned Zhàozhōu (趙州).
Their forces were small,
so the King of Zhào (趙) sent an urgent message to Zhōu Déwēi (周德ēi).
Déwēi (德威) dispatched cavalry commander Lǐ Shàohéng (李紹衡) to meet with Zhào (趙) general Wáng Démíng (王德明) to jointly resist the Liáng (梁) army.
Shīhòu (師厚) and Shǒuqí (守奇) crossed the Yùhé (御河) at Gōnggāo (弓高) and headed east.
Suí (隋) Emperor Yángdì (煬帝) in the fourth year of Dàyè (大業) dug the Yǒngjì-qú (永濟渠),
diverting the Qìnshuǐ (沁水) south to the River (Hé),
and north to Zhuōjùn (涿郡).
Later generations consequently called it the Yùhé (御河).
Zhāng Wànjìn (張萬進) was afraid,
and requested to be moved to Hénán (河南).
Shīhòu (師厚) memorialized to transfer Wànjìn (萬進) to garrison Qīngzhōu (青州),
and appointed Shǒuqí (守奇) as Military Governor of Shùnhuà (順化).
Last year, Cāngzhōu (滄州) Yìchāng-jūn (義昌軍) was renamed Shùnhuà-jūn (順化軍).
24. Wú (吳) sent Huā Qián (花虔), Vice Commander of Xuānzhōu (宣州), with troops to meet Wō Xìn (渦信), Defender of Guǎngdé (廣德), to encamp at Guǎngdé (廣德),
intending to again invade Yīyǐn-jūn (衣錦軍).
Wúyuè’s (吳越) Qián Chuán’guàn (錢傳瓘) then attacked them.
25. In the sixth month,
on the rénshēn (壬申) day, the first day of the month,
the King of Jìn (晉) sent Zhāng Chéngyè (張承業) to Yōuzhōu (幽州)
to discuss military affairs with Zhōu Déwēi (周德威).
26. On the bǐngzǐ (丙子) day,
the Shǔ (蜀) lord appointed the Daoist Dù Guāngtíng (杜光庭) as Golden Purple Grand Master of Emoluments and Grand Remonstrance of the Left,
ennobled him as Duke of Cài (蔡),
and granted him the title Master Guǎngchéng (廣成先生).
Guāngtíng (光庭) was learned and skilled at writing.
The Shǔ (蜀) lord esteemed him,
and often consulted him on political matters.
27. Wúyuè’s (吳越) Qián Chuán’guàn (錢傳瓘) captured Guǎngdé (廣德),
taking Huā Qián (花虔) and Wō Xìn (渦信) captive and returning.
28. On the wùzǐ (戊子) day,
Zhāng Wànjìn (張萬進) was appointed Military Governor of Pínglú (平盧).
29. On the xīnmǎo (辛卯) day,
Yān’s (燕) lord Shǒuguāng (守光) sent an envoy to Zhāng Chéngyè (張承業),
requesting to surrender with his city;
Chéngyè (承業), believing him to be untrustworthy,
refused.
30. Shǔ (蜀) Crown Prince Yuán Yīng (元膺) had a boar-like snout, protruding teeth,
and an irregular gaze,
but was alert, intelligent, and literate,
skilled in horsemanship and archery,
though his nature was headstrong, impatient, suspicious, and cruel.
The Shǔ (蜀) lord ordered Dù Guāngtíng (杜光庭) to select pure, tranquil, and virtuous individuals to serve in the Eastern Palace.
Guāngtíng (光庭) recommended the scholars Xǔ Jì (許寂) and Xú Jiǎnfū (徐簡夫).
The Crown Prince never spoke with them,
spending his days with musicians and young boys in unrestrained play.
His officials dared not remonstrate.
In autumn,
in the seventh month,
the Shǔ (蜀) lord was planning an excursion for the Qīxī (七夕) festival.
On the bǐngwǔ (丙午) day,
the Crown Prince summoned the various princes and high officials for a banquet.
Jí Wáng Zōnghán (集王宗翰), Inner Privy Councilor Pān Qiào (潘峭), and Hanlin Academician Compiler Gāo Yáng (高陽) Máo Wénxī (毛文錫) did not attend.
The Crown Prince was angry and said:
"Jí Wáng (集王) did not come;
it must be Qiào (峭) and Wénxī (文錫) who alienated him."
Xú Yáo (徐瑤) and Cháng Qiān (常謙), commanders of the Dàchāng Army,
who were deeply trusted by the Crown Prince,
repeatedly looked at Junior Protector Táng Dàoxí (唐道襲) as wine was served.
Dàoxí (道襲) was afraid and rose to leave.
At dawn on the dīngwèi (丁未) day,
the Crown Prince entered and reported to the Shǔ (蜀) lord, saying:
"Pān Qiào (潘峭) and Máo Wénxī (毛文錫) are alienating my brothers."
The Shǔ (蜀) lord was angry and
ordered Qiào (峭) and Wénxī (文錫) to be demoted and banished.
Pān Kàng (潘炕), formerly Military Governor of Wǔtài (武泰) and concurrently Grandee Secretary, was appointed Inner Privy Councilor.
When the Crown Prince left,
Dàoxí (道襲) entered.
The Shǔ (蜀) lord told him about the matter.
Dàoxí (道襲) said:
"The Crown Prince plans to rebel.
He intends to summon the generals and princes,
and confine them with troops."
"Guù (錮)" (錮)
means "imprisonment."
The Shǔ (蜀) lord was suspicious,
and thus did not go out;
thus he did not go on the Qīxī (七夕) excursion.
He agreed to this.
Inner and outer areas were put under strict alert.
The Crown Prince initially made no preparations.
Hearing that Táng Dàoxí had summoned troops,
he then used the Tiānwǔ armored guards to protect himself.
He captured Pān Qiào and Máo Wénxī and brought them before him,
flogging them almost to death,
and imprisoned them in the Eastern Palace.
He also captured Pān Qiáo, the Yǐn of Chéngdū,
and imprisoned him at Déxiánmén.
On the day Wùshēn,
Xú Yáo, Cháng Qiān, and Yán Lín, the Huáishèng Army Commander, etc., each led their respective troops to support the Crown Prince in attacking Dàoxí.
When they reached Qīngfēnglóu,
Dàoxí led his Tún Yíng (cantonment) troops out to resist and fight.
Dàoxí was struck by a stray arrow.
They pursued him to the west of the city
and beheaded him.
The Kǎoyì states: According to the Jiǔguó Zhì:
"Jiàn was about to go on an outing on the Qīxī festival.
The day before,
Yuán Yīng summoned the various army commanders and princes to a banquet in his residence,
and also discussed the protocol for accompanying him on Qīxī.
However, Jí Wáng Zōnghán and others did not come."
It also states:
"The next morning,
Yuán Yīng entered and reported to Jiàn: 'Pān Qiào and Máo Wénxī are sowing discord between brothers
and are plotting rebellion.'"
It also states:
"And when he heard that Táng Dàoxí was mobilizing troops,
he then dispatched the court musician Ānxīxiāng to instruct the army commander Quán Shū to lead the Tiānwǔ armored guards for self-protection."
It also states:
"The next day,
Xú Yáo, Cháng Qiān, and Yán Lín, the Huáishèng Army Commander, etc., conspired together
and used their respective troops to force Yuán Yīng to pursue Táng Dàoxí.
Yuán Yīng, in armor on horseback, led his soldiers past the gate of his elder brother, Zōnghè,
and summoned him to advance together.
Zōnghè said: 'This uprising is without just cause,
I dare not obey the command.'"
It also states:
"Jiàn urgently summoned Zōngkǎn, Zōnghè, and the various army commanders,
ordering them to lead troops to suppress the rebels.
They then pursued Táng Dàoxí to the west of the city and beheaded him,
killing all the Tún Yíng troops.
They then ascended the battlements from the Dà'ānmén and entered,
attacking Yáo, Qiān, and others."
Ouyáng Shǐ says:
"Yuán Yīng, with the court musician Ānxīxiāng and the army general Yù Quánshū, led the Tiānwǔ troops for self-protection,
summoned the great generals Xú Yáo and Cháng Qiān to lead troops out to resist Dàoxí,
and fought Dàoxí at Shénwǔmén.
Dàoxí was struck by a stray arrow, fell from his horse, and died."
The Shíguó Jìnián states:
"On the day Dīngwèi,
Yuán Yīng ordered the army commander Yù Quánshū to lead the Tiānwǔ troops for self-protection.
On the day Wùshēn,
Xú Yáo, Cháng Qiān, and Wáng Chéngsuì, the Zuǒ Dàchāng Army Commander, etc., each led their respective troops to support Yuán Yīng in attacking Táng Dàoxí.
Dàoxí, from his private residence, put on armor and mounted his horse.
He passed by Wáng Zōnghè's gate to summon him.
Zōnghè said: 'This uprising is without just cause,
and furthermore, it is not by imperial edict.
You, sir, should proceed slowly.'
Yuán Yīng dispatched the Tiānwǔ general Táng Jù to lead his personal guards in pursuit of Dàoxí to the west of the city and behead him."
According to the Jiǔguó Zhì,
it states
"Xú Yáo and others forced Yuán Yīng to pursue Táng Dàoxí,"
which suggests that Dàoxí was in the palace,
and they wanted to drive him out.
Ouyáng Shǐ states
"Yuán Yīng summoned Yáo and others to lead troops out to resist Dàoxí,
and attacked the Eastern Palace while Yuán Yīng resisted him."
The Jìnián states
"Yáo and others supported Yuán Yīng in attacking Táng Dàoxí,
and Dàoxí, from his private residence, put on armor and mounted his horse."
This suggests Dàoxí was outside in his outer residence,
and Yuán Yīng went to attack him.
However, Dàoxí merely relied on coercing the sovereign to assert his own importance.
Since he had advised the Lord of Shǔ to mobilize troops for self-protection,
how could he have gone out to his outer residence?
He must have remained within the forbidden area.
It was probably Yáo and others who led troops to attack the palace to find Dàoxí.
Dàoxí led the Tún Yíng troops out to resist and fight.
His army was defeated and fled to the west of the city,
where he was killed by Táng Jù.
The Jiǔguó Zhì also states
"Yuán Yīng, in armor on horseback, led his soldiers past the gate of his elder brother, Zōnghè,
and summoned him to advance together,"
which means Yuán Yīng summoned Zōnghè.
The Jìnián states
"Dàoxí, from his private residence, put on armor and mounted his horse, passed by Zōnghè's gate to summon him,"
which means Dàoxí summoned Zōnghè.
However, how could Dàoxí's private residence have troops?
Observing Zōnghè's reply,
it seems he was speaking to the Crown Prince,
not to Dàoxí.
If he were speaking to Dàoxí,
he should have advised him to quickly enter the imperial guard,
how could he have said
"You, sir, should proceed slowly"?
Pān Kàng said
"The Crown Prince has no other intentions.
Your Majesty should personally instruct your ministers to pacify the state."
At that time, when the Lord of Shǔ heard of the disturbance,
he believed Dàoxí's words but also could not bear to punish the Crown Prince,
lacking a decisive command.
Therefore, Kàng said the Crown Prince had no other intentions,
and that the ministers should be summoned to suppress Xú Yáo and others who were causing the chaos.
The Jiǔguó Zhì states
"Ordered Zōngkǎn and others to lead troops to suppress the rebels,
and then pursued Táng Dàoxí to the west of the city and beheaded him."
This means the imperial army beheaded Dàoxí.
If so,
why was Dàoxí quickly posthumously honored and given a posthumous title the next day?
This must be an error.
Inside and outside the palace, there was alarm and disturbance.
Pān Kàng spoke to the Lord of Shǔ, saying:
"The Crown Prince and Táng Dàoxí are merely contending for power;
he has no other intentions.
Your Majesty should personally instruct your ministers to pacify the state."
The Lord of Shǔ then summoned Wáng Zōngkǎn, acting Zhōngshū Lìng, Wáng Zōnghè, and Wáng Zōnglǔ, former Lìzhōu Tuánliànshǐ,
and ordered them to mobilize troops to suppress the rebels Xú Yáo, Cháng Qiān, and others.
Zōngkǎn and others arrayed themselves at the Xīqiúchǎngmén.
Wáng Zōng'àn, acting Shìzhōng, climbed the city wall from the Dà'ānmén
and fought Yáo and Qiān in front of the Huìtóngdiàn,
killing dozens of people.
Yáo died.
Qiān and the Crown Prince fled to Lóngyuèchí.
Lóngyuèchí is also known as Móhēchí.
On the day Jǐyǒu,
the Crown Prince came out to beg for food from a boatman.
The boatman reported this to the Lord of Shǔ,
who urgently dispatched Jí Wáng Zōnghán to console and pacify him.
By the time he arrived,
