the Crown Prince had already been killed by a guard.
The Lord of Shǔ suspected Zōnghán had killed him
and wept uncontrollably.
Those around him feared a change of events.
Coincidentally, Zhāng Gé presented a placard to comfort and instruct the military and civilians.
When the Lord of Shǔ read to
"If the punishment of the axe is not carried out,
the plans for the state will be misguided,"
he wiped away his tears and said:
"How dare I harm public interest for private gain!"
Thereupon, he issued an edict deposing Crown Prince Yuán Yīng as a commoner.
Zōnghán requested the execution of those who had personally killed the Crown Prince.

at the end of the Táng dynasty,
Gé Cóngzhōu defeated the Jìn army at Shāhé,
pursuing them to Zhānggōngqiáo.
Shāhé County is twenty-five *lǐ* south of Xíngzhōu,
thus it can be known that Xíngzhōu's seat was Lónggāng.
The Jìn army retreated,
and the troops of the various garrisons all returned home.
"Troops of the various garrisons"
refers to the troops of Yān, Zhào, and Lù.
Jìn Wáng returned to Jìnyáng.
13 The Shǔ Wǔtài Jiédùshǐ, Wáng Zōngxùn, garrisoned Qiánzhōu.
He was greedy, tyrannical, and lawless.
Upon returning to Chéngdū,
on the day Gēngchén,
he met the Shǔ ruler
and made many demands,
his words being arrogant and rebellious.
The Shǔ ruler was enraged
and ordered his guards to beat him to death.
On the day Wùzǐ,
the Nèi Shūmìshǐ, Pān Qiào, was appointed Wǔtài Jiédùshǐ and Tóng Píngzhāngshì,
and Hànlín Xuéshì Chéngzhǐ Máo Wénxī was appointed Lǐbù Shàngshū
and Pàn Shūmìyuàn.
There was a weir above the gorges.
Someone advised the Shǔ ruler to take advantage of the summer and autumn river floods
to breach it and inundate Jiānglíng.
Máo Wénxī admonished:
"Gāo Jìchāng is not submissive,
but what crime have his people committed?
Your Majesty is now winning over the world with virtue;
how can you bear to let the people of a neighboring state be food for fish and turtles?"
The Shǔ ruler then stopped.
14 The Emperor appointed Fú Wáng Yǒu Zhāng as Wǔníng Jiédùshǐ.
The former Jiédùshǐ, Wáng Yīn,
who had been appointed by Yǒu Guī,
was fearful
and refused to be replaced,
rebelling and allying with Wú.
In the ninth month,
he ordered Huáinán Xīběimiàn Zhāotǎo Yìngjiēshǐ Niú Cúnjié and Kāifēng Yǐn Liú Xún to lead troops to suppress him.
In winter,
the tenth month,
Cúnjié and others encamped at Sùzhōu.
Jiǔyù Zhì: From Xúzhōu south to Sùzhōu is one hundred forty-five *lǐ*.
Niú Cúnjié did not directly attack Xúzhōu but instead moved south to garrison Sùzhōu,
occupying the strategic point of Yǒngqiáo,
thereby cutting off aid from Huáinán.
Cúnjié and others counter-attacked
and defeated them.
The Wú troops retreated.
15 In the eleventh month,
on the day Yǐsì,
Nánzhào invaded Lízhōu.
The Shǔ ruler appointed Kuí Wáng Zōngfàn, concurrently Zhōngshūlìng Zōngbò, and Jiā Wáng Zōngshòu as the three Zhāotǎo to attack them.
On the day Bǐngchén,
they defeated them at Pāncāngzhàng,
beheading their chieftains, Zhào Cuózhèng and others.
On the day Rénxū,
they again defeated them at Shānkǒuchéng.
In the twelfth month,
on the day Yǐhài,
they destroyed their thirteen stockades at Wǔhóulǐng.
The southern border of Lízhōu had eleven cities like Pāncāng and Wǔhóu.
Lù Zhèn's Jiǔguó Zhì: Wáng Zōngbò emerged from Qióngláiguān to Pāncāng,
decisively defeating the barbarian multitudes,
pursuing the fleeing enemy to Shānkǒuchéng.
Thus Pāncāng was south of Qiónglái,
and Shānkǒuchéng was further south of Pāncāng.
On the day Xīnsì
they again defeated them at Dàdùhé.
According to Jiǔyù Zhì,
Lízhōu is blocked on three sides by Dàdùhé;
the south side to Dàdùhé is one hundred *lǐ*,
the southeast side to Dàdùhé is one hundred twenty *lǐ*,
and the southwest side to Dàdùhé is three hundred *lǐ*.
The barbarians scrambled to cross the water,
the bridge broke,
and tens of thousands drowned.
Zōngfàn and others were about to build a pontoon bridge to cross Dàdùhé and attack them,
but the Shǔ ruler summoned them back.
The barbarian lands were deeply treacherous,
and he did not wish to exhaust his army with a distant campaign,
merely driving them out of the border;
this was the Shǔ ruler's intention.
16 On the day Guǐwèi,
the Shǔ Xīngzhōu Cìshǐ and concurrently Běilù Zhìzhì Zhǐhuīshǐ, Wáng Zōngduó, attacked Qíjiēzhōu.
Jiǔyù Zhì: From Xīngzhōu southwest to Jiēzhōu is five hundred ten *lǐ*.
Gùzhèn is northeast of Qīngnílǐng.
Xuē Shǐ Dìlǐ Zhì: The land of Gùzhèn in Fèngzhōu
was elevated to Xióngshèngjūn in the sixth year of Zhōuxiǎndé.
Four thousand heads were taken.
On the day Jiǎshēn,
Zhǐhuīshǐ Wáng Zōngyǎn destroyed Qí Chángchéngguān and four other stockades,
taking two thousand heads.
17 The Qí Jìngnán Jiédùshǐ, Lǐ Jìhuī,
was poisoned by his son Yànlǔ and died.
Yànlǔ then made himself Liúhòu.
Zhēnmíng Yuánnián
(Yǐhài, 915).
The reign title was changed to Zhēnmíng in the eleventh month of this year.
1. In the spring,
the first month,
on the day *Jǐhài*,
the ruler of Shǔ presided at the Déxián Gate to receive the Mán captives,
and granted a great amnesty.
Initially,
the Mán chieftains of Lí and Yǎ, Liú Chāngsì, Hǎo Xuánjiàn, and Yáng Shītài,
although nominally subordinate to Táng,
and having received noble titles and rewards,
were known as the three kings of Wèijīnbǎo.
Shǐ Zhào said: Wèi
means great,
and many.
Now, we observe that Wèi is pronounced *dīng-me-fān*,
and in the Mán language it means many,
and great.
The *Táng Shū* states that to the west of Lí and Qióng prefectures were the Three Kings Mán,
who were likely remnants of the Zuòdū Yí and Báimǎ Dī.
The three clans of Yáng, Liú, and Hǎo served as chiefs for generations,
inheriting the title of king,
and were referred to as the Three Kings' Tribes.
They lived in stacked brick houses,
called Wèishè.
By the Sòng dynasty,
there were also the Zhào and Wáng clans,
who, along with Liú, Hǎo, and Yáng, were called the Five Tribes.
They lived to the west of Lí Prefecture,
over a hundred *lǐ* from the prefecture,
separated by the Fēiyuè Ridge.
Their dwellings were stacked stones forming Wèi,
with provisions, utensils, and armor stored on top.
The tribes had no single ruler,
only obeying the elders.
When they traveled to Hàn territory,
they could all speak Chinese,
hence they were considered more cunning than other Qiāng.
They acted as scouts and guides;
those governing Shǔ were mostly civil officials,
who, although aware of their intentions,
dared not question them.
By this time,
the ruler of Shǔ frequently executed them in the markets of Chéngdū
for leaking military secrets,
and destroyed Wèijīnbǎo.
From then on, Nánzhào no longer encroached upon the border.
2. In the second month,
Niú Cúnsiè and others captured Péngchéng,
and Wáng Yīn's entire clan immolated themselves.
*Kǎoyì* says: The biography of Zhu Yǒuzhēn in the *Zhuāngzōng Lièzhuàn* states:
"In the eleventh month of the fourth year of Qiánhuà, Xúzhōu was captured,
and Yīn immolated himself."
The *Wǔdài Tōnglù*, *Xuē Shǐ Jì*, and the biography of Wáng Yīn all state that it was in the spring of the first year of Zhēnmíng;
we now follow this.
3. In the third month,
on the day *Dīngmǎo*,
Zhào Guāngfēng, who was Right Grandee Secretary and concurrently Minister of the Palace Affairs and Chancellor, was appointed Grand Tutor of the Crown Prince,
and retired from office.
4. Yáng Shīhòu, Prince of Yè, Military Governor of Tiānxíong and concurrently Chancellor, passed away.
In his later years, Shīhòu prided himself on his achievements and relied on his numerous troops,
confiscating wealth and taxes,
selecting the bravest and most skilled soldiers from the army,
and establishing the Yínqiāng Xiàojié Corps of several thousand men.
He provided them with generous stipends,
intending to restore the former grandeur of the household guards.
Wèibó had established household guards since Tián Chéngsì,
and they were abolished by Luó Shàowēi,
only to be re-established by Yáng Shīhòu.
The court secretly feared him,
and upon his death,
privately received congratulations in the palace.
They feared his coercion and rejoiced at his death.
The Office of Rent and Taxation had existed since the middle of the Táng dynasty.
*Wǔdài Huìyào* states: Liáng established the Office of Rent and Taxation,
whose rank was below that of the Chóngzhèng Envoy and
above that of the Xuānhuī Envoy.
Its official was the Judge of Rent and Taxation.
"Wèibó has been a cancer in the heart of Táng,
which for over two hundred years could not be removed,
due to its vast territory and strong military.
Luó Shàowēi and Yáng Shīhòu controlled it,
and the court could not restrain them.
If Your Majesty does not make plans now,
as the saying goes, 'If a carbuncle is not thoroughly lanced,
it will surely gather again.'
This means that a doctor lancing a carbuncle must not fear the patient's pain,
but must completely drain the pus and blood,
only then will new flesh grow and the illness be cured.
Otherwise, it will re-accumulate.
Physicians lance carbuncles with a sharp stone.
It is advisable to divide the six prefectures into two circuits to weaken their power."
*Kǎoyì* says: *Zhuāngzōng Lièzhuàn* states:
"Chancellors Jìng Xiáng, Rent and Taxation Envoy Zhào Yán, and Judge Shào Zàn and others advised Yǒuzhēn to divide the six prefectures of Wèibó into two circuits."
The *Xuē Shǐ* does not mention Jìng Xiáng's name;
we now follow this.
Hè Délún, Military Governor of Pínglú, was appointed Military Governor of Tiānxíong;
the Zhāodé Army was established in Xiāngzhōu,
and Chán and Wèi prefectures were assigned to it.
Xuān Huī Envoy Zhāng Jūn was appointed Military Governor of Zhāodé,
and half of Wèizhōu's troops, officers' residences, and armories were transferred to Xiāngzhōu.
Jūn
was from Hǎizhōu.
After the two arrived at their posts,
the court feared that the people of Wèi would not submit,
so they dispatched Liú Xún, Mayor of Kāifēng, with sixty thousand troops to cross the river from Báimǎ.
Báimǎjin was in Huázhōu.
This was to show force and intimidate them.
The soldiers of Wèi had been hereditary for several centuries;
"several centuries" means that their tradition was long-standing,
not necessarily that it literally spanned several centuries.
They did not wish to be divided and relocated.
Délún repeatedly urged them,
and all who were to move sighed and complained,
gathering in their camps to weep.
On the day *Jǐchǒu*,
Liú Xún was stationed at Nánlè.
Nánlè was originally Chānglè County of Táng Wèizhōu,
later, to avoid the taboo name of Emperor Xiànzǔ of the Later Táng,
it was renamed Nánlè,
and historians subsequently recorded it as such.
The *Jiǔyù Zhì* states: Nánlè County is forty-four *lǐ* south of Wèizhōu.
He was stationed at Jīnbō Pavilion.
The Wèi soldiers conspired among themselves, saying:
"The court fears the strength of our military command
and wishes to devise a plan to cripple and break us.
Our six prefectures have been a frontier command for generations;
our troops have never been dispatched far beyond the river gate."
According to the *Old Táng Shū*, outside Wèizhōu city there was an old embankment called Hémén;
Lè Yànzhēn built the outer wall,
which was about eighty *lǐ* long along the old Hémén embankment.
"It is better to die than to live."
That evening,
the army mutinied.
*Kǎoyì* says: *Zhuāngzōng Lièzhuàn* states:
"On the 27th,
Liú Xún was stationed at Nánlè,
and dispatched Wáng Yànzhāng, commander of the Lóngxiáng Corps, with five hundred cavalry into Wèizhōu.
That night, at the third watch,
the Wèi army mutinied."
The first day of this month was *Xīnyǒu*,
and the *Xuē Shǐ Jì* states that the Wèibó army rebelled on *Jǐchǒu*.
The character "jiǔ" (nine) in the *Zhuāngzōng Lièzhuàn*
was probably mistakenly written as "qī" (seven).
They surrounded Jīnbō Pavilion,
and Wáng Yànzhāng broke through the gates and fled.
At dawn,
the mutineers entered the *yá* city,
killed five hundred of Hè Délún's personal guards,
and seized Délún, placing him on a tower.
A military officer of the Xiàojié Army named Zhāng Yàn
led his faction,
drew their swords,
and merely plundered.
In the summer,
the fourth month,
the Emperor sent Hù Yì, a palace attendant, to pacify and persuade the Wèi army,
promising Zhāng Yàn the title of刺史 (*cìshǐ*).
Yàn requested that Xiāng, Chán, and Wèi prefectures be restored to the old system.
He requested the disbandment of the Zhāodé Army
and the re-subordination of Xiāng, Chán, and Wèi prefectures to Tiānxíong,
as in the old system.
He said that Zhāng Yàn was easy to deal with,
and that if Liú Xún were simply ordered to advance with his troops,
Yàn's head would immediately be presented.
Therefore, the Emperor did not agree,
but only replied with a gracious edict.
When the envoy returned a second time,
Yàn tore the edict and threw it to the ground,
pointed his fingers southwards like a *jǐ* and cursed the court.
The *Zuǒ Zhuàn* states: The Duke *jǐ* his hand.
Dù Yù's commentary says: *Dǐ*
means bending the elbow like the shape of a *jǐ*.
Lù Démíng says: *Dǐ* is pronounced *zhǐ*.
Zhèng Xuán says: A person holding a bow and arrows *jǐ* their elbow.
Kǒng Yǐngdá's *Zhèngyì* says: This means when an archer holds the bow with the left hand and draws it with the right,
the elbow is *jǐ*-shaped.
"The Son of Heaven is foolish and ignorant,
allowing others to lead him by the nose."
"To be led by the nose like an ox" means to be controlled and turned by others,
moving forward or backward entirely at the command of others,
implying that the nose is the point of control.
"If we have no external aid,
we cannot stand alone.
We should pledge allegiance to Jìn."
*Kuǎn*
means sincerity.
5 Lǐ Jìhuī’s adopted son, Bǎohéng, killed Lǐ Yànlǔ.
The *Kǎoyì* says: In the biography of Liú Zhījùn in the *Shǔ Shū*,
“Bǎohéng”
is
written as “Yànkāng”.
We now follow the *Xuē Shǐ*.
He brought the two prefectures of Bīn and Níng to pledge allegiance.
He rebelled against Qí and joined Liáng.
Huò Yànwēi, the Garrison Commissioner of Héyáng, was made Military Governor of Jìngnán.

6 Xú Wēn of Wú made his son Xú Zhīxùn, the Army’s Deputy Commander of the Palace Guard, Deputy Commander of the Huáinán Expeditionary Army and Deputy Commander of all internal and external cavalry and infantry forces.
This sets the stage for Xú Zhīxùn’s arrogance and downfall.
7 Jìn Wáng received a letter from Hè Délún,
and ordered Mǎbù Fù Zǒngguǎn Lǐ Cúnshěn to advance from Zhàozhōu
and occupy Línqīng.
In the fifth month,
Cúnshěn reached Línqīng,
and Liú Xún was stationed at Huánshuǐ.
Línqīng is north of Wèizhōu,
and Huánshuǐ is west of Wèizhōu.
Jìn Wáng led his main army eastward from Huángzélǐng.
*Wèi Shōu Zhì* says,
that in the Liáoyáng County of Lèpíng Commandery there is Huángzélǐng.
Suí changed Liáoyáng to Liáoshān County,
and Táng placed it under Liáozhōu.
Still suspecting the deceit of the Wèi people,
he held his troops back and did not advance.
Délún sent his judicial official Sīkōng Tíng to reward the army,
and secretly told Jìn Wáng:
"To eliminate chaos, the root must be removed."
He then spoke of Zhāng Yàn’s vicious cunning,
and advised Jìn Wáng to eliminate him first,
and then there would be no worries.
The King remained silent.
He had already conveyed his meaning without putting it into words,
fearing eavesdropping and the泄 disclosure of military secrets.
He was a native of Bèizhōu.
Jìn Wáng advanced and encamped at Yǒngjì.
Yǒngjì County is several tens of *lǐ* north of Wèizhōu.
All held weapons to protect themselves,
and went to Yǒngjì to pay their respects.
The King ascended the posthouse tower and said to them:
"You have intimidated your commander,
and cruelly oppressed the common people.
In the past few days, over a hundred groups have come forward to plead their grievances.
I have now raised an army and come
to bring peace to the common people,
not to covet others' land.
Although you have rendered service to me,
I cannot but execute you to appease the Wèi people."
Thereupon, he beheaded Yàn and seven of his confederates,
and the remaining troops trembled with fear.
The King summoned and instructed them, saying:
"The crime extends only to these eight people;
the rest are not questioned.
From now on, you must exert yourselves to be my claws and teeth."
All bowed down,
shouting "Long live!"
The next day,
the King loosened his belt and donned a light fur coat, and advanced.
He ordered Zhāng Yàn’s soldiers to don armor and carry weapons,
and follow him on horseback,
still as the Silver Spear Unit of the tent front.
Jìn Wáng then used the Silver Spear Unit to conquer Liáng,
but also suffered disaster because of the Silver Spear Unit.
When Liú Xún heard that the Jìn army had arrived,
he selected over ten thousand soldiers
and proceeded from Huánshuǐ to Wèixiàn.
Jìn Wáng left Lǐ Cúnshěn to garrison Línqīng,
and sent Shǐ Jiàntáng to garrison Wèixiàn to resist them.
The *Jiǔyù Zhì* says: Wèixiàn is thirty-five *lǐ* west of Wèizhōu.
They set up camps facing Xún across the river.
The river
is the Zhāng Hé.
The Zhāng Hé passes through Wèixiàn,
and is also called the Wèi Hé.
The Emperor heard that Wèibó had rebelled,
and was greatly remorseful and fearful.
He sent Niú Cúnjié, the Military Governor of Tiānpíng, to lead troops to garrison Yángliú.
The *Kǎoyì* says: In the biography of Niú Cúnjié,
"Yángliú"
is
written as "Yángliú"
or
"Yángliú".
We now follow the biography of Péi Dù in Táng and the biographies of various people in *Xuē Shǐ*.
Coincidentally, Cúnjié fell ill and died,
and Wáng Tán, the Military Governor of Kuāngguó, replaced him.
8 Qí Wáng sent Liú Zhījùn, the Military Governor of Zhāngyì, to besiege Bīnzhōu,
and Huò Yànwēi held fast and resisted him.
Previously, Lǐ Bǎohéng had rebelled against Qí and joined Liáng,
and Liáng had replaced him with Huò Yànwēi to govern Bīnzhōu.
9 In the sixth month,
on the first day (gēngyín),
Hè Délún led his generals and officials to invite Jìn Wáng to enter the prefectural city for comfort and inspection.
After entering,
Délún presented his seal and tally,
and requested the King to concurrently lead the Tiānxíong Army.
The King firmly declined,
saying:
"I recently heard that the Biàn bandits were encroaching upon your territory,
so I personally led my army
to come from afar to rescue you;
I also heard that the city had recently suffered great distress,
so I temporarily entered to console and reassure.
If you do not trust me,
but instead offer your seal and tally to me,
this is truly not my original intention."
Délún bowed again and said:
"Now the enemy is close at hand,
referring to Liú Xún’s army pressing upon Wèizhōu.
The people's hearts are not yet settled,
and Délún's close confidants and officials
*Zuǒzhuàn*: The Marquis of Qín sent three thousand men to guard Duke Wén of Jìn,
who were indeed trusted officials.
are isolated and weak,
how can I command the multitude!
Should something happen,
I fear I would betray your great kindness."
The King then accepted.
Délún led his generals and officials to bow in congratulation.
The King, by imperial decree, appointed Délún as Military Governor of Dàtóng,
and sent him to his post.
When Délún arrived at Jìnyáng,
Zhāng Chéngyè detained him.
The Dàtóng Army is north, bordering the frontier.
Hè Délún had just submitted,
and Zhāng Chéngyè did not want him to have a city and an army,
hence he detained him.
This sets the stage for Chéngyè later killing Délún.
At that time, the Silver Spear Unit was still arrogant in Wèichéng.
Wèichéng
is the city of Wèizhōu.
“héng” (横)
is pronounced *hù mèng fān*.
"From now on, anyone forming factions, spreading rumors, or plundering the common people
shall be executed without mercy!"
Lǐ Cúnjìn, the Inspector of Qìnzhōu, was made Tiānxíong Dū Xún'ànshǐ (Chief Investigator of the Tiānxíong Army).
If anyone spread rumors to agitate the populace or forcibly took so much as a single coin from others,
Cúnjìn would behead them and dismember their bodies in the marketplace.
Within ten days,
the city became solemn,
and no one dared to make a disturbance.
Cúnjìn's original surname was Sūn,
given name Chóngjìn,
and he was a native of Zhènwǔ.
Jìn Wáng often went on campaigns,
and all affairs of the Tiānxíong Army's headquarters were entrusted to the judicial official Sīkōng Tíng.
Tíng relied on his talent and influence,
exacted revenge for the slightest offense,
accepted bribes, and lived extravagantly.
Tíng had a cousin in Hénán.
Tíng secretly sent someone to summon him.
The Commissioner of Army Affairs, Zhāng Yù, seized the messenger and reported it to the King.
The King rebuked Tíng, saying:
"Since I obtained Wèibó,
all affairs have been entrusted to you,
how can you deceive me like this!
Could you not have shown me first!"
He bowed and ordered him to return to his residence;
on that day,
he was executed with his clan at the army gate.
With two enemies facing each other,
and sending private letters across the border,
his execution
was appropriate,
but the execution of his clan
was excessive.
Zhèngyán
was a native of Yùnzhōu.
Kǒng Qiān, a clerk of Wèizhōu,
was diligent, quick-witted, and skilled in calculations,
and adept at managing records.
Jìn Wáng made him Commissioner of Financial Affairs.
In the Táng dynasty, many *jiézhèn* concurrently held positions such as Commissioner of Financial Affairs.
Towards the end of the dynasty,
among the officials appointed by the *fānzhèn*, some were officials for budgeting,
others were Commissioners of Financial Affairs.
“zhì” (治)
is pronounced *zhí zhī fān*.
From this, his favor and trust became even more secure.
This sets the stage for Kǒng Qiān's exploitation and disruption of Táng.
The state coffers were depleted,
and the common people were exhausted,
yet he gathered the armies of three prefectures
and fought on the river for
nearly ten years.
The three prefectures
are Bīng, Wèi, and Zhèn.
There was never a shortage,
which was due to Qiān’s efforts.
However, his heavy taxation and levies
caused suffering in the six prefectures,
and resentment was directed at the King,
which was also his doing.
The historian concludes by saying this.
When Zhāng Yànzhī (張彥之) submitted Wèibó (魏博) to Jìn (晉),
the prefect of Bèizhōu (貝州), Zhāng Yuándé (張源德), did not comply.
He allied with Cāngdé (滄德) to the north.
In Qiánhuà (乾化) 3, Yáng Shīhòu (楊師厚) and Liú Shǒuqí (劉守奇) raided the north,
and Cāngdé (滄德) then submitted to Liáng (梁).
They frequently cut off the grain supply routes to Zhèn (鎮) and Dìng (定).
Someone advised the Jìn (晉) King:
"Please first dispatch ten thousand troops to take Yuándé (源德),
then combine with Cāngjǐng (滄景) to the east,
and all the lands by the sea will be ours."
The Jìn (晉) King said:
"Not so.
Bèizhōu (貝州) has strong walls and numerous soldiers,
and it is not easy to attack abruptly.
Dézhōu (德州) is subordinate to Cāngzhōu (滄州) and unprepared.
If we can take it and garrison it,
then Cāng (滄) and Bèi (貝) will be unable to communicate.
(The *Jiǔyù Zhì* (九域志) says: Dézhōu (德州) is two hundred thirty *lǐ* (里) southwest of Bèizhōu (貝州),
and also two hundred thirty *lǐ* (里) northeast of Cāngzhōu (滄州).)
Then we can take the two fortresses."
(The two fortresses
refer to Cāng (滄) and Bèi (貝).)
Marching day and night,
they raided Dézhōu (德州).
The prefect did not expect the Jìn (晉) troops to arrive,
climbed over the wall and fled.
They then captured it,
and appointed Mǎ Tōng (馬通), the *shǒuzhuō jiàng* (守捉將) of Liáozhōu (遼州), as its prefect.
In autumn,
seventh month,
the Jìn (晉) forces attacked Chánzhōu (澶州) by night
and captured it.
(The *Jiǔyù Zhì* (九域志) says: Wèizhōu (魏州) is one hundred forty *lǐ* (里) south of Chánzhōu (澶州).
According to the *Jiǔyù Zhì*'s (九域志) Chánzhōu (澶州), it was the Chánzhōu (澶州) relocated in Hàn Gānyòu (漢乾祐) 1.
Sòng Bái (宋白) said: Chánzhōu (澶州) was originally in the territory of Hàn Dùnqīu (漢頓丘) County,
south of Wèizhōu (魏州),
at the post road of the two rivers.
In Táng Wǔdé (唐武德) 4, Guānchéng (觀城) and Dùnqīu (頓丘) counties of Wèizhōu (魏州) were separated to establish Chánzhōu (澶州),
named after the ancient Chányuān (澶淵).
In Zhēnguān (貞觀) 1, the prefecture was abolished,
but in Dàlì (大曆) 7, Tián Chéngsì (田承嗣) again memorialized to establish it.
In Hàn Gānyòu (漢乾祐) 1, it was moved to the old site of Déshèng (德勝) Stockade,
and Dùnqīu (頓丘) County moved with the prefecture to below its city wall.
At this time, Chánzhōu (澶州) was still governing the old prefectural city of Dùnqīu (頓丘);
today's Dùnqīu (頓丘) Town in Déqīng (德清) Commandery is that place.)
The Jìn (晉) forces captured his wife and children,
treated them very well,
and sent a secret envoy to entice Yànzhāng (彥章).
Yànzhāng (彥章) executed the envoy,
and the Jìn (晉) forces then exterminated his entire family.
The Jìn (晉) King appointed Lǐ Yán (李巖), a general from Wèizhōu (魏州), as the prefect of Chánzhōu (澶州).
(The *Kǎoyì* (考異) says: The *Zhuāngzōng Shílù* (莊宗實錄) writes
"Lǐ Yán" (李嚴),
now we follow Xuē Shǐ (薛史).)
The Jìn (晉) King reviewed the army in Wèixiàn (魏縣),
then led over a hundred cavalry along the river upstream
to observe Liú Xún's (劉鄩) camp.
It happened to be dark and overcast.
Xún (鄩) had hidden five thousand soldiers in the thickets by the river bend.
They burst out with drums and shouts,
surrounding the King many times over.
The King leapt on his horse, shouted loudly,
and led his cavalry to charge and break through,
sweeping away all in their path.
His subordinate generals, Xià Lǔqí (夏魯奇) and others, fought fiercely with short weapons.
From noon until *shēn* (申) (3-5 PM), they finally broke out,
losing seven cavalrymen.
Lǔqí (魯奇) personally killed over a hundred men
and was wounded all over his body.
When Lǐ Cúnshěn's (李存審) relief troops arrived,
they were then able to escape.
The King looked back at his retinue and said:
"We almost became the butt of the barbarians' jokes!"
(Uses the words of Hàn Guāngwǔ (漢光武).)
pronounced *jūyī* (居依) in *fǎnqiè* (反切).)
(*Chī* (嗤),
pronounced *chǒuzhī* (丑之) in *fǎnqiè* (反切).)
"It was just enough to show the enemy Your Majesty's bravery and martial prowess!"
Lǔqí (魯奇) was from Qīngzhōu (青州).
The King consequently loved him even more
and bestowed upon him the surname and given name Lǐ Shàoqí (李紹奇).
Liú Xún (劉鄩), believing that all Jìn (晉) troops were in Wèizhōu (魏州)
and Jìnyáng (晉陽) must be empty,
wanted to seize it with a surprise attack.
He secretly led his troops west from Huángzé (黃澤).
The Jìn (晉) forces were puzzled that Xún's (鄩) army had not come out for several days,
silent and without a trace.
They sent cavalry to scout,
and there was no smoke from fires in the city,
but flags were occasionally seen moving back and forth along the battlements.
The Jìn (晉) King said:
"I heard that Liú Xún (劉鄩) uses troops with
'a hundred schemes for every step'.
This must be a deception."
He sent more scouts,
who discovered that they had bound straw into figures,
holding flags and riding donkeys on the city walls.
(They were just bundles of straw made into figures, holding flags and riding donkeys on the city walls.)
They questioned an old and weak person found in the city,
who said the army had left two days ago.
The Jìn (晉) King said:
"Liú Xún (劉鄩) is skilled at surprise attacks.
(Liú Xún (劉鄩) captured Yǎnzhōu (兗州)
and conquered Tóngguān (潼關),
all by surprise attacks,
hence it is said so.)
However, when intelligence meets intelligence,
there must be one who is exhausted.
If Xún (鄩) attacks Jìnyáng (晉陽),
then his intelligence will be exhausted.
I estimate his march has only reached the foot of the mountains."
(West of Xiàng (相) and Wèi (魏) are all connected mountains.)
It happened to be raining for ten days.
The Huángzé (黃澤) road was treacherous,
the sticky mud more than a foot deep.
Soldiers advanced by pulling on vines and creepers.
(*Jǐnní* (堇泥)
is sticky clay.)
(*Shēn* (深),
pronounced *shìjìn* (式禁) in *fǎnqiè* (反切).)
(*Yuán* (援),
pronounced *yúyuán* (于元) in *fǎnqiè* (反切).)
Two or three out of ten died.
The Jìn (晉) general Lǐ Sì'ēn (李嗣恩) doubled his pace and entered Jìnyáng (晉陽) first.
The city knew of this
and mobilized troops for defense.
When Xún (鄩) reached Lèpíng (樂平),
his dried provisions were almost exhausted;
(Lèpíng (樂平) is only two hundred fifty *lǐ* (里) from Jìnyáng (晉陽).)
(*Qiǔ* (糗),
pronounced *qùjiǔ* (去久) in *fǎnqiè* (反切).)
Pursuit troops were behind them,
and the multitude feared
they would collapse.
Xún (鄩) admonished them, saying:
"Now we are a thousand *lǐ* (里) from home,
deep in enemy territory,
with troops at our front and back,
and the valleys are high and deep,
like falling into a well.
Where will we go if we flee?
Only by fighting with all our might can we perhaps escape;
otherwise, we will repay our lord and parents with our deaths!"
The multitude wept and halted.
Zhōu Déwēi (周德威), hearing that Xún (鄩) had gone west,
led a thousand cavalry from Yōuzhōu (幽州) to rescue Jìnyáng (晉陽).
When he reached Tǔmén (土門),
Xún (鄩) had already arrayed his forces and descended the mountain.
From Xíngzhōu (邢州) at Chénsòngkǒu (陳宋口), he crossed the Zhāngshuǐ (漳水) eastward
and encamped at Zōngchéng (宗城).
(The *Jiǔyù Zhì* (九域志) says: Zōngchéng (宗城) County is one hundred seventy *lǐ* (里) northwest of Wèizhōu (魏州).)
Nearly half of their horses died.
At that time, the Jìn army was short of provisions.
Liú Xún knew that Línqīng had accumulated supplies,
and wanted to seize it to cut off the Jìn's grain route.
He traveled east from Zōngchéng,
and headed obliquely towards Línqīng, several tens of *lǐ* away.
Sòng Bái said: Línqīng
was originally the territory of Qīngquán County in the Hàn dynasty.
In the 21st year of Tài'hé of the Later Wèi dynasty, Línqīng County was established here.
After two nights,
he arrived at Nángōng.
Nángōng County was 62 *lǐ* southwest of Jìzhōu.
Heading southeast towards Línqīng was also several tens of *lǐ*.
He cut off their wrists and released them,
making them say:
"Zhōu Shìzhōng has already occupied Línqīng!"
The Kǎo Yì says: Xuē Shǐ:
"Déwēi heard that Liú Xún had returned east,
and hastened to Nángōng.
Knowing that Xún's army was in Zōngchéng,
he sent over ten horsemen to approach their camp,
capturing several tens of scouts.
He stabbed them all in the back,
bound and released them.
When they arrived,
they told Xún: 'Zhōu Shìzhōng has already occupied Zōngchéng!'
Xún's army was greatly alarmed."
We note that if they were stabbed in the back,
how could these people revive and speak!
We now follow the Zhuāngzōng Shílù and the Xuē Shǐ's Zhuāngzōng Jì.
Furthermore,
Xún was currently in Zōngchéng,
so saying Zhōu Shìzhōng occupied Zōngchéng
must be a mistaken character for Línqīng.
The next morning,
Déwēi passed by Xún's camp without engaging,
and entered Línqīng.
Xún led his army towards Bèizhōu.
At that time, Jìn Wáng led an army and encamped at Bózhōu.
Liú Xún's army was at Tángyì.
Zhōu Déwēi attacked him,
but failed to overcome him.
The next day,
Xún's army was at Shēnxìan.
The Jiǔyù Zhì says: Shēnxìan is 90 *lǐ* east of Wèizhōu.
Liú Xún saw the Jìn army in Bózhōu,
moved his army west,
and gradually approached Wèizhōu.
Sòng Bái said: Shēn was originally a Wèi settlement in the Spring and Autumn period.
In the Hàn dynasty, it was Yángpíng County.
In the Later Zhōu dynasty, Yángpíng was changed to Qīngyì County.
In the Dàyè era, Qīngyì was changed to Shēnxìan,
named after the ancient place.
Liú Xún fortified Shēnchéng,
dug trenches and defended it.
From Shēn to the river, he built a covered walkway to transport provisions.
Shēnxìan is over 20 *lǐ* east of the Yellow River.
Crossing the river to the east,
to the south is the border of Yùn and Pú.
Therefore, he built a covered walkway connecting to the river to transport provisions.
The covered walkway
had walls built on both sides
to prevent the Jìn army from clashing with or intercepting them.
"Zhì" (治)
is pronounced *zhí* as in *zhí zhī*.
Smoke and fire were visible to each other,
and there were several battles a day.
Jìn Wáng loved Yuán Xíngqīn for his bravery and strength.
He requested him from Lǐ Sìyuán, the Cìshǐ of Dàizhōu.
Lǐ Sìyuán reluctantly presented him,
and he was appointed Sǎnyuán Dūbùshǔ.
The title Dūbùshǔ first appeared in the Tōngjiàn;
later it became the title for a general commander of an army.
The Xuē Shǐ says: At that time, there were "Sǎn Zhǐhuī" (散指揮), whose name was "Sǎnyuán" (散員).
Xíngqīn was appointed Dūbùshǔ.
Shào Róng once fought deep into enemy lines,
a sword struck his face,
and he was not yet freed
when Gāo Xíngzhōu rescued him from danger.
The King again wanted to request Xíngzhōu,
but was hesitant to speak.
He secretly sent someone to entice him with official positions and emoluments.
Xíngzhōu declined, saying:
"Dàizhōu raises brave warriors
also for the Great King.
My service to Dàizhōu
is also like serving the Great King."
The Kǎo Yì says: The Zhōu Tàizǔ Shílù:
"Jìn Wáng secretly sent someone to entice him with profit and emoluments.
Xíngzhōu declined, saying:
'The Zǒngguǎn uses people also for the state.
Serving the Zǒngguǎn is like serving the King.
My brothers and I escaped disaster and were reborn,
receiving the Zǒngguǎn's great kindness.
How could I bear to betray him!' "
According to the Míngzōng Shílù,
this year he was still the Cìshǐ of Dàizhōu.
It was not until the 18th year of Tiānyòu that he became Fù Zǒngguǎn.
This mention of "Zǒngguǎn"
is likely an error in the Zhōu Tàizǔ Shílù.
This event is described in the previous scroll, Qiánhuà third year.
So he stopped.
Yǐn Hào, the Cìshǐ of Jiàngzhōu, attacked Jìn's Xízhōu.
In the eighth month,
he again attacked Cízhōu,
but failed in both attempts.
According to the Jiǔyù Zhì,
Jiàngzhōu is 514 *lǐ* northwest of Xízhōu,
and Xízhōu is 160 *lǐ* southwest of Cízhōu.
Hè Huái
captured it,
arrested Lǐ Yán,
and sent him to Dōngdū.
According to Ōu Shǐ Zhífāng Kǎo,
Liáng had no Zhāoyì Army.
Referring to Hè Huái's biography,
he was likely the Liúhòu of Xuānyì.
"Zhāo" (昭)
should be
"Xuān" (宣).
Previously,
Jìn had seized Chányángzhōu,
and appointed Lǐ Yán to guard it.
He sent 10,000 soldiers to assist Liú Xún,
and also to entice the people of Wèi.
Jìn Wáng sent Lǐ Cúnshěn with 5,000 soldiers to attack Bèizhōu.
Zhāng Yuándé had 3,000 soldiers
who went out every night to plunder.
The people of the prefecture suffered greatly from this,
and requested that the city be trenched to allow for peaceful farming.
Cúnshěn then mobilized able-bodied men from eight counties to trench and besiege it.
Bèizhōu administered Qīnghé, Qīngyáng, Wǔchéng, Jīngchéng, Línqīng, Zhāngnán, Lìtíng, and Xiàjīn, eight counties.
Liú Xún had been in Shēn for a long time,
and provisions were inadequate.
The Jìn army repeatedly came to the foot of his camp to challenge him,
but Xún did not come out.
The Jìn army then attacked and cut off his covered walkway.
With over a thousand axes, they cut down the camp's wooden structures.
The Liáng soldiers were alarmed and came out,
whereupon they were captured and the Jìn army returned.
The Emperor issued an edict reprimanding Xún for his protracted war,
excessive expenditure of provisions,
heavy losses,
and failure to engage in decisive battle.
Xún reported:
"I recently wanted to use surprise troops to strike at their heart,
and recover Zhèn and Dìng,
expecting to clear the Hésuò region again within ten days.
Ten days is called *xún shí*.
Prolonged heavy rains for a full *xún* led to depleted provisions and sick soldiers.
I also wanted to occupy Línqīng to cut off their provisions,
but Zhōu Yángwǔ arrived suddenly,
charging and striking like a god.
I am now retreating to secure Shēnxìan,
to rest my soldiers and train them, awaiting an opportune time to advance.
Observing their numerous troops,
skilled in horsemanship and archery,
they are indeed a formidable enemy,
not to be underestimated.
*Qíng* (勍)
is pronounced *qú jīng*.
*Yì* (易)
is pronounced *yǐ shì*.
If there were an exploitable opening,
how could I dare to take my ease and foster the enemy!"
The Emperor again asked Xún for a decisive strategy.
Xún replied:
"I have no strategy now.
I only wish that each person be given ten *hú* of grain,
and the enemy can be defeated."
Liú Xún wanted to defeat Jìn through attrition.
He reprimanded Xún:
"General, are you hoarding rice
to defeat the enemy,
or to relieve hunger?"
Thereupon, he sent a palace envoy to oversee the battle.
Liú Xún assembled his generals and asked:
"The Emperor stays deep within the forbidden palace,
ignorant of military affairs.
He merely consults with young, newly promoted individuals.
Military strategy lies in adapting to changing circumstances,
not in rigid predetermination.
Now the enemy is still strong;
to fight them would surely be disadvantageous.
What should we do?"
The generals all said:
"Victory or defeat should be decided at once;
why prolong the delay!"
Liú Xún was silent,
displeased.
He withdrew
and said to his confidants:
"The lord is dim, his ministers sycophantic;
the generals are arrogant, the soldiers lax.
I do not know where I shall die!"
Liú Xún's assessment of the enemy and consideration of victory
was not a bad plan;
it was merely that his hands were tied, preventing him from carrying out his original strategy.
He again gathered the generals at the army gate,
placing a vessel of river water before each person
and ordering them to drink it.
The衆 could not fathom its meaning.
Liú Xún explained to them:
"If one vessel is already difficult,
can the surging river
ever be completely drunk up!"
The衆 turned pale.
A few days later,
Liú Xún led over ten thousand men to approach Zhèn and Dìng, setting up camp.
The people of Zhèn and Dìng were alarmed and disturbed.
Lǐ Cúnshěn of Jìn, with two thousand cavalry, attacked them transversely.
Lǐ Jiànjí assisted with a thousand silver-spear men.
Liú Xún suffered a great defeat
and fled back.
The Jìn people pursued him
to the foot of his camp,
capturing and beheading thousands.
Liú Xún wished to attack Zhèn and Dìng by surprise,
but was defeated by the Jìn people.
Liú Xún's strategy was again exhausted.
12 Liú Yán took a wife from Chǔ.
King Yīn of Chǔ dispatched Cún, the Military Governor of Yǒngshùn, to escort her.
13 On the Yǐwèi day,
the Shǔ ruler appointed Wáng Zōngwǎn, concurrently Grand Chancellor, as overall commander of the northern campaign army;
Wáng Zōngbò, concurrently Grand Chancellor, as pacification commissioner
to attack Qínzhōu.
He appointed Wáng Zōngyáo, concurrently Grand Chancellor, as pacification commissioner for the northeast front;
and Wáng Zōnghán, concurrently Grand Chancellor, as deputy commissioner
to attack Fèngzhōu.
At that time, both Qín and Fèng prefectures belonged to Qí.
14 On the Gēngxū day,

Wú appointed Xú Wēn, Military Governor of Zhènhǎi, as overall commander of all land and naval, cavalry and infantry forces within the territory, Grand Pacification Commissioner for the two Zhè districts, acting Grand Mentor, and Duke of Qí.
He was stationed at Rùnzhōu,
with Shēng, Rùn, Cháng, Xuān, Shè, and Chí — six prefectures — under his supervision.
All military and national affairs were to be deliberated and decided as before.
The historians say that Xú Wēn, by holding a strategic stronghold externally,
controlled the power of the Wú state internally.
This hastened Xú Zhīxùn's death.
15 Initially,
the Emperor, as Prince Jūn, married the daughter of Zhāng Guībà, Military Governor of Héyáng.
Upon his ascension,
he wished to establish her as Empress.
However, the Empress refused,
citing that the Emperor had not yet performed the southern suburban sacrifice.
The ancients believed
that after offering sacrifice to the Supreme Emperor in the suburbs,
one could then rule the people on behalf of Heaven.
On the Rénwǔ day,
her illness worsened.
She was enfeoffed as Virtue (Dé).
That evening,
she passed away.
Prince Kāng, Yǒujìng,
had double pupils.
Believing himself destined to be Emperor,
he plotted rebellion.
In winter,
the tenth month,
on the Xīnhài night,
when Virtue was about to be buried,
Yǒujìng placed several confidants in hiding in the sleeping palace.
The Emperor became aware of this,
escaped barefoot over the wall,
summoned the imperial guards to search the palace,
found and personally slew them.
On the Rénzǐ day,
Yǒujìng was apprehended
and executed.
From this, the Emperor grew estranged from and suspicious of the imperial clan.
He solely relied on Zhào Yán and the brothers of Virtue, Hàn Dǐng and Hàn Jié, as well as their cousins Hàn Lún and Hàn Róng.
All held close positions,
participating in deliberations.
Whenever troops were dispatched, he always made them supervise.
Yán and others, relying on their power, abused it,
sold offices and manipulated justice,
and sowed discord among the old generals and chancellors.
Although Jìng Xiáng and Lǐ Zhèn were in charge of administration,
much of what they said was not adopted.
Zhèn often feigned illness and did not participate in affairs
to avoid the families of Zhào and Zhāng.
Governance became increasingly chaotic
until the state's downfall.
The historians say that the Liáng had reasons for its self-destruction;
it was not that Jìn was able to destroy it.
16 Liú Xún sent soldiers to feign surrender to Jìn,
plotting to bribe the cook to poison the Jìn King.
The plot was exposed,
and the Jìn King executed him
and five of his associates.
17 In the eleventh month,
on the Jǐwèi night,
a fire broke out in the Shǔ palace.
Since the capture of Chéngdū, precious goods stored in the hundred-foot tower
were all reduced to ashes.
Zōng Kǎn, overall commander of all armies and concurrently Grand Chancellor, and others led the guards to try and put out the fire,
but the Shǔ ruler closed the gates and did not let them in.
He feared that some might take advantage of the fire-fighting to cause trouble.
The historians speak of the Shǔ ruler's suspicion and caution.
On the Gēngshēn day,
the fire had still not gone out.
The Shǔ ruler went out of Yìxīng Gate to meet his ministers
to reassure the populace.
He toured the capital,
and after speaking,
returned to the palace and closed the gates.
The fire had not yet gone out,
and he dared not relax his guard.
also read "Fú" (扶又翻).
18 On the Rénxū day,
Shǔ granted a general amnesty.
19 On the Yǐchǒu day,
the era name was changed.
This record states that Liáng changed its era name to Zhēnmíng.
The "Kǎo Yì" (考異) says: The "Wúyuè Bèishǐ" (吳越備史) states:
"On the Rénchén day of the first month,
the era name was changed,
and a general amnesty was granted."
This follows Xuē's "Shǐ" (史) and the Imperial Annals of the Last Emperor.
On the 20th day of the Jǐsì month,
Wáng Zōnghàn, the King of Shǔ, led his troops out of Qīngnílǐng,
and captured Gùzhèn.
The Jiǔyù Zhì states: Gùzhèn is in Héchí Xiàn, Fèngzhōu.
The Jiǔyù Zhì states: Níyángzhèn is in Lìtíng Xiàn, Chéngzhōu.
They retreated and held Lùtáishān.
Today, Lùyùshān is ten lǐ east of Chéngzhōu.
On the Xīnwèi day,
Wáng Zōngwǎn and others defeated Qínzhōu soldiers at Jīnshāgǔ,
captured their general Lǐ Yàncháo and others,
and, capitalizing on their victory, pressed towards Qínzhōu.
Wáng Zōngduó, the Cìshǐ of Xīngzhōu, captured Jiēzhōu,
and received the surrender of its Cìshǐ, Lǐ Yàn'ān.
On the Jiǎxū day,
Wáng Zōngwǎn captured Chéngzhōu,
and captured its Cìshǐ, Lǐ Yàndé.
When the Shǔ army reached Shàngrǎnfáng,
Lǐ Jìchóng, the Jiédùshǐ of Qínzhōu, sent his son Yànxiù to offer the tally and seal in surrender.
Zōngjiàng entered Qínzhōu.
The Jiǔyù Zhì states: From Qínzhōu southeast to Fèngzhōu is 320 lǐ;
from Qínzhōu southwest to Chéngzhōu is 265 lǐ;
from Chéngzhōu southwest to Jiēzhōu is 250 lǐ.
"Zōngjiàng"
should be
"Zōngwǎn."
Liú Zhījùn attacked Huò Yānwēi at Bīnzhōu,
but failed to capture it for half a year.
In the fifth month of this year, Liú Zhījùn attacked Bīnzhōu.
Zhījùn's wife and children were all moved to Chéngdū;
Zhījùn lifted the siege and returned to Fèngxiáng,
but fearing eventual disaster,
at night he led seventy of his close guards,
broke through the gate, and left.
On the Gēngchén day,
he defected to the Shǔ army.
Wáng Zōngwǎn advanced his troops from Héchí and Liǎngdāng,
joining Wáng Zōngyáo to attack Fèngzhōu.
On the Guǐwèi day,
they captured it.
Shǔ thus gained the territory of Qín, Fèng, and Chéng three prefectures.
Sòng Bái said: Héchí Xiàn belonged to Wǔdū during the Hàn dynasty.
The Huáyáng Guózhì states: Héchí is also called Qiúchí.
According to this, Qiúchíshān is on the border of Chéngzhōu.
Today, Héchí Xiàn belongs to Fèngzhōu,
and is somewhat far from the county seat.
The place where the current county seat is located is called Héchíshuǐ,
hence the county is named after it.
Liǎngdāng was
the ancient Dàodào Xiàn of Hàn.
The Shuǐjīng states: Liǎngdāngshuǐ originates from Dàsǎnlǐng in Chéncāng Xiàn,
and flows southwest into Gùdàochuān.
Also, Héchí Xiàn has Liǎngdāngshuǐ,

should probably be
"Shuòzhōu".
The *Kǎoyì* states: In the Kaiyuan era,
Zhènwǔ Jūn was located 350 *lǐ* northwest of Shuòzhōu, within the city of Dānyú Dūhùfǔ,
and was subordinate to the Shuòfāng Jìedùshǐ.
In the first year of Qiányuán, the Zhènwǔ Jìedùshǐ was established,
governing Zhènběi Dàdūhù and Lín and Shèng two prefectures.
The Later Táng Zhènwǔ Jìedùshǐ also held the titles of Ānběi Dūhù and Inspector of Lín and Shèng prefectures, etc.
After the Shí Jìn, all held the title of Cìshǐ of Shuòzhōu.
According to this, it governed Wèizhōu,
but the year of relocation is unknown.
Cúnzhāng executed their envoy.
The Qìdān advanced to attack Yúnzhōu,
and Cúnzhāng resisted with all his might.
Yúnzhōu was Dàtóng Jūn.
19th year, 9th month.
Jìn Wáng returned to Jìnyáng.
The King was benevolent and filial,
so although he was engaged in operations north of the Yellow River,
he frequently returned to Jìnyáng to visit Cáo Fūrén,
two or three times a year.
20th year, Jìn forces pressed Cāngzhōu.
Dài Sīyuǎn, Jìedùshǐ of Shùnhuà, abandoned the city and fled to Dōngdū.
Héshuò entirely fell to Jìn,
Cāngzhōu was isolated,
and Dài Sīyuǎn could not defend it.
Jìn Wáng ordered Lǐ Sìyuán to lead troops to pacify and garrison it,
and Sìyuán sent Zhāng to Jìnyáng.
Jìn Wáng transferred Lǐ Cúnshěn to be Jìedùshǐ of Hénghǎi,
to garrison Cāngzhōu.
Cāngdé thus belonged to Jìn,
and Shùnhuà was again changed to Hénghǎi,
following the old Táng designation.
Sìyuán appointed Ān Chónghuǐ as Zhōngménshǐ.
Within Jìn Wáng’s domain,
all Jìedù offices had a Zhōngménshǐ.
Their role was that of the Tiāncháo Shūmìshǐ.
Chónghuǐ also dedicated himself to Sìyuán.
Chónghuǐ was
a Hú person from Yìngzhōu.
21st year, Jìn Wáng personally led troops to relieve Yúnzhōu.
When he reached Dàizhōu,
the Qìdān heard of it and withdrew.
The King also returned.
He appointed Lǐ Cúnzhāng as Jìedùshǐ of Dàtóng.
22nd year, Jìn forces had besieged Bèizhōu for over a year;
Jìn had besieged Bèizhōu in the 8th month of the previous year.
He wanted to surrender.
He consulted with his troops.
The troops, fearing that surrendering only when exhausted
might not save them from death,
refused.
They together killed Yuán Dé
and held the city firmly.
Food ran out in the city,
and they ate people as provisions.
Then they told the Jìn general:
“We fear death if we surrender.
Please allow us to surrender wearing armor and bearing weapons,
and release us once the situation is settled.”
The Jìn general agreed.
Their 3,000 troops came out to surrender.
After they had laid down their armor,
they were surrounded and killed,
all perished.
Jìn Wáng appointed Máozhāng as Cìshǐ of Bèizhōu.
At this point, all of Héběi fell to Jìn,
except Líyáng, which was held by Liáng.
Líyáng was by the river,
Liáng's forces still maintained contact and support,
and Liú Xún defended it,
which is why it could hold its own.
Wéi,
pronounced "yú wěi fān".
23rd year, Jìn Wáng went to Wèizhōu.
24th year, Wú’s Guāngzhōu general Wáng Yán killed Cìshǐ Dài Zhào.
"Zài"
should probably be
"Dài".
Zhāng Chóng, Guāncháshǐ of Lúzhōu, without waiting for orders,
led troops to Guāngzhōu.
Yán abandoned the city and fled.
Lǐ Hòu was provisionally appointed to govern Guāngzhōu.
Chóng was
a native of Shènxian.
25th year, on the Gēngshēn day,
the new Shǔ palace was completed.
It was located north of the old palace.
26th year, Wáng Tán, Jìedùshǐ of Tiānpíng and concurrent Zhōngshūlìng, known as Lángxié Zhōngyì Wáng,
recruited many bandits
and kept them under his command as personal guards.
On the Jǐmǎo day,
the bandits, taking advantage of Tán's unpreparedness,
burst into the residence and killed Tán.
Péi Yàn, the Deputy Jìedùshǐ, led the army garrison to attack and execute them.
The military administration was thereby secured.
In the winter of the 27th year,
10th month,
on the *Jiǎshēn* day,
Wáng Zōngwǎn (王宗綰), King of Shǔ, and others sallied forth from Dàsàn Pass,
utterly defeating the Qí (岐) troops.
They captured and beheaded tens of thousands,
and then seized Bǎojī (寶雞).
On the *Jǐchǒu* day,
Wáng Zōngbò (王宗播) and others sallied forth from Gù Pass
and reached Lǒngzhōu (隴州).
Gù Pass
refers to Dàzhèn Gù Pass (大震故關).
On the *Bǐngyín* day,
Lǐ Jìjí (李繼岌), the military commissioner of Bǎoshèng (保勝) and acting attendant, feared the suspicion of the King of Qí.
Qí (岐) had established the Bǎoshèng Army in Lǒngzhōu.
He abandoned Lǒngzhōu and fled to the Shǔ (蜀) army.
The Shǔ (蜀) troops advanced to attack Lǒngzhōu,
appointing Jìjí as the Fourth Recruiter of the Northwestern Route Mobile Headquarters.
Liú Zhījùn (劉知俊) met Wáng Zōngwǎn (王宗綰) and others to besiege Fèngxiáng (鳳翔),
but the Qí (岐) troops did not come out.
Coinciding with heavy snow,
the Shǔ (蜀) lord recalled the army.
He restored Lǐ Jìjí's (李繼岌) original name, Sāng Hóngzhì (桑弘志).
Hóngzhì (弘志)
was a native of Líyáng (黎陽).
In the 28th year, on the *Dīngyǒu* day,
Zhèng Yù (鄭玉), a junior minister of the Ministry of Rites, was made a junior minister of the Central Secretariat and concurrently acting chancellor.
Yù (玉)
was the great-nephew of Qǐng (綮).
For Zhèng Qǐng (鄭綮), see volume 259, first year of Qiánníng (乾寧) of Táng Zhāozōng (唐昭宗).
The “Divergent Records” states: Xuē Shǐ’s (薛史) “Annals of the Last Emperor of Liáng” (梁末帝紀) does not record the year and month of Yù's (玉) first appointment as chancellor.
In the 10th month of this year, on the *Dīngyǒu* day,
Zhèng Yù (鄭玉), a junior minister of the Central Secretariat and acting chancellor, was concurrently appointed minister of the Ministry of Punishments and acting chancellor.
Then in the 4th month of the 4th year of Zhēnmíng (貞明), on the *Jǐyǒu* day,
it again says Zhèng Yù (鄭玉), a junior minister of the Central Secretariat and acting chancellor, was concurrently minister of the Ministry of Punishments.
It is suspected that he became chancellor in the 2nd year of Zhēnmíng (貞明)
and transferred to minister of the Ministry of Punishments in the 4th year.
His biography states:
“He was successively promoted to junior minister of the Ministry of Rites,
and appointed acting chancellor during the Zhēnmíng (貞明) period.”
“Táng Yú Lù” (唐餘錄), “Annals of Emperor Jùn” (均帝紀) states:
“In the 10th month of the 2nd year of Zhēnmíng (貞明), on the *Dīngyǒu* day,
Zhèng Yù (鄭玉), a junior minister of the Ministry of Rites, was made a junior minister of the Central Secretariat and acting chancellor.”
We follow this now.
Furthermore, Gāo Ruòzhuō’s (高若拙) “Hòu Shǐ Bǔ” (後史補) states:
“Yù (玉) passed the examinations on his nineteenth attempt,
his name being the nineteenth person,
and his rank was also the same.
From passing the examination, it took him nineteen years to become chancellor.”
Now, according to the records, Yù (玉) passed the examination in the 3rd year of Guānghuà (光化).
From the 3rd year of Guānghuà (光化) to this year, it was only seventeen years,
which also does not match.
In the 29th year, on the *Jǐhài* day,
Shǔ (蜀) granted a general amnesty.
In the 30th year, the King of Jìn (晉) sent an envoy to Wú (吳)
to muster troops to attack Liáng (梁).
In the 11th month,
Wú (吳) appointed Xú Zhìxùn (徐知訓), the deputy commander of the mobile army, as the Commander-in-Chief of the Huáinán (淮南) Mobile Headquarters.
He and Zhū Jǐn (朱瑾) and others led troops to Sòng (宋) and Bó (亳) to rendezvous with Jìn (晉).
After crossing the Huái (淮) River,
they dispatched proclamations to the prefectures and counties,
and advanced to besiege Yǐngzhōu (潁州).
In the 31st year, 12th month,
on the *Wùshēn* day,
Shǔ (蜀) granted a general amnesty,
changing the era name for the coming year to Tiānhàn (天漢),
and the dynastic title to Dàhàn (大漢).
In the 32nd year, Yīn (殷), King of Chǔ (楚), hearing that the King of Jìn (晉) had pacified Hébĕi (河北),
sent an envoy to establish friendly relations.
The King of Jìn (晉) also sent an envoy in response.
In the 33rd year,
Qìngzhōu (慶州) rebelled and defected to Qí (岐).
Qìngzhōu (慶州) was originally Qí (岐) territory,
but because Lǐ Bǎohéng (李保衡) had attached Bīnníng (邠寧) to Liáng (梁) last year,
it became Liáng's (梁) possession.
An imperial edict appointed Hè Huái (賀懷), the commander of the Left Dragon and Tiger Guards, as the Commander-in-Chief of Cavalry and Infantry of the Western Route Mobile Headquarters.
He led troops to suppress them,
defeated the Qí (岐) troops,
and captured the two prefectures of Níng (寧) and Yǎn (衍).
Yǎnzhōu (衍州)
was established by Lǐ Màozhēn (李茂貞) of Qí (岐),
located between Níng (寧) and Qìng (慶).
Sòng (宋) abolished Yǎnzhōu (衍州) and made it Dìngpíng (定平)鎮,
belonging to Bīnzhōu (邠州).
The “Divergent Records” states: In Xuē Shǐ’s (薛史) biography of Hè Huái (賀懷):
“In the 2nd year of Zhēnmíng (貞明), Qìngzhōu (慶州) rebelled

and was occupied by Lǐ Jìzhì (李繼陟). The Emperor ordered Hè Huái (賀懷), commander of the Left Dragon and Tiger Guards, to be the Commander-in-Chief of Cavalry and Infantry of the Western Route Mobile Headquarters and concurrently Supervisor of all armies.
He and Zhāng Jūn (張筠) defeated thirty thousand troops of Jīng (涇) and Fèng (鳳),
and captured the two prefectures of Níng (寧) and Yǎn (衍).”
This was not a minor event,
but it is absent from the “Annals of the Last Emperor” (末帝紀) and the biography of Lǐ Màozhēn (李茂貞),
appearing only in the biography of Huái (懷).
We now use it as our basis.
In the 34th year, Zhāng Chéngyè (張承業), the supervisor of Hédōng (河東), became influential and powerful.
His nephews, Guàn (瓘) and five others, traveled from Tóngzhōu (同州) to rely on him.
The King of Jìn (晉), for Chéngyè’s (承業) sake,
all promoted and employed them.
Chéngyè (承業) managed his household very strictly.
One of his nephews was a bandit
who killed a cattle seller.
Chéngyè (承業) immediately beheaded him.
The King urgently sent someone to save him,
but it was too late.
The King appointed Guàn (瓘) as the prefect of Línzhōu (麟州).
Chéngyè (承業) said to Guàn (瓘):
“You were originally a commoner of Chēdù (車度),
and a bandit with Liú Kāidào (劉開道).”
Liú Kāidào (劉開道) must refer to Liú Zhījùn (劉知俊),
who was commander of the Kaidào (開道) forces for Liáng (梁)
and once stationed in Tóngzhōu (同州).
“Chē” (車)
is pronounced *chǐzhē* (尺遮翻).
“If you do not reform now,
your death is imminent!”
From then on, Guàn (瓘) did not dare to be corrupt or tyrannical wherever he went.
In the 35th year, Qián Chuánxiàng (錢傳珦), the commander of the vanguard within the household of Wúyuè (吳越), married a woman from Mǐn (閩).
From then on, Mǐn (閩) and Wúyuè (吳越) established friendly relations.
In the 36th year, Mǐn (閩) minted lead coins
to circulate alongside copper coins.
37 Initially,
the people of Yān suffered from Liú Shǒuguāng’s cruelty and tyranny,
and many soldiers defected to the Qìdān;
when Shǒuguāng was besieged in Yōuzhōu,
the details are in the previous volume.
The Qìdān grew stronger day by day.
Qìdān King Ābǎojī declared himself emperor,
and his people called him Tiānhuáng Wáng,
establishing his wife, the Shùlǜ clan, as empress,
and appointing various officials;
at this point,
he changed the reign title to Shéncè.
The Kǎoyì states: The Jìnián Tōngpǔ says:
"The old histories do not record Ābǎojī's establishment of a reign title.
Currently, among the Qìdān, there is a calendar
that records 120 years.
In the winter of Jǐngyòu third year, this humble servant was an envoy to the north, to Yōu and Jì,
and obtained their calendar.
Upon examining the year sequence,
Yǐhài was the first year,
and the next year was clearly designated the first year of Shéncè,
followed later by Tiānzàn.
According to the Wǔdài Qìdān Zhuàn,
it was only from Yēlǜ Déguāng that the name Tiānxiǎn was recorded.
It is suspected that at that time, their records were not obtained,
or else the barbarians, ashamed that Ābǎojī had no title,
posthumously created one for him.
Ābǎojī
was also called Tiānhuáng Wáng among the barbarians." The Lǔtíng Zá jì says:
"Tàizǔ, in one swift campaign, annexed the Xī kingdom,
yet still established the Xī people as the Xī kings as before,
and ordered the Qìdān to supervise their military.
He also extinguished Bóhǎi,
captured its king Dà Yīnyuàn,
and made his eldest son the Bóhǎi Dōngdān Wáng,
titled Rén huáng Wáng.
He himself was called Tiānhuáng Wáng,
and first established the reign title as Tiānzàn,
and also Shéncè,
and the state was called Dà Liáo.
In the large tribe where he resided, he built a tower,
calling it the Xīlóu,
which is now called Shàngjīng;
he also built a tower to its south at Mùyèshān,
calling it the Nánlóu;
he also built a tower a thousand *lǐ* to its east,
calling it the Dōnglóu;
he also built a tower three hundred *lǐ* to its north,
calling it the Běilóu;
Tàizǔ often roamed and hunted between the four towers in all four seasons."
It also says:
"After Ābǎojī transformed his household into a state,
he first designated the royal clan as Hèngzhàng,
with the surname Shìlǐmòlǐ,
which, when translated into Hàn Chinese, is Yēlǜ Shì.
He bestowed the empress's clan with the surname Xiāo Shì.
The royal clan could only intermarry with the empress's clan;
if other tribes did not follow the orders of the Northern Lord,
they were not allowed to intermarry with these two clans."
Ōuyáng Shǐ says:
"Ābǎojī, using his wife Shùlǜ's strategy,
sent people to tell the tribal chiefs: 'I have salt ponds,
from which all tribes eat.
However, the tribes know the benefit of eating salt but do not know that the salt has an owner,
is this acceptable?
You should come and reward me.'
The tribes thought this reasonable,
and all gathered at the salt ponds with wine.
Ābǎojī hid soldiers nearby,
and when they were deep in their cups, the hidden soldiers attacked,
killing all the tribal chiefs,
and thus he established himself,
never to be replaced again."
That Ābǎojī declared himself emperor, the former histories do not record the year and month.
In the Zhuāngzōng Lièzhuàn and Qìdān Zhuàn, it is placed after Zhuāngzōng's enthronement and Lǐ Cúnshěn's defense of Fányáng;
the Hàn Gāozǔ Shílù and Táng Yúlù both state that Ābǎojī devised a plan to unite the tribes,
and then declared himself emperor,
placing it during the Qiánníng era before Liú Rén'gōng's governance of Yōuzhōu;
Xuē Shǐ places it at the end of Zhuāngzōng's Tiānyòu era.
According to the Jìnián Tōngpǔ,
the first year of Ābǎojī's Shéncè was a Bǐngzǐ year,
which was the thirteenth year of Zhuāngzōng's Tiānyòu,
and the second year of Liáng Zhēnmíng,
seemingly not at the end of Tiānyòu nor after Zhuāngzōng's enthronement.
The Biānyílù states that in the fifth month of Kāipíng second year, Tàizǔ, in a record of bestowing a gift upon Ābǎojī, still called him "Qīng,"
and also mentioned
"this humble servant serves our court,
hoping the state will send an envoy to officially enfeoff him,"
he must not yet have declared himself emperor.
How could it have been before Liú Rén'gōng governed Yōuzhōu?
The Táng Yúlù entirely adopts the Qìdān events from the Hàn Gāozǔ Shílù to form its biography,
which is the most erroneous.
The exact year of his declaration as emperor is unknown,
but since he changed his reign title,
it is placed here.
Empress Shùlǜ was courageous, decisive, and resourceful.
Whenever Ābǎojī led troops or managed the multitude,
Empress Shùlǜ often participated in his plans.
Ābǎojī once crossed the desert to attack the Dǎngxiàng;
the Dǎngxiàng were west of the desert.
Qì,
pronounced Qī Jì.
Dǎng,
pronounced Dǐ Lǎng.
The Huángtóu and Chòubó two Shìwěi, taking advantage of the vacuum, joined forces to raid him;
Huángtóu
was a strong Shìwěi tribe;
Chòubó
was a Shìwěi tribe named after its dwelling place.
He marshaled his troops to await their arrival,
fiercely attacked,
and utterly defeated them,
thereby gaining fame among all the barbarian tribes.
Empress Shùlǜ had a mother and an aunt,
both of whom sat on couches to receive her bows,
saying:
"I only bow to Heaven,
not to people."
The King of Jìn was then campaigning in Héběi,
wishing to ally with the Qìdān for support,
and always treated Ābǎojī as an uncle,
and Empress Shùlǜ as an aunt.
This was because Jìn Wáng Kèyòng and Ābǎojī had become sworn brothers.
In his later years, Liú Shǒuguāng was in decline and distress,
and sent his staff officer Hán Yánhuī to seek aid from the Qìdān.
The Kǎoyì states: The Hàn Gāozǔ Shílù's Yánhuī Zhuàn says:
"In the Tiānyòu era, military commissioner Liú Shǒuguāng attacked Zhōngshān unsuccessfully,
and wishing to ally with the Northern barbarians,
sent Yánhuī as an envoy to the barbarians."
Liú Shù believed that after Liú Shǒuguāng occupied Yōuzhōu, he never attacked Dìngzhōu.
Only in the third year of Táng Guānghuà, when Biàn general Zhāng Cúnjìng captured Yíng and Mò
and attacked Dìngzhōu,
Liú Rén'gōng sent Shǒuguāng to rescue Dìngzhōu,
but he was defeated by Cúnjìng.
It is feared that this was at that time,
when Rén'gōng was the commander of Yōu,
not Shǒuguāng.
However, when Liú Rén'gōng and his son were strong and prosperous, they often bullied the Qìdān,
how could they be willing to send an envoy to ally with them!
In the first year of Gānhuà, Shǒuguāng attacked Yì Dìng,
and Wáng Chǔzhí sought help from Jìn,
so the King of Jìn sent Zhōu Déwēi to attack him.
It was probably at this time that he sent Yánhuī to ally with the Qìdān.
However, since there is no clear evidence,
it simply states "declining and distressed,"
appended here.
He was made to herd horses in the wilderness.
Yánhuī,
a man from Yōuzhōu, was intelligent and resourceful,
and quite skilled in writing.
Empress Shùlǜ spoke to the Qìdān lord, saying:
"Yánhuī is able to uphold his integrity and not yield;
he is a worthy man of today.
How can he be degraded by being a groom!
He should be treated with respect and employed."
The Qìdān lord summoned Yánhuī and spoke with him,
was pleased,
and consequently made him his chief strategist,
consulting him on all actions.
Yánhuī first taught the Qìdān to establish a government,
build cities and outer walls,
and set up markets and residential areas,
to settle the Hàn people,
ensuring each had a spouse,
and to cultivate barren land.
Consequently, the Hàn people each settled into their livelihoods,
and the number of fugitives decreased.
The Qìdān subdued various states with their might,
and Yánhuī played a part in this.
A short while later,
Yán Huī (延徽) fled to Jìnyáng (晉陽).
The King of Jìn (晉) wanted to place him in the military headquarters,
but the secretary Zhǎng Shūjì Wáng Jiān (掌書記王緘) disliked him.
Yán Huī (延徽) felt uneasy,
and requested to return east to visit his mother.
He returned from Jìnyáng (晉陽) to Yōuzhōu (幽州),
going from west to east.
省 (shěng),
read as Xī Jǐng Fān (悉景翻).
He stayed at the home of a local, Wáng Démíng (王德明).
Wáng Démíng (王德明) was the adopted son of Zhào Wáng Róng (趙王鎔),
who was Zhāng Wénlǐ (張文禮) of Yān (燕).
Yán Huī (延徽) said,
"Now all of Héběi (河北) belongs to Jìn (晉).
I must return to the Qìdān (契丹)."
Démíng (德明) said,
"Having rebelled and returned,
will you not face death?"
He meant that having rebelled against the Qìdān (契丹) and returned to the Central Plains,
now going back to the Qìdān (契丹) again,
he feared he would be killed by them.
復 (fù),
read as Fú Yòu Fān (扶又翻);
same below.
"When I left them,
it was as if they had lost a hand or an eye.
Now that I am going back to them,
their hand and eye will be restored.
How could they harm me!"
After visiting his mother,
he then re-entered Qìdān (契丹).
The Qìdān (契丹) ruler, hearing of his arrival,
was greatly pleased,
as if he had descended from heaven.
Patting him on the back, he said,
"Where did you go previously?"
Yán Huī (延徽) said,
"I missed my mother
and wanted to ask for leave to return,
but feared you would not permit it,
so I returned privately."
The Qìdān (契ān) ruler treated him even more favorably.
When he proclaimed himself emperor,
he made Yán Huī (延徽) his prime minister,
who was successively promoted to Zhōngshū Lìng (中書令).
The Oū Shǐ Sìyí Fùlù (歐史四夷附錄) says: Ābǎojī (阿保機) made Yán Huī (延徽) his prime minister,
calling him Zhèngshì Lìng (政事令).
The Qìdān (契丹) referred to him as
"Chóngwén Xiànggōng (崇文相公)."
The King of Jìn (晉) sent an envoy to Qìdān (契丹).
Yán Huī (延徽) sent a letter to the King of Jìn (晉),
explaining his reasons for going north,
and further said,
"It is not that I do not long for an enlightened lord,
nor that I do not miss my homeland.
The reason I did not stay
was precisely my fear of Wáng Jiān's (王緘) slanders."
He then entrusted his aged mother to the king,
and further said,
"With Yán Huī (延徽) here,
the Qìdān (契丹) will certainly not graze their horses south."
Jiǎ Yì's (賈誼) Guò Qín Lùn (過秦論) states: The Hú (胡) people dared not go south to graze their horses.
The Qìdān (契丹) not deeply invading as bandits
was due to Yán Huī's (延徽) efforts.
However, during the reign of Zhuāngzōng (莊宗),

Wáng did not consent.
Yán Kěqiú repeatedly urged Wēn to have his second son, Zhīxún, replace Xú Zhīgào in managing Wú's government.
Zhīgào conspired with Luò Zhīxiáng
and had Kěqiú sent out as Cǐshǐ of Chǔzhōu.
After Kěqiú received the order,
he arrived at Jīnlíng,
met Wēn,
and persuaded him, saying:
"We uphold the orthodox calendar of Táng
and constantly use 'restoration' as our pretext.
Now Zhū and Lǐ are contending;
the Zhū clan is daily weakening,
and the Lǐ clan is daily strengthening.
If the Lǐ clan gains the realm one day,
can we face north and serve them as subjects?
It would be better to establish the state of Wú first to secure the people's hopes."
Wēn was greatly pleased,
and retained Kěqiú
to assist in managing all state affairs,
instructing him to draft the ceremonial protocols.
He drafted the procedures for establishing the state.
He then gave his daughter in marriage to Kěqiú's son, Xù.
33 Jìn Wáng wanted to advance quickly to Dàliáng,
but the Liáng army blocked his front,
reinforcing their defenses and refusing to fight for over a hundred days.
In the twelfth month,
on the first day of Gēngzǐ,
Jìn Wáng advanced his troops,

He advanced from Májiā Dù to press towards Xíngtái Cūn.
Initially,
Hè Huái (賀懷), the commander-in-chief of the Northern Front Mobile Army, was skilled at leading infantry,
and Xiè Yànzhāng (謝彥章), the commander of the battle formations, was skilled at leading cavalry.
Hè Huái (賀懷) resented being considered their equal.
History states that Hè Huái (賀懷) was jealous of talent and thereby caused national affairs to go awry.
惡 (è),
pronounced wū lù.
Hè Huái (賀懷) and Yànzhāng (彥章) were drilling troops in the field,

At this point,

Hè Huái (懷) repeatedly wanted to fight,

and by some chance stumble,

Xiè Yànzhāng (謝彥章) wanted to prolong the engagement to wear out the Jìn (晉) army,
while Hè Huái (賀懷) wanted to decide the outcome in a single battle.
From this perspective,
there was indeed a gap in their wisdom and insight.
蹉 (cuō),
pronounced qī hé.
跌 (diē),
pronounced tú jié.
Hè Huái (懷)

He (Yànzhāng) was also an excellent cavalry general.

The national capital refers to Dàliáng (大梁).
and fortunately engage them in battle,

The King wanted to personally lead ten thousand cavalry directly to Dàliáng (大梁),

to hastily pursue advantage

35Hè Huái (賀懷) heard that the King of Jìn (晉) had already moved west,

Húliǔ Pō (胡柳陂) is in Pú Zhōu (濮州),

Zhōu Déwēi (周德ēi) said:
"The enemy has come a long way, doubling their march,

Our camp and palisades are already secure,

This place is very close to Dàliáng (大梁),

filled with resentment and indignation.
If we do not control them with strategies,

Your Majesty should hold back the troops and not fight.
Déwēi (德威) requests to harass them with cavalry,

This was the strategy Zhōu Déwēi (周德威) used to defeat Wáng Jǐngrén (王景仁).
If the King of Jìn (晉) had been able to use it,

why would they have had to wait for Lǐ Sìyuán (李嗣源) to take Dōngpíng (東平)?
"Before, by the Hé (河), I regretted not seeing the enemy.

Why are you so timid, sir!"
He looked at Lǐ Cúnshěn (李存審) and said:

He immediately led his personal troops out first.
Déwēi (德威) had no choice

Since the King of Jìn (晉) had already gone out first,
if Zhōu Déwēi (周德威) did not follow him with troops,
he would be seen as hesitating and not advancing,
so he truly had no other choice.
History comments on his state of mind.
"I have nowhere to die now."
Hè Huái (賀懷) advanced with his formations in place,
stretching for tens of *lǐ*.
The King led the Silver Spear Division (Yínqiāng Dū, 銀槍都) to penetrate their formation,
charging, disrupting, and cutting down the enemy,
going back and forth for over ten *lǐ*.
Wáng Yànzhāng's (王彥章) army, the Commander of the Left Flank Cavalry of the Mobile Army and Defense Commissioner of Zhèngzhōu (鄭州), was defeated first,
fleeing west towards Púyáng (濮陽).
The Liáng (梁) cavalry were the first to be defeated and flee.
趣 (qū),
pronounced qī yù;
same below.
Seeing the Liáng (梁) banners,
they panicked and dispersed.
The Jìn (晉) baggage train saw the Liáng (梁) cavalry heading west,
assumed they were attacking,

The Yōuzhōu (幽州) troops were also in disarray,
trampling each other;
Zhōu Déwēi (周德威) could not control them,

Since the formation was in disarray,
even though Zhōu Déwēi (周德威) was brave,
he was only one man against many.
He also died.
The Jìn (晉) troops no longer had any organized units.
The Liáng (梁) troops gathered from all sides,
and their momentum was very strong.
The King of Jìn (晉) took up a position on a high hill to gather the scattered soldiers.
By midday,
the army had rallied again.
By occupying a high hill, the scattered soldiers would gather at the sight of banners and the sound of drums,
thus their army rallied again.
"Rallied again" means
that their troops had been defeated and weakened,
but then sprang back into action and rose again.
Hè Huái (賀懷) led his troops to occupy it.
The King of Jìn (晉) said to his officers and soldiers:
"Whoever takes this hill today will win.
I will seize it with you all."
He immediately led his cavalry to ascend first.
Lǐ Cóngkē (李從珂) and the Silver Spear general Wáng
Jiàn (建) followed with infantry.
The Liáng (梁) troops scattered downwards,

In military tactics,
those who occupy high ground to overlook the enemy win.
Since the Jìn (晉) troops had captured the earthen hill,
Hè Huái (賀懷) had lost the geographical advantage.
珂 (kē),
pronounced qiū hé.
As the sun approached dusk,

The generals believed that all the armies had not yet assembled,

Yán Bǎo, Military Governor of Tiānpíng and Commander of the Southeastern Front, said:

‘Under the mountain’ refers to the foot of the earthen hill.
This refers to the troops Hè Huái arrayed at the western foot of the mountain.
If we take advantage of the high ground to strike them from above,
we will surely defeat them.
Now that the King is deep in enemy territory,
if a detached force suffers a setback,
referring to Zhōu Déwēi’s troops being defeated.
He will certainly be taken advantage of.
Those armies not yet assembled, upon hearing that Liáng has recaptured it,

Whenever one decides victory or estimates the enemy,

This means that if Jìn launched a major attack and was defeated and retreated,

“The bandits have no camp,

Wáng Jiànjí donned his armor and advanced with his long spear,

Sìzhāo and Jiànjí, with their cavalry, charged into the enemy lines with a great roar.

Wú Qióng, the Magistrate of Yuánchéng,

The Liáng soldiers trampled over each other,

Zhuāng
is the great-grandson of Zhèng.

Zhèng,
pronounced like ‘zhèng’.

Sàng,
