On the *rénshēn* day,
he arrived at Lǎngzhōu.
A woman named Hé Kāng from that prefecture was very beautiful.
She was about to be married,
but the Shǔ Lord took her.
He bestowed a hundred bolts of silk upon her husband's family,
and her husband died of grief.
The *Jì* states: "Princes do not stoop to 'fishing for beauty'."
The commentary explains: "This means not taking women from within their own state."
To take women from within one's own state is called "fishing for beauty."
When a ruler takes from within his state,
it is like catching fish;
he takes whatever falls into the net,
without selection.
Wáng Yǎn's seizure of others' wives
was perhaps even more egregious than "fishing"!
On the *guǐwèi* day,
he arrived at Zǐzhōu.
16 Zhào Wáng Róng relied on his family's generations of governing Chéngdé,
and thus having the hearts of the Zhào people.
He grew up in wealth and nobility,
living a life of ease and indulgence.
He built mansions, gardens, and ponds,
achieving the height of luxury for his time.
He spent much time in entertainment and leisure,
not personally attending to government affairs.
Everything was left to his subordinates to complete.
He stayed secluded in his mansion,
and power shifted to those around him.
The military governor, Lǐ Ài, and the eunuch, Lǐ Hóngguī, held sway both inside and outside the court.
Lǐ Ài outside,
Lǐ Hóngguī inside.
Initially,
Liú Rénqīng sent his military aide Zhāng Wénlǐ to accompany his son Shǒuwén, who was garrisoned in Cāngzhōu.
When Shǒuwén went to Yōuzhōu to visit his father,
Wénlǐ subsequently seized the city and revolted.
The people of Cāng attacked him,
and he fled to Zhènzhōu.
This describes events at the end of the Táng dynasty,
narrating Zhāng Wénlǐ's origin.
省 (*shěng*),
pronounced like *xījǐng*.
Wénlǐ claimed to be skilled in military matters.
Zhào Wáng Róng admired him,
adopted him as his son,
and changed his name to Démíng.
He entrusted all military affairs to him.
Démíng led the mobile troops to follow Jìn Wáng.
This event began in the 267th scroll, during the first year of Tàizǔ Qiānhuà.
He sent the Grand Commander Fú Xí to return in his place,
making him the city defense commissioner.
In his later years, Róng was fond of Buddhism and seeking immortality.
He devoted himself to expounding Buddhist scriptures,
received Daoist talismans,
held numerous rituals and offerings,
and refined elixirs of immortality.
He lavishly decorated residences in Xīshān
and frequently visited them for pleasure.
The Xīshān of Zhènzhōu was called Fángshān,
and on it was a temple to Xī Wángmǔ.
Róng desired to seek immortality,
and thus frequently traveled there.
He would often not return for several months,
and the accompanying generals, officers, and soldiers often numbered no less than ten thousand.
The constant travel and provisions
caused suffering to both military and civilians.
That month,
he returned from Xīshān
and stayed at Húyíng Zhuāng.
Shí Xīméng advised the king to return to his palace.
Lǐ Hóngguī said to the king:
"Jìn Wáng is engaged in bloody battles across the Hé,
sometimes fighting south of the Hé,
sometimes north of the Hé—
hence 'across the Hé'.
He personally braves arrows and stones,
while Your Majesty dedicates funds intended for the army to non-urgent expenses.
Moreover, these are difficult times,
and people's hearts are unpredictable.
Your Majesty has long left the mansion empty
and gone out for prolonged excursions.
If by chance a traitor were to cause trouble,
closing the gates and resisting,
what would we do?"
The king was about to return,
when Xīméng secretly told the king:
"Hóngguī is fabricating suspicions,
uttering insolent words to coerce Your Majesty,
merely wishing to aggrandize himself externally
and expand his authority."
The king then stayed,
with no intention of returning even after two nights.
The *Shī* poem *Jiǔyù* says: "staying for two nights."
Máo's commentary says: "two nights is called *xìn*."
This meaning differs from
the *Zuǒzhuàn*'s statement: "a night's stay for an army is *xìn*."
He donned armor and drew his blade,
and came before the tent to tell the king:
"The soldiers have been exposed for too long;
we wish to return with Your Majesty!"
Hóngguī then stepped forward and said:
"Shí Xīméng incessantly urges Your Majesty to continue the excursions,
and it is even heard that he plans to secretly plot regicide.
I request his execution to appease the masses."
The king did not listen.
The palace guards then loudly roared,
beheaded Xīméng,
and presented his head.
The king was both angry and afraid,
and hastily returned to his mansion.
That evening,
he dispatched his eldest son, Vice-Ambassador Zhāo Zuò, and Wáng Démíng to lead troops to surround the residences of Hóngguī and Lǐ Ài,
exterminating their clans.
Dozens of families were implicated and punished.
He also killed Sū Hánhéng,
arrested his associates,
and thoroughly investigated the rebellion.
The personal guard was greatly alarmed.
This sets the stage for Zhāng Wénlǐ to incite the soldiers to kill Wáng Róng.
治 (*zhì*),
pronounced like *zhízhī*;
same below.
17 When the city of Jīnlíng for Wú was completed,
Chén Yànqiān presented the expense ledgers.
Xú Wēn said:
"Since I have entrusted this to you,
I will no longer concern myself with the accounts."
He burned them all.
18 Initially,
Mǐn Wáng Shěnzhī, acting on imperial authority, promoted his cousin, Quánzhōu Cìshǐ Yánbīn, to additionally hold the title of Pínglú Jiédùshǐ.
Yánbīn governed Quánzhōu for seventeen years,
and the officials and people were content.
At that time, a white deer and purple ganoderma were found.
The monk Hàoyuán considered these omens of a king.
Yánbīn, because of this, became arrogant and indulgent.
He secretly sent envoys by sea to pay tribute
and sought to become the Jiédùshǐ of Quánzhōu.
When the matter was discovered,
Shěnzhī executed Hàoyuán and his associates,
and demoted Yánbīn, sending him back to his private residence.
19 Hàn Zhǔ Yán sent envoys to establish friendly relations with Shǔ.
20 Wúyuè Wáng Liú sent envoys to request a marriage for his son, Chuánxiù, with Chǔ.
Chǔ Wáng Yīn agreed.
Longdé first year
(*xīnsì*, 921 CE)
The era name was changed in the fifth month of this year.
1 In spring,
the first month,
on the *jiǎwǔ* day,
the Shǔ Lord returned to Chéngdū.
The Shǔ Lord had departed on his tour in the seventh month of the previous year,
only now returning.
2 Initially,
when the Shǔ Lord was crown prince,
Gāozǔ had arranged a marriage for him with the daughter of Gāo Zhīyán, the Minister of War.
She was not favored.
The Shǔ Lord Wáng Jiàn's temple name was Gāozǔ.
She was especially neglected and estranged.
At this time, she was sent back home.
Zhīyán was so shocked that he collapsed
and died of not eating.
The Wéi family member
was Xú Gēng's granddaughter,
possessing extraordinary beauty.
When the Shǔ Lord visited Madam Xú,
he saw her and was pleased.
The Empress Dowager then took her into the imperial harem.
The Shǔ Lord did not wish to marry into his mother's family,
so it was claimed she was Wéi Zhàodù's granddaughter.
Wéi Zhàodù had been appointed by imperial decree to govern Shǔ during the reign of Táng Xīzōng,
hence the fabrication.
She was successively promoted to Yuán.
The Lord of Shǔ regularly arranged brocade screens,
played polo within them,
often going far away without outsiders knowing.
He burned various incenses,
day and night without cease.
After a long time, he grew weary of it,
and instead burned Chinese honey locust pods to disrupt the scent.
He tied silk to form mountains,
with palaces, halls, and towers upon them.
If they were damaged by wind or rain,
he would replace them with new ones.
Sometimes he would enjoy drinking on the silk mountains,
staying for ten days or more without descending.
Before the mountains, a canal was dug leading into the forbidden palace.
Sometimes he would return by boat at night,
ordering over a thousand palace women holding wax torches to stand on the front boats,
facing backward to illuminate the way.
The water surface was as bright as day.
Sometimes he would drink heavily within the forbidden palace,
with drums and wind instruments playing boisterously,
continuing until dawn.
This was his custom.
3. On the Jiǎchén day, Wēn Zhāotú, Military Governor of Jìngshèng, was transferred to be Military Governor of Kuāngguó,
garrisoned at Xǔchāng.
Zhāotú had always served Zhào Yán,
and thus obtained this important commandery.
Wēn Zhāotú sought a transfer of commandery,
as seen in the previous year.
Jìngshèng
was a border commandery of Liáng,
and comprised only two counties.
Kuāngguó
was the Zhōngwǔ Jūn of Táng,
administering Xǔ, Chén, and Rǔ prefectures,
and had always been an important commandery.
Zhào Yán bestowed this important commandery upon Zhāotú,
and relied on him in times of crisis for support.
Yet it was Zhāotú who later executed Yán.
How can one not be wary
of relationships based on power and profit!
4. The Lord of Shǔ and the Lord of Wú repeatedly sent letters urging the Prince of Jìn to claim emperorship.
The Prince of Jìn showed the letters to his officials and aides, saying:
"In the past, Grand Preceptor Wáng also once sent a letter to my late king,
urging him, since the Táng imperial house had fallen,
to declare himself emperor of a region.
Grand Preceptor Wáng
refers to the Lord of Shǔ by his Táng official title.
The matter of Wáng Jiàn's letter can be seen in volume 267, first year of Kāipíng.
Yí (遺)
means 'to send', as per Jì Fān.
'In the past, when the Son of Heaven went to Shímén,
I raised troops to execute treacherous ministers,
the event can be seen in volume 260, second year of Qiánníng of Emperor Zhāozōng of Táng.
My might shook the world.
Zhèn (振)
means "to move."
I could have drafted the document for the Nine Bestowals and abdication myself;
who could have stopped me!
But considering my family has been loyal and filial for generations,
having rendered service to the imperial house,
I swore to die rather than do it.
You, in the future, must make it your duty to restore the Táng altars of soil and grain,
and be careful not to emulate what these people are doing!'
His words are still ringing in my ears.
I dare not hear such a proposal."
Then he wept.
Afterwards, his generals, aides, and regional military governors kept urging him to ascend the throne.
So he ordered the relevant officials to buy jade to make ritual objects.
Fǎwù (法物)
refers to things like the Eight Imperial Treasures.
This can be seen in volume 254, first year of Guǎngmíng of Emperor Xīzōng of Táng.
It had been hidden for forty years.
At this time,
Chuánzhēn thought it was ordinary jade
and was about to sell it.
Someone recognized it
and said:
"It is an imperial treasure!"
Chuánzhēn then went to the Xíngtái to present it.
Sòng Bái said: In the early Tóngguāng era,
Chuánzhēn, a monk from Kāiyuán Temple in Wèizhōu, presented an imperial treasure.
When its inscription was verified, it was indeed the Eight Bestowed Treasures.
The Prince of Jìn, as the Director of the Department of State Affairs, had established a Xíngtái in Wèizhōu.
Zhāng Chéngyè, hearing of this in Jìnyáng,
went to Wèizhōu to remonstrate, saying:
"My King's family has been loyal to the Táng dynasty for generations.
It is said that Zhíyí, Guóchāng, and Kèyòng all contributed their strength to the Táng dynasty.
That is why this old slave has been collecting wealth and provisions for the King for over thirty years.
In the second year of Qiánníng of Emperor Zhāozōng of Táng,
Zhāng Chéngyè first oversaw the Hédōng army.
By this year, it had been twenty-seven years.
Jùn,
pronounced 'jǔ yùn' [as in 舉蘊],
also 'jū yùn' [as in 居運].
We swore to annihilate the rebellious bandits [Zhū Wēn]
and restore the ancestral altars of the present dynasty.
'Present dynasty' [Běncháo],
refers to Táng.
Cháo,
pronounced 'zhí yáo' [as in 直遙].
The Zhū clan still exists,
yet Your Majesty suddenly ascends the great throne.
This is entirely contrary to the original intention of our campaigns.
Who in the world would not be disheartened by this?
Why does Your Majesty not first destroy the Zhū clan,
avenge the deep enmity of the former emperors,
and then seek out a descendant of Táng to establish him?
Then, take Wú in the south,
and Shǔ in the west.
At this time, the Yáng clan occupied Jiāng and Huái,
with the state name Wú;
the Wáng clan occupied Liáng and Yì,
with the state name Shǔ.
Uniting them into one family,
at that time,
even if Gāozǔ and Tàizōng were to be reborn,
who would dare to stand above Your Majesty?
The longer you cede, the firmer your acquisition will be.
This old slave has no other ambition,
but having received great kindness from the late King,
I wish to establish a foundation for Your Majesty for ten thousand years."
The King said:
"This is not what I desire,
but what can be done about the wishes of my subordinates?"
Chéngyè knew it was impossible to stop him,
and wept bitterly, saying:
"The feudal lords fought bloody battles
originally for the Táng imperial house.
This is what Zhāng Chéngyè called the 'original intention of campaigns.'
You have led this old slave astray!"
He then returned to Jìn Wáng
Yì,
fell ill and never recovered.
Zhāng Chéngyè was
a loyal minister of Táng.
How could he be treated as a mere eunuch!
The Kǎoyì states: The Zhuāngzōng Shílù records:
"When His Majesty first obtained the imperial seal,
the generals advised His Majesty to restore the Táng calendar and legitimacy.
Chéngyè hastened from Tàiyuán to see His Majesty and said: 'Your Highness and your father have fought bloody battles for over thirty years,
ostensibly to repay the country and avenge,
for the Táng ancestral altars.
Now the arch-culprit [Zhū Wēn's son] is not yet annihilated,
military provisions are insufficient,
and the several prefectures of Héshuò are exhausted by levies.
To hastily assume the grand title now
would consume the resources for maintaining the army,
and distress the exhausted populace.
Your servant believes this is one reason it is not permissible.
Since Your Highness has transformed your house into a state,
and newly established a court,
the ceremonial rites and institutions must conform to the standards of the Tàicháng [Court of Imperial Sacrifices].
Currently, the Ministry of Rites has no suitable person.
Should the old regulations be lost,
people will scoff at it.
This is a second reason it is not permissible.'
Thereupon, tears streamed down his lapels.
His Majesty said: 'This is not what I desire,
but what can be done about the wishes of the generals?'
From then on, Chéngyè was often ill,
becoming increasingly critical,
and died in office."
The Zhuāngzōng Lièzhuàn states:
"His Majesty received the recommendations for advancement from all circuits,
intending to usurp the imperial throne.
Chéngyè believed that the Jìn kings had rendered service to the state for three generations,
and the late King was angered by the rebellious minister's usurpation,
restoring the former state.
As the rebel was not yet pacified,
it was inappropriate to lightly accept the endorsement.
While he was suffering from illness,
he was carried in a palanquin to Yègōng [Yè Palace]
and strongly remonstrated with His Majesty."
The general gist is consistent with the Shílù.
Xuē Shǐ and Táng Yúlù are also consistent with the Zhuāngzōng Lièzhuàn.
The Wǔdài Shǐ Quēwén states:
"Chéngyè said to Zhuāngzōng: 'Our King's family has served the Táng house for generations,
being most loyal and filial.
Since Zhēnguān,
whenever the royal house faced difficulties,
they never failed to respond.
That is why this old slave has been collecting wealth and provisions for our King for over thirty years,
and recruiting soldiers and horses,
swearing to annihilate the rebellious bandit Zhū Wēn,
and restore the ancestral altars of the present dynasty.
Now that Héshuò is barely settled,
and the Zhū clan still exists,
is it permissible for our King to suddenly ascend the great throne?'
Zhuāngzōng said: 'What can be done about the wishes of the generals?'
Chéngyè knew it was impossible to stop him through remonstrance,
and so he wept bitterly, saying: 'The feudal lords fought bloody battles
originally for the Lǐ family;
now our King takes it for himself,
you have led this old slave astray!'
He then returned to Tàiyuán,
and died without eating."
Qín Zàisī's Luòzhōng Jìyì states:
"Chéngyè remonstrated with the Emperor, saying: 'Why does Your Majesty not wait until Zhū Liàngniè is executed,
and further pacify Wú and Shǔ,
making the world one family,
and first seek out a descendant of the Táng clan to establish him?
Then, if you again cede the world to a deserving person,
who would dare to accept it?
The longer you cede by a month, the firmer it becomes by a month;
the longer you cede by a year, the firmer it becomes by a year.
Even if Gāozǔ were reborn,
and Tàizōng returned,
what more could they do?
Now, Your Majesty suddenly establishes yourself,
instantly losing the previous purpose of upholding righteousness and campaigning,
and people's morale will slacken.
This old man is a eunuch.
I do not covet Your Majesty's official positions and wealth,
but simply because I received the heavy trust of the late King,
I wish to establish a foundation for the late King for ten thousand years.'
Zhuāngzōng could not follow his advice,
so [Chéngyè] excused himself with illness, returned to Tàiyuán, and died."
Ouyáng Shǐ combines the intentions of the Quēwén and Jìyì.
According to the Shílù and other books,
Chéngyè only lamented the excessive expenses and the incompleteness of the ceremonial objects,
which seems too shallow.
As stated in the Quēwén,
Chéngyè served Zhuāngzōng and his father for several decades,
and the close relatives of the Táng imperial house were already gone.
How could he not know their intention to take the throne for themselves?
Praising Chéngyè might also be excessive.
Furthermore, according to the Chuánzhēn, the precious seal was presented in the first month of Tiānyòu 18,
and Chéngyè died in the eleventh month of Tiānyòu 19.
The statement that he 'immediately returned to Tàiyuán and died without eating'
is also not factual.
As for the words in the Jìyì,
Chéngyè's loyal counsel to Zhuāngzōng
is closer to the truth,
so we follow it now.
5 In the second month,
Wú changed its era name to Shùnyì.
6 After the King of Zhào killed Lǐ Hóngguī and Lǐ Āi,
he entrusted governance to his son, Zhāo Zuò.
Zhāo Zuò was arrogant and obstinate by nature.
Once he gained great power,
he exterminated all those who had previously been allied with Hóngguī.
Five hundred of Hóngguī's troops wanted to flee.
They gathered, wept, and spoke in whispers,
unsure where to go.
It so happened that all the armies were due to receive stipends,
but the King of Zhào, incensed by his personal guard's killing of Shí Xīméng,
withheld payment from them alone,
increasing the multitude's fear.
Wáng Démíng had long harbored rebellious intentions.
Taking advantage of their fear, he incited them, saying:
"The King has ordered me to bury all of you alive.
I pity you for dying innocently,
'dying innocently' [bìngmìng]
means being executed all at once.
Otherwise, I would incur the King's wrath.
What should we do?"
All of them were moved to tears.
If Zhāng Wénlǐ were moved, he would take revenge on Zhào Wáng Róng.
That evening,
some of the imperial guards who were quartered at Tánchéng’s west gate
drank together and plotted.
Tánchéng
was to the north of Chángshān Yáchéng.
Ōuyáng Gōng’s poem "Zhenyang 残杏" says,
"The northern pond is but a few steps away, but my illness prevents me from reaching it;
how can I find leisure to ride a horse and seek the wilderness?"
The note says: The northern pond (Běitán)
is the pond behind the Chángshān Palace;
it is the only scenic spot in the prefecture.
Because there was a pond (tán),
its city was called Tánchéng.
Among the brave and strong ones there, one said:
"We understand the intention of Wáng Tàibǎo."
Wáng Tàibǎo
refers to Wáng Démíng.
"What Démíng said to the imperial guards
was intended to incite them to rebellion."
They immediately scaled the city wall and entered.
As Zhào Wáng was burning incense and receiving talismans,
two men cut off his head and came out,
then set fire to the mansion.
The military officer Zhāng Yǒushùn led his men to Démíng’s residence
and requested him to be the Liúhòu.
Démíng then restored his original name, Zhāng Wénlǐ,
and completely annihilated Wáng’s clan.
In the first year of Chángqìng of Táng Mùzōng (921),
Wáng Tíngcòu occupied Chéngdé Jūn,
which lasted for four generations and five commanders before its downfall.
Liáng Nǚ, wife of Zhāozùo, see volume 262, Táng Zhāozōng Guānghuà third year.
7 In the third month,
the Wú people returned Wúyuè Wáng Qián Liú’s younger cousin, the Lóngwǔ Tǒngjūn Qián Yì, to Qiántáng.
Qián Yì captured, see volume 265, Táng Tiānyòu second year.
Qiántáng
was the capital of Wúyuè Guó.
From (從),
pronounced Cái Yòng.
Lǐ Tāo captured, see volume 268, Gānhuà third year.
Guǎnglíng
was the capital of Wú Guó.
History says that Qián and Yáng both released their captives to solidify their peace and goodwill.
Liú appointed Yì as the Zhènhǎi Jiédù Fùshǐ.
The punishment for a defeated army,
its non-enforcement has indeed been long.
8 Zhāng Wénlǐ dispatched an envoy to report the rebellion to Jìn Wáng
and also presented a memorial urging him to advance,
thereby requesting the jiéyuè.
Jìn Wáng was feasting and enjoying himself.
Upon hearing this,
he threw down his cup and wept sorrowfully,
wishing to punish him.
His subordinates believed that Wénlǐ’s crime was indeed great,
but "we are currently contending with Liáng,
and should not create another enemy so close to us.
It is advisable to comply with his request for now to pacify him."
The King had no choice.
Summer,
fourth month,
he sent the Jiédù Pànguān Lú Zhì to, by imperial decree, appoint Wénlǐ as the Chéngdé Liúhòu.
Although Jìn Wáng wanted to appease him,
Zhāng Wénlǐ could not feel secure himself.
This laid the groundwork for raising an army to punish Wénlǐ.
9 Huì Wáng Yǒunéng, the Císhǐ of Chénzhōu, rebelled
and raised an army to advance towards Dàliáng.
Jiǔyù Zhì: Chénzhōu is 340 li north of Dàliáng.
Qù (趣),
pronounced Qī Yù.
Yǒunéng reached Chénliú.
Jiǔyù Zhì: Chénliú Xiàn is 52 li east of Dàliáng.
He fled back to Chénzhōu,
where all the armies surrounded him.
10 Fifth month,
on the day Bǐngxū, the first day of the lunar month,
the reign title was changed.
The reign title was changed to Lóngdé.
11 Initially,
Liú Xún and Zhū Yǒuqīan were allied by marriage.
When Xún received the imperial order to attack Yǒuqīan,
the event is mentioned in the previous year.
He first sent an envoy with a letter,
explaining the consequences of his actions;
he waited for over a month,
but Yǒuqīan did not comply,
and only then did he advance his troops.
Yǐn Hào and Duàn Níng had always resented Xún.
They consequently slandered him to the Emperor, saying:
"Xún is dawdling and harboring the enemy,
awaiting reinforcements."
Yǐn Hào, Duàn Níng, and Liú Xún jointly attacked Zhū Yǒuqīan.
Because Xún had tried to persuade Yǒuqīan but failed to secure his submission,
and then met Jìn troops and retreated in defeat,
they were able to slander him.
After Xún’s defeat and return,
he pleaded illness and requested to be relieved of military command.
An imperial edict allowed him to seek medical treatment in Xīdū.
Liáng designated Luòyáng as Xīdū.
On the day Dīnghài,
he died.
History says that Liáng cut off its own claws and teeth.
Kǎoyì says: Zhuāngzōng Shílù states
"he died of illness caused by worry and indignation."
Xuē Shǐ says
"Zhāng Zōngshì, acting on a secret imperial decree,
forced him to drink poisoned wine and he died";
this account is now followed.
12 Sixth month,
on the day Yǐmǎo, the first day of the lunar month,
there was a solar eclipse.
13 Autumn,
seventh month,
Huì Wáng Yǒunéng surrendered;
on the day Gēngzǐ,
an imperial edict pardoned him from death,
demoting him to Fánglíng Hóu.
14 After Jìn Wáng granted the request of the Fānzhèn,
he sought out former officials of Táng
to fill the various official posts.
Zhū Yǒuqīan sent the former Lǐbù Shàngshū Sū Xún to the Xíngtái.
Sū Xún allied with Zhū Yǒuqīan,
see volume 266, Tàizǔ Kāipíng first year.
Upon entering the yáchéng,
he immediately bowed towards the governmental offices,
calling it "worshipping the palace."
When he saw the King, he shouted "Long live!" and danced,
weeping and declaring himself a subject.
The next day,
he further presented thirty large writing brushes,
calling them
"sun-drawing brushes."
According to Táng regulations, all imperial edicts were "sun-drawn" by the Emperor.
Sū Xún was scorned by Zhū Quánzhōng for pandering to the discussion of abdication,
but Lǐ Cúnxù actually liked him,
indicating that his discernment was inferior to Quánzhōng’s.
He immediately appointed Xún to his original post as the Hédōng Jiédù Fùshǐ.
Zhāng Chéngyè deeply detested him.
15 Although Zhāng Wénlǐ had accepted Jìn’s appointment,
he felt insecure internally,
and again sent a secret envoy through Lú Wénjìn to seek aid from Qìdān;
he also sent another secret envoy to report, saying:
"The Wáng clan was slaughtered by the rebellious troops,
but the princess is unharmed.
Now your servant has summoned Qìdān from the north,
and begs the imperial court to dispatch ten thousand elite armored troops to assist,
crossing the river from Dé and Dì,
then the Jìn people will flee with no time to spare."
The Emperor was doubtful and undecided.
Jìng Xiáng said:
"If Your Majesty does not seize this opportunity to recover Héběi,
then the Jìn people will never be defeated again.
It is advisable to comply with his request; this opportunity must not be missed."
Zhào, Zhāng, and others all said:
"Now the formidable enemy is close by the river,
and even if we use all our military strength to resist them,
we still fear we cannot hold out.
How can we spare ten thousand men to rescue Zhāng Wénlǐ!
Furthermore, Wénlǐ is trying to play both sides,
wishing to secure himself;
what benefit is that to us!"
The Emperor then stopped.
History says that Zhào and Zhāng did not think far enough ahead,
thus bringing disaster to the nation and their families.
The Jìn people repeatedly captured waxed pills and silk letters from Wénlǐ on the frontier and at the river fords.
Those captured on the frontier were letters communicating with Qìdān;
those captured at the river fords were letters communicating with Liáng.
Wénlǐ was ashamed and afraid.
Wénlǐ was wary of the former generals of Zhào,
and executed many of them.
Fú Xí was leading ten thousand Zhào soldiers under the Jìn King at Déshèng.
Wénlǐ requested that Xí be recalled,
and replaced with another general.
He also made Xí's son, Méng, a Staff Officer of the Dūdūfǔ,
and sent people with money and silk to reward the generals and soldiers of the campaign, so as to please them.
Zhāng Wénlǐ had apparently established his own Dūdūfǔ in Zhèn, Jì, Shēn, and Zhào,
hence the staff officers.
Láo,
pronounced lì dào.
(Xí) wept and pleaded to stay.
The Jìn King said:
"I and the King of Zhào were allied in suppressing the rebels.
The alliance between Jìn and Zhào
is recorded in volume 267, under Tàizǔ, Kāipíng fourth year.
I did not expect disaster to arise suddenly from within;
I am truly pained by this.
If you do not forget your former lord,
can you avenge him?
I will assist you with troops and provisions."
Xí and over thirty of his generals prostrated themselves on the ground, weeping bitterly, and said:
"Our former lord bestowed swords upon us,
commanding us to repel the bandits and enemies.
'Former lord'
refers to Wáng Róng.
Since he has died,
he is called 'former lord.'
'Shǐ,'
pronounced shū lì;
same below.
Our grievances and indignation have no outlet;
we wish to draw our swords and commit suicide,
but that would be of no benefit to the deceased.
'Gù,'
means to reflect.
'Deceased'
also refers to Wáng Róng.
'Assistants'
means to assist the Jìn King with military force.
We, Xí and others, dare not trouble the troops of the Overlord's Residence.
The Jìn King was in Wèizhōu,
acting as the盟主 méngzhǔ (alliance leader) of the various Fānzhèn of Héběi,
hence his residence was called the Báfǔ.
(We wish) to repay the Wáng clan's generations of kindness;
we will die without regret!"
In the eighth month,
on the day Gēngshēn,
the Jìn King appointed Xí as Liúhòu of Chéngdé,
and also ordered Yán Bǎo, Jìedùshǐ of Tiānpíng, and Shǐ Jiàntáng, Cìshǐ of Xiāngzhōu, to lead troops to assist him,
advancing north from Xíngmíng.
Wénlǐ had previously fallen ill with an abdominal carbuncle.
On the day Jiǎzǐ,
the Jìn army captured Zhàozhōu.
Cìshǐ Wáng Chuí surrendered.
The Jìn King reappointed him as Cìshǐ.
When Wénlǐ heard of this,
he died from shock and fear.
His son Chǔjǐn secretly concealed the death,
and conspired with his faction, Hán Zhèngshí, to resist Jìn with all their might.
In the ninth month,
the Jìn army crossed the Hūtuó River,
and besieged Zhènzhōu.
Fàn Chéngdà's northern mission record says: "Five lǐ past the Hūtuó River is Zhènzhōu."
They captured Zhāng Yǒushùn, Cìshǐ of Shēnzhōu.
On the day Rénchén,
Shǐ Jiàntáng died from a stray arrow.
The Jìn King wished to divide his forces to attack Zhènzhōu.
Dài Sīyuǎn, the Commander of Northern Campaign, heard of this,
and planned to gather all the troops from Yángcūn to assault the northern wall of Déshèng.
The Jìn King obtained intelligence from a surrendered Liáng soldier,
and learned of the plan.
In winter,
the tenth month,
on the day Jǐwèi,
the Jìn King ordered Lǐ Sìyuán to ambush at Qīchéng,
and Lǐ Cúnshěn to garrison Déshèng.
First, cavalry was used to lure them,
feigning weakness and timidity.
The Liáng army advanced eagerly.
The Jìn King prepared his central army to await them.
When the Liáng army arrived,
the Jìn King charged with three thousand iron cavalry,
and the Liáng army was utterly defeated.
Sīyuǎn fled towards Yángcūn.
Soldiers were killed or wounded by the Jìn army, or trampled each other,
fell into the river, or broke through the ice,
losing over twenty thousand men.
The Jìn King appointed Lǐ Sìyuán as Vice Commander-in-Chief of Fan and Han Cavalry and Infantry, and Co-Administrator of Affairs.
Initially, Wáng Chǔzhí, the Jìedùshǐ of Yìwǔ and concurrent Grand Secretary, had no son.
The sorcerer Lǐ Yìngzhī found a young boy, Liú Yúnláng, in Xíngyì.
Xíngyì was originally Kǔxíng County in the Former Hàn,
renamed Hànchāng in the Later Hàn,
Wèichāng in Cáo Wèi,
Suíchāng in Suí,
Tángchāng in the fourth year of Wǔdé of Táng,
and Xíngyì in the first year of Tiānbǎo,
belonging to Dìngzhōu.
Yāo,
pronounced yī yáo.
Xíng,
pronounced xíng.
"This child has a noble countenance."
He was made to adopt him as a son,
and named him Dū.
When he grew up, he was clever, eloquent, and full of tricks.
Chǔzhí loved him,
established a new army,
and made him command it.
Chǔzhí had an illegitimate son, Yù,
who was not favored,
and fled to Jìn.
The Jìn King Kèyòng married a daughter to him.
A concubine's son is illegitimate.
Qī,
pronounced qī xì.
His other sons were all young.
Chǔzhí made Dū the Deputy Ambassador of the Jìedùshǐ,
intending to make him his successor.
When the Jìn King Cúnxù attacked Zhāng Wénlǐ,
Chǔzhí, because Zhèn and Dìng had always been like lips and teeth,
feared that if Zhèn fell, Dìng would be isolated.
He strongly advised
that since they were currently defending against the Liáng bandits,
it would be appropriate to pardon Wénlǐ for now.
The Jìn King replied that Wénlǐ had assassinated his lord,
and by righteous principles, could not be pardoned.
Moreover, he had secretly drawn in Liáng forces,
which might also be detrimental to Yìdìng.
Chǔzhí was troubled by this.
Since Xīnzhōu bordered Qìdān,
he secretly sent someone to tell Yù,
(Xīnzhōu,
a remote frontier,
bordering Qìdān to the north.)
Yǔ,
pronounced niú jù.
to incite them to invade the frontier,
specifically to relieve the siege of Zhènzhōu.
Although Wáng Yù could not relieve the siege of Zhènzhōu,
he was able to act as a guide for Qìdān to raid Jìn.
(Yù) did not listen.
Yù had long resented Dū for usurping his family succession.
So he asked Chǔzhí to be made successor,
and Chǔzhí agreed.
The people of the military headquarters all did not want to summon Qìdān.
Dū also worried that Yù would seize his position.
So he secretly conspired with the clerk Hé Zhāoxùn to abduct Chǔzhí.
It happened that Chǔzhí was feasting with Zhāng Wénlǐ east of the city.
It is noted that Zhāng Wénlǐ was already under attack at this time.
How could he come to Dìngzhōu to feast with Wáng Chǔzhí?
The person Chǔzhí was feasting with must have been Wénlǐ's envoy.
The character 'shǐ'
should be added after 'Wénlǐ'.
[Chapter: The twelve-line edition has the two characters 'shǐ zhě';
the B twelve-line edition is the same;
the Kǒng edition is the same;
Zhāng's collation is the same.]
Dū ambushed with several hundred of the new army in the mansion,
and loudly acclaimed (as if in rebellion) to abduct him,
saying:
"The generals and soldiers do not wish to summon Qìdān by means of the city;
we request that His Excellency return to the Western Residence."
Then he imprisoned Chǔzhí and his wives and concubines in the Western Residence.
In all official residences, the east was considered superior.
The Western Residence was a place for peaceful retirement.
At the end of the Táng dynasty, Wáng Chǔcún led Yìwǔ,
and his brothers succeeded him.
It was at this point that the lineage failed.
Dū made himself Liúhòu,
and reported the full situation to the Jìn King.
The Jìn King then replaced Chǔzhí with Dū.
This later became the basis for Wáng Dū to summon Qìdān during Emperor Míngzōng's reign.
17 Wú Xú Wēn urged Wú King to sacrifice to the southern suburbs.
Some said:
“The rites and music are not yet fully prepared;
moreover, Táng sacrificed to the southern suburbs,
and the cost was enormous,
which we cannot afford now.”
Wēn said:
“How can there be a king who does not serve Heaven!
I have heard that sincerity is most valued in serving Heaven,
what is the need for great expense!
Each time Táng performed the suburban sacrifice,
they opened the southern gate,
pouring a hundred *hú* of fat into its pivots.
Pouring fat into the pivots,
desiring them to be smooth and easy to turn,
and for the gate to make no sound.
How can this be worth emulating!”
The historian says Xú Wēn, though unlearned,
understood the intention of the former kings in instituting rites.
On the *jiǎzǐ* day,
Wú King sacrificed to the southern suburbs,
with Tàizǔ as co-sacrificed deity.
Wú King honored his
[father]
on the *yǐchǒu* day,
proclaimed a general amnesty;
and promoted Xú Zhīgào to *Tóng Píngzhāng Shì*,
concurrently leading the *Jiāngzhōu Guānchásǐ*.
Soon after, Jiāngzhōu was made Fènghuà Commandery,
with Zhīgào leading as *Jiédùshǐ*.
Xú Zhīgào rose from *Tuánliàn* to *Guānchá*,
and soon after from *liánchē* to *jiànjié*.
Xú Wēn heard that the *Shòuzhōu Tuánliànshǐ* Cuī Tàichū was harsh and alienated the people,
and wanted to summon him.
Xú Zhīgào said:
“Shòuzhōu is a major frontier town;
summoning him might cause rebellion.
It would be better to have him come to court,
and then detain him.”
Wēn angrily said:
“If I cannot control one Cuī Tàichū,
what about others!”
The historian says Xú Wēn’s stratagems surpassed those of Zhīgào.
18 In the eleventh month,
Jìn King sent Lǐ Cúnshěn and Lǐ Sìyuán to guard Déshèng,
and personally led troops to attack Zhènzhōu.
Zhāng Chǔjǐn sent his younger brother Chǔqí and staff officer Qí Jiǎn to apologize and request submission,
but Jìn King refused,
attacking with full force,
but failed to overcome it in ten days.
Jìn King only knew how to win battles in the field in an instant,
but did not know the difficulty of attacking cities.
(Zhāng Chǔjǐn) hastened to Dìngzhōu,
intending to seek help from Wáng Chǔzhí.
Jìn troops pursued him to Hángtáng,
and beheaded him.
Hángtáng
was Hán Nán Hángtáng County in Hàn times;
in Táng, it belonged to Zhènzhōu.
*Jiǔyù Zhì* states: it is fifty-five *lǐ* north of the prefecture.
19 Since Qìdān Lord had already permitted Lú Wénjìn to deploy troops,
Zhāng Wénlǐ, through Lú Wénjìn, sought aid from Qìdān,
as mentioned above.
(Lú Wénjìn said to Qìdān Lord): “Zhènzhōu has beauties like clouds,
and gold and silks like mountains.
If the Tiānhuáng Wáng goes quickly,
then all will be his;
otherwise,
it will belong to Jìn King.”
Qìdān Lord thought this was true,
and dispatched all his available troops south.
The historian says Qìdān was enticed by profit and came,
not yet having the intention to conquer the Central Plains.
(Yēlǜ Ābǎojī’s brother said): “I have the wealth of sheep and horses in the Western Tower,
and its joy is inexhaustible;
why must I weary my army with a distant expedition to take risks for profit!
I have heard that Jìn King’s military prowess
is unmatched in the world;
should there be danger and defeat,
what regret would be too late!”
Qìdān Lord did not listen.
In the twelfth month,
on the *xīnwèi* day,
(Qìdān) attacked Yōuzhōu,
Lǐ Shàohóng garrisoned the city and defended himself.
In Zhēnmíng Fifth Year,
Jìn King ordered Lǐ Shàohóng to take charge of Yōuzhōu military affairs.
(Qìdān) besieged Zhuōzhōu,
captured it in ten days,
seized the *Cìshǐ* Lǐ Sìbì,
and advanced to attack Dìngzhōu.
From Yōuzhōu southwest to Zhuōzhōu is one hundred and twenty *lǐ*;
from Zhuōzhōu to Dìngzhōu is two hundred and eighty *lǐ*.
Jìn King personally led five thousand of his elite troops from Zhènzhōu to relieve it,
and sent the *Shénwǔ Dūzhīhuīshǐ* Wáng Sītóng to lead troops to garrison south of Lángshān to resist them.
Lángshān is two hundred *lǐ* northwest of Dìngzhōu,
and eighty *lǐ* northeast to Yìzhōu.
20 Gāo Jìchāng sent the *Dūzhīhuīshǐ* Ní Kěfú with ten thousand soldiers to repair the outer wall of Jiānglíng.
Jìchāng inspected it,
rebuked the slowness of the progress,
and caned him.
Jìchāng’s daughter was Kěfú’s son Zhījìn’s wife.
Jìchāng said to his daughter:
“Go tell your father-in-law: I merely wished to impress the troops and get things done.”
He gave him several hundred *liǎng* of silver.
21 In this year,
Hàn appointed *Shàngshū Zuǒchéng* Ní Shǔ as *Tóng Píngzhāng Shì*.
22 The *Chén* and *Xù Mán* invaded Chǔ.
Chǔ’s *Níngyuǎn Jiédù Fùshǐ* Yáo Yànzhāng campaigned and pacified them.
In Tàizǔ Gānhuà First Year,
Yáo Yànzhāng had already abandoned Róngzhōu and returned to Tánzhōu,
but continued to hold the position of *Níngyuǎn Jiédù Fùshǐ*.
1 In spring,
the first month,
on the *rénwǔ* day (the first day of the month),
Wáng Dū went to see Wáng Chǔzhí in the western residence.
Chǔzhí clenched his fist and struck his chest,
saying:
“Rebel!
What wrong have I done to you!”
Since he had no weapon,
he tried to bite his nose,
but Dū pulled his sleeve and escaped.
Soon after,
Chǔzhí died of grief and indignation.
2 On the *jiǎwǔ* day,
Jìn Wáng arrived south of Xīnchéng.
According to Wèi Shōu's *Dìxíng Zhì*,
Xīnchéng was in Wújí Xiàn,
which at the time belonged to Qí Zhōu.
Xīnlè,
the ancient subsidiary state of Xiānyú,
was Xīnshì Xiàn during the Hàn dynasty.
The Suí dynasty renamed it Xīnlè.
During the Táng dynasty, it belonged to Dìng Zhōu.
The *Jiǔyù Zhì* states: it is fifty *lǐ* southwest of the prefecture.
Sòng Bái said: Xīnlè Xiàn
was established in the sixteenth year of Kāihuáng during the Suí dynasty.
As for Xīnlè,
during the reign of Hàn Chéng Dì, the mother of Zhōngshān Xiào Wáng, Féng Zhāoyí, followed the king to his state.
She built a palace in Lèlǐ,
in Xī Xiāng,
and it was called Xīlè Chéng.
Later, due to a linguistic corruption,
"Xī"
was pronounced
as "Xīn",
hence the name Xīnlè.
The generals and soldiers all turned pale.
Some soldiers deserted,
and even if the commanding general executed them, it could not be stopped.
All the generals said:
"The invaders have come with their entire nation's force.
Our troops are few and cannot match them.
Furthermore, we hear that Liáng bandits are invading our interior.
We should return our army to Wèizhōu to save our foundation,
or perhaps abandon the siege of Zhènzhōu
and enter Jǐngxíng to the west to avoid them."
Jìn Wáng hesitated, unable to decide.
Guō Chóngtāo said:
"The Qìdān were enticed by Wáng Yù.
They originally came for wealth and goods,
not to relieve the emergency at Zhènzhōu.
The King has recently defeated Liáng forces;
in the fifth year of Zhēnmíng, he defeated Héhuái at Húliǔ,
and also defeated Wáng Zàn at Qīchéng.
That same year, he defeated Dài Sīyuǎn at Déshèng.
When the Qìdān hear that the King has arrived,
their morale will be low and their spirits will be broken.
If we can only defeat their vanguard,
they will surely flee."
Lǐ Sìzhāo arrived from Lùzhōu
and also said:
"Now, with a strong enemy before us,
we must advance and not retreat.
We must not act rashly and shake the morale of the people."
Jìn Wáng said:
"The rise of emperors and kings
is determined by Heaven's mandate.
What can the Qìdān do to me!
I have pacified Shāndōng with tens of thousands of troops.
The land of Héběi
is east of Tàiháng and Chángshān.
How can I face the Four Seas [if I retreat]!"
Thereupon, he personally led five thousand iron cavalry to advance.
Upon reaching north of Xīnchéng,
half of them emerged from a mulberry forest.
The more than ten thousand Qìdān cavalry saw them
and fled in panic.
The Qìdān had always feared Jìn Wáng
and did not expect his arrival,
hence their panicked flight.
After traveling several tens of *lǐ*,
they captured the son of the Qìdān ruler.
At that time, the Shāhé Bridge was narrow and the ice thin,
so many Qìdān fell in and drowned.
That evening,
Jìn Wáng stayed at Xīnlè.
The Qìdān ruler's "chariot tent" was below the city of Dìngzhōu.
The Qìdān ruler rode a Xī chariot,
and a felt tent was erected over it,
where he slept and resided.
This was called a "chariot tent".
The Qìdān army retreated en masse to defend Wàngdū.
Wàngdū is sixty *lǐ* northeast of Dìngzhōu.
Fàn Chéngdà's *Běishǐ Lù* states: From Zhēndìng Fǔ, seventy *lǐ* across the Shāhé to Xīnlè Xiàn,
then another forty-five *lǐ* to Dìngzhōu,
and another fifty *lǐ* to Wàngdū Xiàn.
The *Shuǐjīng Zhù* states: East of Wàngdū Xiàn, there is a mountain standing in isolation.
The *Dìwáng Shìjì* states: This was where Yáo's mother, Qìngdū, resided,
and it was called Dūshān.
Zhāng Yàn said: Yáoshān is in the north,
and Yáo's mother Qìngdūshān is in the south.
When one ascends Yáoshān, one can see Dūshān,
hence Wàngdū Xiàn was named after it.
When Jìn Wáng arrived at Dìngzhōu,
Wáng Dū came to greet him before his horse,
and requested to marry his beloved daughter to Prince Jìjí.
On the *wùxū* day,
Jìn Wáng led his troops to Wàngdū.
The Qìdān met them in battle.
Jìn Wáng led a thousand cavalry of his personal guard to advance first,
encountering five thousand cavalry led by the Xī chieftain, Tūněi,
and was surrounded by them.
Jìn Wáng fought fiercely,
breaking in and out several times.
The battle continued from noon until the *shēn* hour without ceasing.
Lǐ Sìzhāo heard of it
and led three hundred cavalry to attack them from the flank.
The invaders retreated,
and the King was then able to escape.
Thereupon, he unleashed his troops in a furious assault.
The Qìdān were utterly defeated,
and were pursued northward to Yìzhōu.
The *Jiǔyù Zhì* states: From Dìngzhōu north to Yìzhōu is one hundred forty *lǐ*.
The plains were several *chǐ* deep [in snow],
and the Qìdān men and horses had no food.
The dead lay continuously along the road.
The Qìdān ruler pointed a finger to the sky
and said to Lú Wénjìn:
"Heaven has not allowed me to reach this point."
Having been defeated and then encountering snow,
he attributed it to Heaven.
*Shǔ* (屬)
should be pronounced *zhīyù* (之欲).
Jìn Wáng led his troops in pursuit,
following their movements.
He saw their encampments,
where straw was spread on the ground,
arranged in neat circles and squares,
all appearing as if woven and cut.
Even after they left,
not a single branch was out of place.
He sighed, saying:
"The invaders' laws are so strict that they can achieve such order.
This is something the Central Plains cannot match."
When Jìn Wáng arrived at Yōuzhōu,
he sent two hundred cavalry to follow the Qìdān,
saying:
"Return once the invaders have crossed the border."
The cavalry, relying on their bravery, pursued and attacked them.
All were captured,
with only two cavalrymen escaping via another route.
Advancing an army is easy;
retreating an army is difficult.
To retreat and still maintain order
is truly difficult.
The strength of the Qìdān
must be attributed to this!
The Qìdān ruler blamed Wáng Yù
and brought him back in chains,
because Wáng Yù had misled him into invading.
*Zhí* (縶)
should be pronounced *shélì* (涉立).
Lǐ Sìhóng, the Jìn Prefect of Dàizhōu, led troops to pacify Guī, Rú, Wǔ, and other prefectures.
It should be known: Guīzhōu is two hundred twenty *lǐ* southeast of Yōuzhōu,
while Rú and Wǔ are northwest of Guīzhōu.
When the Qìdān entered the passes,
all three prefectures fell,
so Lǐ Sìhóng recaptured them.
3 When Jìn Wáng was attacking Zhènzhōu in the north,
Lǐ Cúnshěn said to Lǐ Sìyuán:
"The Liáng people heard that our forces in the south are few
(Jìn Wáng led his troops to campaign in the north,
leaving Lǐ Cúnshěn and others to guard Chán and Wèi.
These are the troops in the south.)
They will certainly attack Wèizhōu.
What are the two of us doing gathered here?
It is better to divide our armies to prepare for them."
Thereupon, they divided their forces and stationed them at Chánzhōu.
At that time, Chánzhōu's administrative seat was Dùnqiū.
Sìyuán led his troops there first,
encamping below the temple of Dí Gōng.
Táng Dī Rénjié had been the Prefect of Wèizhōu
and had governed with benevolence.
The people of the prefecture built a temple for him.
He made preparations for them.
When Sīyuǎn arrived at Wèidiàn,
Sìyuán sent his general Shí Wànquán to lead cavalry to challenge him to battle.
Sīyuǎn, knowing they were prepared,
then crossed the Huán Shuǐ to the west,
captured Chéng'ān,
plundered extensively, and returned.
He then led fifty thousand troops to attack the north city of Déshèng,
digging deep trenches and building multiple ramparts,
cutting off its access.
He launched a fierce attack day and night,
but Lǐ Cúnshěn resisted with all his might.
Jìn Wáng heard that Déshèng was in danger,
and in the second month,
he hurried there from Yōuzhōu,
reaching Wèizhōu in five days.
Sīyuǎn heard of this,
burned his camp, and fled back to Yángcūn.
4 The Shǔ ruler enjoyed making incognito visits,
going everywhere from wine shops to brothels.
Disliking being recognized,
he issued an order that all officials and commoners wear large, specially cut hats.
5. Yán Bǎo (閻寶), Jìn Tiānpíng Jiédùshǐ (晉天平節度使) and Shìzhōng (侍中), built a palisade to besiege Zhènzhōu (鎮州),
and diverted the Hūtuó River (滹沱水) to encircle it.
Communication was cut off both internally and externally,
and the city ran out of food.
On the day bǐngwǔ (丙午),
over five hundred men were dispatched to seek provisions.
Yán Bǎo allowed them to leave,
intending to ambush and capture them;
but these men then attacked the long palisade.
"These men"
generally refers to the more than five hundred Zhèn (鎮) soldiers.
Yán Bǎo was unprepared,
and soon several thousand more soldiers arrived.
As his armies had not yet assembled,
the Zhèn (鎮) men broke through the long palisade and came out,
setting fire to Yán Bǎo's camp.
Yán Bǎo could not resist,
and retreated to protect Zhàozhōu (趙州).
The Jiǔyù Zhì (九域志) states: Zhènzhōu (鎮州) is 190 lǐ (里) south of Zhàozhōu (趙州).
They seized his fodder and grain,
which lasted for several days.
The Jìn Wáng (晉王) heard of this
and appointed Lǐ Sìzhāo (李嗣昭), Zhaōyì Jiédùshǐ (昭義節度使) and Zhōngshū Lìng (中書令), as the Běimiàn Zhāotǎoshǐ (北面招討使),
to replace Yán Bǎo.
6. In summer,
fourth month,
Wáng Chénggāng (王承綱), a Shu (蜀) army officer, had a daughter about to marry,
but the Shu Zhǔ (蜀主) took her into the palace.
Wáng Chénggāng pleaded for her return,
but the Shu Zhǔ (蜀主) was angered
and exiled him to Màozhōu (茂州).
When the daughter heard that her father had been punished,
she committed suicide.
The Shu Zhǔ (蜀主) took Hé Kāng (何康)'s daughter,
and her husband died because of it;
he took Wáng Chénggāng (王承綱)'s daughter,
and Wáng Chénggāng (王承gāng) was punished because of it,
and the daughter killed herself because of it: the Tōngjiàn (通鑑) repeatedly records this to serve as a warning.
7. On the day jiǎxū (甲戌),
Zhāng Chǔjǐn (張處瑾) dispatched a thousand soldiers to receive grain at Jiǔmén (九門).
Lǐ Sìzhāo (李嗣昭) set an ambush at the old camp.
The old camp
was Yán Bǎo's (閻寶) camp.
Almost all were killed or captured.
The remaining five hid among the ruined walls.
Lǐ Sìzhāo (李嗣昭) circled on horseback and shot at them.
A Zhèn (鎮) soldier shot an arrow that struck him in the head.
Lǐ Sìzhāo (李嗣āo)'s quiver ran out of arrows,
so he pulled the arrow from his head and shot it,
killing a man with one shot.
As dusk fell,
he returned to camp,
his wound bleeding incessantly.
He died that evening.
The Jìn Wáng (晉王) heard of this
and abstained from wine and meat for several days.
Yù (御)
means "to partake of."
The official Rèn Yuán (任圜)
was ordered to oversee the armies attacking Zhènzhōu (鎮州).
His commands were uniform,
so the Zhèn (鎮) people did not know of Lǐ Sìzhāo (李嗣昭)'s death.
Rèn Yuán (任圜)
was from Sānyuán (三原).
History speaks of Rèn Yuán (任圜)'s talent.
The Jìn Wáng (晉王) appointed Lǐ Cúnjìn (李存進), Tiānxíong Mǎbù Dōuzhīhuīshǐ (天雄馬步都指揮使) and Zhènbǔ Jiédùshǐ (振武節度使), as the Běimiàn Zhāotǎoshǐ (北面招討使).
He ordered Lǐ Sìzhāo (李嗣昭)'s sons to escort the coffin back to Jìnyáng (晉陽) for burial;
but his son Jìnéng (繼能) refused the order,
and, leading his father's personal troops numbering several thousand,
independently escorted the coffin from the active camp back to Lùzhōu (潞州).
The Jìn Wáng (晉王) sent his younger brother by the same mother, Cúnwò (存渥), on horseback to pursue and persuade them.
The brothers were all indignant
and wanted to kill Cúnwò (存渥).
Lǐ Sìzhāo (李嗣昭) had defended Lùzhōu (潞州) to the death, thus saving it,
nursed the wounded and disabled,
and repaired the military government offices,
accumulating meritorious service.
He died on the battlefield,
yet the Jìn Wáng (晉王) merely ordered his sons to escort the coffin back to Jìnyáng (晉陽) for burial,
without any commendation for the dead or consolation for the living.
This is why the brothers were all indignant.
Cúnwò (存渥)
was the Jìn Wáng (晉王)'s younger brother by the same mother.
Lǐ Sìzhāo (李嗣昭) had seven sons: Jìchóu (繼儔), Jìtāo (繼韜), Jìdá (繼達), Jìzhōng (繼忠), Jìnéng (繼能), Jìxí (繼襲), Jìyuǎn (繼遠).
Jìchóu (繼儔) was Zézhōu Cìshǐ (澤州刺史)
and was supposed to inherit the title, but he was always timid and weak.
Jìtāo (繼韜) was fierce and cunning.
He imprisoned Jìchóu (繼儔) in a separate room
and falsely induced soldiers to declare him as Liúhòu (留後).
Jìtāo (繼韜) feigned humility
and reported the matter to the Jìn Wáng (晉王).
The Jìn Wáng (晉王), finding military affairs at a critical juncture,
with Zhènzhōu (鎮州) not yet subdued
and Liáng (梁) forces again attacking and harassing on the river,
meant that military affairs were at a critical juncture.
Yīn (殷)
means "flourishing."
changed the Zhaōyì (昭義) army to Ānyì (安義),
and appointed Jìtāo (繼韜) as Liúhòu (留後).
This laid the groundwork for Lǐ Jìtāo (李繼韜)'s rebellion against Jìn (晉) and defection to Liáng (梁).
The Kǎoyì (考異) says: "According to records, Lùzhōu (潞州) was originally called Zhaōyì Jūn (昭義軍).
Now that Jìtāo (繼韜) is the Ānyì (安義) Liúhòu (留後), it must be that the Jìn Wáng (晉王) changed the name to avoid his father's taboo name."
When Jìtāo (繼韜) surrendered to Liáng (梁),
Liáng (梁) also appointed him as Kuāngyì Jiédùshǐ (匡義節度使).
People today still refer to Zézhōu (澤州) as Ānyì (安義).
8. Yán Bǎo (閻寶) was ashamed and indignant,
due to the defeat at Zhènzhōu (鎮州).
He died on the day jiǎxū (甲戌).
9. The Hàn Zhǔ (漢主) Yán (巖), following a sorcerer's words,
traveled to Méikǒu Zhèn (梅口鎮) to avoid disaster.
This place was near the western border of Mǐn (閩).
The Jiǔyù Zhì (九域志) states: "Méikǒu Zhèn (梅口鎮) is in Chéngxiāng Xiàn (程鄉縣) of Méizhōu (梅州),
bordering Mǐn (閩)'s Tīngzhōu (汀州)."
Jìn (近)
means "near."
When he was still several tens of lǐ (里) away,
a scout informed him,
and Yán (巖) barely escaped by fleeing.
10. In the fifth month,
on the day yǐyǒu (乙酉),
Lǐ Cúnjìn (李存進) of Jìn (晉) arrived at Zhènzhōu (鎮州)
and camped at Dōngyuán Dù (東垣渡).
Zhēndìng (真定) was originally Dōngyuán (東垣).
Hàn Gāodì (漢高帝) changed its name to Zhēndìng (真定),
but the ferry crossing still retained the name Dōngyuán (東垣).
11. Lǐ Cúnrú (李存儒), Jìn Wèizhōu Cìshǐ (晉衞州刺史),
whose original surname was Yáng (楊) and given name Pó'ér (婆兒),
gained favor with the Jìn Wáng (晉王) as an entertainer.
He possessed considerable physical strength,
and the Jìn Wáng (晉王) bestowed upon him a surname and given name,
appointing him as Cìshǐ (刺史);
he specialized in extortion and exploitation.
The soldiers guarding the city were all required to pay a monthly fee to be excused from duty.
They were required to pay a monthly fee and were thus exempted from guard duty.
Duàn Níng (段凝), Zhuāngzhái Shǐ (莊宅使), and Zhāng Lǎng (張朗), Bùjūn Dōuzhīhuīshǐ (步軍都指揮使), led troops across the river at night to raid him.
They ascended the city walls at dawn,
captured Lǐ Cúnrú (李存儒),
and thus took Wèizhōu (衞州).
Dài Sīyuǎn (戴思遠) then joined Duàn Níng (段凝) in attacking and capturing Qímén (淇門), Gòngchéng (共城), and Xīnxiāng (新鄉).
Gòngchéng (共城) and Xīnxiāng (新鄉) were both counties belonging to Wèizhōu (衞州).
The Jiù Tángshū Dìlǐ Zhì (舊唐書地理志) states: "During the Suí (隋) dynasty, land from Jí (汲) and Huòjiā (獲嘉) counties was carved out
to establish Xīnxiāng Xiàn (新鄉縣) at the site of the ancient Xīnlè Chéng (新樂城)."
Gòngchéng Xiàn (共城縣) was the Hàn (漢) Gòng Xiàn (共縣),
and during the Táng (唐) it became Gòngchéng Xiàn (共城縣).
The Jiǔyù Zhì (九域志) states: "Wèizhōu (衞州) administered Jí Xiàn (汲縣)."
In the sixth year of Xīníng (熙寧), Xīnxiāng Xiàn (新鄉縣) was abolished as a county and made a town,
belonging to Jí Xiàn (汲縣).
Jí Xiàn (汲縣) also had Qímén Zhèn (淇門鎮).
Gòngchéng (共城) was fifty-five lǐ (里) northwest of the prefecture.
Gòng (共)
is pronounced gōng.
The area south of Xiāngzhōu (相州)
all fell into Liáng (梁) hands.
The Jiǔyù Zhì (九域志) states: "Chánzhōu (澶州) is 240 lǐ (里) west of Wèizhōu (衞州)."
Xiāngzhōu (相州) is 150 lǐ (里) south of Wèizhōu (衞州).
The Liáng (梁) army regained strength.
The Emperor appointed Zhāng Lǎng (張朗) as Wèizhōu Cìshǐ (衞州刺史).
Zhāng Lǎng (張朗)
was from Xúzhōu (徐州).
12. In the ninth month,
on the first day, wùyín (戊寅),
Zhāng Chǔjǐn (張處瑾) ordered his younger brother Chǔqiú (處球) to take advantage of Lǐ Cúnjìn (李存進)'s unpreparedness,
leading seven thousand soldiers to suddenly arrive at Dōngyuán Dù (東垣渡).
At that time, Jìn (晉) cavalry were also heading towards Zhènzhōu Chéng (鎮州城),
so the two forces did not encounter each other.
When the Zhèn (鎮) soldiers reached Lǐ Cúnjìn (李存進)'s camp gate,
Lǐ Cúnjìn (李存進) hastily led over ten men to fight on the bridge.
The Zhèn (鎮) soldiers retreated,
and the Jìn (晉) cavalry cut off their rear,
attacking them from both sides.
Almost all the Zhèn (鎮) soldiers were annihilated,
and Lǐ Cúnjìn (李存進) also died in battle.
At that time,
the Jìn (晉) army was the strongest in the world,
and Zhèn (鎮) was known for its cowardice.
The Jìn Wáng (晉王), wielding the mandate to punish the wicked and suppress the rebellious,
should have taken it in one swift blow.
The Zhèn (鎮) people, forgetting the hundred years of nurturing grace from the Wáng (王) family,
were fighting for the momentary lives of Zhāng Wénlǐ (張文禮) and his son.
Shǐ Jiàntáng (史建瑭) had perished earlier,
Yán Bǎo (閻寶) had been defeated and retreated later,
and Lǐ Sìzhāo (李嗣昭) and Lǐ Cúnjìn (李存進) had successively had their bodies brought back: these four were all valiant generals of Jìn (晉).
So, were the Zhèn (鎮) brave and the Jìn (晉) cowardly?
No,
the Zhèn (鎮) people bore the guilt of regicide and
knew that on the day the city fell, they would certainly be executed side by side.
Therefore, they fought with all their might to resist Jìn (晉).
Jìn (晉), with its constantly victorious army, faced a populace determined to die,
and although its soldiers were elite and its generals brave, they died without being able to conquer.
This is why the ancients, when punishing crimes,
dispersed the peripheral factions
and limited the punishment to the chief culprits,
precisely out of this consideration.
Zhènzhōu's food and strength were exhausted.
Chǔjǐn sent an envoy to Xíngtái to request surrender.
Before a reply was received,
Cúnshěn's troops arrived beneath the city walls.
On the night of Bǐngwǔ,
Lǐ Zàifēng, a general within the city, acted as an inside supporter,
secretly lowering ropes to admit the Jìn troops.
By dawn, they had all entered,
seizing Chǔjǐn, his brothers, family, and his associates Gāo Méng, Lǐ Zhù, and Qí Jiǎn, and sending them to Xíngtái.
The Zhào people all requested to eat them,
and Zhāng Wénlǐ's corpse was dismembered in the marketplace.
A former attendant of Zhào Wáng found Zhào Wáng's remains in the ashes.
Jìn Wáng ordered them to be sacrificed to and buried.
The Zhào general Fú Xí was appointed as Chéngdé Jiédùshǐ,
Wū Zhèn as Zhàozhōu Cìshǐ,
Zhào Rénzhēn as Shēnzhōu Cìshǐ,
and Lǐ Zàifēng as Jìzhōu Cìshǐ.
Zhèn
was a native of Xìndū.
Fú Xí dared not accept Chéngdé,
and declined, saying:
"The former envoy has no descendants and is not yet buried.
I, Xí, should wear zhǎncuī mourning attire to bury him.
A minister wears zhǎncuī for his lord."
衰，
倉回翻。
After the burial,
he would then go to Xíngtái.
The Zhào people requested that Jìn Wáng concurrently hold the position of Chéngdé Jiédùshǐ,
and he assented.
Jìn Wáng carved out Xiāng and Wèi prefectures to establish the Yìníng Jūn,
and appointed Xí as Jiédùshǐ.
Xí declined, saying:
"The Wèibó Bàfǔ
cannot be divided.
I wish to obtain one command in Hénán,
which I, Xí, will take myself."
Indeed, in this world there are many who can speak but cannot act.
Fú Xí's principles were not perfunctory,
but in the end, he could not take one command in Hénán.
This is why a Jūnzǐ values fulfilling his words.
Lǐ Cúnshěn was additionally appointed concurrently as Shìzhōng.
13In the 11th month,
on Wùyín,
Zhāng Chéngyè, Jìn's Tèjìn and Hédōng Jiānjūnshǐ, passed away.
Cáo Tàifūrén went to his residence,
and observed mourning rites for him,
like a child or nephew.
Zhāng Chéngyè had pacified the rebellions of Lǐ Kèníng and Cún Hào,
and for this reason, Cáo Tàifūrén was deeply grateful to him.
為，
于偽翻。
She did not eat for several days.
Hé Zàn, the Hédōng Liúshǒu Pànguān, was ordered to temporarily manage the affairs of the Hédōng Jūnfǔ.
14In the 12th month,
Jìn Wáng appointed Zhāng Xiàn of Jìnyáng, Wèibó Guānchá Pànguān, to concurrently serve as Zhènjì Guānchá Pànguān,
and to provisionally manage the affairs of the Zhènzhōu Jūnfǔ.
Wèizhōu had many unpaid taxes.
Jìn Wáng admonished Sīlù Zhào Jìliáng of Jìyīn.
Under the Táng system,
various prefectures had various departments like Sīlù, Sīshì, Sībīng, and Sīgōng,
which were called Pànsī.
Jìyīn
was a Hàng jùn name;
the Suí established Jìyīn Xiàn;
during the Táng, it was attached to Cáozhōu.
濟，
子禮翻。 "
Your] Highness, when do you intend to pacify Hénán?"
The King angrily said:
"Your duty is to supervise taxes.
Your duty is not fulfilled.
How dare you interfere with my military affairs!"
Jìliáng replied:
"Your Highness is planning to attack and conquer, but does not care for the common people.
If the common people lose heart,
I fear that even Héběi will not belong to Your Highness,
let alone Hénán!"
The King was pleased,
and thanked him.
From then on, he valued him greatly,
and included him in every council.
15In this year,
the Qìdān changed their era name to Tiānzàn.
16The greatly enfeoffed King Gōngyì
was cruel and ruthless by nature.
The naval commander Wáng Jiàn killed him,
and established himself,
again calling himself Gāolì Wáng.
He made Kāizhōu the Dōngjīng,
and Píngrǎng the Xījīng.
Jiàn was frugal and generous,
and the people of the state were at peace.
Xú Jìng's Gāolì Tújīng states: The ancestor of Gāolì Wáng Jiàn
was from a prominent Gāolì clan.
When the Gāo clan's rule declined,
the people of the state, considering Jiàn to be worthy,
established him as their ruler.
In the second year of Hòutáng Chángxīng,
he styled himself as acting regent (Quán Zhī Guóshì),
and sought investiture from Míngzōng.
Thereupon, Jiàn was appointed Dàyì Jūnshǐ,
and enfeoffed as Gāolì Wáng.
According to Xú Jìng, who was sent as an envoy to Gāolì during the Xuānhé period,
and presented the Tújīng,
his records were brief and imprecise.
Due to listening to local rumors,
he thus claimed that Jiàn gained the state after the Gāo clan,
unaware that Jiàn actually killed Gōngyì to obtain the state.
For details, see the Kǎoyì for the fifth year of Zhēnmíng.
Punctuation by Dèng Guǎngmíng, re-collated by Niè Chóngqí.
